docs.title: What is the DTaaS Platform?
docs.text:
The Digital Twin as a Service (DTaaS) software platform is used to Build, Use and Share digital twins (DTs).

Build: construct DTs on DTaaS from the reusable DT assets available on the platform.

Use: run DTs on the DTaaS platform.

Share: share ready-to-use DTs with other users, or share the services that one DT offers.

This walkthrough shows the DTaaS v1.1 interface and workflow:

An overview of the DTaaS platform is available as a short introduction video and slides.

docs.title: General Questions
docs.text:
What is the DTaaS platform?

The DTaaS platform is a software platform for creating and running digital twins. The features page gives an overview of what DTaaS can do.

What is the scope and current capabilities of the DTaaS platform?
  1. DTaaS is a web-based interface for invoking the tools needed to work with one or more DTs.
  2. DTaaS lets users run DTs in their private workspaces. These user workspaces are based on the Ubuntu 20.04 operating system.
  3. DTaaS can help create reusable DT assets only if the DT asset authoring tools run in the Ubuntu 20.04 xfce desktop environment.
  4. From the DTaaS platform's perspective, DTs are executables. Users are free to work with DTs in whatever way suits them. DTaaS suggests creating DTs from reusable assets and offers a suggested structure for DTs. The examples show the DTaaS workflow in more detail. This suggested workflow is not mandatory.
  5. DTs can run as services with a REST API from within user workspaces, which makes service-level DT composition possible.
What can not be done inside the DTaaS platform?
  1. DTaaS does not help install DTs obtained from external sources.
  2. Windows-only tools cannot run inside DTaaS workspaces.
Is there any fundamental difference between commercial solutions like Ansys Twin Builder and the DTaaS platform?

Commercial DT platforms like Ansys Twin Builder integrate models, simulation and sensors tightly. This leaves fewer choices in DT design and implementation, and it brings vendor lock-in. DTaaS, on the other hand, lets users split a DT into reusable assets and combine these assets flexibly.

Is licensed software such as Matlab provided?

Proprietary and commercially licensed software is not available on the platform by default. However, each user has a private workspace based on a Linux xfce desktop environment. Users can install proprietary and commercially licensed software in their workspaces. A screencast shows Matlab Simulink running within the DTaaS platform. Licensed software installed by one user is not available to other users.

docs.title: Digital Twin Assets
docs.text:
Can the DTaaS platform be used to create new DT assets?

The core purpose of DTaaS is to help users create DTs from assets already available in the library. However, users can use the services available in their workspace to install asset authoring tools there. These authoring tools can then be used to create and publish new assets. User workspaces are private and are not shared with other users. Thus, any licensed software tools installed in a workspace are only available to that user.

docs.title: Digital Twin Models
docs.text:
Can the DTaaS platform create new DT models?

DTaaS is not a model creation tool, and it does not create digital twin models itself. It can still help users create them: model creation tools can be placed inside DTaaS, and any Linux desktop or terminal tool can run inside DTaaS. Thus, models can be created inside DTaaS and executed using tools that run on Linux. Windows-only tools cannot run in DTaaS.

How can the DTaaS platform help to design geometric model? Does it support 3D modelling and simulation?

DTaaS by itself does not produce any models. It provides a platform and an ecosystem of services that let digital twins run as services. Since each user has a Linux OS at their disposal, they can also run digital twins that have a graphical interface. In short, the DTaaS platform is neither a modelling nor a simulation tool. If such tools are required, they must be brought onto the platform. For example, if Matlab is needed, the user must bring the licensed Matlab software.

Can the DTaaS platform support only the information models (or behavioural models) or some other kind of models?

The DTaaS platform is agnostic to the kind of models used. DTaaS can run all kinds of models, including behavioural and data models. As long as the models and matching solvers can run on a Linux OS, they can be used in DTaaS. In some cases, models and solvers (tools) are bundled together to form monolithic DTs. The DTaaS platform can run such DTs as well. DTaaS does not provide dedicated solvers. If a solver can be installed in the workspace, the platform does not need to provide one.

Does it support XML-based representation and ontology representation?

Not at present. The team is looking for users who need this capability. Given concrete requirements and an example, the team can discuss how to realise it in DTaaS.

docs.title: Communication Between Physical Twin and Digital Twin
docs.text:
How can the DTaaS platform control the physical entity? Which technologies it uses for controlling the physical world?

At an abstract level, data flows from the physical entity to the digital entity and back to the physical entity. The person designing the digital entity decides how this communication happens. DTaaS provides communication services that make this communication easier. The InfluxDB and RabbitMQ services hosted on DTaaS may be used for two-way communication between digital and physical entities. RabbitMQ has its MQTT plugin enabled, so it also works as an MQTT broker.

How is a physical entity such as shape, size, weight, structure, or chemical attributes measured using DTaaS? Is any specific technology used in this case?

The measurements are made at the physical twin and then sent to the digital twin. A digital twin platform like DTaaS can only facilitate the communication of these measurements from the physical twin. DTaaS provides InfluxDB and RabbitMQ (which also acts as an MQTT broker) for this purpose. These are among the most widely used services for digital twin communication. DTaaS also permits the use of other communication technologies and services hosted elsewhere on the Internet.

How can real-time data differ from static data and what is the procedure to identify dynamic data? Is there any UI or specific tool used here?

The DTaaS platform cannot tell whether data is static or dynamic. It can store names, units and any other text description of the quantities of interest (weight of batter, voltage output, etc.). It can also store the data sent by the physical twin. The user has to make the distinction between static and dynamic data. Only metadata can reveal more about the nature of the data. A tool may help in very specific cases, but it still needs metadata. If a person makes this distinction, the need for metadata goes down but does not go away entirely. Some manufacturer-supported DT platforms tightly integrate data and model. In such cases, the tool itself manages the metadata. DTaaS is a generic platform for running digital twins. If a tool runs on a Linux desktop or command line, DTaaS can support it. The tool (e.g., Matlab) can then manage the metadata requirements itself.

docs.title: Digital Twin DevOps Automation
docs.text:
Can a DT execute forever?

The web UI imposes a 10-minute timeout on an execution. Users can also terminate an execution manually. The best option is for a DT to run a terminate script, which ends the execution and returns the logs.

Is the DT execution really scalable?

The capacity of the DT execution infrastructure depends on GitLab and on the compute power available to the GitLab runners. GitLab itself does not limit the number of runners.

If many GitLab runners are attached to a GitLab repository, which one is used?

This is indeterminate. The order and location of a DT's execution cannot be relied on.

docs.title: Data Management
docs.text:
Can the DTaaS platform collect data directly from sensors?

Yes, via the platform services.

Does DTaaS support data collection from different sources like hardware, software and network? Is there any user interface or any tracking instruments used for data collection?

The DTaaS platform provides InfluxDB, PostgreSQL, RabbitMQ, MQTT, MongoDB and ThingsBoard services. Both the physical twin and the digital twin can use these services to communicate. IoT (time-series) data can be collected using the InfluxDB and MQTT broker services. InfluxDB has a user interface for analysing the collected data. Users can also upload their own data files into DTaaS.

Is the DTaaS platform able to transmit data to cloud in real time?

Yes, via the platform services.

Which transmission protocol does the DTaaS platform allow?

InfluxDB, RabbitMQ, MQTT and anything else that can be used from cloud service providers.

Does the DTaaS platform support multisource information and combined multi sensor input data? Can it provide analysis and decision-supporting inferences?

Information from multiple sources can be stored. The InfluxDB service hosted on DTaaS has the Influx / Flux query language for sensor fusion, analysis and inference.

Which kinds of visualisation technologies can the DTaaS platform support (e.g. graphical, geometry, image, VR/AR representation)?

Graphical, geometric and image visualisation. If the visualisation needs specific licensed software, the user must provide the licence for it. DTaaS does not support AR/VR.

docs.title: Platform Native Services on the DTaaS Platform
docs.text:
Is the DTaaS platform able to detect the anomalies about-to-fail components and prescribe solutions?

This is the job of a digital twin. If a ready-to-use digital twin exists for this purpose, DTaaS lets others use it. Anomaly detection can be done with platform services such as Grafana, ThingsBoard and InfluxDB.

docs.title: Comparison with other DT Platforms
docs.text:
All the DT platforms seem to provide different features. Is there a comparison chart?

Here is a qualitative comparison of DT integration platforms:

Legend: high performance (H), mid performance (M) and low performance (L)

DT Platforms License DT Development Process Connectivity Security Processing power, performance and Scalability Data Storage Visualisation Modelling and Simulation Microsoft Azure DT Commercial Cloud H H H M H H H AWS IOT Greengrass Open source commercial H H H M H H H Eclipse Ditto Open source M H M H H L L Asset Administration Shell Open source H H L H M L M PTC Thingworx Commercial H H H H H M M GE Predix Commercial M H H M L M L The DTaaS Platform Open source H H L L M M M 
Adapted by Tanusree Roy from Tables 4 and 5 of the following paper.

Ref: Naseri, F., Gil, S., Barbu, C., Cetkin, E., Yarimca, G., Jensen, A. C.,
... & Gomes, C. (2023). Digital twin of electric vehicle battery systems:
Comprehensive review of the use cases, requirements, and platforms.
Renewable and Sustainable Energy Reviews, 179, 113280.
All the comparisons between DT platforms seems so confusing. Why?

The confusion comes from the fact that different DT platforms (Azure DT, GE Predix) provide different kinds of DT capabilities. GE Predix can run all kinds of models natively, even next to (on) the PTs. The Azure DT service cannot do this natively. The user must integrate it with other Azure services or third-party services to get the capabilities that GE Predix provides natively in one interface. The right platform therefore depends on the specific requirements.

docs.title: GDPR Concerns
docs.text:
Does the platform adhere to GDPR compliance standards? If so, how?

The DTaaS platform does not store any personal information about users. It stores only usernames to identify users, and these usernames do not contain enough information to deduce a user's true identity.

Which security measures are deployed? How is data encrypted (if exists)?

The multi-user server installation requires an HTTPS-terminating reverse proxy between the users and the DTaaS platform installation. Administrators can install HTTPS certificates into the application. The codebase can produce an HTTPS-enabled application, and users can also install their own certificates obtained from certificate authorities such as Let's Encrypt.

What security measures does the cloud provider offer?

The DTaaS platform can be installed on a corporate server hosted behind network firewalls, so that only permitted user groups have network access and physical access to the server.

How is user access controlled and authenticated?

The multi-user server installation of DTaaS has two levels of authorisation. The first level is server-side OAuth 2.0 authorisation through Traefik forward-auth over a secure HTTPS connection. The second level is the OAuth 2.0 PKCE authorisation flow in the web client. A GitLab instance provides both. DTaaS does not store the account and authorisation information of users.

Does the platform manage personal data? How is data classified and tagged based on the sensitivity? Who has access to the critical data?

The platform does not store personal data of users.

How are identities and roles managed within the platform?

The platform has two roles: administrator and user. The administrator manages the user roles.

docs.title: Third-Party Software
docs.text: Some known issues come from third-party software included in the DTaaS platform. They are listed below.

docs.title: GitLab
docs.text:
The GitLab OAuth 2.0 authorisation service has no way to sign out of a third-party application. After a user logs out of the DTaaS platform, GitLab still shows the user as signed in. The next time the user clicks the Sign In button on the DTaaS platform page, the GitLab login page is not displayed. Instead, the user goes directly to the Library page. Close the browser window after use to avoid this. Alternatively, open the linked GitLab instance (ex: https://intocps.org/gitlab) and sign out there. To exit the DTaaS platform completely, the user has to sign out of both the DTaaS platform and GitLab.

The same applies to the Workspace installation.

docs.text:
The following projects have funded this project.

  • Sustainable Water-based Cooling in Megacities (SWiM) - a project sponsored by the Grundfos Foundation.
  • Security for the Digital Twin as a Service Platform - a project sponsored by the Thomas B. Thriges Foundation.
  • CP-SENS (Cyber-Physical Sensing for Machinery and Structures) - a Grand Solution project funded by the Innovation Fund Denmark under the grant agreement 2081-00006B.
  • DIGITbrain (Digital Twins for Manufacturing SMEs) - a project funded by the European Union's Horizon 2020 research and innovation programme under grant agreement No 952071.
  • Digital Twins for Cyber-Physical Systems (DiT4CPS) - a project sponsored by the Grundfos Foundation.

docs.text: The DTaaS platform uses a range of third-party software components. Each component remains subject to its upstream licence terms.

docs.title: Deployment and Runtime Software
docs.text:
The core deployment stack currently references the following software:

Software Package Usage Licence Docker CE mandatory Apache 2.0 Traefik mandatory MIT Traefik Forward Auth optional MIT GitLab CE optional MIT GitLab Runner optional MIT Dex optional Apache 2.0 Keycloak optional Apache 2.0 RabbitMQ optional MPL 2.0 MongoDB optional SSPL v1 Grafana optional AGPL v3 InfluxDB optional Apache 2.0 / MIT PostgreSQL optional PostgreSQL Licence ThingsBoard optional Apache 2.0

docs.title: Development Environments
docs.text:
In addition to runtime software, the development and documentation workflows use the following tools.

Software Package Usage Licence Node.js mandatory Node.js licence npm mandatory Artistic Licence 2.0 Yarn optional BSD 2-Clause Material for MkDocs mandatory MIT JupyterLab optional BSD 3-Clause MicroK8s optional Apache 2.0

docs.title: Client Packages With Copyleft Terms
docs.text:
Most client dependencies are permissively licensed and are declared in client/package.json. Two are named here because their terms carry obligations that a redistributor has to meet, and a name in a lock file is not a notice.

Software Package Usage Licence @into-cps-association/bim-kit mandatory INTO-CPS Association Public Licence web-ifc mandatory MPL 2.0

web-ifc is the IFC geometry kernel, and it reaches the client through bim-kit, which embeds its WebAssembly build so that a deployment serves no extra file. Embedding it does not change its terms.

MPL 2.0 is file-level copyleft and is compatible with redistributing DTaaS under the INTO-CPS Licence. What it requires of anyone shipping a build:

  • The source of the MPL-covered files has to be available to whoever receives that build. Upstream is linked above, and the version in use is the one client/yarn.lock resolves for web-ifc.
  • The notice has to travel with the artifact. Embedding the kernel inside a JavaScript chunk makes its provenance invisible in the built output, which is the reason this table exists instead of a pointer to package.json.
  • A modified MPL file stays MPL. bim-kit uses web-ifc as a dependency and does not fork it, so the boundary is the package boundary.

docs.title: Package Dependencies
docs.text:
Additional third-party dependencies for client, servers, CLI, and tooling are declared in:

  • client/package.json
  • servers/**/package.json
  • cli/pyproject.toml
  • deploy/services/cli/pyproject.toml
  • script/docs/mkdocs-requirements.txt

Upstream dependency licences should be consulted in those manifests when detailed licence auditing is required.

docs.title: CLI Configuration Reference
docs.text: This page is the reference for dtaas.toml, the configuration file that every DTaaS CLI command reads. Generate a template with dtaas config generate, fill it in, and check it with dtaas config validate before running any other command. The installation workflow is covered in Install with DTaaS CLI.

docs.title: Which sections does my deployment need?
Server deployments
docs.text:
Section localhost insecure-server secure-server secure-server-gitlab [common] Required Required Required Required [common.security] Not used Optional (tls = false) Required Required [common.resources] Optional Optional Optional Optional [gitlab] Optional Optional Optional Optional [[users]] Optional Required Required Required [frontend] Not used Required Required Required [localhost] Required Not used Not used Not used [insecure-server] Not used Required Not used Not used [secure-server] Not used Not used Required Not used [secure-server-gitlab] Not used Not used Not used Required

dtaas user add reads [common.security].tls for every deployment type to choose the per-user compose template. For insecure-server, leave the section out or set tls = false; tls = true gives the new users the HTTPS template, which the HTTP-only deployment does not serve.

docs.title: Workspace deployments
docs.text: Section workspace-localhost workspace-secure-server [common] Required Required [common.security] Not used Required [common.resources] Optional Optional [gitlab] Optional Optional [[users]] Optional Required [workspace-localhost] Required Not used [workspace-secure-server] Not used Required

docs.title: Annotated dtaas.toml
docs.text:
The file below shows every key with inline comments. Copy it as a starting point and delete the sections that your deployment type does not use (see the tables above).

# ── Metadata (top level) ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Describes the instance. git-repo, the URL of the DTaaS repository, is
# required for all deployment types; validate checks no other key here.
name     = "Digital Twin as a Service (DTaaS)"
version  = "2.2.1"
owner    = "The INTO-CPS-Association"
git-repo = "https://github.com/into-cps-association/DTaaS.git"

# ── Common settings (all deployment types) ────────────────────────────────────
[common]
# Public hostname of the server. Use "localhost" for local deployments,
# a fully-qualified domain name (e.g. "dtaas.example.com") for servers,
# or a bare IP address.
server-dns = "dtaas.example.com"

# Absolute path to the DTaaS installation directory on the deployment host.
# Must exist before running validate.
path = "/opt/dtaas"

# ── TLS settings (required for: secure-server, secure-server-gitlab,
#                               workspace-secure-server) ──────────────────────
[common.security]
tls = true

# Absolute path to the directory containing fullchain.pem and privkey.pem.
# Used by deployment generate (seeds certs/) and platform update --certs.
certs-src = "/etc/letsencrypt/live/dtaas.example.com"

# ── Per-user container resource limits (optional, all types) ──────────────────
[common.resources]
# Enforce the limits below. Set to false to add users without any caps.
# The 4 fields are then optional and ignored. Defaults to true when omitted.
set_limits = true
cpus       = 4        # CPU cores; may be fractional, e.g. 0.5
mem_limit  = "4G"     # memory limit unit required: G, m, k …
pids_limit = 4960     # maximum number of processes per container (integer)
shm_size   = "512m"   # shared memory unit required

# ── Starting users (all deployment types) ─────────────────────────────────────
# One self-contained [[users]] block per user, hand-edited once at install
# time. Presence in this file is the desired state there are no add/delete
# lists. Additional users added later with `dtaas user add` live in the
# CLI-owned dtaas.users.registry.json instead.
# Usernames must match GitLab accounts and be unique across the array.
#
# email enables traefik-forward-auth routing rules automatically;
# groups/load_balance carry per-user tags. password is optional: it is the
# initial GitLab password when `dtaas user add <username>` provisions this
# starting user's account. Avoid committing a real secret here; prefer
# supplying it at runtime instead.
[[users]]
username     = "alice"
email        = "alice@example.com"
groups       = ["default", "dtaas"]
load_balance = true

[[users]]
username     = "bob"
email        = "bob@example.com"
groups       = ["default", "dtaas"]
load_balance = false
# password   = "Kq7v-Rm3x-Zt9w"   # initial GitLab password, see above

# ── React web client OAuth app (insecure-server, secure-server,
#                                secure-server-gitlab) ────────────────────────
# This is a SEPARATE OAuth application from the traefik-forward-auth app
# configured in [insecure-server] / [secure-server] below.
# Redirect URI: https://<server-dns>/Library
# Scopes: api read_user read_repository openid profile   Type: not Confidential
[frontend]
react-app-client-id = "dtaas-client"
react-app-oauth-url = "https://gitlab.example.com"

# ── GitLab user provisioning (optional, all types) ───────────────────────────
# Off by default. When provision = true, `dtaas user add` also creates
# each new user's GitLab account and a Personal Access Token (see
# "Add Users" in cli.md). The provisioning token must belong to an
# administrator and carry the api scope (plus admin_mode on an instance with
# Admin Mode enabled); supply it via the DTAAS_GITLAB_PAT environment variable
# rather than committing it here. A [gitlab].pat key is the fallback when the
# variable is unset or empty. ssl_verify may be a CA-bundle path for a GitLab
# behind an internal CA; false disables verification (a warning is printed)
# and true (default) uses the system trust store.
[gitlab]
provision  = false
api_url    = "https://gitlab.example.com"
# pat      = "glpat-xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx"   # prefer DTAAS_GITLAB_PAT
# ssl_verify = "/etc/ssl/certs/corp-ca.pem" # or true (default) / false

# ── localhost deployment (dev / demo only) ────────────────────────────────────
# GitLab OAuth app for the web client; auth-authority is the GitLab URL.
[localhost]
default-user   = "alice"
client-id      = "dtaas-local"
auth-authority = "https://gitlab.example.com"

# ── insecure-server deployment (HTTP, demo only not internet-facing) ─────────
# GitLab OAuth app for traefik-forward-auth.
# Redirect URI: http://<server-dns>/_oauth
# Scopes: openid profile read_user   Type: Confidential
[insecure-server]
oauth-url           = "https://gitlab.example.com"
oauth-client-id     = "abc123"
oauth-client-secret = "s3cr3t"
oauth-secret        = "random-signing-string"   # random; used to sign session cookies

# ── secure-server deployment (HTTPS/TLS production-ready) ───────────────────
# Same GitLab OAuth app as insecure-server, with Redirect URI using https.
[secure-server]
oauth-url           = "https://gitlab.example.com"
oauth-client-id     = "abc123"
oauth-client-secret = "s3cr3t"
oauth-secret        = "random-signing-string"

# ── secure-server-gitlab deployment (bundled GitLab production-ready) ───────
# oauth-url points at the bundled GitLab, served under /gitlab.
[secure-server-gitlab]
oauth-url           = "https://dtaas.example.com/gitlab"
oauth-client-id     = "abc123"
oauth-client-secret = "s3cr3t"
oauth-secret        = "random-signing-string"

# ── workspace-localhost deployment (Dex on localhost dev / demo only) ───────
[workspace-localhost]
default-user   = "alice"
client-id      = "workspace-local"
auth-authority = "http://localhost:5556/dex"

# ── workspace-secure-server deployment (Keycloak production-ready) ──────────
[workspace-secure-server]
keycloak-admin          = "admin"
keycloak-admin-password = "change-me"
keycloak-realm          = "dtaas"
keycloak-issuer-url     = "https://keycloak.example.com/realms/dtaas"
keycloak-client-id      = "workspace"
keycloak-client-secret  = "s3cr3t"
oauth-secret            = "random-signing-string"
# Not written to config/client.js (auth-authority is only checked to be
# a URL). Set REACT_APP_CLIENT_ID and REACT_APP_AUTH_AUTHORITY there by hand.
client-id               = "dtaas-frontend"
auth-authority          = "https://keycloak.example.com/realms/dtaas"

docs.title: Validation rules
docs.text:
dtaas config validate reads dtaas.toml (from --output-dir first, then the current directory) and reports all problems at once:

Field Rule git-repo Must be an http(s) URL [common].server-dns Must be localhost, an IP, or a fully qualified hostname [common].path Must be an absolute path to an existing directory [common.security].certs-src When present, must be an absolute path to an existing directory [common.resources].set_limits false turns the limits off; any other value, or no key, keeps them on [common.resources].cpus Positive number (e.g. 4 or 0.5) [common.resources].pids_limit Integer [common.resources].mem_limit, shm_size Byte size with required unit (e.g. 4G, 512m) [[users]] When present, must be an array of tables; usernames must be unique [[users]].username Required, valid username [[users]].email Required, valid RFC 5321/5322 address (no DNS lookup) [[users]].groups When present, must be a list of strings [[users]].load_balance When present, must be true or false [[users]].password When present, must be a string (the starting user's initial GitLab password, used when user add names them) [gitlab].provision When present, true or false (default false) [gitlab].api_url Must be an http(s) URL; required when provision is true, optional otherwise [gitlab].pat When present, must be non-empty (remove the key to use DTAAS_GITLAB_PAT) [gitlab].ssl_verify When present, true, false, or a CA-bundle path string Deployment-section URLs When present, must be http(s) URLs Deployment-section default-user When present, must be a valid username

Deployment-section URLs are react-app-oauth-url, oauth-url, auth-authority and keycloak-issuer-url in [frontend], [localhost], [insecure-server], [secure-server], [secure-server-gitlab], [workspace-localhost] and [workspace-secure-server]. Each is checked only when its section is present. config validate checks every section in the file, while platform update --config checks only the section of the installed deployment type, plus [frontend].

For workspace-secure-server, no command writes client-id or auth-authority into config/client.js; auth-authority is only checked to be a URL. Edit REACT_APP_CLIENT_ID and REACT_APP_AUTH_AUTHORITY in that file by hand.

path and certs-src are checked against the local filesystem, so run validate on the deployment host. If a check fails with a permission error (for example, certs-src under the root-owned /etc/letsencrypt), the CLI prints the command to re-run with sudo.

The [common.resources] limit fields (cpus, pids_limit, mem_limit, shm_size) are required only when set_limits is true, the default. With set_limits = false they are optional and ignored, but any value that is present is still validated.

docs.title: Configuration substitution
docs.text:
When dtaas.toml is present, deployment generate substitutes its values into the generated files. platform update --config repeats the same substitution on an installed deployment. Each --type reads from its matching top-level section in dtaas.toml. Depending on the type, values go into the dotenv files (config/.env, config/conf.server), the React client config (config/client.js, or config/env.local.js for workspace-localhost) and the Dex config (config/dex-config.yaml for workspace-localhost).

For the server types, the [frontend] section supplies REACT_APP_CLIENT_ID and REACT_APP_AUTH_AUTHORITY for the DTaaS web client. That is a separate OAuth application from the traefik-forward-auth credentials in [insecure-server], [secure-server] and [secure-server-gitlab]. The redirect URIs in config/client.js are built from [common].server-dns, and the first two [[users]] records fill USERNAME1 and USERNAME2.

If dtaas.toml is not found, the command prints a note and the generated files keep their placeholder values.

docs.title: TLS certificate placement
docs.text: For the TLS types (secure-server, secure-server-gitlab, workspace-secure-server), deployment generate also fills the certs/ directory in the output. It reads [common.security].certs-src from dtaas.toml and copies the latest fullchain.pem and privkey.pem from there.

docs.title: User files
docs.text:
User management spans three files, each with a single owner. The split follows the one Terraform makes between .tf and terraform.tfstate files:

File Owner Contents Git dtaas.toml [[users]] Human, at install time Starting users: one self-contained record per user (username, email, groups, load_balance, optional password) Hand-edited; keep out of Git, as it can hold credentials dtaas.users.registry.json CLI (user add / delete / pause / stop / resume) Additional users under users: the same fields, plus desired_status (running/paused/stopped) and any GitLab markers. Its starting_users section holds the GitLab markers alone, for starting users that user add has provisioned on GitLab Tracked, CLI-written, never hand-edited .dtaas.state.json CLI, at provisioning time Observed runtime facts: container id, status, provisioned-at, config hash Ignored, runtime cache
  • dtaas.toml is written by a person and never rewritten by the CLI, so its comments and reviewed values stay as they are.
  • dtaas.users.registry.json is a database that the CLI owns and updates atomically, the way useradd owns /etc/passwd. Change its users with dtaas user add --file users.csv, delete, pause, stop and resume, not by hand. The users.csv written by dtaas config generate is the bulk input for add and delete. desired_status is running for a user who has never been paused or stopped, and user add and config reconcile --fix do not start any user whose desired_status is something else.
  • .dtaas.state.json is a disposable cache of what is running, refreshed on every add and delete. It is git-ignored and safe to delete.

docs.title: Checking for drift
docs.text:
dtaas config reconcile compares dtaas.users.registry.json (the users who should be provisioned) with the live compose.users.yml services (the users who are provisioned). It reports missing, unexpected, drifted, absent and desired-status drift; see config reconcile for what each means. When everything matches, it prints In sync: no drift detected.

Without --fix, the command is read-only. --fix reprovisions missing and drifted users, restarts absent users' containers, and pauses, stops or starts every provisioned user to match its desired_status. It never touches unexpected services; remove those with dtaas user delete.

Pausing or stopping a user with dtaas user pause or stop is recorded as that user's desired_status. A later reconcile treats the suspension as the desired state instead of reporting it as drift.

docs.title: GitLab provisioning settings
docs.text:
The [gitlab] section turns on GitLab account provisioning for dtaas user add. For what the command does and prints in each case, see GitLab provisioning.

[gitlab]
provision  = true
api_url    = "https://gitlab.example.com"
# pat      = "glpat-xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx"   # prefer DTAAS_GITLAB_PAT
# ssl_verify = "/etc/ssl/certs/corp-ca.pem" # or true (default) / false
Key Default Meaning provision false true makes user add create each user's GitLab account and token api_url none The GitLab instance; required when provision is true pat none The admin token, used only when DTAAS_GITLAB_PAT is unset or empty ssl_verify true true uses the system trust store, a path uses that CA bundle, false turns verification off

docs.title: Admin token
docs.text:
The CLI uses DTAAS_GITLAB_PAT whenever it is exported and not empty, and [gitlab].pat otherwise, so a rotated token needs no edit to a dtaas.toml the whole installation shares. When both are set to different tokens, a Note: line says the exported one is used. The token must belong to a GitLab administrator and carry the api scope, plus admin_mode on an instance with Admin Mode enabled.

For a self-hosted GitLab behind an internal CA, point ssl_verify at the CA bundle rather than turning it off. With ssl_verify = false, the admin token and every user's initial password cross the network without certificate checks, and the CLI prints a warning on each run.

docs.title: Initial passwords
docs.text:
Each new account needs an initial password. The CLI takes the first one it finds:

  1. --password on the command line, or the password column of the users.csv given with --file.
  2. [[users]].password in dtaas.toml, for a starting user.
  3. A hidden prompt, asked twice, when a single user is added.

A password is used once, to create the account. The CLI never writes it to dtaas.users.registry.json, .dtaas.state.json or a log. A run in which a named user has no password and no account from an earlier run is refused before anything changes. --password is visible in shell history and in the process list, so prefer the prompt, or the CSV column with chmod 600 users.csv (the CLI sets that mode only on the sample users.csv that config generate writes).

[[users]].password and the CSV column hold passwords in plaintext. When a run takes a password from dtaas.toml or users.csv and that file is readable by other users, the CLI prints a warning with the chmod 600 command (on Linux and macOS; Windows file modes do not say who can read a file). Once a starting user's account exists, the CLI also reminds you to remove their [[users]].password: it stays a valid GitLab login until the user changes it.

docs.title: Files written
docs.text:
gitlab_user_tokens.json holds the token issued to each user, keyed by username. It is written to the current directory, next to dtaas.toml (not to --output-dir), with mode 0600, and each user's token is added the moment it is issued:

{
  "alice": "glpat-xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx",
  "bob": "glpat-yyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyy"
}

A run adds to the file and never rewrites the other entries. Should a user's entry ever be replaced, the old token is kept under a "<username> (superseded <timestamp>)" key and a warning says to revoke it in GitLab if it is still active. user delete revokes the deleted users' tokens on GitLab, starting users' included, and then drops their entries; a token that could not be revoked keeps its entry. Their GitLab accounts stay.

Before creating any account, user add checks that this file can be read and written, and removes a leftover gitlab_user_tokens.json.tmp from an interrupted run. A token that still cannot be saved is revoked on GitLab at once, and the run issues no further tokens.

dtaas.users.registry.json records, per user, the GitLab account id (gitlab_user_id) and whether a token was issued (gitlab_pat_issued). That is how a re-run knows what is already done: a user with an account id but no token gets a new token for that account, with no password needed, after any token an earlier run issued but never saved is revoked, and a user with a token gets nothing more. Starting users carry the same two markers in the separate starting_users section, since they have no entry under users:

{
  "users": {
    "alice": {
      "email": "alice@intocps.org",
      "groups": [
        "additional"
      ],
      "load_balance": true,
      "desired_status": "running",
      "gitlab_user_id": 42,
      "gitlab_pat_issued": true
    }
  },
  "starting_users": {
    "username1": {
      "gitlab_user_id": 7,
      "gitlab_pat_issued": true
    }
  }
}

dtaas.toml, users.csv and gitlab_user_tokens.json are gitignored and written with mode 0600, since they can hold the admin token, user passwords and user tokens respectively.

The registry and gitlab_user_tokens.json are read and rewritten without a lock, so run one dtaas command at a time per installation: two user add runs at once can lose each other's changes.

docs.title: Install DTaaS with the CLI
docs.text:
The DTaaS command line interface (CLI) is the recommended way to install and operate a DTaaS deployment. A single dtaas entry point generates deployment projects, validates configuration, starts and stops deployments, manages users and rotates certificates for all supported scenarios.

This page covers the standard installation workflow and every dtaas command. The complete dtaas.toml field reference, with the validation rules, an annotated example file and the user-file model, is in the Config Reference.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Install the CLI inside a virtual environment.

python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate     # Linux / macOS
# .venv\Scripts\activate      # Windows

pip install dtaas
dtaas --help                  # verify
dtaas --version               # which build is installed

The package needs Python 3.10 or newer.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
From a clean machine to a running deployment:

# 1. Generate dtaas.toml + a sample users.csv
dtaas config generate

# 2. Edit dtaas.toml: server DNS, paths, OAuth credentials, users

# 3. Validate; fix any reported errors before continuing
dtaas config validate

# 4. Generate deployment files for your chosen scenario
dtaas deployment generate --type secure-server

# 5. Bring the deployment up
dtaas platform install

Tear it down again with dtaas platform uninstall. Add --remove-user-files to also delete the per-user workspace directories. That flag asks for confirmation; pass --yes to skip the prompt.

docs.title: Deployment types
docs.text:
--type When to use Support level localhost Local development or demo, single user dev/demo only insecure-server Multi-user HTTP demo insecure/demo only secure-server Multi-user HTTPS production-supported secure-server-gitlab HTTPS with bundled GitLab production-supported workspace-localhost Workspace with Dex on localhost dev/demo only workspace-secure-server Workspace with Keycloak production-supported

Warning

Types marked dev/demo only or insecure/demo only run over plain HTTP with default or static credentials. Do not expose them to the internet or shared networks. Production-supported types still require the manual hardening steps documented in the README.md and configuration notes (CONFIG.md, or CONFIGURATION.md for workspace-secure-server) shipped with each generated project.

The generated packages match the manual installation scenarios. The CLI fills in the configuration and file structure that the manual path asks you to prepare by hand.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
The CLI reads all its settings from dtaas.toml. It looks for the file in --output-dir first and then in the current working directory, so one top-level dtaas.toml can serve a deployment generated into a subdirectory.

The main sections are:

  • [common]: the server DNS name and the absolute path of the DTaaS installation directory.
  • [common.security]: the tls flag and certs-src, the source directory for TLS certificates.
  • [common.resources]: default resource limits for user workspace containers (cpus, mem_limit, pids_limit, shm_size), with a set_limits flag that turns enforcement off. Adjust them to the host capacity and your tenancy policy.
  • [[users]]: the starting users, one record each.
  • [gitlab]: optional GitLab account provisioning for user add (see GitLab provisioning).
  • [frontend]: the OAuth application of the DTaaS web client, for the server types.
  • One section per deployment type, such as [secure-server], which holds the OAuth credentials for that type.

Run dtaas config validate after every edit. It reports all problems at once; see Validation Rules for the full list.

docs.title: Abridged configuration
docs.text:
An abridged dtaas.toml:

name="Digital Twin as a Service (DTaaS)"
version="2.2.1"
owner="The INTO-CPS-Association"
git-repo="https://github.com/into-cps-association/DTaaS.git"

[common]
server-dns="localhost"
# Absolute path to the DTaaS installation. Separate it with / or \\, never a
# single \, which fails with "Invalid unicode value".
path="/home/XXX/DTaaS"
# Windows example
#path="C:\\Users\\XXX\\DTaaS"

[common.security]
tls=true
certs-src='/etc/letsencrypt/archive/intocps.org'

[common.resources]
# Enforce the per-user limits below; false creates users with no CPU, memory
# or process caps and ignores the fields.
set_limits=true
cpus=4 # Virtual CPU
mem_limit="4G"
pids_limit=4960 # Number of processes
shm_size="512m" # Shared memory size

[[users]]
username="username1"
email="username1@intocps.org"
groups=["default","dtaas"]
load_balance=true

[gitlab]
provision=false
api_url="https://gitlab.com"
ssl_verify=true
#pat="glpat-xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx"

[frontend]
react-app-client-id="your_client_id_here"
react-app-oauth-url="https://gitlab.com"
...

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Edits to dtaas.toml affect only user containers created after the change.
  • To apply new limits to existing containers, recreate or restart the user containers, for example by deleting and re-adding the user with the CLI or by restarting the container with Docker Compose.
  • Give memory and shared memory values a unit (M, G).

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Every command follows a dtaas <noun> <verb> grammar with four nouns, listed in workflow order:

Noun Acts on config dtaas.toml and the user registry deployment The generated deployment files platform The installed core services, as one unit user Additional users, one at a time

The config, deployment and platform commands accept --output-dir (default .). The user commands always act on the current directory, so run them from the deployment directory.

If a command fails because a path is root-owned (for example TLS certificates under /etc/letsencrypt), the CLI suggests re-running it as sudo -E env PATH="$PATH" dtaas <command>.

docs.title: config generate / config validate
docs.text:
dtaas config generate    # writes dtaas.toml + a sample users.csv
dtaas config validate    # checks an existing dtaas.toml

generate writes dtaas.toml and a sample users.csv (bulk input for user add --file) into --output-dir. --force overwrites an existing dtaas.toml. validate reports every problem in the file at once; see Validation Rules.

Options:

Option Default Description --output-dir PATH . For generate: target directory (created if missing). For validate: search location --force off (generate only) Overwrite an existing dtaas.toml

docs.title: config reconcile
docs.text:
Reports drift between dtaas.users.registry.json (the users who should be provisioned) and the live compose.users.yml services (the users who are provisioned):

dtaas config reconcile

It lists users in these categories:

  • missing: registered but not provisioned.
  • unexpected: provisioned but not in the registry. This can come from a manual edit or a partial delete, so investigate it.
  • drifted: provisioned, but the live config no longer matches what .dtaas.state.json recorded at the last provisioning.
  • absent: provisioned (the user has a compose service), but the container is gone, for example after an interrupted user add.
  • desired-status drift: provisioned, but the live container state does not match the user's registry desired_status (for example desired 'paused' but container is 'running').

When everything matches, it prints In sync: no drift detected. If Docker is unreachable, the command warns that it could not verify container state and reports only the drift it can read from the compose file. It never reports In sync in that case.

Without --fix, the command is read-only. With --fix, it reprovisions missing and drifted users, restarts the containers of absent users, and then pauses, stops or starts every provisioned user to match its desired_status:

dtaas config reconcile --fix

--fix runs the same code as dtaas user add, so it acts on the current directory. Combining it with an --output-dir other than the current directory is rejected. It also refuses to run when Docker is unreachable.

--fix never touches unexpected services, because removing something that is running should be a deliberate action. Use dtaas user delete for those.

Options:

Option Default Description --output-dir PATH . Installation directory to inspect --fix off Reprovision missing/drifted registry users, and enforce desired status, after reporting

docs.title: deployment generate
docs.text:
Copies the project structure for one deployment scenario (docker-compose.yml, config examples and supporting files) into a target directory. It also writes the user-workspace templates and the files/template/ skeleton, and, for the types that run the logger, creates logs/logger/ (see platform install).

dtaas deployment generate --type <name>

Options:

Option Default Description --type NAME (required) Deployment scenario (see Deployment Types) --output-dir PATH . Target directory (created if missing) --force off Overwrite files that already exist

Examples:

# Localhost demo in the current directory
dtaas deployment generate --type localhost

# Production HTTPS server in a subdirectory
dtaas deployment generate --type secure-server --output-dir ./my-server

# Regenerate, overwriting existing files
dtaas deployment generate --type insecure-server --output-dir ./demo --force

Generated files besides the scenario's compose tree:

Item Purpose users.server.yml Docker Compose template for HTTP deployments users.server.secure.yml Docker Compose template for HTTPS/TLS deployments users.resources.yml Per-user resource-limit overlay, merged in when set_limits is true files/template/ Skeleton copied into each new user workspace

When dtaas.toml is present, its values are substituted into the generated files (dotenv files, the client config and, for TLS types, the certs/ directory). See Configuration Substitution for details. If dtaas.toml is not found, the command prints a note and the generated files keep their placeholder values.

Verify the Docker image tag

users.server.yml and users.server.secure.yml pin a workspace image tag (e.g. intocps/workspace:main-56c6f68). Check Docker Hub and update the tag to a current, stable version before deploying.

docs.title: platform install
docs.text:
Starts a generated deployment.

dtaas platform install

The command runs docker compose up -d against the docker-compose.yml in the installation directory. Before that, it makes sure a workspace directory exists for every [[users]] record, creating any missing one from files/template/, and sets its ownership to 1000:100.

For the localhost, insecure-server, secure-server and secure-server-gitlab types, it also creates logs/logger/, where the logger microservice writes its events, and gives it to 1000:1000, the user that runs the logger. This is the logger step of the manual installation guides, so an installation done with the CLI needs no extra step. Only logs/logger/ changes owner: secure-server-gitlab also mounts logs/ into GitLab, so logs/ itself is left alone.

Both ownership changes use sudo on Linux and macOS and are skipped on Windows. Before sudo runs, the command says what it is for, since sudo may ask for your password. logs/logger/ is left alone when it already belongs to 1000:1000, for example when you are that user. When a change fails, for example because sudo is not available, the command prints a warning with the commands to run by hand and carries on:

Setting the owner of logs/logger/ to 1000:1000 with sudo (it may ask for your password)
Warning: could not set the owner of logs/logger/
  Run: sudo chown -R 1000:1000 -- /home/admin/dtaas/logs/logger

When logs/ or logs/logger/ is a symbolic link, the command does not change its owner and prints a warning instead.

Options:

Option Default Description --output-dir PATH . Installation directory containing the generated deployment

Because the CLI looks for dtaas.toml in --output-dir first and then in the current working directory, a single top-level dtaas.toml can serve a deployment generated into a subdirectory:

dtaas platform install --output-dir ./insecure

The command fails with an error if docker-compose.yml is missing, dtaas.toml cannot be found or the Docker daemon is unreachable.

docs.title: platform uninstall
docs.text:
Tears the whole installation down, stopping and removing containers and networks.

dtaas platform uninstall

Containers of users added with user add run as a separate Compose project. The command removes them first so that they do not hold the shared network open. Per-user workspace files are kept by default.

To also delete the per-user workspace directories and the CLI-owned dtaas.users.registry.json and .dtaas.state.json:

dtaas platform uninstall --remove-user-files

This is destructive, so the command asks for confirmation. Skip the prompt in non-interactive scripts with --yes:

dtaas platform uninstall --remove-user-files --yes

Options:

Option Default Description --output-dir PATH . Installation directory --remove-user-files off Also delete per-user workspace dirs + registry/state files --yes / -y off Skip the confirmation prompt for --remove-user-files

Note

--remove-user-files removes only the per-user directories inside <output-dir>/files/. It keeps files/common/ and files/template/, so a later platform install can recreate the user directories. It refuses to follow a symlinked files/. Double-check --output-dir before using this flag.

docs.title: Lifecycle operations
docs.text:
These commands work on an installed deployment. status reports its state; stop/start and pause/resume suspend and resume it. None of them remove containers or networks; uninstall does that. They exit 0 on success, including when nothing is installed, and non-zero on failure, so CI and ops scripts can call them safely.

platform stop, start, pause and resume act on the core services only and never touch per-user containers. Suspend or resume additional users with dtaas user stop/pause/resume. platform status still reports the whole installation, core services and user containers.

Lifecycle command matrix:

Command docker compose verb Effect Containers kept? Reverse with platform install up -d Create and start every service n/a platform stop / platform uninstall platform status ps (read-only) Report per-service state; no change n/a n/a platform stop stop Terminate the processes, keep the containers yes platform start platform start start Start previously stopped containers yes platform stop platform pause pause Freeze the processes (memory preserved) yes platform resume platform resume unpause Thaw previously paused processes yes n/a platform uninstall down Stop and remove containers and networks no platform install

stop vs pause

stop sends SIGTERM/SIGKILL: the processes end, and a restart runs them from scratch (reverse with platform start). pause uses the kernel cgroup freezer: the processes are suspended in place with their memory intact and resume instantly (reverse with platform resume), but a paused container still holds its resources. Use stop to free CPU and pause for a short suspension. pause expects running containers and fails if the deployment is already stopped.

docs.title: platform status
docs.text:
Reports the state of every service, for both the core services and the user containers.

dtaas platform status

PROJECT     SERVICE            STATE
deployment  traefik            running
deployment  client             running
deployment  gitlab             not created
users       alice              paused

The state is one of running, paused, stopped (a terminated container, which Docker calls exited), restarting or not created (a service defined in docker-compose.yml that has no container yet).

For automation, --json prints the same records as JSON:

dtaas platform status --json

[
  {"project": "deployment", "service": "traefik", "state": "running"}
]

For the user containers alone, use dtaas user status.

Options:

Option Default Description --output-dir PATH . Installation directory --json off Emit machine-readable JSON instead of the table

docs.title: platform stop / platform start
docs.text:
stop stops the core services with docker compose stop; start brings the stopped containers back with docker compose start. Containers and networks are kept, so stop is not an uninstall.

dtaas platform stop
dtaas platform start

After stop, the command notes how many per-user containers are still running and suggests dtaas user stop --all. Both commands print There is no existing DTaaS / Workspace installation and exit 0 when nothing is installed (no containers in any state), so they are safe to call repeatedly.

Options:

Option Default Description --output-dir PATH . Installation directory

docs.title: platform pause / platform resume
docs.text:
pause freezes the running core-service containers in place with docker compose pause; resume thaws them with docker compose unpause. Memory is preserved and resuming is almost instant.

dtaas platform pause
dtaas platform resume

Like stop, pause notes any per-user containers still running. Both commands report the absent installation and exit 0 when nothing is installed (no containers in any state).

Options:

Option Default Description --output-dir PATH . Installation directory

docs.title: platform update --certs
docs.text:
Replaces the TLS certificates of a running deployment in place, without regenerating the project or copying files by hand.

dtaas platform update --certs

The command reads [common.security].certs-src from dtaas.toml, then:

  1. Validates the new certificate pair (parseable, private key matches the certificate, no expired intermediates).
  2. Stops the traefik service to release open file handles.
  3. Swaps the validated files into <output-dir>/certs/, backing up the live pair and restoring it on any failure.
  4. Restricts the private key to 0600 (POSIX; prints a warning on Windows).
  5. Restarts traefik and waits for it to come back up.

If validation fails, the live certificates are left untouched. The command is safe to run repeatedly.

Options:

Option Default Description --certs (required) Refresh the deployment's TLS certificates --output-dir PATH . Installation directory

docs.title: platform update --config
docs.text:
Re-applies the values in dtaas.toml to the service config files of an installed deployment without regenerating the project.

dtaas platform update --config

The command runs the same substitution as deployment generate. If any file changed, it recreates all deployment services with docker compose up -d --force-recreate. It detects the deployment type from docker-compose.yml.

# Preview changes without writing or restarting
dtaas platform update --config --dry-run

# Apply changes and restart
dtaas platform update --config

# Update a deployment in a subdirectory
dtaas platform update --config --output-dir ./my-server

--config validates dtaas.toml before changing anything and refuses to apply an invalid file. A second run with no dtaas.toml changes reports No configuration changes and restarts nothing. If secrets are still template placeholders after the update, the command lists them.

Options:

Option Default Description --config (required) Re-apply dtaas.toml to installed service config files --dry-run off Report what would change without writing or restarting --output-dir PATH . Installation directory

--certs and --config can be combined in one invocation; at least one of them is required.

docs.title: User management
docs.text:
User management spans three files, each with a single owner; see User Files for the full model.

  • dtaas.users.registry.json is the CLI-owned record of every additional user (added after installation with user add), including their desired_status (running/paused/stopped). Only user add, delete, pause, stop and resume change it; do not edit it by hand.
  • .dtaas.state.json is a git-ignored, disposable cache of what is running: per-user container id, status and a config hash, refreshed on every add and delete. It is safe to delete; the CLI rebuilds it on the next provisioning run. config reconcile compares it against the registry to detect drift.

docs.title: Add users
docs.text:
The starting users an instance is installed with are declared in dtaas.toml as [[users]] records (see Abridged Configuration). You edit them once at installation time, and the CLI never rewrites them.

Users added later are not written to dtaas.toml. Add them with dtaas user add, either one at a time:

dtaas user add --email alice@intocps.org --group dtaas --load-balance alice

--group is repeatable, not comma-separated. Pass it once per group to add a user to several groups:

dtaas user add --email alice@intocps.org --group dtaas --group testers alice

or in bulk from a CSV file (dtaas config generate writes a sample users.csv next to dtaas.toml):

dtaas user add --file users.csv

username,email,groups,load_balance,password
alice,alice@intocps.org,additional,true,
bob,bob@intocps.org,additional;beta-testers;load-balanced-tier1,false,

groups is a ;-separated list and load_balance is true or false. The password column is used only with GitLab provisioning (see below). Give either a USERNAME or --file, not both. A bare dtaas user add with neither is rejected, so it cannot reprovision the whole registry by accident.

Both forms merge the users into the CLI-owned dtaas.users.registry.json with desired_status set to running. Only the newly added users are started; users already running are left alone, so adding one user never recreates the others. A username already in the registry is reported ('alice' already exists, skipping) and never added twice or overwritten. A username declared in dtaas.toml's [[users]] is reported as a starting user, whose workspace dtaas.toml manages; with GitLab provisioning on, naming one creates its GitLab account (see below). A run that adds nobody ends with No new users added. and exits 0.

To reprovision every registry user at once (for example after compose.users.yml was lost), use dtaas config reconcile --fix.

Options:

Option Default Description USERNAME — Add one user (requires --email, except for a dtaas.toml starting user) --file PATH / -f — Bulk-add users from a CSV --email TEXT — Email for USERNAME (enables forward-auth routing); read from [[users]] for a starting user, and another address given for one is reported and not applied --group TEXT additional Group tag for USERNAME; repeat the flag for multiple groups --load-balance / --no-load-balance on Mark USERNAME for load balancing --password TEXT — Initial GitLab password for USERNAME; only used when GitLab provisioning is enabled (see below). It wins over [[users]].password. Prefer the users.csv password column or the interactive prompt, because a command-line value is visible in shell history and the process list

For each registry user, the command copies files/template/ into files/<username>, creating the directory when it is missing, and sets its ownership to 1000:100 where it has the permission to; without that permission it leaves the ownership as it is and carries on.

When a user has an email, the CLI adds the matching traefik-forward-auth routing rule to config/conf.server, so you do not need to edit conf.server by hand. A user added from a users.csv row with an empty email cell gets no rule. Restart the container for the change to take effect:

docker compose --env-file config/.env up -d --force-recreate traefik-forward-auth

docs.title: GitLab provisioning (optional)
docs.text: When [gitlab].provision = true in dtaas.toml (off by default), user add also creates a GitLab account for each user it adds and issues that account a Personal Access Token (PAT). The containers are provisioned first; a GitLab failure never undoes them, but it does make the command exit non-zero. The [gitlab] keys, the password sources and the files written are described in GitLab provisioning settings.

docs.title: Set up the admin token
docs.text:
Provisioning needs an admin token, set up once per installation by a GitLab administrator:

1. Use an administrator account. In Admin area > Users, click Edit on the account and check that User type is Administrator.

2. Create its token, signed in as that account, under User settings > Access > Personal access tokens (Add new token). Tick the api scope, and admin_mode too if the instance has Admin Mode enabled, then export the token where you run dtaas:

export DTAAS_GITLAB_PAT="glpat-xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx"

Choose an expiry you will rotate, because provisioning stops working the day the token lapses. When DTAAS_GITLAB_PAT and [gitlab].pat hold different tokens, the exported one is used and the CLI prints Note: using the admin token from DTAAS_GITLAB_PAT.

docs.title: Scenarios
docs.text:
Each scenario shows what dtaas user add prints. The output of docker compose while containers start is left out.

Add one user. Without --password, the CLI asks for the initial GitLab password with hidden input, twice:

$ dtaas user add --email alice@intocps.org alice
GitLab password for 'alice':
Repeat for confirmation:
GitLab account and token created for 'alice'.
  The token is in gitlab_user_tokens.json.
Users added successfully

Add users from a CSV. Fill in the password column of users.csv, then make the file readable by you alone:

username,email,groups,load_balance,password
alice,alice@intocps.org,additional,true,Kq7v-Rm3x-Zt9w
bob,bob@intocps.org,additional;beta-testers,false,Wd4p-Hs8n-Qc2y

$ chmod 600 users.csv
$ dtaas user add --file users.csv
GitLab account and token created for 'alice'.
  The token is in gitlab_user_tokens.json.
GitLab account and token created for 'bob'.
  The token is in gitlab_user_tokens.json.
Users added successfully

A starting user. Naming a [[users]] user of dtaas.toml creates only their GitLab account and token. Their workspace already runs from docker-compose.yml, their email is the one in dtaas.toml, and their password is [[users]].password or, when that is unset, the prompt:

$ dtaas user add username1
'username1' is a dtaas.toml starting user.
  Its workspace is managed there, not by 'user add'.
GitLab account and token created for 'username1'.
  The token is in gitlab_user_tokens.json.
No new users added.

An --email that differs from the one in dtaas.toml is not applied, and the run says so:

$ dtaas user add --email other@intocps.org username1
Warning: the email given for 'username1' is not used.
  dtaas.toml declares username1@intocps.org for this starting user, and that is the address GitLab gets.
...

A user with no password. When a named user has no password and no account from an earlier run, the whole run is refused before anything is registered or started. Fill in the password column and run the same command again:

$ dtaas user add --file users.csv
Error: No GitLab password for 'bob'.
  [gitlab].provision is enabled in dtaas.toml, so a new user needs an initial GitLab password: add a 'password' column to their users.csv row (and chmod 600 the file), pass --password for a single user, or set [[users]].password for a dtaas.toml starting user.

A password GitLab refuses. GitLab refuses a password that is too short or built from common words, for example one that contains pass or the username. The user's container is up, but their account is not created. The line under GitLab account creation failed. is GitLab's own reason, for example:

$ dtaas user add --file users.csv
GitLab account and token created for 'alice'.
  The token is in gitlab_user_tokens.json.
GitLab provisioning failed for 'bob'.
  GitLab account creation failed.
    Failed to create user 'bob': 400: {'password': ['must not contain commonly used combinations of words and letters']}
Error: Error while adding users
  GitLab provisioning failed for: bob
    Their containers were still provisioned.

Retry after a failure. Fix the cause (here, bob's password in users.csv) and run the same command again. Both users are already registered, so their containers are left alone; alice already has a token and is skipped, and only bob's account is created:

$ dtaas user add --file users.csv
'alice' already exists, skipping
'bob' already exists, skipping
GitLab account step skipped for 'alice'.
  A Personal Access Token was already issued on an earlier run (see gitlab_user_tokens.json). A re-run does not reissue one.
GitLab account and token created for 'bob'.
  The token is in gitlab_user_tokens.json.
No new users added.

A retry never leaves a second live token for a user, so repeating the command after a partial failure is always safe. When the account was created but its token was not saved, the retry first revokes any token named dtaas that an earlier run issued, then issues a new one to that same account (the registry keeps its id) instead of creating the account again. No password is needed for that, so naming the user again is enough:

$ dtaas user add --email alice@intocps.org alice
'alice' already exists, skipping
GitLab token issued for 'alice'.
  The token is in gitlab_user_tokens.json.
No new users added.

A token that is lost or revoked is replaced in GitLab directly.

A token that cannot be saved. Before creating any account, user add checks gitlab_user_tokens.json. A leftover gitlab_user_tokens.json.tmp from an interrupted run is removed with a warning; a file that is not a JSON object, or cannot be written, stops the GitLab step for every user. Should a save still fail after a token was issued (a full disk, for example), that token is revoked at once, and no further token is issued in that run:

GitLab token for 'alice' not saved; revoked.
  [Errno 28] No space left on device
  Once tokens can be saved to gitlab_user_tokens.json again, run 'dtaas user add alice' to issue a new one.
GitLab provisioning stopped for: bob
  Tokens cannot be saved to gitlab_user_tokens.json, so no further token is issued this run.
Error: Error while adding users
  GitLab provisioning failed for: alice, bob
    Their containers were still provisioned.

If the token cannot be revoked either, the first line reads GitLab token for 'alice' not saved, still valid. and says to revoke it in GitLab.

An account that already exists. When the username, or the email, is already taken on GitLab, the account is left as it is and no token is issued: this run did not create it and does not know its credentials. The container is still provisioned, and the command fails. Delete the account in GitLab, or use another username or email, then run the same command again:

$ dtaas user add --email carol@intocps.org carol
GitLab password for 'carol':
Repeat for confirmation:
GitLab provisioning failed for 'carol'.
  GitLab account already exists; no token issued.
    The username is already registered, or its email is already on another account, and this CLI did not create it, so its credentials are unknown. Delete that account in GitLab, or use another username or email, then run 'user add' again. GitLab said: 409: Username has already been taken
Error: Error while adding users
  GitLab provisioning failed for: carol
    Their containers were still provisioned.

No admin token. Without DTAAS_GITLAB_PAT or [gitlab].pat, the containers are still provisioned, the GitLab step is skipped for everyone, and the command fails. Export the token and run the same command again:

$ dtaas user add --email alice@intocps.org alice
GitLab password for 'alice':
Repeat for confirmation:
GitLab provisioning skipped for every user.
  No GitLab PAT configured for provisioning.
    Export DTAAS_GITLAB_PAT, or set [gitlab].pat in dtaas.toml.
Error: Error while adding users
  GitLab provisioning failed for: alice
    Their containers were still provisioned.

A token GitLab rejects. When GitLab answers 401 (an invalid or expired token) or 403 (a token whose owner is not an administrator, or that lacks a scope), each user's failure ends with a hint on the token:

GitLab provisioning failed for 'alice'.
  GitLab account creation failed.
    Failed to create user 'alice': 403: 403 Forbidden
    Check DTAAS_GITLAB_PAT (or [gitlab].pat): creating users and managing their tokens needs a non-expired personal access token with the 'api' scope, owned by an administrator account, and the 'admin_mode' scope as well on an instance with Admin Mode enabled.

docs.title: What the user receives
docs.text: Each issued token is named dtaas, has the read_repository and write_repository scopes only, and expires after 365 days. It is saved to gitlab_user_tokens.json the moment it is issued; see Files written for that file and the registry markers. Hand each user their token, which they use to clone and push their repositories, and their initial password.

docs.title: Resource limits (optional)
docs.text:
By default each user container gets the CPU, memory, process and shared-memory caps from [common.resources], merged in from the users.resources.yml overlay. To add users without any caps, set set_limits = false in that section:

# Constrained users (default): limits enforced
[common.resources]
set_limits = true
cpus       = 4
mem_limit  = "4G"
pids_limit = 4960
shm_size   = "512m"

# Unconstrained users: no caps written, limit fields optional
[common.resources]
set_limits = false

The CLI reads the flag on every user add, so one deployment can host both constrained and unconstrained users if you change set_limits between runs.

docs.title: Delete users
docs.text:
Pass one or more usernames to dtaas user delete:

dtaas user delete alice bob

or delete in bulk from the same CSV format (only the username column is used):

dtaas user delete --file users.csv

Give either USERNAMES or --file; one of them is required. Add --dry-run to see which users would be removed without deleting anything:

dtaas user delete alice bob --dry-run

Each deleted user is deprovisioned (container stopped, compose service and forward-auth rule removed) and dropped from dtaas.users.registry.json. Users who are not provisioned are reported and skipped, but they are still removed from the registry.

The CLI removes the traefik-forward-auth routing rules of deleted users from config/conf.server. Restart the container for the change to take effect:

docker compose --env-file config/.env up -d --force-recreate traefik-forward-auth

The GitLab account stays

user delete removes the user from the DTaaS installation and revokes the Personal Access Tokens named dtaas that the CLI issued to them, so they lose repository access. Their GitLab account stays, so the user can still sign in there. A revoked token is dropped from gitlab_user_tokens.json. Revoking uses the same admin token as user add, even when [gitlab].provision is now off. To remove an account, a GitLab administrator deletes it in GitLab. Do that before adding the same username again: user add cannot issue a token for an account it did not create.

A dtaas.toml starting user is handled the same way on GitLab: its token is revoked and its markers are cleared. Its workspace is one of the installation's own, defined in docker-compose.yml, so user delete keeps its container and forward-auth rule.

GitLab token revoked for 'alice'.
  The GitLab account stays. Delete it in GitLab before adding the same username again.
Users deleted successfully

When a token cannot be revoked (GitLab unreachable, admin token missing or refused), the rest of the delete still completes, the token stays in gitlab_user_tokens.json, and the command fails naming the user. Revoke that token in GitLab:

GitLab token not revoked for 'alice'.
  No GitLab PAT configured for provisioning.
    Export DTAAS_GITLAB_PAT, or set [gitlab].pat in dtaas.toml.
  The token is still valid and stays in gitlab_user_tokens.json; revoke it in GitLab.
Error: Error while deleting users
  GitLab tokens not revoked for: alice
    Their workspaces were still deleted.

Options:

Option Default Description USERNAMES — One or more usernames to remove --file PATH / -f — Bulk-delete users listed in a CSV (only the username column is used) --dry-run off Preview the removal without making any changes

docs.title: user pause / stop / resume
docs.text:
Suspend or resume specific additional users without touching the rest of the installation. Target one or more USERNAMES, a --file/-f users.csv (only the username column is read, as with user delete), or every additional user with --all.

dtaas user pause alice bob
dtaas user stop alice
dtaas user resume alice bob
dtaas user pause --file users.csv
dtaas user stop --all
Command docker compose verb Effect Reverse with user pause pause Freeze the named users' containers (memory preserved) user resume user stop stop Terminate the named users' containers, keep them user resume user resume unpause or start, as needed Thaw a paused user, or restart a stopped one —

Each command also records a desired_status ("paused"/"stopped"/"running") in dtaas.users.registry.json for the users it acted on. This makes the suspension durable: a later dtaas user add or dtaas config reconcile --fix checks desired_status and does not restart a user you paused or stopped. Only user resume (or editing the registry by hand) sets it back to "running".

Only additional users can be targeted. Naming a dtaas.toml starting user is an error. To suspend or resume the whole installation, starting users included, use dtaas platform pause/stop/resume together with --all here.

A username that is not in the registry, or is registered but not provisioned (for example because user add never ran for it), is reported and skipped, and the rest of the batch continues:

'carol' is not a registered user, skipping
alice, bob paused successfully

Options:

Option Default Description USERNAMES — One or more usernames to target --file PATH / -f — Bulk-target users listed in a CSV (only the username column is used) --all off Target every additional user; cannot be combined with USERNAMES or --file

docs.title: user status
docs.text:
Reports the state of every additional user's container, or of one named user. It is the per-user part of platform status, using the same table and --json format.

dtaas user status
dtaas user status alice
dtaas user status --json

A username that is not in dtaas.users.registry.json is rejected, so a typo is not mistaken for a stopped user. A registered user without a container is reported as not provisioned. The command exits 0 whenever it can read the deployment.

Options:

Option Default Description USERNAME — Report only this user --json off Emit machine-readable JSON instead of the table

docs.title: Additional points to remember
docs.text:
• user add writes every registry user into compose.users.yml but starts only the users added in that run. Users whose desired_status is not running are never started.
  • config reconcile --fix with an empty registry does nothing.
  • Usernames may contain ., _ and - and must start with a letter or digit. Whitespace, path separators and shell metacharacters are rejected.
  • user add does not enable AuthMS authentication.

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text: • Validation accepts usernames that contain ., but . is a special character in Docker Compose labels, so containers for such users can fail to provision. A future release will replace . with - or _ in the generated labels.
