  • Workspace secure server config

docs.title: GitLab Integration Guide
docs.text:
This guide connects a local GitLab instance to a DTaaS server installation and sets GitLab up as the OAuth provider for DTaaS.

Afterwards, the GitLab instance is the OAuth provider for both the DTaaS client application and the Traefik forward-auth backend authorisation.

Important

The DTaaS client uses the react-oidc-context node package, which incorrectly makes authorisation redirects use the HTTPS URL scheme. This is a known issue with the package, and it forces the DTaaS server to use HTTPS, either at https://localhost or at https://intocps.org. The rest of this guide uses intocps.org to stand for either localhost or a custom domain.

docs.title: Integration Paths
docs.text:
There are two integration paths:

  1. Integrated package: see the installation page of the dtaas-secure-server-integrated-gitlab-xx.zip package. GitLab is then available over HTTPS at https://intocps.org/gitlab.
  2. Platform Services CLI: see the CLI docs. GitLab is then available over HTTPS on the configured port, at https://intocps.org:${GITLAB_PORT}/gitlab (custom domain, default port 8090).

docs.title: 1. Create OAuth Tokens in GitLab
docs.text:
Follow these guides to create OAuth application tokens for the backend and the client.

This step produces the credentials of the applications named DTaaS Server Authorization and DTaaS Client Authorization, which the next step uses.

docs.title: 2. Use Valid OAuth Application Tokens
docs.text: Put the OAuth application details into the configuration files: the DTaaS Client Authorization details go into config/client.js, and the DTaaS Server Authorization details go into config/.env.

docs.title: 3. Create Users
docs.text: Create GitLab users that match USERNAME1 / USERNAME2 in config/.env.

docs.title: 4. Restart Services
docs.text: docker compose --env-file config/.env up -d --force-recreate client traefik-forward-auth

docs.title: GitLab Runner Integration
docs.text:
For Windows hosts, see runner-windows.md.

This page creates a gitlab-runner that executes digital twins. You can install several such runners and link them to the integrated GitLab.

The diagram shows the intended installation.

A path such as /user1 is the URL route of that service, for example https://intocps.org/user1. The thick arrow is the forward-auth check: Traefik asks traefik-forward-auth to authorise each request before it routes it.

There are two installation scenarios:

  1. Localhost Installation: the integrated runner runs locally with a GitLab instance hosted at https://localhost/gitlab.
  2. Server Installation: the integrated runner works with a GitLab instance on a production server. That server may be a remote machine rather than the host, and may use TLS with a self-signed certificate.

In a server installation, GitLab can run on a second server, and the runners on further remote servers, as the diagram shows.

The steps below set up an integrated runner that can execute digital twins from the Digital Twins Preview Page.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
A GitLab Runner picks up CI/CD jobs by communicating with a GitLab instance. To set up a GitLab instance that integrates with a DTaaS platform, see the GitLab instance document and the GitLab integration guide.

The rest of this page assumes a running DTaaS platform with a GitLab instance.

docs.title: Runner Scopes
docs.text:
A GitLab Runner can have one of three scopes:

Runner Scope Description Instance Runner Available to all groups and projects in a GitLab instance. Group Runner Available to all projects and subgroups in a group. Project Runner Associated with one specific project.

Instance runners are the simplest to set up and are recommended, but any type works. The official GitLab documentation describes the three types.

docs.title: Obtaining A Registration Token
docs.text:
First, obtain the token that registers the runner with the GitLab instance. Open the GitLab instance (remote or local) and follow the steps for the chosen runner scope:

Runner Scope Steps Instance Runner 1. On the Admin dashboard, navigate to CI/CD > Runners.2. Select New instance runner. Group Runner 1. On the DTaaS group page, navigate to Settings > CI/CD > Runners.2. Ensure the Enable shared runners for this group option is enabled.3. On the DTaaS group page, navigate to Build > Runners.4. Select New group runner. Project Runner 1. On the DTaaS group page, select the project named after the GitLab username.2. Navigate to Settings > CI/CD > Runners.3. Select New project runner.

Each scope then shows a page for creating the runner:

  1. Under Platform, select the Linux operating system.
  2. Under Tags, add a linux tag.
  3. Select Create runner.

The following screen appears:

Save the generated runner authentication token.

docs.title: Configuring the Runner
docs.text:
The runner compose files are in deploy/services/runner:

Scenario Compose file Variables it reads Localhost compose.runner.local.yml DTAAS_DIR Server compose.runner.server.yml DTAAS_DIR, SERVER_DNS

Both files mount the TLS certificate of the GitLab host from ${DTAAS_DIR}/deploy/docker/certs/.... That directory no longer exists in the repository, so edit the certificate volume in the compose file to point to the certificate in use, for example deploy/dtaas/docker/secure-server_with_integrated-gitlab/certs/fullchain.pem for the integrated package. In the server scenario, remove the certificate volume if GitLab does not use a self-signed certificate.

The runner must be registered with the GitLab instance before the two can communicate. deploy/services/runner/runner-config.toml contains this template:

concurrent = 20

[[runners]]
  name = "dtaas-runner-1"
  description = "dtaas-runner-1"
  url = "https://intocps.org/gitlab/" # Edit this
  token = "xxx" # Edit this
  executor = "docker"
  request_concurrency = 10
  [runners.docker]
    tls_verify = false
    image = "ruby:2.7"
    privileged = false
    disable_entrypoint_overwrite = false
    oom_kill_disable = false
    volumes = ["/cache"]
    network_mode = "host" # Disable this in secure contexts
  1. Set url to the URL of the GitLab instance.
  2. Set token to the runner authentication token obtained earlier.
  3. In the server installation scenario, remove the line network_mode = "host".

The GitLab documentation lists the advanced configuration options.

docs.title: Start the GitLab Runner
docs.text:
Run these commands from the DTaaS repository directory. Each pair starts and then stops the gitlab-runner container.

  1. Localhost Installation

    export DTAAS_DIR=$(pwd)
docker compose -f deploy/services/runner/compose.runner.local.yml up -d
docker compose -f deploy/services/runner/compose.runner.local.yml down

  2. Server Installation

    export DTAAS_DIR=$(pwd)
export SERVER_DNS=intocps.org
docker compose -f deploy/services/runner/compose.runner.server.yml up -d
docker compose -f deploy/services/runner/compose.runner.server.yml down

The runner inside the container starts automatically. To check that it works, open the page where the runner was created. An Instance Runner, for example, looks like this:

The GitLab runner is now ready to accept jobs from the GitLab instance.

docs.title: Pipeline Trigger Token
docs.text:
The Digital Twins Preview Page uses the GitLab API, which requires a Pipeline Trigger Token. Open the project in the DTaaS group and navigate to Settings > CI/CD > Pipeline trigger tokens. Add a new token with any description.

The Digital Twins Preview Page can now manage and execute digital twins.

docs.title: Setting up GitLab Runners with Docker on Windows for DTaaS
docs.text:
This guide sets up and configures GitLab runners with Docker on Windows for the DTaaS platform. The diagram shows the intended installation.

A path such as /user1 is the URL route of that service, for example https://intocps.org/user1. The thick arrow is the forward-auth check: Traefik asks traefik-forward-auth to authorise each request before it routes it.

docs.title: 1. Install GitLab Runner
docs.text:
Download and install GitLab Runner for Windows from GitLab's official download page.

# Navigate to your download directory
cd C:\path\to\download\folder

# Run the GitLab Runner
.\gitlab-runner.exe install

# Start the service
.\gitlab-runner.exe start

docs.title: 2. Getting a token
docs.text:
To obtain the GitLab token, open the project page (e.g. https://dtaas-digitaltwin.com/gitlab/dtaas/USERNAME) and:

  1. Go to Settings > CI/CD > Runners.
  2. Press New Project Runner.
  3. Add the tag linux.
  4. Leave the other settings unchanged and press Create Runner.
  5. GitLab displays the token. Save it.

docs.title: 3. Register the Runner for DTaaS
docs.text:
Register the runner with the URL of the GitLab instance and the token:

# Register the runner for DTaaS
.\gitlab-runner.exe register --url "https://intocps.org/gitlab" --token ""

# When prompted, enter:
# - Name: [Your machine name or any preferred name]
# - Executor: docker
# - Default Docker image: ruby:2.7
# - Tags: linux

DTaaS digital twins need a Linux environment: their pipelines run shell scripts with commands such as chmod +x.

docs.title: 4. Configure the config.toml
docs.text: Most of the setup happens in the config.toml file. It is usually at C:\Users\YourUsername\.gitlab-runner\config.toml, or in the directory where the gitlab-runner executable was installed and run.

docs.title: DTaaS Configuration for Windows Hosts
docs.text:
The recommended configuration for running DTaaS digital twins on Windows is:

concurrent = 1
check_interval = 0
connection_max_age = "15m0s"
shutdown_timeout = 0

[session_server]
  session_timeout = 1800

[[runners]]
  name = "Some name"
  url = "https://dtaas-digitaltwin.com/gitlab"
  id = 3
  token = "YOUR_RUNNER_TOKEN"
  token_obtained_at = 2025-03-17T19:50:25Z
  token_expires_at = 0001-01-01T00:00:00Z
  executor = "docker"
  [runners.custom_build_dir]
    enabled = false
  [runners.cache]
    MaxUploadedArchiveSize = 0
    [runners.cache.s3]
    [runners.cache.gcs]
    [runners.cache.azure]
  [runners.feature_flags]
    FF_NETWORK_PER_BUILD = false
  [runners.docker]
    tls_verify = false
    image = "ruby:2.7"
    privileged = false
    disable_entrypoint_overwrite = false
    oom_kill_disable = false
    disable_cache = false
    volumes = ["/cache"]
    shm_size = 0
    network_mtu = 0
  tags = ["linux"]

docs.title: 5. Restart the Runner
docs.text:
Restart the runner to apply the configuration:

.\gitlab-runner.exe stop
.\gitlab-runner.exe start

docs.title: Verifying the Setup
docs.text:
Check that the runner is configured correctly:

.\gitlab-runner.exe verify

A successful check prints something like:

Verifying runner... is valid        runner=YourRunnerToken

docs.title: Understanding the DTaaS Project Setup
docs.text:
DTaaS runs digital twins as follows:

  1. Digital twins live in the digital_twins directory.
  2. Each digital twin has lifecycle scripts (create, execute, terminate, clean).
  3. The GitLab CI/CD pipeline triggers these scripts based on user actions.
  4. The scripts need a Linux environment.

docs.title: Common Errors
docs.text:
GitLab CI/CD pipelines on Windows with Docker can fail with these errors:

ERROR: Failed to remove network for build
ERROR: Job failed: invalid volume specification: "c:\\cache"

The usual causes are:

  1. An incorrect Docker executor configuration
  2. Windows-style paths, which Docker does not accept
  3. A mismatch between the runner's executor type and the pipeline requirements

Use the Docker (Linux) executor even on a Windows host, because the digital twin scripts are written for Linux, and write volume paths in Linux form (/cache).

docs.title: Check Client Configuration
docs.text:
A common error is an incorrect configuration of the React website. The client has a checklist page that verifies its configuration.

Visit: https://<SERVER_DNS>/config/developer

A correct configuration shows the following result.

An incorrect client website URL shows the following result.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
Some installations need to stop users from changing the common assets. To make the common area read only, change the volume definitions of the user workspace services.

Note

Make these changes before installing the application.

docs.title: How
docs.text:
To make the common assets read only, change the user services in the secure-server docker-compose.yml file as follows.

  ...
  user1:
    ....
    volumes:
      - ./files/common:/workspace/common:ro
    ....

  user2:
    ....
    volumes:
      - ./files/common:/workspace/common:ro
    ....

The :ro suffix at the end of the line makes the common assets read only.

To apply the same restriction to new users, make the same change to any additional userX service blocks in deploy/dtaas/docker/secure-server/docker-compose.yml. Users added with the DTaaS CLI get their volumes from the users.server.yml and users.server.secure.yml templates in the installation directory, so add :ro to the /workspace/common volume there as well.

docs.title: Renewing LetsEncrypt Certificates
docs.text: LetsEncrypt certificates expire every three months and must be renewed. This guide covers renewal for the current DTaaS package layouts.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Administrative access to the host
  • certbot installed
  • Access to Docker commands

docs.title: Step 1: Renew certificates
docs.text:
sudo certbot renew --dry-run
sudo certbot renew

docs.title: CLI shortcut for generated deployments
docs.text:
If the DTaaS CLI created the deployment (dtaas deployment generate) and [common.security].certs-src in dtaas.toml points to the directory holding the renewed fullchain.pem / privkey.pem (e.g. /etc/letsencrypt/live/your-domain.com), one command replaces the manual copy and restart below:

dtaas platform update --certs --output-dir /path/to/deployment

The command validates the renewed pair: it must parse, the key must match the certificate, and neither the leaf nor any intermediate may have expired. It then stops traefik, swaps the new files into the deployment's certs/ directory (restoring the previous pair if anything goes wrong), restarts traefik and waits for it to come back up. On POSIX hosts it also restores 0600 on the private key; on Windows it prints a warning, because file permissions cannot be enforced there. If validation fails, the live certificates stay untouched. See the DTaaS CLI page for details.

The manual steps below apply to the deploy/dtaas/docker/* package layouts and the services project.

docs.title: Step 2: Deploy to DTaaS server package
docs.text:
For the secure server package (deploy/dtaas/docker/secure-server):

sudo cp /etc/letsencrypt/live/your-domain.com/fullchain.pem \
  /path/to/DTaaS/deploy/dtaas/docker/secure-server/certs/fullchain.pem
sudo cp /etc/letsencrypt/live/your-domain.com/privkey.pem \
  /path/to/DTaaS/deploy/dtaas/docker/secure-server/certs/privkey.pem

For the integrated package (deploy/dtaas/docker/secure-server_with_integrated-gitlab):

sudo cp /etc/letsencrypt/live/your-domain.com/fullchain.pem \
  /path/to/DTaaS/deploy/dtaas/docker/secure-server_with_integrated-gitlab/certs/fullchain.pem
sudo cp /etc/letsencrypt/live/your-domain.com/privkey.pem \
  /path/to/DTaaS/deploy/dtaas/docker/secure-server_with_integrated-gitlab/certs/privkey.pem

docs.title: Step 3: Restart Traefik in DTaaS package
docs.text:
Server package:

cd /path/to/DTaaS/deploy/dtaas/docker/secure-server
docker compose --env-file config/.env up -d --force-recreate traefik

Integrated GitLab package:

cd /path/to/DTaaS/deploy/dtaas/docker/secure-server_with_integrated-gitlab
docker compose --env-file config/.env up -d --force-recreate traefik

docs.title: Step 4: Deploy to services project (if used)
docs.text:
If the platform services run from a project generated by dtaas-services, refresh that project's certs/ directory. Set CERTS_SRC in config/services.env to the certbot directory that holds the renewed certificates, then run from the project directory:

cd /path/to/services-project
sudo -E env PATH="$PATH" dtaas-services host setup

host setup copies the newest certificate pair from CERTS_SRC into certs/ as fullchain.pem and privkey.pem, and rebuilds the per-service certificate files and permissions.

docs.title: Step 5: Restart affected services project containers
docs.text:
cd /path/to/services-project
docker compose -f compose.services.yml --env-file config/services.env up -d --force-recreate

If the ThingsBoard or GitLab compose stacks run in the same project:

docker compose -f compose.thingsboard.yml --env-file config/services.env up -d --force-recreate
docker compose -f compose.gitlab.yml --env-file config/services.env up -d --force-recreate

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
curl -I https://your-domain.com

Check the logs of the traefik service if needed.

docs.title: Self-Signed Certificates
docs.text: This guide configures DTaaS to work with self-signed TLS certificates. Internal servers that are not reachable from the public Internet need them, because they cannot get certificates from public certificate authorities such as Let's Encrypt.

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
When DTaaS is installed with a self-signed certificate, the traefik-forward-auth service must trust that certificate in order to complete the OAuth 2.0 token exchange with the GitLab instance. Otherwise, authentication fails with a certificate error, and the logs of the traefik-forward-auth service contain this error:

level=error msg="Code exchange failed with provider"
error="Post https://intocps.org/gitlab/oauth/token:
x509: certificate signed by unknown authority"

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Administrative access to the host
  • A DTaaS installation using the secure server package

docs.title: Step 1: Update the DNS Configuration
docs.text:
Containers in the secure-server package use the host's DNS configuration. If the GitLab instance uses an internal DNS name that the public Internet cannot resolve, add the correct nameserver to /etc/resolv.conf on the Docker host so that the host can resolve it. Ask the IT department for the correct values. For example:

search client.intocps.org
nameserver 10.20.25.125

docs.title: Step 2: Create Local TLS Certificates with mkcert
docs.text:
Install mkcert if it is not already present, preferably with the OS package manager:

# Debian / Ubuntu 22.04+
sudo apt install mkcert

# macOS (via Homebrew)
brew install mkcert

Alternatively, download the binary from the mkcert releases page and verify its SHA-256 checksum against the value published on that page before installing:

wget https://github.com/FiloSottile/mkcert/releases/download/v1.4.4/mkcert-v1.4.4-linux-amd64
# Verify the checksum from https://github.com/FiloSottile/mkcert/releases/tag/v1.4.4
sha256sum mkcert-v1.4.4-linux-amd64
sudo mv mkcert-v1.4.4-linux-amd64 /usr/local/bin/mkcert
sudo chmod +x /usr/local/bin/mkcert

Create a local root CA and server certificates:

mkcert -install
mkcert "intocps.org" "*.intocps.org" "localhost" "127.0.0.1" "::1"
cp ~/.local/share/mkcert/rootCA.pem rootCA.crt

Replace intocps.org with the actual hostname of the DTaaS installation.

docs.title: Step 3: Build a Custom traefik-forward-auth Image
docs.text:
The traefik-forward-auth container must trust the local root CA. Create a Dockerfile in the same directory as rootCA.crt:

# Stage 1: prepare the root CA certificate
FROM alpine:latest AS cert-builder
RUN apk add --no-cache ca-certificates
COPY rootCA.crt /usr/local/share/ca-certificates/
RUN update-ca-certificates

# Stage 2: copy the updated certificate bundle into the final image
FROM thomseddon/traefik-forward-auth:latest
COPY --from=cert-builder /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt \
     /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt
CMD ["traefik-forward-auth"]

Build the image:

docker build -t traefik-forward-auth-local:latest .

docs.title: Step 4: Use the Custom Image
docs.text:
In deploy/dtaas/docker/secure-server/docker-compose.yml, replace the image reference image: thomseddon/traefik-forward-auth:latest with:

image: traefik-forward-auth-local:latest

docs.title: Step 5: Recreate the forward-auth Container
docs.text:
docker compose --env-file config/.env \
  up -d --force-recreate traefik-forward-auth

docs.title: External GitLab with Self-Signed Certificates
docs.text:
If the GitLab OAuth provider is hosted on a separate server (for example, gitlab.intocps.org) and also uses a self-signed certificate, generate that certificate using the same mkcert root CA:

mkcert "gitlab.intocps.org" "localhost" "127.0.0.1" "::1"

The custom traefik-forward-auth image already trusts the mkcert root CA, so the OAuth token exchange succeeds.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Certificates created with mkcert are trusted only on the machine where mkcert -install was run. Other clients that access the DTaaS installation must also import rootCA.crt into their trust store.
  • If the server has a valid public TLS certificate, this guide is not needed. Use the standard Let's Encrypt renewal guide instead.

docs.title: Install DTaaS on Localhost (GUI)
docs.text:
This guide runs DTaaS on localhost through a graphical user interface (GUI). It suits a single user who wants to run DTaaS on their own computer.

Two installation scenarios are available:

Scenario Auth Provider External Account Required DTaaS Localhost GitLab OAuth Yes (gitlab.com) Workspace Localhost Dex (local) No

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Docker Desktop or Docker Engine with the Compose plugin
  • Portainer Community Edition (setup below)

docs.title: Download Packages
docs.text:
Download the package for your scenario:

  1. dtaas-localhost-xx.zip for the DTaaS localhost installation, or
  2. workspace-dex-localhost-xx.zip for the Workspace localhost installation

Tip

The guide uses Linux-style paths such as /Users/username/DTaaS. On Windows use an equivalent path, for example C:\DTaaS.

docs.title: Start Portainer
docs.text:
Portainer Community Edition provides a graphical interface for managing Docker containers at https://localhost:9443.

Follow the official Portainer CE documentation or run these commands:

docker volume create portainer_data
docker run -d -p 8000:8000 -p 9443:9443 --name portainer --restart=always \
  -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock \
  -v portainer_data:/data portainer/portainer-ce:2.21.4

Open https://localhost:9443 and complete the Initial Setup to create an administrator account.

Tip

To restart Portainer later, run docker start portainer.

docs.title: 1. DTaaS Localhost
docs.text: Unzip the dtaas-localhost-xx.zip package, which contains the installation files. This scenario uses GitLab OAuth for authentication and needs a GitLab account on https://gitlab.com.

docs.title: 1.2 Create Configuration Files
docs.text:
Copy the example files:

cp config/.env.example config/.env
cp config/client.js.example config/client.js

docs.title: 1.3 Environment Variables
docs.text:
Edit config/.env:

Variable Example Description DEFAULT_USER user1 Workspace path prefix and folder name COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME dtaas Docker Compose project name

docs.title: 1.4 Client Configuration
docs.text:
This step is optional. If the localhost installation needs its own OAuth 2.0 application, follow these steps to create one. Then edit config/client.js and set the OAuth application credentials from the GitLab account:

Variable Example Description REACT_APP_CLIENT_ID (OAuth app id) GitLab OAuth application ID REACT_APP_AUTH_AUTHORITY https://gitlab.com/ OAuth authority URL

docs.title: 1.5 Create User Workspace
docs.text:
Create a workspace directory for the user set in DEFAULT_USER:

cp -R files/template files/<DEFAULT_USER>
sudo chown -R 1000:100 files/*

The logger microservice writes its events to logs/logger. Create the directory and give it to uid 1000, the user that runs the logger:

mkdir -p logs/logger
sudo chown -R 1000:1000 logs/logger

docs.title: 1.6 Create the Portainer Stack
docs.text:
1. Navigate to Stacks and click Add Stack.
  2. Name the stack, for example dtaas-localhost.
  3. Select the Upload build method.
  4. Upload the compose file (docker-compose.yml).
  5. Load the environment file (config/.env).

Tip

If the .env file is not visible, select All Files in the file explorer dialog.

Click Deploy the stack. Portainer creates a stack with this name, which looks like this:

docs.title: 1.7 Use
docs.text: Open http://localhost in a web browser and sign in with the configured GitLab credentials.

docs.title: 1.8 Limitations
docs.text: This scenario does not include the library microservice or backend forward-auth.

docs.title: 2. Workspace Localhost
docs.text:
Unzip the workspace-dex-localhost-xx.zip package, which contains the installation files.

This scenario uses Dex as a local identity provider. It needs no external account and comes with default credentials.

docs.title: 2.1 Configuration
docs.text:
Copy the example files:

cp config/.env.example config/.env
cp config/dex-config.yaml.example config/dex-config.yaml

docs.title: 2.2 Environment Variables
docs.text:
Edit config/.env:

Variable Example Description COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME dtaas Docker Compose project name DEFAULT_USER user Default user login profile for Dex

Tip

The local login users are defined in config/dex-config.yaml.

docs.title: 2.3 Create the Portainer Stack
docs.text:
1. Navigate to Stacks and click Add Stack.
  2. Name the stack, for example workspace-localhost.
  3. Select the Upload build method.
  4. Upload the compose file (docker-compose.yml).
  5. Load the environment file (config/.env).

Click Deploy the stack.

docs.title: 2.4 Use
docs.text:
Open http://localhost in a web browser. Sign in with the default Dex credentials:

  • Email: user@intocps.org
  • Password: user

docs.title: 2.5 Limitations
docs.text:
• This scenario does not include the library microservice.
  • DevOps features are not available.
  • See the custom user instructions to change the default credentials.

docs.title: References
docs.text: Image sources: Traefik logo, reactjs, gitlab

docs.title: OAuth 2.0 for Traefik Gateway
docs.text:
The Traefik gateway serves the DTaaS, and it secures every service that is part of the application. The security is based on Traefik forward-auth.

The illustration shows the docker containers and the authorisation setup.

The traefik forward-auth can use any OAuth 2.0 provider. The DTaaS uses GitLab as the authorisation provider, with the OAuth 2.0 web / server application authorisation flow.

The configuration steps are:

1. Choose GitLab Server:

  • OAuth 2.0 authorisation must be set up on a GitLab server. An on-premises GitLab installation is preferable to the commercial https://gitlab.com.
  • The GitLab Omnibus Docker can be used for this purpose.
  • The OAuth 2.0 application should be configured as an instance-wide authorization type. Select the options to generate a client secret and to make it a trusted application.

2. Determine Website Hostname:

Decide the hostname of the website before setting up OAuth 2.0 on GitLab. A self-hosted GitLab instance is recommended, because other parts of the DTaaS platform can use it too.

3. Determine Callback and Logout URLs:

For the web / server authorisation flow to function correctly, two URLs are required: a callback URL and a logout URL.

  • The callback URL tells the OAuth 2.0 provider where to redirect signed-in users. It is the landing homepage of the DTaaS platform (either http://intocps.org/_oauth/ or http://localhost/_oauth/).
  • The logout URL signs users out of GitLab and clears their authorisation in traefik forward-auth (either http://intocps.org/_oauth/logout or http://localhost/_oauth/logout). Do not enter the logout URL in the GitLab OAuth 2.0 application setup.

4. Create OAuth 2.0 Application:

The OAuth 2.0 application setup on GitLab is at Edit Profile -> Application https://gitlab.intocps.org/-/profile/applications.

When creating the OAuth 2.0 application on GitLab, select the read_user scope.

5. Copy Application Credentials:

After creating the OAuth 2.0 application, GitLab generates an application ID and a client secret. Both are long hexadecimal strings needed in the configuration files.

6. Checklist: Required Information from OAuth 2.0 Application:

The following information is needed from the OAuth 2.0 application registered on GitLab:

GitLab Variable Name Variable Name in .env of docker compose file Default Value OAuth 2.0 Provider OAUTH_URL https://gitlab.intocps.org/ Application ID OAUTH_CLIENT_ID xx Application Secret OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET xx Callback URL (to be directly entered in GitLab OAuth 2.0 registration) Forward-auth secret OAUTH_SECRET random-secret-string (password for forward-auth, can be changed to a preferred string) Scopes read_user

docs.title: Development Environment
docs.text: The developer Docker environment in developer/check/ and the server installation scenarios require traefik forward-auth.

docs.title: Configure Authorisation Rules for Traefik Forward-Auth
docs.text: The Traefik forward-auth microservice needs rules that manage authorisation for different URL paths. The rules go in the conf.server file. There are broadly three kinds of URLs:

docs.title: Public Path Without Authorisation
docs.text:
An example of a public page:

rule.noauth.action=allow
rule.noauth.rule=Path(`/public`)

Here, 'noauth' is the rule name. Change it to suit the rule; each rule needs a unique name. The 'action' property is set to "allow" to make the resource public. The 'rule' property defines the path or route to the resource.

docs.title: Common to All Users
docs.text:
To set up a page that requires GitLab OAuth 2.0 but is available to all users of the GitLab instance:

rule.all.action=auth
rule.all.rule=Path(`/common`)

The 'action' property is set to "auth", so users must sign in with GitLab OAuth 2.0 before they can access the resource.

docs.title: Selective Access
docs.text:
Selective access allows only a few users to reach a URL path. To set up selective access to a page:

rule.onlyu1.action=auth
rule.onlyu1.rule=Path(`/user1`)
rule.onlyu1.whitelist = user1@localhost

The 'whitelist' property of a rule is a comma-separated list of the email IDs allowed to access the resource. Users can still sign in with either their username or email ID, but the email ID of their account must be in the whitelist. Only the users in the whitelist can access the resource.

docs.title: User management
docs.text: Use the DTaaS CLI to add users to and remove users from a DTaaS instance.

docs.title: Limitation
docs.text: The traefik-forward-auth microservice does not reload the rules in the conf._ file. Restart traefik-forward-auth* after any change to the _conf file. The restart invalidates all existing user sessions.

docs.title: Configure Library Microservice
docs.text:
The microservice reads its configuration from a YAML file. The template configuration file is:

port: '4001'
mode: 'local' or 'git'
local-path: '/home/Desktop/files'
log-level: 'debug'
apollo-path: '/lib' or ''
graphql-playground: 'true' or 'false'

#Only needed if git mode
git-repos:
  - <username>:
      repo-url: '<git repo url>'
  ...
  - <username>:
      repo-url: '<git repo url>'

The local-path variable is the path to the local directory that the library microservice serves to users.

With graphql-playground: 'true', a browser that opens apollo-path gets GraphiQL, a web page for writing and running GraphQL queries. This is also the behaviour when the option is left out. With 'false', the microservice serves no such page and accepts only the GraphQL queries themselves.

Replace the default values with values suited to the deployment and save the configuration as a YAML file, for example libms.yaml.

docs.title: Operation Modes
docs.text: The mode sets the backend storage for the files. There are two modes, local and git. In local mode, users get the files in local-path. In git mode, the remote git repositories are cloned and served to users as local files.

docs.title: git mode
docs.text:
A fragment of the config for git mode is:

...
git-repos:
  - user1:
      repo-url: 'https://gitlab.com/dtaas/user1.git'
  - user2:
      repo-url: 'https://gitlab.com/dtaas/user2.git'
  - common:
      repo-url: 'https://gitlab.com/dtaas/common.git'

Here, user1, user2 and common are the local directories into which the remote git repositories are cloned. The repository name need not match the local directory name. For example, the above configuration makes the library microservice clone the https://gitlab.com/dtaas/user1.git repository into the user1 directory. Any git server reachable over HTTP(S) is supported. The .git suffix is optional.

Replace the default values with values suited to the deployment.

By default, libms looks for a libms.yaml file in the working directory from which it is run. To use a configuration file at another location, pass -c <path-to-file>.

The npm package page has more on using the library microservice.

docs.title: Host Library Microservice
docs.text:
The lib microservice is a simplified file manager that serves files over GraphQL and HTTP APIs. It lists directory contents and transfers files to and from users.

This page explains how to run the library microservice as a standalone docker container.

docs.title: Outside the DTaaS Platform
docs.text: The package can be used independently of the DTaaS. In this case no particular file structure is needed. A directory named files, placed in the directory from which compose.lib.yml will be run, is enough.

docs.title: Inside the DTaaS Platform
docs.text:
DTaaS users expect the following file system structure for their reusable assets.

A skeleton file structure is available in the DTaaS codebase. Copy it to create a file system for users. Name the directory files and place it in the directory from which compose.lib.yml will be run.

The container runs as uid 1000 and writes into this directory, so on Linux hosts give the directory to that user:

sudo chown -R 1000:1000 files

docs.title: Use
docs.text:
Use the docker compose file to start the service.

# To bring up the container
docker compose -f compose.lib.yml up -d
# To bring down the container
docker compose -f compose.lib.yml down

docs.title: Service Endpoints
docs.text:
The GraphQL URL: localhost:4001/lib

The HTTP URL: localhost:4001/lib/files

The service API documentation is available on user page.

docs.title: Host Library Microservice
docs.text:
The lib microservice is a simplified file manager that serves files over GraphQL and HTTP APIs. It lists directory contents, and it uploads and downloads files.

This page explains how to install the npm package of the library microservice and run it as a standalone service.

docs.title: Outside the DTaaS Platform
docs.text: The package can be used independently of the DTaaS. In this case no particular file structure is needed; any directory will do.

docs.title: Inside the DTaaS Platform
docs.text:
DTaaS users expect the following file system structure for their reusable assets.

A skeleton file structure is available in the DTaaS codebase. Copy it to create a file system for users.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
The npm package is available in GitHub packages registry and on npmjs. Prefer the package on npmjs over GitHub.

Install the package with one of the two following commands.

docs.title: npmjs
docs.text: sudo npm install -g @into-cps-association/libms  # requires no login

docs.title: GitHub
docs.text:
# requires login
sudo npm config set @into-cps-association:registry https://npm.pkg.github.com
sudo npm install -g @into-cps-association/libms

The github package registry asks for a username and password. The username is the GitHub username and the password is a GitHub personal access token with the read:packages scope.

docs.title: Use
docs.text:
Display help.

$libms -h
Usage: libms [options]

The lib microservice is a file server. It supports file transfer
over GraphQL and HTTP protocols.

Options:
  -c, --config <file>  provide the config file (default libms.yaml)
  -H, --http <file>    enable the HTTP server with the specified config
  -h, --help           display help for libms

Neither option is mandatory.

See configuration for the configuration conventions. By convention the configuration is saved in a libms.yaml file. If -c is not given, libms looks for libms.yaml in the working directory from which it is run. To run libms with that default file, run

$libms

To run libms with a custom config file,

$libms -c FILE-PATH
$libms --config FILE-PATH

If the configuration file has another name, for example libms-config.yaml, run

$libms -c "config/libms-config.yaml"

Press Ctrl+C to halt the application. To run the microservice in the background, use

$nohup libms [-c FILE-PATH] & disown

The lib microservice is now running and ready to serve files.

docs.title: Protocol Support
docs.text:
libms supports the GraphQL protocol by default. It can also serve files to a browser over HTTP. Enable this with the -H http.json flag; the sample http config can be used.

$nohup libms [-H http.json] & disown

The usual file upload and download options then become available.

docs.title: Service Endpoints
docs.text:
The GraphQL URL: localhost:PORT/lib

The HTTP URL: localhost:PORT/lib/files

The service API documentation is available on user page.

docs.title: Host Logger Microservice
docs.text:
The logger microservice ingests workflow log events produced by the DTaaS client and stores them as JSON Lines (.jsonl) files.

This page explains how to run the logger microservice as a standalone docker container.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Place a logger.yaml configuration file in the directory from which compose.logger.yml will be run. Download the sample configuration and use it as a template:

curl -o logger.yaml \
  https://raw.githubusercontent.com/INTO-CPS-Association/DTaaS/feature/distributed-demo/servers/logger/config/logger.yaml.sample

The captured events go to a logs directory in the same location. The logger runs as the node user (uid 1000), so create the directory and, on Linux hosts, give it to uid 1000:

mkdir logs
sudo chown -R 1000:1000 logs

If the logs directory does not exist, Docker creates it as root. Images before 0.1.2 cannot write into such a directory.

docs.title: Use
docs.text:
Use the docker compose file to start the service.

# To bring up the container
docker compose -f compose.logger.yml up -d
# To bring down the container
docker compose -f compose.logger.yml down

docs.title: Service Endpoints
docs.text:
The health check URL: localhost:4003/logger/health

The event ingestion URL: localhost:4003/logger

The configuration options are described in the npm package page and the service is described on the user page.

docs.title: Logger Microservice NPM Package
docs.text:
The logger microservice package is @into-cps-association/logger-ms. Install it from npmjs:

npm install -g @into-cps-association/logger-ms

Start it with logger-ms. It reads logger.yaml from the working directory if the file exists; use -c <file> to give another configuration file.

To build and start it from source instead, run these commands in servers/logger/:

yarn install
yarn build
yarn start

By default, the logger binds to 127.0.0.1:4003 and accepts unauthenticated ingest. Set LOGGER_AUTH_TOKEN for non-browser producers that can send bearer headers. The bundled browser client uses navigator.sendBeacon, which cannot set custom headers, so enforce browser ingest authentication at the reverse proxy.

For the full configuration reference, see servers/logger/README.md.

docs.title: Platform Services
docs.text:
Digital twins running inside DTaaS often need third-party services, and we recommend installing them alongside the platform. These services can only be installed in secure (TLS) mode.

The following services can be installed:

  • Influx time-series database and dashboard service
  • Grafana visualisation and dashboard service
  • RabbitMQ AMQP broker and its management interface. The MQTT plugin of this broker is enabled, so it can also be used as an MQTT broker.
  • MongoDB database server
  • ThingsBoard IoT device management and data visualisation platform (with PostgreSQL backend)
  • GitLab OAuth2 identity provider and Git repository service

docs.title: DTaaS Services CLI
docs.text: The dtaas-services command-line tool manages the DTaaS platform services: MongoDB, InfluxDB, RabbitMQ, Grafana, ThingsBoard and GitLab.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Generates a project structure with config and data directories.
  • Sets up TLS certificates and file permissions with one command.
  • Starts, stops and reports the status of all services.
  • Creates user accounts in InfluxDB, RabbitMQ, MongoDB, PostgreSQL, ThingsBoard and GitLab.
  • Runs on Linux, macOS and Windows.
  • Reads its settings from config/services.env.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Python 3.10 or higher
  • Docker and Docker Compose
  • TLS certificates

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Install the package inside a Python virtual environment:

pip install dtaas-services

This installs the dtaas-services command.

To verify the installation:

dtaas-services --help

Commands follow the form dtaas-services <noun> <verb>. The nouns are project, host, service and user, listed in the order you use them.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
1. Go to the desired setup location and generate the project structure:
dtaas-services project generate

This creates: * config for the service configuration * data, where the services store their data * log for the GitLab and ThingsBoard logs * certs for the TLS certificates the services need * compose.services.yml for the main services, including PostgreSQL * compose.thingsboard.yml for ThingsBoard * compose.gitlab.yml for GitLab

  1. Update config/services.env with the environment values:
  2. HOSTNAME: public hostname of the DTaaS server (used for certificate paths)
  3. CERTS_SRC: directory that holds the TLS certificates to copy
  4. GITLAB_PORT: port for the local GitLab instance (default: 8090)
  5. GITLAB_ROOT_NEW_PASSWORD: strong password to set for the GitLab root admin
  6. TB_SYSADMIN_NEW_PASSWORD: new password for the ThingsBoard system admin
  7. TB_TENANT_ADMIN_PASSWORD: new password for the tenant admin
  8. port numbers for each service
  9. USERID and GROUPID: user and group ID that the Grafana container runs as

  10. OAuth configuration (optional, to customise the GitLab OAuth app registrations): edit config/gitlab_oauth.json to adjust app names, redirect URIs, scopes or confidentiality settings before running dtaas-services service install -s gitlab. dtaas-services project generate creates this file. To use a different filename, set OAUTH_APPS=<filename> in config/services.env; the file is still looked up in config/.

  11. Update config/credentials.csv with user accounts (format: username,password,email).

Options:

  • --path Directory to generate the project structure in (default: current directory)
  • --force Refresh the packaged files of an existing project (see below)

Example:

dtaas-services project generate --path /path/to/project

docs.title: Refreshing an existing project
docs.text:
By default an item that already exists is skipped, so re-running the command is safe but picks up nothing new. After upgrading the package, --force refreshes the files that ship with it:

dtaas-services project generate --force

It overwrites the three compose.*.yml files and the packaged files under config/. It never touches data/, log/ or certs/, and it never overwrites these files, which are reported as kept:

  • services.env, credentials.csv, gitlab_oauth.json
  • gitlab_tokens.json, gitlab_user_tokens.json, password.env.current
  • mongod.conf.secure, rabbitmq.conf, rabbitmq.enabled_plugins

The first six hold your settings and live credentials; the last three are service configuration you may have hardened locally. Overwritten files and existing directories keep the permissions they already had, so a tightened config/ stays tightened. To adopt the packaged version of a kept file, copy it aside, delete it and run the command again.

Review the refreshed files before starting the services, and re-run dtaas-services host setup if certificate or service file permissions were affected.

docs.title: Service Setup
docs.text:
After generating the project and configuring the settings, run:

dtaas-services host setup

This command:

  • copies the TLS certificates to the correct locations
  • sets up MongoDB certificates and permissions
  • sets up InfluxDB certificates and permissions
  • sets up RabbitMQ certificates and permissions
  • sets up ThingsBoard certificates and permissions

Run the clean command right after it:

dtaas-services service clean

docs.title: Managing Services
docs.text:
The service commands start, stop, restart, remove and report the status of the services.

Example:

dtaas-services service start

To act on one service only, name it:

dtaas-services service stop -s influxdb

Remove services and their volumes:

dtaas-services service remove --volumes
# Specify
dtaas-services service remove --volumes -s <service_name>

service status prints a table by default. For scripting, --json prints a JSON array on stdout, one object per container, so services that share a container label are all listed:

dtaas-services service status --json

[
  { "service": "gitlab", "container": "gitlab", "status": "running" },
  { "service": "grafana", "container": "grafana", "status": "removed" }
]

Failures are still reported as text on stderr, so a script can read stdout only.

Note: -s accepts a comma-separated list. A selector that names no service, such as -s "" from an unset shell variable, is an error rather than a silent "all services", so a mistyped selector cannot remove or clean more than you intended. Omit the flag entirely to act on all services.

docs.title: User Account Management
docs.text:
1. Edit config/credentials.csv with user accounts (format: username,password,email).

  2. Add users to all supported services:

    dtaas-services user add

    This creates user accounts in InfluxDB, RabbitMQ, MongoDB, PostgreSQL, ThingsBoard and GitLab. A service that is not running is skipped. For GitLab, a Personal Access Token is created for each new user and saved to config/gitlab_user_tokens.json.

  3. Add users to a specific service:

    dtaas-services user add -s rabbitmq

docs.title: ThingsBoard
docs.text:
We recommend ThingsBoard for digital twins that need IoT device management. It can only be installed in secure (TLS) mode.

The ThingsBoard setup uses two services:

  • ThingsBoard, an IoT device management and data visualisation platform
  • PostgreSQL, the database server for ThingsBoard

docs.title: ThingsBoard Installation
docs.text:
Warning: Running dtaas-services service install -s thingsboard more than once re-runs the ThingsBoard schema migration against an already populated PostgreSQL database, which can corrupt it. To reinstall from scratch, first run dtaas-services service clean -s "postgres,thingsboard" to wipe all data, then re-run the install command. Note: Name the service explicitly with -s <service> when installing. Run the clean command before the installation.

# It starts PostgreSQL if it is not running, and it checks its health.
dtaas-services service install -s thingsboard

dtaas-services service start -s thingsboard

# After installation, wait some time before adding users.
# This creates the tenant, tenant admin, and users.
dtaas-services user add -s thingsboard

Reset the ThingsBoard sysadmin and tenant admin passwords to the values configured in config/services.env:

dtaas-services user reset-password -s thingsboard

This command:

  • changes the sysadmin password from the default ("sysadmin") to TB_SYSADMIN_NEW_PASSWORD
  • changes the tenant admin password from the default ("tenant") to TB_TENANT_ADMIN_PASSWORD

docs.title: GitLab Installation
docs.text:
Prerequisites:

  • The GitLab container joins the dtaas-services Docker network (platform-services in the compose files), which is created when the other platform services start. Start them first with dtaas-services service start before installing GitLab.
  • Set REACT_APP_AUTH_AUTHORITY in the client config file to https://<hostname>:<GITLAB_PORT>/gitlab.

Note: The DTaaS client uses react-oidc-context, which forces redirects to use HTTPS. GitLab must therefore be served over HTTPS at https://<hostname>:<GITLAB_PORT>/gitlab.

To install and configure the local GitLab instance:

dtaas-services service install -s gitlab

GitLab takes 5 to 10 minutes to become healthy after the first start. The install command checks GitLab readiness and returns immediately:

  • If GitLab is healthy, the command runs the post-install setup (PAT creation, OAuth app registration and root password reset) and saves the tokens to config/gitlab_tokens.json.
  • If GitLab is still starting, the command prints a status hint and exits. Check progress with dtaas-services service status -s gitlab and re-run dtaas-services service install -s gitlab once the status shows running.

Note: After a successful setup, config/gitlab_tokens.json is backed up to config/backup_gitlab_tokens.json and the root_password entry is removed from the live tokens file. If the GitLab installation becomes corrupted before the root password is changed, the initial password can be found in the backup file config/backup_gitlab_tokens.json. If that file is also missing, re-install GitLab to generate a new initial password. Warning: The CLI manages config/password.env.current, which tracks the current service passwords. Do not edit or delete this file manually; doing so may cause the password reset commands to fail.

To complete the OAuth2 integration with DTaaS and set up GitLab Runner, follow the integration guide and the runner setup guide for either Linux or Windows.

Reset the GitLab root admin password to the value configured in config/services.env (GITLAB_ROOT_NEW_PASSWORD):

dtaas-services user reset-password -s gitlab

The command reads the new password from GITLAB_ROOT_NEW_PASSWORD and applies it through the GitLab API.

docs.title: GitLab Post-Install Flow
docs.text:
The dtaas-services service install -s gitlab command performs these steps:

  1. Starts the GitLab Docker container.
  2. Checks whether GitLab is healthy.
  3. Reads the auto-generated root password from the container (/etc/gitlab/initial_root_password).
  4. Creates an initial Personal Access Token.
  5. Creates the server and client OAuth applications.
  6. Saves the root password, token and OAuth application details to config/gitlab_tokens.json.
  7. Resets the root password to GITLAB_ROOT_NEW_PASSWORD.
  8. Backs up the tokens file to config/backup_gitlab_tokens.json and removes the root password from config/gitlab_tokens.json.

docs.title: Manual Compose Operations
docs.text:
After generating a services project, you can also run the services directly with the compose files:

  • compose.services.yml
  • compose.thingsboard.yml
  • compose.gitlab.yml

Start manually:

docker compose -f compose.services.yml --env-file config/services.env up -d
docker compose -f compose.thingsboard.yml --env-file config/services.env up -d
docker compose -f compose.gitlab.yml --env-file config/services.env up -d

Stop manually:

docker compose -f compose.services.yml --env-file config/services.env down
docker compose -f compose.thingsboard.yml --env-file config/services.env down
docker compose -f compose.gitlab.yml --env-file config/services.env down

docs.text: ThingsBoard needs time to initialise after it starts. Wait before adding users or changing passwords.

docs.title: Workspace Deployment Scenarios
docs.text: Workspace deployments cover how users reach their workspaces and which identity provider signs them in.

docs.title: Available Workspace Scenarios
docs.text: Scenario Purpose Dex localhost Single-user local workspace deployment Keycloak secure server Multi-user secure server deployment with OIDC

docs.title: Writes From the Client, and Jupyter XSRF Protection
docs.text:
The Building Models page writes a converted model back into the user's library through the workspace's own Jupyter Contents API. This is the only place where the web client writes to a workspace.

The Jupyter server can guard writes with a token that it sets as the _xsrf cookie and expects echoed in an X-XSRFToken header. The workspace image DTaaS ships sets no such cookie and accepts the write. The client sends the header when the cookie is readable and leaves it out when it is not. Writes from the client depend on this deployment assumption.

On a workspace that enables the protection, the cookie is HttpOnly, so scripts cannot read it, the header is omitted and every write is refused. The page still draws the model; it converts the model again on the next visit instead of loading a stored file. The refusal is logged to the browser console, so the two cases can be told apart.

If you enable XSRF protection on a workspace and want conversions to persist, produce the .glb files outside the browser with ifc-to-glb from the ifc-utils repository. This is also the better route for a large model.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Use the workspace scenarios when you mainly need workspace authentication and per-user routes.
  • The DTaaS package deployments include the full DTaaS web platform. See localhost, secure multi-user and secure multi-user with integrated GitLab.

docs.title: Custom User
docs.text: This document explains how to change the username and password of the localhost DTaaS installation.

docs.title: Update Configuration
docs.text:
Copy config/dex-config.yaml.example to config/dex-config.yaml. Update these fields in config/dex-config.yaml:

  • email
  • hash (bcrypt hash of the chosen password)
  • username, name, preferredUsername

The Dex configuration is described in dex.md.

Edit config/.env.

Variable Example Value Explanation DEFAULT_USER 'user' Dex username set in dex-config.yaml

The username must match in both files when Dex uses its local password database:

  • In config/.env, choose DEFAULT_USER=<user>.
  • In config/dex-config.yaml, set the static user's username and preferredUsername to the same value.

This keeps the user-scoped DTaaS routes in line with the OIDC identity claims.

Changing DEFAULT_USER changes only the workspace URL route (/<DEFAULT_USER>) and the MAIN_USER of the workspace container. The workspace files still come from files/user, because docker-compose.yml mounts ./files/user at /workspace; do not rename that directory.

docs.title: Run
docs.text:
Start the application:

docker compose --env-file config/.env up -d

Stop the application:

docker compose --env-file config/.env down

docs.title: Use
docs.text:
Open http://localhost in a web browser. Sign in with the new user credentials from the Dex configuration file (config/dex-config.yaml).

All DTaaS functionality except the DevOps features is available through the single page client.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text: See https://into-cps-association.github.io/DTaaS/development/index.html for the complete documentation.

docs.text:
Scopes in local password database mode:

  • Supported: openid profile email groups offline_access
  • Not supported by the Dex local password database: read_user read_repository api

docs.text:

Traefik logo: https://www.laub-home.de/wiki/

docs.title: Dex configuration guide
docs.text: The dex-config.yaml.example file is the Dex configuration template. Copy config/dex-config.yaml.example to config/dex-config.yaml.

docs.title: Files
docs.text: • dex-config.yaml.example: template for local password database mode

docs.title: issuer
docs.text:
Set to http://localhost:5556/dex.

This must match the URL used by the web client (REACT_APP_AUTH_AUTHORITY).

docs.title: storage.type: memory
docs.text: Keeps state in memory for local development. Tokens, keys and sessions reset when the Dex container is recreated.

docs.title: web.http: 0.0.0.0:5556
docs.text: Dex listens on container port 5556.

docs.title: web.allowedOrigins: ['*']
docs.text: Permissive CORS setting for localhost development.

docs.title: staticClients
docs.text:
One client is configured:

  • id: mock
  • redirectURIs: ['http://localhost/Library']
  • public: true (no client secret, which suits a browser SPA)

docs.title: expiry.idTokens: "2h"
docs.text: ID tokens are valid for two hours.

docs.title: oauth2.skipApprovalScreen: true
docs.text: Skips the consent page during login.

docs.title: enablePasswordDB: true and staticPasswords
docs.text:
Enables Dex local user authentication with static users.

Configured user fields:

  • email: login identifier used on the Dex login screen
  • hash: bcrypt hash of the password
  • username/name/preferredUsername: identity claims returned by Dex
  • groups: included when the groups scope is requested
  • userID: stable Dex subject identifier

In dex-config.yaml.example, the sample user's password is user (bcrypt-hashed).

docs.title: Generate a bcrypt password hash
docs.text:
Use the generated value for the hash field in staticPasswords.

Install the Python dependency if needed:

python3 -m pip install bcrypt

Generate a bcrypt hash interactively:

python3 - <<'PY'
import bcrypt
import getpass

password = getpass.getpass('Password: ').encode('utf-8')
print(bcrypt.hashpw(password, bcrypt.gensalt()).decode('utf-8'))
PY

Copy the printed hash into config/dex-config.yaml as the value of hash.

docs.title: Username alignment with config/.env
docs.text:
DTaaS user-scoped routes use the DEFAULT_USER value from config/.env. DEFAULT_USER sets only the workspace URL route (/<DEFAULT_USER>) and the MAIN_USER of the workspace container. The workspace files always come from files/user: docker-compose.yml mounts ./files/user at /workspace whatever the value of DEFAULT_USER.

In local password database mode, keep these aligned:

  • config/.env: DEFAULT_USER=<user>
  • config/dex-config.yaml: set the static user's username and preferredUsername to the same <user>

This prevents path mismatches in user-scoped URLs.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
These instructions run DTaaS on localhost, served over HTTP. This installation suits a single user running DTaaS on their own computer.

Download workspace-dex-localhost-xx.zip from the latest release / pre-release page.

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
The installation setup is shown here.

A path such as /user is the URL route of that service, for example http://localhost/user.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Docker Engine v27 or later
  • Ports 80 and 5556 available on the host
  • At least 2GB RAM available

docs.title: Quick Demo
docs.text:
Run all the commands below from the extracted package directory.

Copy the example configuration files first:

cp config/.env.example config/.env
cp config/dex-config.yaml.example config/dex-config.yaml

The workspace container runs as uid 1000 and gid 100. Give it ownership of the user files it mounts:

sudo chown -R 1000:100 files

Start the demo:

docker compose --env-file config/.env up -d

Open http://localhost in a web browser and log in with the default credentials:

  • User email: user@intocps.org
  • Password: user

Stop the demo:

docker compose --env-file config/.env down

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
1. All DTaaS functionality except the DevOps features is available through the single page client.
  2. The installation has default user credentials. See the instructions for changing them.

docs.text: See https://into-cps-association.github.io/DTaaS/development/index.html for the complete documentation.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
Image sources:

Traefik logo: https://www.laub-home.de/wiki/

Dex IdP: https://dexidp.io/

docs.title: DTaaS Configuration
docs.text:
This document describes the configuration needed for the docker compose file. It has pre-install and post-install parts. Complete the pre-install tasks before bringing up the docker compose services, and the post-install tasks after.

Pre-install Configuration Tasks:

  • Environment
  • Domain
  • TLS Certificates
  • Usernames
  • Forward Auth

Post-install Configuration Tasks:

  • Keycloak Integration
  • Web Client

docs.title: Environment
docs.text:
The compose commands in the setup guides read their environment from an environment file. An example of this file is at config/.env.example.

Create a copy of this example file without the example suffix:

cp config/.env.example config/.env

docs.title: Domain
docs.text:
Decide whether the deployment is local or remote.

Wherever <DOMAIN_NAME> or intocps.org appears in this guide, replace it with the domain name of the remote machine. The remote machine must have a domain name and be reachable from the internet.

Open config/.env and replace the current value of the SERVER_DNS variable with the domain name:

# Server Configuration
# Replace with the actual domain name
SERVER_DNS=<DOMAIN_NAME>

docs.title: TLS Certificates
docs.text:
Ensure that valid TLS certificates are present on the machine. The fullchain.pem and privkey.pem files must be in the certs/ directory. Traefik reads them through config/tls.yml.

There are several ways to obtain TLS certificates. On a web server you can use Certbot from Let's Encrypt:

# Install certbot
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install certbot

# Generate certificates
sudo certbot certonly --standalone -d <DOMAIN_NAME>

# Copy certificates to the project
sudo cp /etc/letsencrypt/live/<DOMAIN_NAME>/fullchain.pem ./certs/
sudo cp /etc/letsencrypt/live/<DOMAIN_NAME>/privkey.pem ./certs/
sudo chown $USER:$USER ./certs/*.pem
chmod 644 ./certs/fullchain.pem
chmod 600 ./certs/privkey.pem

docs.title: Usernames
docs.text:
The usernames of the main workspace users are set in the environment variable file config/.env. Change the default values (user1 and user2) to the desired usernames:

# Username Configuration
# These usernames will be used as path prefixes for user workspaces
# Example: https://intocps.org/user1, https://intocps.org/user2
USERNAME1=user1
USERNAME2=user2

NOTE: These usernames must match the names of the Keycloak users used in the forward auth configuration.

docs.title: Traefik Forward Auth Configuration
docs.text:
The config/forward-auth-conf.example file contains an example configuration for the forward-auth service.

Create a copy of this example file without the example suffix:

cp config/forward-auth-conf.example config/forward-auth-conf

Then update the Traefik forward auth configuration file with the usernames and emails of the Keycloak users that correspond to user1 and user2.

rule.user1_access.action=auth
rule.user1_access.rule=PathPrefix(`/<USERNAME_USER1>`)
rule.user1_access.whitelist = <EMAIL_USER1>

rule.user2_access.action=auth
rule.user2_access.rule=PathPrefix(`/<USERNAME_USER2>`)
rule.user2_access.whitelist = <EMAIL_USER2>

NOTE: The usernames set in the Usernames configuration step must be the same as those in the Traefik forward auth configuration file.

docs.title: Keycloak Integration
docs.text:
The default docker-compose.yml uses Keycloak for authentication through OIDC (OpenID Connect). The traefik-forward-auth and DTaaS client docker services use Keycloak for authentication and authorisation. Each one needs an OAuth2 application in the integrated Keycloak service.

For detailed Keycloak setup instructions, see keycloak-setup.md

docs.title: Configure Environment Variables
docs.text:
1. Edit config/.env and fill in the Keycloak credentials:
# Keycloak Admin Credentials
KEYCLOAK_ADMIN=admin
KEYCLOAK_ADMIN_PASSWORD=changeme

# Keycloak Realm
KEYCLOAK_REALM=dtaas

# Keycloak Client Credentials (obtain from Keycloak after creating client)
KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_ID=dtaas-workspace
KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_SECRET=your_client_secret_here

# Keycloak Issuer URL
KEYCLOAK_ISSUER_URL=https://<DOMAIN_NAME>/auth/realms/<REALM>

# Secret key for encrypting OAuth session data
# Generate a random string (at least 16 characters)
# for example, using the following command
# openssl rand -base64 32
OAUTH_SECRET=your-oauth-secret

docs.title: DTaaS Web Client Config
docs.text:
The DTaaS web client is configured with a small JavaScript file. An example is at config/client.js.example.

Create a copy of this example file without the example suffix:

cp config/client.js.example config/client.js

Then edit the new web client config file and update the following values.

docs.title: Client OAuth2 Setup
docs.text:
The DTaaS web client is a React SPA that authenticates with Keycloak using the Authorization Code flow with PKCE. Follow the Create OAuth2 Client for DTaaS Client Service instructions to create the public PKCE client in Keycloak, then update config/client.js:

REACT_APP_CLIENT_ID: 'dtaas-client',          // Client ID set in Keycloak
REACT_APP_AUTH_AUTHORITY: 'https://<DOMAIN_NAME>/auth/realms/dtaas',
REACT_APP_REDIRECT_URI: 'https://<DOMAIN_NAME>/Library',
REACT_APP_LOGOUT_REDIRECT_URI: 'https://<DOMAIN_NAME>/',
REACT_APP_GITLAB_SCOPES: 'openid profile',    // OIDC scopes requested from Keycloak

openid and profile are standard OIDC scopes that Keycloak provides by default. openid is required for OIDC authentication and issues the ID token. profile adds the profile claims, including preferred_username and the profile claim mapped from the profile user attribute that Create Users sets.

The web client takes the username from the first of these claims that is present: preferred_username, username, nickname, login, the part of email before @, the part of upn before @, the last path segment of the profile URL, and sub. The profile URL is also shown as the user's profile link. The variable is named REACT_APP_GITLAB_SCOPES for historical reasons; it carries the Keycloak OIDC scopes.

Replace <DOMAIN_NAME> with the value set in the Domain section, and replace dtaas with the Keycloak realm name if you chose a different one.

docs.text:

  • Docker Compose Documentation
  • OAuth 2.0 Specification

docs.title: Workspace with Traefik, OAuth2, and TLS
docs.text: This guide explains how to deploy the workspace container with the Traefik reverse proxy, OAuth2 authentication and TLS/HTTPS support for secure multi-user deployments.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Docker Engine v27 or later
  • Docker Compose v2.x
  • Sufficient system resources (at least 1GB RAM per workspace instance)
  • Valid TLS certificates (production) or self-signed certificates (testing)
  • A domain name pointing to the server (production) or localhost (testing)

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
User Request → Traefik → Forward Auth → Keycloak (OIDC)
               ↓
         User Workspace

The docker-compose.yml file sets up:

  • Traefik reverse proxy with TLS termination (ports 80, 443) and an automatic HTTP to HTTPS redirect
  • Keycloak identity provider, served under /auth
  • OAuth2 authentication through traefik-forward-auth
  • the DTaaS web client
  • Workspace containers for each user (user1, user2) behind authentication, using the workspace image
  • Two Docker networks, dtaas-frontend and dtaas-users, which separate the frontend services from the user workspaces

docs.title: Initial Configuration
docs.text: Follow the steps in configuration.md to create a suitable configuration.

docs.title: Create Workspace Files
docs.text:
Every deployment option needs user directories for the workspace files. Create them for the USERNAME1 and USERNAME2 values set in config/.env.

# create required files
cp -R files/template files/<USERNAME1>
cp -R files/template files/<USERNAME2>
# set file permissions for use inside the container
sudo chown -R 1000:100 files

docs.title: Start Services
docs.text:
To start all services with TLS:

docker compose --env-file config/.env up -d

This:

  1. starts the Traefik reverse proxy with TLS on ports 80 (HTTP → HTTPS redirect) and 443 (HTTPS)
  2. starts Keycloak and the DTaaS web client
  3. starts the traefik-forward-auth service for OAuth2 authentication
  4. starts the workspace instances for user1 and user2, protected by authentication

docs.title: Accessing Workspaces
docs.text: Once all services are running, open the workspaces through Traefik over HTTPS:

docs.title: User Workspace (workspace)
docs.text:
• VNC Desktop: https://intocps.org/user1/tools/vnc?path=user1%2Ftools%2Fvnc%2Fwebsockify
  • VS Code: https://intocps.org/user1/tools/vscode
  • Jupyter Notebook: https://intocps.org/user1
  • Jupyter Lab: https://intocps.org/user1/lab

docs.title: Service Discovery
docs.text:
The workspace has a /services endpoint that returns a JSON list of the available services, so frontend applications can discover them.

Example: Get the service list for user1

curl https://intocps.org/user1/services

Response:

{
  "desktop": {
    "name": "Desktop",
    "description": "Virtual Desktop Environment",
    "endpoint": "tools/vnc?path=user1%2Ftools%2Fvnc%2Fwebsockify"
  },
  "vscode": {
    "name": "VS Code",
    "description": "VS Code IDE",
    "endpoint": "tools/vscode"
  },
  "notebook": {
    "name": "Jupyter Notebook",
    "description": "Jupyter Notebook",
    "endpoint": ""
  },
  "lab": {
    "name": "Jupyter Lab",
    "description": "Jupyter Lab IDE",
    "endpoint": "lab"
  }
}

The endpoint values are filled in with the username from the MAIN_USER environment variable. For user1, this variable is set from USERNAME1 in config/.env.

docs.title: Authentication Flow
docs.text:
1. The user opens a workspace URL.
  2. Traefik forwards the request to traefik-forward-auth.
  3. If the user is not authenticated, they are redirected to the OAuth2 provider.
  4. The user logs in with the OAuth2 provider.
  5. The provider redirects back with an authorisation code.
  6. traefik-forward-auth exchanges the code for a token and creates a session.
  7. The user is redirected to the original URL and gains access.

docs.title: Stopping Services
docs.text:
To stop all services:

docker compose --env-file config/.env down

To stop and remove volumes:

docker compose --env-file config/.env down -v

docs.title: Adding More Users
docs.text:
To add more workspace instances, add a new service in docker-compose.yml:

  user3:
    image: intocps/workspace:main-56c6f68
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      - MAIN_USER=${USERNAME3:-user3}
    volumes:
      - "./files/common:/workspace/common"
      - "./files/${USERNAME3:-user3}:/workspace"
    labels:
      - "traefik.enable=true"
      - "traefik.http.routers.u3.entryPoints=web-secure"
      - "traefik.http.routers.u3.rule=Host(`${SERVER_DNS:-localhost}`) && PathPrefix(`/${USERNAME3:-user3}`)"
      - "traefik.http.routers.u3.tls=true"
      - "traefik.http.routers.u3.middlewares=traefik-forward-auth"
    networks:
      - users

Add the USERNAME3 variable to config/.env:

# Username Configuration
# These usernames will be used as path prefixes for user workspaces
# Example: https://intocps.org/user1, https://intocps.org/user2
USERNAME1=user1
USERNAME2=user2
USERNAME3=user3 # <--- replace "user3" with your desired username

Add a Forward Auth rule for user3 to config/forward-auth-conf:

rule.user3_access.action=auth
rule.user3_access.rule=PathPrefix(`/user3`)
rule.user3_access.whitelist = user3@localhost

The username and email must match the workspace user.

Create the user's directory:

cp -r files/template files/<USERNAME3>
sudo chown -R 1000:100 files/<USERNAME3>

Bring up the user workspace:

docker compose --env-file config/.env up -d --force-recreate user3

docs.title: Certificate Issues
docs.text:
Problem: "NET::ERR_CERT_INVALID" in the browser

Solutions:

  • Verify that the certificate files exist in the ./certs/ directory
  • Check the certificate file permissions
  • Ensure that config/tls.yml references the correct certificate paths
  • For self-signed certificates, add a security exception in the browser

docs.title: OAuth2 Issues
docs.text:
Problem: Redirect loop after OAuth2 login

Solutions:

  • Verify that the OAuth2 callback URL matches https://intocps.org/_oauth
  • Check that the SERVER_DNS environment variable is set correctly
  • Ensure that SERVER_DNS is correct (COOKIE_DOMAIN is derived from it)
  • Verify that the OAuth2 application is approved and active

docs.title: Port Conflicts
docs.text:
Problem: Ports 80 or 443 already in use

Solutions:

  • Check for other services: sudo netstat -tlnp | grep -E ':(80|443)'
  • Stop conflicting services
  • Or change the port mappings in the compose file (not recommended for production)

docs.text:

  • OAuth 2.0 Specification

docs.title: Install
docs.text: This guide explains how to deploy the workspace application for secure multi-user deployments with Keycloak for authentication.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Docker Engine v27 or later
  • Sufficient system resources (at least 2GB RAM per workspace instance)
  • Ports 80 and 443 available on the host
  • Valid TLS certificates
  • A domain name pointing to the server

Download workspace-keycloak-production-xx.zip from the latest release / pre-release page.

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
The installation setup is shown here.

A path such as /user1 is the URL route of that service, for example https://intocps.org/user1. The thick arrow is the forward-auth check: Traefik asks traefik-forward-auth to authorise each request before it routes it.

docs.text:

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Follow the pre-installation steps in configuration.md to create a valid configuration.

Start the application:

docker compose --env-file config/.env up -d

docs.title: Temporary Issues
docs.text:
The following startup issues are expected at this stage and go away after the post-installation steps:

  • The traefik-forward-auth service keeps restarting.
  • Visiting https://intocps.org shows HTTP ERROR 500.

Now complete the post-installation steps in configuration.md, then restart traefik-forward-auth:

docker compose --env-file config/.env up -d --force-recreate traefik-forward-auth

The application is now available at https://intocps.org. Log in with the user credentials set in Keycloak.

Stop the application:

docker compose --env-file config/.env down

To stop and remove volumes:

docker compose --env-file config/.env down -v
