docs.title: Keycloak Setup Guide for DTaaS
docs.text: This guide explains how to configure Keycloak for authentication in the DTaaS workspace deployment.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Keycloak uses the OIDC/OAuth2 standards and supports single sign-on, multi-factor authentication and user federation. The deployment is configured through environment variables.

The configuration uses:

  • Keycloak as the identity provider (IdP) with OIDC support
  • Traefik Forward Auth to protect routes using OIDC
  • Traefik as the reverse proxy

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
User Request → Traefik → Forward Auth → Keycloak (OIDC)
               ↓
         Protected Service

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text: This guide uses either <DOMAIN_NAME> or intocps.org as a placeholder for the server hostname of the installation.

docs.title: 1. Configure Environment Variables
docs.text:
The Keycloak-specific environment variables are:

Variable Purpose Example KEYCLOAK_ADMIN Admin username admin KEYCLOAK_ADMIN_PASSWORD Admin password changeme KEYCLOAK_REALM Realm name dtaas KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_ID OIDC client ID dtaas-workspace KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_SECRET OIDC client secret <from-Keycloak> KEYCLOAK_ISSUER_URL OIDC issuer URL https://intocps.org/auth/realms/dtaas

KEYCLOAK_REALM is informational: docker-compose.yml does not use it. The realm that DTaaS uses is the one named at the end of KEYCLOAK_ISSUER_URL (/realms/<realm>).

Edit the Keycloak configuration in config/.env:

# Keycloak Admin Credentials (for initial setup)
KEYCLOAK_ADMIN=admin
KEYCLOAK_ADMIN_PASSWORD=changeme

# Keycloak Realm (informational; the realm in KEYCLOAK_ISSUER_URL is used)
KEYCLOAK_REALM=dtaas

# Keycloak Client Configuration (will be created in post-install step)
KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_ID=dtaas-workspace
KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_SECRET=<generated-secret>

docs.title: 2. Configure Keycloak
docs.text: The following instructions are part of the post-install step.

docs.title: Access Keycloak Admin Console
docs.text:
1. Go to https://intocps.org/auth
  2. Click Administration Console
  3. Log in with the credentials from the config/.env file (default: admin / changeme)

docs.title: Create a Realm
docs.text:
1. In the top-left dropdown (currently showing "Master"), click Create Realm
  2. Realm name: dtaas (or match the realm named in KEYCLOAK_ISSUER_URL in config/.env)
  3. Click Create
  4. Click Realm Settings -> User Profile
  5. Click Create attribute with
  6. name: profile
  7. display name: profile
  8. Permission: who can edit selected on admin
  9. Click Create

docs.title: Create Users
docs.text:
1. In the left sidebar, click Users
  2. Click Create new user
  3. Fill in the user details:
  4. Username: user1 (or the desired username)
  5. Email: the user's email
  6. First name / Last name: required
  7. Email verified: OFF
  8. Profile: https://intocps.org/auth/realms/dtaas/<USERNAME> The profile URL is the <REACT_APP_AUTH_AUTHORITY> URL from client.js with /<USERNAME> appended
  9. Click Create
  10. Set a password:
  11. Go to the Credentials tab
  12. Click Set password
  13. Enter a password
  14. Temporary: OFF (so users do not have to change it on first login)
  15. Click Save
  16. Repeat for additional users (e.g., user2)

docs.title: Create OAuth2 Client for Traefik Forward-Auth Service
docs.text:
1. In the left sidebar, click Clients
  2. Click Create client
  3. Configure the client:
  4. Client type: OpenID Connect
  5. Client ID: dtaas-workspace (match KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_ID in config/.env)
  6. Click Next
  7. Capability config:
  8. Client authentication: ON
  9. Authorization: OFF
  10. Authentication flow: enable Standard flow
  11. Click Next
  12. Login settings:
  13. Root URL: https://intocps.org
  14. Valid redirect URIs:
    • https://intocps.org/_oauth/*
    • https://intocps.org/*
  15. Valid post logout redirect URIs: https://intocps.org/*
  16. Web origins: https://intocps.org
  17. Click Save
  18. Get the client secret:
  19. Go to the Credentials tab
  20. Copy the Client secret value
  21. Update KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_SECRET in the config/.env file

docs.title: Create OAuth2 Client for DTaaS Client Service
docs.text:
The DTaaS web client is a React single-page application (SPA) that uses the Authorization Code flow with PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange). It needs a public client (no client secret) with PKCE enforced.

  1. In the left sidebar, click Clients
  2. Click Create client
  3. Configure the client:
  4. Client type: OpenID Connect
  5. Client ID: dtaas-client
  6. Click Next
  7. Capability config:
  8. Client authentication: OFF (public client, no secret needed)
  9. Authorization: OFF
  10. Authentication flow: enable Standard flow only
  11. Click Next
  12. Login settings:
  13. Root URL: https://intocps.org
  14. Valid redirect URIs: https://intocps.org/*
  15. Valid post logout redirect URIs: https://intocps.org/*
  16. Web origins: https://intocps.org
  17. Click Save
  18. Enforce PKCE:
  19. Go to the Advanced tab of the client
  20. Under Advanced Settings, set Proof Key for Code Exchange Code Challenge Method to S256
  21. Click Save
  22. Verify scopes:
  23. Go to the Client Scopes tab of the client
  24. Confirm that profile is listed as an assigned scope

docs.title: 3. Restart Services
docs.text:
After configuring Keycloak, restart the services to apply the new client secret:

docker compose --env-file config/.env down
docker compose --env-file config/.env up -d

docs.title: 4. Test Authentication
docs.text:
1. Go to https://intocps.org
  2. The browser should redirect to the Keycloak login page
  3. Log in with one of the created users
  4. The browser should redirect back to the DTaaS landing page

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
To use an external Keycloak instance (recommended for production):

  1. Update KEYCLOAK_ISSUER_URL in config/.env:
KEYCLOAK_ISSUER_URL=https://keycloak.intocps.org/auth/realms/dtaas
  1. Update the client redirect URIs in Keycloak to use the production domain.

docs.title: Secure Credentials
docs.text:
• Change the default Keycloak admin password
  • Use strong client secrets
  • Store secrets securely (Docker secrets or external secret managers)
  • Rotate secrets regularly

docs.title: Database Backend
docs.text:
For production, configure Keycloak with a database such as PostgreSQL or MySQL:

keycloak:
  environment:
   - KC_DB=postgres
   - KC_DB_URL=jdbc:postgresql://postgres:5432/keycloak
   - KC_DB_USERNAME=keycloak
   - KC_DB_PASSWORD=secure_password

docs.title: Cannot Access Keycloak Admin Console
docs.text:
• Ensure that the Keycloak service is running: docker compose --env-file config/.env ps
  • Check the Keycloak logs: docker compose --env-file config/.env logs keycloak
  • Verify that ports 80 and 443 are reachable

docs.title: Authentication Loop/Redirect Issues
docs.text:
• Verify that KEYCLOAK_ISSUER_URL contains the correct realm name
  • Ensure that the redirect URIs in the Keycloak client include /_oauth/*
  • Confirm that SERVER_DNS is correct (COOKIE_DOMAIN is derived from it)
  • Clear the browser cookies and retry

docs.title: "Invalid Client" Error
docs.text:
• Verify that KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_ID matches the client ID in Keycloak
  • Ensure that KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_SECRET is correct
  • Confirm that client authentication is enabled for the client

docs.title: Forward Auth Not Working
docs.text:
• Check the traefik-forward-auth logs: docker compose --env-file config/.env logs traefik-forward-auth
  • Verify that the environment variables are set correctly
  • Ensure that Keycloak is reachable from the traefik-forward-auth container

docs.title: Custom Claims and Scopes
docs.text:
To access custom user attributes:

  1. In Keycloak, create client scopes with mappers
  2. Assign the scopes to the client
  3. Configure traefik-forward-auth to request the additional scopes

docs.title: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)
docs.text: Keycloak supports RBAC, but the traefik-forward-auth service does not use it by default.

docs.title: Single Sign-On (SSO)
docs.text: Keycloak supports SSO across multiple applications. Configure additional clients for other services as needed.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Keycloak Documentation
  • Traefik Forward Auth
  • OIDC Specification

docs.title: DTaaS Brand Assets
docs.text: The product mark, the two lockups, and the colours, in the formats a person actually asks for. Everything here is generated from one description of the geometry, so a change to the mark cannot leave one variant behind.

docs.title: What the Mark Is
docs.text:
One figure, built on one side and drawn on the other. A twin is one thing in two states, so the mark is one body and not two.

The drawn half is a continuous outline and not a dashed one. A dash breaks into specks at the sixteen pixels a browser tab gives it, which was checked by rendering and not assumed.

The primary form carries its own field. That is how the university uses colour: au.dk puts the AU logo white on a solid blue header, its cards are solid blue with white text, and a secondary colour appears as a whole block. Nowhere does it put a secondary colour as a hairline on white, which is also where that colour fails the three to one contrast floor. A mark with its own ground works on a light page and a dark one, which is why there is no separate light form.

docs.title: Which File to Use
docs.text: You want Use To place it in a diagram or a slide dtaas-brand.drawio, one page per variant Anything on the web, at any size the .svg files A fixed size, or a tool that cannot read SVG png/, seven sizes for the mark and four heights for each lockup A favicon dtaas-mark.svg, which is what both mkdocs configs use. client/public/favicon.svg is the application's own copy of the same geometry A documentation page header dtaas-logo-full-192h.png#only-light and dtaas-logo-full-white-192h.png#only-dark, two images in a row, so the page shows the one that suits the reader's colour scheme. The two files are copies of the ones in png/, written beside each page by the update-docs-diagrams skill A README in an installation package under deploy/ The copies of dtaas-logo-full.svg and dtaas-logo-full-white.svg in that package folder, with #gh-light-mode-only and #gh-dark-mode-only. A package is downloaded on its own, so it keeps its own copies. Copy them again after a change to the lockups

docs.title: The Variants
docs.text:
Three forms, each in three colourways.

Form File When Mark alone dtaas-mark*.svg A tab, an avatar, anywhere under about 48 px where a wordmark would be unreadable Mark with DTaaS dtaas-logo*.svg A toolbar, a README header, a slide footer Mark with Digital Twin as a Service dtaas-logo-full*.svg A title slide, a poster, the first time a reader meets the product Colourway Suffix What it is On Primary none The figure on its own navy field, white with a cyan drawn half Anything. It brings its own ground White -white The figure alone, white with a cyan drawn half, no field A photograph or a coloured block that is already the ground Mono -mono The figure alone, one colour, no field One colour printing, a fax, an engraving

The field is #002546, the navy the university's own site uses for a solid block. It appears ninety times in cdn.au.dk/2016/assets/css/app.css, as text and as background, where AU blue appears thirteen. The drawn half is #37a0cb, the cyan of the secondary palette, which is read on that navy and never on white.

docs.title: The Colours
docs.text:
These are the values in client/src/theme/tokens.ts, and that file is the source of truth. They are repeated here so a designer opening this folder does not have to read TypeScript.

Name Value What it is Primary #003d73 AU blue, Pantone 287, RGB 0 61 115, as the university publishes it Primary dark #002546 The navy the university's own site uses for a solid field, and the mark's ground Mark accent #37a0cb The cyan of the secondary palette, on the mark's drawn half Primary tint #eaf1fb Behind a selected row or a quiet panel Accent #00aba4 The turquoise of the secondary palette

The palette is also the last page of the drawio file, as swatches.

docs.title: Rebuilding
docs.text:
The SVG files are the source. The PNG files and the drawio file are built from them, so edit the generator and never the output.

The two Python files are one-shot generators. They resolve their output from their own location, so they can be run from anywhere, and they read the colours from client/src/theme/tokens.ts instead of repeating them, so there is one place to change a colour and not two. They are not part of the application and are not covered by its checks.

render_png.py takes the Chrome or Chromium binary from CHROME and falls back to the usual paths on macOS and on Linux, so it runs in CI as well as here. It prints which binary it used.

Run all three, in this order, from anywhere. Each resolves its paths from its own location.

python3 docs/assets/brand/build_brand.py    # the SVG variants
python3 docs/assets/brand/build_drawio.py   # the drawio file
python3 docs/assets/brand/render_png.py

The PNG files are rasterised with headless Chrome, which resolves the same font stack a browser would, so the wordmark matches what the site shows. A browser that cannot resolve the image writes a blank file and exits zero, so the script checks the size of every file it writes and stops on the first empty one.

docs.title: Where It Is Already Used
docs.text:
Changing the mark changes these, so check them after a rebuild.

Where File The documentation site header mkdocs.yml, mkdocs-github.yml, logo: The documentation site tab the same files, favicon: The PDF export cover mkdocs.yml, cover_logo: The landing page of the published site docs/redirect-page.html, the white mark beside the name in text, and the mark as its tab icon, copied to the site root by script/docs/pages.py The application toolbar client/src/components/BrandMark.tsx, which carries the geometry inline The application tab client/public/favicon.svg

The last two are separate copies of the same geometry, on purpose: a component takes its colour from the theme and a browser tab has no theme to take it from.

docs.title: Which File Is Portable, And Which Is Not
docs.text:
This is the one caveat in the kit, and it decides which file to hand somebody.

File Portable? dtaas-mark*.svg Yes, with no conditions. It carries no text png/* Yes, with no conditions. The text is already pixels dtaas-logo*.svg and dtaas-logo-full*.svg Only where Inter is installed

The lockup SVG files carry their wordmark as a <text> element and not as outlines, and their viewBox is computed from Inter's metrics. On a machine without Inter the wordmark falls back to another face and no longer fits that box. Converting the text to outlines needs a font tool this project does not carry, and the fonts on this machine are licensed to the university and not to the association.

So: a web page that loads Inter, or this application, can use the lockup SVG. Anything else, a slide, a poster, a document, a partner's site, takes the PNG. If a resolution-independent lockup is needed outside those contexts, that is a font-tooling task and it is not done here.

docs.title: If the Drawio File Opens Empty
docs.text: The page content has to be an <mxGraphModel> element inside each <diagram>, and not a string assigned to its text. Written as text, every angle bracket is escaped and draw.io opens a file it can parse and a drawing it cannot find. After any change to the generator, open the result and look at it.

docs.title: Diagrams
docs.text:
The architecture and installation diagrams of the documentation, drawn in the colours of the interface theme. dtaas-diagrams.drawio is the source, with one diagram per page, and the PNG files in the documentation are exported from it.

The scripts that make and export the file are the update-docs-diagrams agent skill, in .agents/skills/update-docs-diagrams/. Its SKILL.md gives the steps, and every command below runs from the repository root.

docs.title: Pages
docs.text:
A page named after a path under docs/ is exported to that path. The other pages are diagrams the documentation does not show yet, kept so they can be placed later.

docs.title: Light and Dark Variants
docs.text:
Every page under docs/ is exported twice, except a page in LIGHT_ONLY. write_dark in design/dark.py turns each light fill, including the white drawio draws when a shape names none, into the slate page of the site with a fifth of its own colour, so tints keep their hue. Dark lines and dark stencil icons become light, text takes the light or the dark text colour by contrast with its new fill, and the DTaaS lockup and the GitLab logo become their white versions. The traefik and Docker logos have no white version, so they are drawn unchanged on a light plate, listed in DARK_LETTERING. An embedded SVG whose every colour falls below 3 to 1 on slate, such as the navy wind turbines, is redrawn in the light line colour. Text drawn in the colour of its ground stays hidden, as it is in the light image. The pages show the pair with #only-light and #only-dark, and the PDF prints the light one.

The export stops when a cell of a placed page has text below 4.5 to 1 or a line or border below 3 to 1 in the dark variant, unless the cell is listed in CONTRAST_EXCEPTIONS in config/pages.py with its reason. The list is empty: every dark image meets both minimums.

A page listed in LIGHT_ONLY in config/pages.py gets no dark variant, and the reason for each is written beside it there. Its image is exported on an opaque white page, so the slate scheme shows it as it is, on white.

docs.title: Layout Check
docs.text:
Before it draws anything, the export checks every placed page as drawio draws it, from the SVG drawio exports for that page, and stops on a problem not listed in LAYOUT_EXCEPTIONS in config/pages.py. diagrams.py check runs the same checks without writing images. The rules, in the layout/ package of the scripts:

  • A connector runs in horizontal and vertical segments.
  • Two connectors do not meet a box at one point from different sides. Branches of one trunk, which leave a box together, are allowed.
  • A connector does not pass behind a box that is not one of its ends.
  • A label fits in its box, and loose text crosses no border, covers no picture and sits on no line unless its background masks it.

The connectors and the place of every label come from the SVG, so a path is checked where drawio routes it. The width of a label is estimated from the advance widths of Inter, and the rules leave a few percent of margin for the kerning the estimate leaves out. A turned label is not checked.

Pages drawn free hand are listed in FREE_FORM, where only the label rules apply: architecture.png and current-status-developer.png, a hub with spokes and curves, the two OAuth sequence diagrams, whose messages cross the lifelines, and author.png, a flow drawn along a diagonal. The lines of the network pictogram inside Communication are listed in LAYOUT_EXCEPTIONS.

docs.title: Design Rules
docs.text:
Every page follows the rules of docs/assets/brand/README.md, with sizes taken from the width the documentation shows an image at. The restyle step applies them and can be run again on its own output without changing anything.

  • Lines, arrows and borders are primary #003d73 or grey 700 #333b4c. The turquoise and cyan of the palette, and the tints, are only fills, because as a line on white they stay under the three to one contrast floor.
  • A heavy arrow in primary marks the main path of a page: the forward-auth check on the installation pages, the flows between twins and services in federated-dtaas.png, and the platform links in architecture.png and devops.png. Every other arrow is grey 700 at the normal width.
  • Text is Inter, never italic, bold only for a title, and at least 4.5 to 1 on its fill. A fill drawn see-through is replaced by the solid colour it shows.
  • Every label is at least 14 pixels when the image is shown 700 pixels wide, the narrowest content column of the site. A wide diagram therefore needs larger fonts in drawio units than a narrow one.
  • The label of a box is in Title Case, with the short joining words inside a line (of, and, to, with) in lower case. The label of a connector, a UML guard and a note on a sequence diagram state a relation or a condition, so they read as a sentence ("May have", "User login verified"). A URL, a path, a name with an underscore or an inner capital keeps its case. GitLab, WebApp and Node.js have one spelling, and systemd and authcode stay lower case. title_case and sentence_case in design/wording.py hold the rules.
  • A label background only masks a line, in the colour of what lies behind it: the fill of the smallest box holding both ends of the connector, or the page. A label inside its own shape has no background, so it never shows as a white patch on a coloured box. label_ground in design/masks.py holds the rule.
  • One forward-auth box, one corner radius and one line width for every box, one style for every arrow, and one icon per idea:
Idea Icon A person mxgraph.ios7.icons.user The web application mxgraph.ios7.icons.globe Docker img/lib/mscae/Docker.svg GitLab the official logo in the skill's assets/ A physical or digital twin mxgraph.signs.transportation.car_3 and mxgraph.ios7.icons.home A twin that is running mxgraph.signs.sports.running

A UML diagram keeps its stick figure and a C4 diagram its person, since they belong to the notation. A product logo, such as Traefik or Keycloak, stays its owner's.

  • A note about the picture is page text and not part of the picture.
  • The DTaaS mark sits at the top right corner of the DTaaS boundary, the largest box of the page, which also gets the thicker boundary line. A page that already shows the full lockup as its title gets no second mark. A page in NO_MARK gets neither: its largest box is drawn like every other box.

docs.title: Updating a Diagram
docs.text:
1. Open dtaas-diagrams.drawio in drawio and edit the page.
  2. Apply the rules and shrink any new raster logo. The restyle undoes the hand edits listed in hand-edits.md, so run it on a copy that holds only the new or changed page and bring that page back:
python3 .agents/skills/update-docs-diagrams/scripts/diagrams.py restyle \
  docs/assets/diagrams/dtaas-diagrams.drawio \
  docs/assets/diagrams/dtaas-diagrams.drawio
uv run --with-requirements .agents/skills/update-docs-diagrams/scripts/requirements.txt python .agents/skills/update-docs-diagrams/scripts/diagrams.py shrink \
  docs/assets/diagrams/dtaas-diagrams.drawio \
  docs/assets/diagrams/dtaas-diagrams.drawio
  1. Export every page to its place in the documentation:
python3 .agents/skills/update-docs-diagrams/scripts/diagrams.py export

The export needs the drawio desktop application. It finds it through DRAWIO, then drawio on the PATH, as on Linux, then its install place on macOS and Windows. On a Linux machine without a display, run the command under xvfb-run -a. On Windows, run python in place of python3. Every image is 1600 pixels wide, twice the widest content column.

  1. Open every exported image and check that nothing overlaps. The scripts set colours, fonts and sizes, and a larger font can need a box moved by hand.

The export draws text with the fonts installed on the machine. Install Inter first, or drawio falls back to another face without a warning. The diagrams use two weights, 400 and 700, and the documentation site already carries both as woff2 in docs/assets/fonts. fonttools turns each into a font the system can install:

for weight in 400 700; do
  uv run --with-requirements .agents/skills/update-docs-diagrams/scripts/requirements.txt \
    fonttools ttLib.woff2 decompress -o "Inter-$weight.ttf" \
    "docs/assets/fonts/inter-latin-$weight-normal.woff2"
done

Copy the two files to ~/Library/Fonts on macOS or ~/.local/share/fonts on Linux. On Windows, make the two files in PowerShell, then open each one and choose Install:

foreach ($weight in 400, 700) { uv run --with-requirements .agents/skills/update-docs-diagrams/scripts/requirements.txt fonttools ttLib.woff2 decompress -o "Inter-$weight.ttf" "docs/assets/fonts/inter-latin-$weight-normal.woff2" }

docs.title: How the File Was Made
docs.text:
The file was converted once from a drawio file that held every installation diagram on a single page, in the drawio default colours. The steps that did it are kept so the conversion can be repeated on a later version of that file:

python3 .agents/skills/update-docs-diagrams/scripts/diagrams.py retheme original.drawio themed.drawio
python3 .agents/skills/update-docs-diagrams/scripts/diagrams.py split themed.drawio split.drawio
python3 .agents/skills/update-docs-diagrams/scripts/diagrams.py restyle split.drawio styled.drawio
uv run --with-requirements .agents/skills/update-docs-diagrams/scripts/requirements.txt python .agents/skills/update-docs-diagrams/scripts/diagrams.py shrink \
  styled.drawio dtaas-diagrams.drawio

The steps that take files on the command line accept only .drawio files under the current directory.

retheme maps each colour to a colour of the theme, through the COLOURS table of config/theme.py, which reads the brand colours from client/src/theme/tokens.ts, and replaces the old wordmark with the logo in docs/assets/brand. split gives each diagram its own page. restyle applies the design rules above. shrink scales every embedded raster logo down to the pixels the export draws, turns a JPEG into a PNG with a transparent background, and stores each logo with a palette, which took the file from 3.5 MB to about 750 KB.

Every edit made by hand after a step, page by page, is recorded in hand-edits.md. A restyle run on a whole page undoes them, which is why the restyle runs on new or changed pages only.

docs.title: Hand Edits to the Diagrams
docs.text:
The edits made by hand in drawio after a step of the .agents/skills/update-docs-diagrams skill, page by page. The rules and the steps are in README.md.

These edits were made by hand in drawio, because each one concerns a single page and a script for it would be longer than the change:

  • The pages were renamed after the image each one replaces.
  • /lib instead of /libms, /user1 on user workspace 1, and intocps.org instead of intocps.com, as the compose files in deploy/ have them.
  • The service at / is Client on every page, the name of the client service in every compose file.
  • admin/gitlab/gitlab-integrated-install.png, admin/gitlab/gitlab-integrated-runner.png and admin/gitlab/gitlab-independent-install.png gained the Logger at /logger, which the secure server packages route. On the independent page Server 2 became narrower so the page stays under 600 units wide, where 12-unit text is still 14 pixels.
  • The WebApp picture, a bitmap with its label drawn in another typeface, is the drawio globe icon with an Inter label.
  • Labels were moved clear of lines and frames after the switch to Inter, which is wider than Helvetica. Route labels such as /logger and /auth sit between two connector lines with space on both sides, and the server tags moved left of the DTaaS mark with a clear gap.
  • developer/system/multi-domain.png was laid out again so its labels fit at 25 drawio units: the columns are wider, compose, configuration and execution are rows instead of rotated columns, and the label of each stack of cards is on the card in front.
  • A Storage box hidden under the Dashboard of the Generic column of the multi-domain page was removed. It drew nothing.

The pages the documentation does not show follow the same rules, but they were not checked label by label for overlaps.

docs.text:
Fifteen more pages bring every diagram of the examples to the theme. docs.title: Contributors Guide
docs.text: This guide describes how to contribute to the Digital Twin as a Service (DTaaS) project, from opening an issue to creating a pull request (PR), review and merge. Please read the Code of Conduct before contributing.

docs.title: Project Goals
docs.text:
The DTaaS platform supports the creation, management and execution of Digital Twins (DTs) through a service-oriented architecture that promotes reuse of DT assets [1]. This documentation explains the software design and development processes of the project to members of the development team.

Additional resources:

  • Developer Slides
  • Developer Overview Video
  • DTaaS DevOps Workflows
  • Research Paper

Codebase Overview maps the directories of the monorepo.

docs.title: Development Environment
docs.text: The recommended development setup is the devcontainer defined in .devcontainer/devcontainer.json. It runs the containerised environment from developer/devenv/, which holds every toolchain needed to build and test the projects. Reopen in Container runs developer/devenv/init.sh on the host first. Outside VS Code, run that script once and follow developer/devenv/README.md.

docs.title: Development Workflow
docs.text:
Contributors follow this procedure:

  1. Fork the main repository into a personal GitHub account.
  2. Configure Qlty, Codecov and SonarQube for the fork. Codecov does not need a secret token for public repositories.
  3. Use Node.js 26 and Python 3.14.
  4. Follow the Fork, Branch, PR workflow.
  5. Develop in the fork and open a PR from the working branch to the feature/distributed-demo branch of the fork. The PR triggers the GitHub Actions, Qlty, SonarQube and Codecov checks.
  6. Fix every issue the automated checks report.
  7. Once the checks pass, open a PR to the feature/distributed-demo branch of the upstream DTaaS repository.
  8. Project administrators or maintainers review and merge the PR.

Each PR should either satisfy a well-defined user story or improve code quality.

Local Testing lists the build and test commands to run before opening a PR.

docs.title: Coding Agents and Editors
docs.text:
The project makes extensive use of coding agents. The primary usage scenarios include:

  • Co-development assistance
  • Code review support
  • Draft pull requests for prototyping ideas

Every coding agent reads the same instructions: AGENTS.md for the general coding guidelines and PROJECT.md for the repository-specific ones. Task-specific instructions are Agent Skills in .agents/skills/. Coding Agents describes these files and the available skills.

Contributors should disclose code generated by coding agents, particularly when such code embeds significant programming logic.

The following practices are strictly prohibited:

  • Contributing unknown or unreviewed code
  • Failing to understand the implications of generated code

Summary: Contributors must fully understand their contributions and should not delegate critical thinking to coding agents.

docs.title: Code Quality
docs.text:
Code quality is checked by:

  • Static Analysis: Qlty reports linting issues. Install the Qlty CLI and run qlty check --no-fail --sample 5 --no-formatters to list them locally. Qlty analyses only the files that differ from the default branch (feature/distributed-demo).
  • Security Scans: SonarQube reports code quality and security issues.
  • Test Coverage: Codecov collects coverage reports.
  • Continuous Integration: every GitHub Actions workflow must pass.

docs.title: Qlty
docs.text:
Qlty performs static analysis, linting and style checks.

New issues appear on the PR page. The issues and code sections of the Qlty dashboard list the rest.

Qlty Cloud skips pull requests opened from forks, because GitHub withholds its token from them. The Qlty workflow (.github/workflows/qlty.yml) runs the Qlty CLI on every pull request instead. It fails on new actionlint findings in changed workflows, and reports dependency advisories (osv-scanner) and code smells in the job log and summary without failing.

Contributions should not introduce new quality issues. Fix any that appear, using the suggestions from Qlty. Add an ignore flag only in exceptional cases.

docs.title: Codecov
docs.text: Codecov tracks test coverage for the whole project. The testing documentation describes the testing practices and workflows.

docs.title: GitHub Actions
docs.text: The project defines several GitHub Actions workflows. Every pull request and direct commit must pass all of them. Secrets for GitHub Actions lists the secrets and variables a fork needs for the publishing jobs.

docs.title: References
docs.text: [1] Talasila, Prasad, et al. "Composable digital twins on Digital Twin as a Service platform." Simulation 101.3 (2025): 287-311.

docs.title: Vagrant Deployment
docs.text: This page summarises the Vagrant setup in this repository. The full instructions are in deploy/vagrant/README.md.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: The Vagrant setup installs DTaaS in a virtual machine, so it runs on any operating system that supports Vagrant. The same machine can serve as a reproducible development and evaluation environment.

docs.title: Host Requirements
docs.text:
Recommended host capacity:

  • 16 GB RAM
  • 8 vCPUs
  • 50 GB available disk space

Required tooling:

  • Vagrant
  • vagrant-disksize plugin

docs.title: Provisioning Modes
docs.text:
deploy/vagrant has two provisioning scripts:

  • user.sh for the user installation (default)
  • developer.sh for additional developer tooling

To enable developer provisioning, uncomment the developer.sh line in deploy/vagrant/Vagrantfile. Vagrant may time out while provisioning both scripts; in that case, run developer.sh from inside the virtual machine.

docs.title: Basic Workflow
docs.text:
Run the following from the deploy/vagrant directory:

vagrant up
vagrant ssh
sudo bash /vagrant/route.sh

route.sh sets a cron job inside the virtual machine that removes the conflicting default route.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: The file deploy/vagrant/config.json sets the hostname, MAC address, disk size, VM name, memory and number of CPUs of the virtual machine.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• DTaaS installation scenarios
  • DTaaS package deployments: docs/admin/dtaas/
  • Workspace deployments
  • Platform services

docs.title: Codebase Overview
docs.text: DTaaS is a monorepo. It holds the web client, the backend services, shared libraries, deployment packages, admin tooling, documentation and release scripts.

docs.title: Top-level layout
docs.text:
DTaaS/
├── .agents/skills/        # Agent Skills for coding agents
├── .claude/skills/        # Claude Code stubs for the skills
├── .github/               # Workflows, issue templates, Dependabot configuration
├── cli/                   # Python admin CLI package
├── client/                # React and TypeScript frontend
├── deploy/                # Scenario-based deployment packages and services CLI
├── developer/             # Development container and Docker workflow
├── docs/                  # MkDocs source documentation
├── lib/                   # Shared libraries
│   ├── dt-automation/     # Digital twin automation npm package
│   └── gitlab_common/     # GitLab Python library for the CLIs
├── script/                # Automation for docs, environment setup, and releases
└── servers/               # Backend services
    ├── execution/runner/  # Runner microservice
    ├── lib/               # Library microservice
    └── logger/            # Logger microservice

docs.title: Directory roles
docs.text: Directory Purpose .agents/ Agent Skills; see Coding Agents. cli/ Python package for administrative user and workspace operations. client/ Main DTaaS web application with route, store, model, and test layers. deploy/ Installable DTaaS, workspace, runner, and platform-services packages. developer/ The devenv development container and the check Docker workflow. docs/ Documentation source used by mkdocs.yml and mkdocs-github.yml. lib/ The dt-automation npm package and the gitlab_common Python library. script/ Helper scripts for docs publishing, environment setup, and release tasks. servers/ NestJS services: the library, runner and logger microservices. .github/ CI workflows, repository templates and Dependabot configuration.

docs.title: Codebase entry points
docs.text:
The pages in this section follow the parts of the monorepo:

  • Client for the React frontend structure and test commands.
  • DevOps Framework and Client DevOps Integration for GitLab-backed digital twin lifecycle flows.
  • DTaaS CLI for the Python admin CLI package.
  • DTaaS Services for the platform-services provisioning CLI.
  • Library Microservice and Runner Microservice for backend service implementation details.
  • Publish Packages for package-release workflows.

The logger microservice (servers/logger/) has no page in this section yet. Its design notes are in servers/logger/ARCHITECTURE.md and servers/logger/DEVELOPER.md.

docs.title: Agent and automation files
docs.text:
Coding agents read AGENTS.md, which holds the general coding guidelines, and PROJECT.md, which holds the build and test commands, verification steps, shipping cycle and pull request checks specific to this repository. CLAUDE.md imports both for Claude Code.

Task-specific instructions are Agent Skills in .agents/skills/, with a stub for each in .claude/skills/ for Claude Code. .github/copilot-instructions.md points GitHub Copilot to AGENTS.md and PROJECT.md. See Coding Agents.

docs.title: Command Line Interface
docs.text:
The Command Line Interface (CLI) lets administrators manage a DTaaS installation from the shell. It covers the whole deployment lifecycle: generating and validating the configuration, generating deployment files for each supported scenario, installing and uninstalling a deployment, updating certificates and configuration in place, and adding, removing, pausing and resuming users.

The user guide is the admin CLI page, and the full command reference is in cli/README.md. This page describes the internal structure for contributors.

docs.title: Command Surface
docs.text:
Every command follows the grammar dtaas <noun> <verb>. The four nouns are listed in workflow order.

dtaas
├── config
│   ├── generate                  # write dtaas.toml + users.csv
│   ├── validate                  # check dtaas.toml, report all errors
│   └── reconcile                 # report or fix registry drift
├── deployment
│   └── generate --type X         # generate a deployment package
├── platform
│   ├── install                   # docker compose up of a deployment
│   ├── uninstall                 # tear down (optionally user files)
│   ├── update                    # --certs and/or --config, in place
│   ├── status                    # state of the installation
│   ├── stop / start              # core services only
│   └── pause / resume            # core services only
└── user
    ├── add                       # provision user workspaces
    ├── delete                    # deprovision user workspaces
    ├── status                    # state of additional users
    └── pause / stop / resume     # suspend or resume single users

docs.title: Package Structure
docs.text:
The CLI package is organised as follows:

cli/
├── src/                          # Application source code
│   ├── __init__.py               # Package initialization
│   ├── cmd.py                    # Root 'dtaas' group, wires the nouns
│   ├── cmd_config.py             # 'config' commands
│   ├── cmd_deployment.py         # 'deployment' commands
│   ├── cmd_platform.py           # 'platform install/uninstall/update'
│   ├── cmd_lifecycle.py          # 'platform status/stop/start/...'
│   ├── cmd_user.py               # 'user add/delete/status'
│   ├── cmd_user_lifecycle.py     # 'user pause/stop/resume'
│   ├── cmd_options.py            # Shared Click options
│   ├── cmd_utils.py              # Shared command helpers
│   ├── cmd_user_utils.py         # User input resolution
│   ├── cmd_user_emails.py        # Emails given but not applied
│   ├── cmd_user_passwords.py     # Initial GitLab passwords
│   ├── cmd_deploy_utils.py       # Deployment command helpers
│   ├── pkg/                      # Implementation modules
│   │   ├── build.py              # Vendors shared code into src/
│   │   ├── certs.py              # Certificate placement
│   │   ├── cert_update.py        # In-place certificate rotation
│   │   ├── cert_validate.py      # Certificate pair validation
│   │   ├── config.py             # dtaas.toml parsing and access
│   │   ├── config_update.py      # In-place configuration re-apply
│   │   ├── config_validate.py    # Configuration validation rules
│   │   ├── config_validate_gitlab.py # [gitlab] validation rules
│   │   ├── constants.py          # Constant definitions
│   │   ├── deploy.py             # Install/uninstall orchestration
│   │   ├── deploy_config.py      # Scenario configuration mapping
│   │   ├── _deploy_data.py       # Per-scenario substitution specs
│   │   ├── gitlab/               # Optional GitLab user provisioning
│   │   ├── lifecycle.py          # Platform status/stop/start/pause
│   │   ├── messages.py           # Shape of user command output
│   │   ├── project.py            # Template copying for 'generate'
│   │   ├── registry.py           # User registry (JSON)
│   │   ├── registry_csv.py       # users.csv parsing
│   │   ├── state.py              # Runtime state cache
│   │   ├── user_files.py         # User file cleanup on uninstall
│   │   ├── users.py              # User add handler
│   │   ├── users_compose.py      # Per-user compose generation
│   │   ├── users_delete.py       # User delete handler
│   │   ├── users_gitlab.py       # GitLab account and token setup
│   │   ├── users_gitlab_records.py # Saved tokens and markers
│   │   ├── users_gitlab_targets.py # Users to provision in GitLab
│   │   ├── users_lifecycle.py    # Per-user pause/stop/resume
│   │   ├── users_utils.py        # User management helpers
│   │   ├── utils.py              # File I/O and utilities
│   │   └── validators.py         # Shared validation helpers
│   └── templates/                # dtaas.toml, users.csv and compose
│       └── ...                   # templates for user workspaces
├── tests/                        # Test suites and fixtures
├── pyproject.toml                # Poetry project configuration
└── README.md                     # Command reference

docs.title: Architecture and Design
docs.text:
The CLI is a Python package that uses the Click framework for command parsing. Each noun is a Click group in its own cmd_<noun>.py module, and cmd.py attaches the groups to the root dtaas group. Command modules parse options, load and validate the configuration, and call functions in pkg/. Docker operations go through python-on-whales.

dtaas.toml is the single source of truth. Every command reads it through the Config class in pkg/config.py, and platform update --config re-applies it to an installed deployment so that the deployment does not drift from it.

The CLI also keeps two files of its own. dtaas.users.registry.json (pkg/registry.py) records the additional users added with user add, and .dtaas.state.json (pkg/state.py) caches what is known about the provisioned user containers.

GitLab account provisioning in pkg/gitlab/ is built on the gitlab_common library. src/pkg/build.py vendors it from lib/gitlab_common/ into the source tree, so run it before running the tests:

poetry run python src/pkg/build.py && poetry run pytest

docs.title: Main Modules
docs.text: Module Purpose cmd.py Root group; attaches the four noun groups cmd_user.py User add/delete/status command definitions pkg/config*.py TOML parsing, validation, in-place updates pkg/project.py Template copying (config generate, deployment generate) pkg/deploy.py Install/uninstall orchestration pkg/lifecycle.py Platform status, stop, start, pause, resume pkg/cert_*.py Certificate validation and rotation pkg/users*.py User workspace lifecycle pkg/registry.py Registry of additional users pkg/state.py Runtime state of user containers pkg/utils.py YAML/TOML I/O, template substitution

docs.title: Sequence Diagram
docs.text:
The following diagram shows how dtaas user add provisions a user:

sequenceDiagram
    actor Admin
    participant CLI as Click CLI
    participant Config as pkg/config.py
    participant Registry as pkg/registry.py
    participant Users as pkg/users.py
    participant Utils as pkg/utils.py
    participant Docker as Docker Compose
    participant FS as File System

    Admin ->> CLI: dtaas user add alice --email ...
    activate CLI

    CLI ->> Config: Config()
    activate Config
    Config ->> Utils: import_toml("dtaas.toml")
    Utils -->> Config: config data
    deactivate Config

    CLI ->> Registry: stage the new user
    CLI ->> Users: add_users(config_obj, start_only, passwords)
    activate Users

    Users ->> Registry: load_registry()
    Registry -->> Users: user list

    Users ->> Config: get_server_dns() / get_path()
    Config -->> Users: server DNS, installation path

    Users ->> Config: get_resource_limits() / get_tls()
    Config -->> Users: resource limits, TLS setting

    Users ->> FS: Copy workspace files for each user
    Users ->> Users: generate compose service entries

    Users ->> Utils: export_yaml(compose)
    Utils ->> FS: Write user compose file

    Users ->> Docker: docker compose up -d (new users only)
    Docker -->> Users: Containers started

    Users -->> CLI: None (success)
    deactivate Users

    CLI -->> Admin: "Users added successfully"
    deactivate CLI

docs.title: Error Handling Pattern
docs.text:
The CLI handles errors in two ways:

  1. Most modules under src/pkg/ raise exceptions.
  2. config.py and utils.py return (result, Exception | None) pairs, and callers check the error before using the result.

The command modules turn both kinds of error into click.ClickException, so the user sees a short message instead of a traceback. Test commands with Click's CliRunner rather than subprocess.

docs.title: Resource Limits Configuration
docs.text:
Administrators can limit the resources each user container may use, so that one user cannot take over a shared server. The limits are set in the [common.resources] section of dtaas.toml. The set_limits flag turns enforcement on and off. When it is false, user containers are created without limits and the other fields are ignored. The defaults come from the dtaas.toml template:

Parameter Description Default cpus CPU core allocation 4 mem_limit Memory limit 4G pids_limit Maximum process count 4960 shm_size Shared memory size 512m

docs.title: Client DevOps Integration
docs.text: This page describes how the React client manages digital twins through GitLab.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
The DevOps integration in the client:

  • discovers Digital Twin and library assets in GitLab repositories,
  • creates, updates and deletes DT files,
  • triggers and stops CI/CD pipeline executions,
  • collects pipeline status and logs for the execution views.

docs.title: Current Module Map
docs.text:
The implementation lives in lib/dt-automation/src/:

  • gitlab/backend.ts: GitlabAPI, the concrete BackendAPI implementation.
  • gitlab/instance.ts: GitlabInstance, which holds the project context and trigger token.
  • gitlab/execution/: pipeline polling, status checks and log fetching.
  • digitalTwin.ts: DT lifecycle operations and execution hooks.
  • DTAssets.ts, fileHandler.ts, libraryAsset.ts, libraryManager.ts: file and asset management primitives.
  • util/digitalTwinPipelineExecution.ts: start and stop execution paths.
  • util/digitalTwinExecutionHistory.ts: execution history and log updates.
  • state/: Redux state for execution history and status views.
  • interfaces/backendInterfaces.ts: backend contracts and shared types.

docs.title: Architectural Roles
docs.text:
Context, API access and DT domain behaviour sit in separate classes.

  • GitlabAPI calls the GitLab REST API through @gitbeaker/rest (files, pipelines, groups and projects, jobs, logs, multi-action commits).
  • GitlabInstance resolves projectId and commonProjectId, retrieves the trigger token and exposes accessors for execution data.
  • DigitalTwin combines DT asset and file operations with pipeline execution and execution-history updates.
  • DTAssets, LibraryAsset, LibraryManager and FileHandler handle low-level file and repository interactions.

UI code therefore does not depend on GitLab implementation details.

docs.title: Execution Flow
docs.text:
1. A session creates and initializes GitlabInstance.
  2. The UI performs DT actions through DigitalTwin and the backend utility modules.
  3. Pipeline start and stop calls go through GitlabInstance and GitlabAPI.
  4. Status polling and job log fetching update the execution history state.
  5. UI components render current and past execution results.

docs.title: File Operations and Commit Strategy
docs.text:
The client supports both per-file operations and batched commits.

  • Single-file operations use createRepositoryFile, editRepositoryFile and removeRepositoryFile.
  • Multi-file updates should use commitMultipleActions to produce one commit when scaffolding or reconfiguring a DT.

A batched commit keeps a lifecycle update atomic and avoids a long trail of single-file commits.

docs.title: Main Contracts
docs.text:
The BackendAPI contract includes:

  • pipeline trigger, cancel and status,
  • pipeline job listing and job log retrieval,
  • repository file create, read, update and delete, and tree listing,
  • group and project discovery,
  • multi-action commits (commitMultipleActions).

When extending DevOps behaviour, update the interface contracts first, then the GitLab implementation and its call sites.

docs.title: Contributor Guidance
docs.text:
• Keep GitLab-specific details inside lib/dt-automation/src/gitlab/.
  • Keep route and page components focused on presentation and user interaction.
  • Reuse the utility and state modules for execution history instead of adding ad hoc polling to UI components.
  • Add or update unit and integration tests when changing backend contracts.

docs.title: React Client
docs.text: The DTaaS web client is a React and TypeScript single page application. Users compose digital twins, browse assets, edit configuration and run digital twins through GitLab pipelines from it.

docs.title: Current Stack
docs.text:
• React 19
  • React Router 7
  • Redux Toolkit 2
  • Material UI 9
  • Vite 8 for the development server and production build
  • Gitbeaker REST client for GitLab APIs
  • Jest 30 and React Testing Library for unit and integration tests, Playwright for end-to-end tests

docs.title: Current Source Layout
docs.text:
client/
├── src/
│   ├── index.tsx
│   ├── AppProvider.tsx
│   ├── routes.tsx
│   ├── components/
│   ├── database/
│   ├── page/
│   ├── route/
│   ├── store/
│   ├── theme/
│   ├── util/
│   └── utils/
├── test/
│   ├── __mocks__/
│   ├── unit/
│   ├── integration/
│   └── e2e/
├── config/
├── public/
├── index.html
├── vite.config.ts
└── package.json

The route/ directory holds one folder per page, including bim/ for the Building Models page. The Material UI theme and design tokens live in theme/.

The shared backend package lives under lib/dt-automation/ and the client consumes it from npm as @into-cps-association/dt-automation. The Building Models page comes from @into-cps-association/bim-kit, which is maintained in the ifc-utils repository. Client Extensions describes both packages and the proposed extension architecture.

docs.title: Backend Integration Layer
docs.text:
The dt-automation package wraps the GitLab-backed operations.

The main classes are:

  • GitlabAPI: low-level GitLab REST wrapper.
  • GitlabInstance: project and trigger-token context.
  • DigitalTwin: DT-level operations and execution history integration.
  • LibraryAsset: access to reusable library assets.

commitMultipleActions batches file updates, so one commit can carry several create, update and delete operations.

docs.title: Build and Test Commands
docs.text:
Run from client/:

yarn syntax
yarn build
yarn config:test
yarn test:unit
yarn test:int
yarn test:e2e

Use the test:unit and test:int scripts rather than bare jest. The scripts pass --setupFilesAfterEnv, which installs the react-redux mock that many tests need.

docs.title: Notes for Contributors
docs.text:
• Keep GitLab-specific logic in backend implementation modules.
  • Keep route and view components focused on presentation and user workflows.
  • Prefer typed interfaces in lib/dt-automation/src/interfaces/ when extending API contracts.

docs.title: DevOps Framework
docs.text:
The DevOps framework lets the DTaaS client manage the lifecycle of a Digital Twin through the GitLab API and GitLab CI/CD pipelines. With it the client:

  • discovers DT definitions and reusable assets in repositories,
  • creates and updates DT files in Git repositories,
  • triggers pipelines that execute DTs,
  • collects pipeline and job status and logs to show in the UI.

docs.title: Where the Code Lives
docs.text:
The code is in lib/dt-automation/src/. The main modules are:

  • gitlab/backend.ts: GitLab API wrapper.
  • gitlab/instance.ts: backend session and project context.
  • digitalTwin.ts: DT-level operations and execution tracking.
  • interfaces/backendInterfaces.ts: backend contracts and API shapes.
  • util/: execution history and file-management helpers.

Client DevOps Integration describes these modules in more detail.

docs.title: GitLab API Support
docs.text:
The GitLab backend implementation supports:

  • pipeline trigger and cancellation,
  • repository file create, edit and delete operations,
  • group and project discovery,
  • pipeline job listing and log retrieval,
  • pipeline status polling,
  • batching several file changes into one commit with commitMultipleActions.

With the batched commit, the user sees DT creation or an update as one atomic change.

docs.title: Execution Flow
docs.text:
1. GitlabInstance resolves the project IDs and the trigger token.
  2. The UI operation calls DT logic in DigitalTwin.
  3. DigitalTwin uses the backend APIs to prepare files and trigger the pipeline.
  4. The execution history is updated and shown in the UI.
  5. Job logs and statuses are fetched and rendered for diagnosis.

docs.title: Pipeline Contract
docs.text: The client triggers pipelines with two variables: DTName, the selected digital twin, and RunnerTag, the tag of the GitLab runner that should execute it. The GitLab CI pipelines must read these variables so that each DT runs on the intended runner.

docs.title: Practical Guidance
docs.text:
• Prefer backend interface methods over ad hoc API calls in UI code.
  • Use the batched commit method when updating several files.
  • Keep execution history updates in the utility modules so that status reporting stays consistent.

docs.title: DTaaS Services Codebase
docs.text: This page describes the code of the dtaas-services CLI, which sets up and runs the DTaaS platform services.

docs.title: Location and Purpose
docs.text:
Source package:

  • deploy/services/cli

The CLI:

  • generates a services project structure that is ready to run,
  • sets up certificates and service permissions,
  • installs, starts, stops, restarts, removes and cleans service containers,
  • runs the post-start setup for ThingsBoard and GitLab,
  • creates users and resets service passwords from the CSV and environment configuration.

docs.title: Runtime Command Surface
docs.text:
Every command follows the grammar dtaas-services <noun> <verb>. The entry point is dtaas_services/cmd.py, which registers the nouns in install order:

  • project generate
  • host setup
  • service install, service start, service stop, service restart, service status, service remove, service clean
  • user add
  • user reset-password

The old top-level spellings (generate-project, setup, start and so on) are registered by commands/aliases.py. They print a deprecation warning and forward to the <noun> <verb> command.

Poetry script mapping (pyproject.toml):

[tool.poetry.scripts]
dtaas-services = "dtaas_services.cmd:services"

docs.title: Command Layer
docs.text:
The files in dtaas_services/commands/ define the Click commands and the high-level flows:

  • project_ops.py: project scaffold generation (project generate).
  • host_ops.py: TLS certificate and permission setup (host setup).
  • service_ops.py: the service verbs (install, start, stop, restart, status, remove, clean).
  • install_helpers.py: selector validation and the ThingsBoard and GitLab install flows used by service install.
  • user_ops.py: user provisioning and password reset.
  • aliases.py: deprecated top-level spellings that warn and forward to their <noun> <verb> replacement.

docs.title: Core Library Layer
docs.text:
The files in dtaas_services/pkg/ hold reusable logic:

  • config.py: environment and configuration loading.
  • template.py: project scaffolding and template copying.
  • force_overwrite.py: what project generate --force may replace, what it must never replace, and copies that preserve permissions.
  • cert.py: certificate placement and normalization.
  • password_store.py: tracks the current admin password of each supported service.
  • lib/*: compose command execution and service state management.

docs.title: Service Modules Layer
docs.text:
dtaas_services/pkg/services/ implements service-specific behaviour:

  • gitlab/: health checks, root password setup, PAT creation, OAuth application setup and GitLab user provisioning.
  • thingsboard/: setup, sysadmin and tenant workflows, and user setup from the credentials file.
  • influxdb/, rabbitmq.py, mongodb.py, postgres/: permissions, readiness checks and account bootstrap routines.

docs.title: Shared GitLab Layer
docs.text:
gitlab_common holds GitLab operations that do not depend on the deployment (get_gitlab_client, validate_user_row, create_user, create_user_pat, revoke_user_pats, with_hint). Every function takes explicit arguments and changes no environment, filesystem, console or process-global state.

Its single source of truth is lib/gitlab_common/, a standalone Poetry package with its own tests. Each consumer copies it into its own tree instead of depending on it:

lib/gitlab_common/gitlab_common/     <-- edit and test here
| copied by dtaas_services/pkg/build.py |
        v
dtaas_services/gitlab_common/        <-- gitignored, never committed

Run poetry run python -m dtaas_services.pkg.build before testing or packaging. CI does this through run-build-script: true. It is a plain script, not a Poetry build hook, because a hook makes poetry-core emit a platform-specific wheel instead of py3-none-any. Copying the code instead of using a path dependency keeps dtaas-services and the DTaaS CLI independent of each other. It also keeps local paths out of the published wheel metadata, which PyPI rejects.

Deployment-specific glue stays in pkg/services/gitlab/: URL derivation from GITLAB_PORT and HOSTNAME, token-file persistence, docker health checks and Rich console output. Two consequences are deliberate:

  • pkg/services/gitlab/_api.py suppresses urllib3's InsecureRequestWarning when SSL_VERIFY=false. gitlab_common does not, so importing the shared module never silences warnings for unrelated consumers.
  • gitlab_common defaults Personal Access Tokens to least-privilege repository-only scopes. pkg/services/gitlab/users.py asks for the broader api scope explicitly through PatOptions.

docs.title: Configuration Inputs
docs.text:
A generated project is driven by:

  • config/services.env: ports, hostnames, SSL behaviour and service credentials.
  • config/credentials.csv: user list (username,password,email).
  • TLS certificates copied into the generated certs/ layout.

The main GitLab-related environment variables are HOSTNAME, GITLAB_PORT, SSL_VERIFY and GITLAB_ROOT_NEW_PASSWORD.

docs.title: Typical Workflow
docs.text:
1. Generate project files:
  2. dtaas-services project generate
  3. Edit configuration:
  4. config/services.env
  5. config/credentials.csv
  6. Set up certs and permissions:
  7. dtaas-services host setup
  8. Start selected services:
  9. dtaas-services service start [-s ...]
  10. Run post-install setup where needed:
  11. dtaas-services service install -s thingsboard
  12. dtaas-services service install -s gitlab
  13. Provision users:
  14. dtaas-services user add

docs.title: Testing and Quality
docs.text:
The package uses pytest with strict markers, and test discovery starts in deploy/services/cli/tests.

Run the checks from deploy/services/cli:

poetry install
poetry run python -m dtaas_services.pkg.build
CI=true poetry run pytest --ignore=tests/system_tests

The build step vendors gitlab_common; without it the tests cannot be collected. The CLI checks for root before it validates arguments, so a non-root run needs CI=true. The tests in tests/system_tests call docker and are excluded here.

docs.title: Contributor Notes
docs.text:
• Keep command modules thin and put business logic in pkg/.
  • Add service-specific behaviour in pkg/services/<service>/ or peer modules, not in generic command handlers.
  • Commands should print messages the user can act on, and should not leave partial side effects without reporting them.
  • When adding service operations, include tests under tests/test_services and command-level tests under tests/test_commands.

docs.title: Library Microservice
docs.text:
The Library Microservice gives access to workspace files in two ways: a GraphQL API, and an HTTP file server that users can open in a web browser. It reads files from the local file system or from GitLab, and its API follows the GitLab GraphQL API. Both users and digital twins use it to reach the reusable assets in the platform library.

Warning

This microservice is still under heavy development. It is not yet a satisfactory replacement for the file server currently in use.

docs.title: Architecture and Design
docs.text: The microservice is built with the NestJS framework and Apollo GraphQL. It uses the Strategy pattern: a factory picks one of several file storage backends (local file system or GitLab). The GraphQL API of the library microservice is meant to be compatible with the GitLab GraphQL service.

docs.text:

├── src/                           # Application source code
│   ├── main.ts                    # Application entry point

docs.title: GraphQL Resolver
docs.text:
The FilesResolver class exposes two GraphQL queries:

Query Purpose listDirectory Returns directory contents (files and folders) readFile Returns file content as raw text

docs.title: File Service Interface
docs.text:
The IFilesService interface defines the contract for all file backends:

interface IFilesService {
  listDirectory(path: string): Promise<Project>;
  readFile(path: string): Promise<Project>;
  getMode(): CONFIG_MODE;
  init(): Promise<any>;
}

docs.title: Backend Implementations
docs.text: Backend Purpose LocalFilesService Accesses files from local filesystem GitFilesService Accesses files from GitLab repository

docs.title: Factory Pattern
docs.text: FilesServiceFactory.create() picks the backend whose getMode() matches the mode setting in the configuration file (local or git). files.module.ts calls it once, when NestJS builds the FILE_SERVICE provider, and the resolver receives the chosen service through dependency injection. An unknown mode stops the service with an Invalid MODE error.

docs.title: Class Diagram
docs.text:
classDiagram
    class FilesResolver {
    -filesService: IFilesService
    +listDirectory(path: string): Promise<Project>
    +readFile(path: string): Promise<Project>
    }

    class FilesServiceFactory {
    +create(configService: IConfig, fileServices: IFilesService[]): IFilesService$
    }

    class LocalFilesService {
    -configService: Config
    -dataPath: string
    -getFileStats(fullPath: string, file: string): Promise<Project>$
    +listDirectory(path: string): Promise<Project>
    +readFile(path: string): Promise<Project>
    }

    class Config {
    +getMode(): string
    +getLocalPath(): string
    }

    class IFilesService{
    listDirectory(path: string): Promise<Project>
    readFile(path: string): Promise<Project>
    }

    IFilesService <|-- FilesResolver: uses
    IFilesService <|.. LocalFilesService: implements
    IFilesService <|-- FilesServiceFactory: creates
    Config <|-- FilesServiceFactory: uses
    Config <|-- LocalFilesService: uses

docs.title: Sequence Diagram
docs.text:
The factory has already chosen LocalFilesService at startup, so a request goes straight from the resolver to the backend.

sequenceDiagram
    actor Client
    actor Traefik

    box LightGreen Library Microservice
    participant FR as FilesResolver
    participant IFS as IFilesService
    participant LFS as LocalFilesService
    end

    participant FS as Local File System DB

    Client ->> Traefik : HTTP request
    Traefik ->> FR : GraphQL query
    activate FR

    FR ->> IFS : listDirectory(path) or readFile(path)
    activate IFS

    IFS ->> LFS : listDirectory(path) or readFile(path)
    activate LFS

    LFS ->> FS : Access filesystem under the configured local path
    alt Filesystem error
        FS -->> LFS : Filesystem error
        LFS ->> LFS : Throw new InternalServerErrorException
        LFS -->> IFS : Error
    else Successful file operation
        FS -->> LFS : Return filesystem data
        LFS ->> IFS : return Promise<Project>
    end
    deactivate LFS

    alt Error thrown
    IFS ->> FR : return Error
    FR ->> Traefik : return Error
    Traefik ->> Client : HTTP error response
    else Successful operation
    IFS ->> FR : return Promise<Project>
    FR ->> Traefik : return Promise<Project>
    Traefik ->> Client : HTTP response
    end
    deactivate IFS

    deactivate FR

docs.title: Build and Test
docs.text:
Run from servers/lib/:

yarn build && yarn test:all

yarn test:nocov also runs test/cloudcmd, which needs a configured .env and a running libms under pm2.

docs.title: Publish Packages
docs.text: DTaaS is a monorepo that publishes npm packages, Docker images, Python packages and installation packages.

docs.title: Package Channels
docs.text:
• npm packages (public): @into-cps-association/*, published to both GitHub Packages and the npm registry
  • Docker images: GitHub Container Registry and Docker Hub
  • Python packages: the DTaaS CLI and the platform-services CLI on PyPI
  • Installation packages: zip files attached to each GitHub release by the Release Packages workflow

docs.title: JavaScript/TypeScript Packages
docs.text:
The package roots are:

  • servers/lib -> @into-cps-association/libms
  • servers/execution/runner -> @into-cps-association/runner
  • servers/logger -> @into-cps-association/logger-ms
  • lib/dt-automation -> @into-cps-association/dt-automation
  • client -> @into-cps-association/dtaas-web, which is published as a Docker image rather than an npm package

The workflow of each package (lib-ms.yml, runner.yml, logger-ms.yml and dt-automation.yml) first runs the lint, build and test jobs. It then calls the reusable publish-npm.yml workflow once for GitHub Packages and once for the npm registry. publish-npm.yml runs yarn install, yarn build and yarn publish --access public with the registry token passed in as the NPM_TOKEN secret.

Publishing happens on a push or manual run on the feature/distributed-demo branch. The logger workflow also publishes from any feature/* or release-v* branch.

The dt-automation workflow also checks the tarball contents and installs the packed tarball into an empty project before publishing.

docs.title: Private Registry Workflow (Development)
docs.text:
Use a private registry such as Verdaccio to test publish and unpublish behaviour before a public release.

A typical local flow:

docker run -d --name verdaccio -p 4873:4873 verdaccio/verdaccio
npm adduser --registry http://localhost:4873
npm set registry http://localhost:4873/

docs.title: Docker Artifacts
docs.text:
All Dockerfiles for the published images live in developer/check/. The reusable workflows docker-build.yml, docker-ghcr.yml and docker-dockerhub.yml build them. The client.yml, lib-ms.yml and logger-ms.yml workflows publish the dtaas-web, libms and logger-ms images for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64. Each platform is built on a native runner and pushed by digest; a final job tags one multi-platform manifest that points at both. Deployment-level compose definitions are under deploy/.

When changing runtime dependencies, check that the images build and the deployment scenarios start before tagging a release.

docs.title: Python Packages
docs.text:
Two Poetry-based CLIs are published to PyPI:

  • cli (dtaas), by the CLI for DTaaS workflow (python-cli.yml)
  • deploy/services/cli (dtaas-services), by the Platform Services CLI workflow (platform-services-cli.yml)

Both call the reusable python-reusable.yml workflow for tests and builds, and publish on a push or manual run on the feature/distributed-demo branch. The lib/gitlab_common library is tested by the gitlab-common.yml workflow and is not published on its own.

Use Poetry for versioning and keep the lock files up to date so that builds are reproducible.

docs.title: Installation Packages
docs.text:
The installation packages attached to each GitHub release are built by the Release Packages workflow (.github/workflows/release-packages.yml) with script/release-packages.sh. Each package is <package>-<version>.zip, holding every tracked file of its source directory under deploy/dtaas/docker/ or deploy/workspace/.

The workflow builds and verifies the packages whenever deploy/dtaas/, deploy/workspace/, the script or the workflow changes, and keeps them for two days as one release-packages artifact of the workflow run. Publishing a GitHub release also attaches them to the release. Do not edit or re-zip them by hand; change the source directory instead.

To build and check the packages locally:

git lfs install --local
git lfs pull --include="deploy/dtaas/**,deploy/workspace/**"
script/release-packages.sh build dev dist
script/release-packages.sh verify dev dist

git lfs install --local sets up the Git LFS filters. Without them, the fetched images look like uncommitted changes and the script refuses to build.

To replace the packages of an existing release, check out its tag, build the packages with the script from the default branch into a fresh directory and upload them:

git switch --detach v1.0
git lfs install --local
git lfs pull --include="deploy/dtaas/**,deploy/workspace/**"
git show origin/feature/distributed-demo:script/release-packages.sh > /tmp/release-packages.sh
rm -rf dist-1.0
bash /tmp/release-packages.sh build 1.0 dist-1.0
bash /tmp/release-packages.sh verify 1.0 dist-1.0
gh release upload v1.0 dist-1.0/*-1.0.zip --clobber --repo INTO-CPS-Association/DTaaS

--clobber replaces only assets with the same name. Releases up to v1.0 carry packages without a version in their name, such as dtaas-localhost.zip, so delete those after the upload:

for name in dtaas-localhost dtaas-server dtaas-secure-server \
  dtaas-secure-server-integrated-gitlab workspace-dex-localhost \
  workspace-keycloak-production; do
  gh release delete-asset v1.0 "$name.zip" --yes --repo INTO-CPS-Association/DTaaS
done

docs.title: Release Guidance
docs.text:
• Bump versions deliberately, and only for the packages that changed.
  • Prefer the automated CI publishing where it exists.
  • After publishing, install the package and run it once to check that it works.

docs.title: Runner Microservice
docs.text: The Runner microservice executes scripts for digital twins in the DTaaS platform. It accepts HTTP requests to run pre-configured commands and returns the execution status and logs to the caller.

docs.text:
servers/execution/runner/
├── src/                           # Application source code
│   ├── main.ts                    # Application entry point
│   ├── app.module.ts              # Root NestJS module
│   ├── app.controller.ts          # REST API controller
│   ├── execa-manager.service.ts   # Command execution manager
│   ├── execa-runner.ts            # Command runner implementation
│   ├── queue.service.ts           # Command queue service
│   ├── runner-factory.service.ts  # Runner instance factory
│   ├── validation.pipe.ts         # Request validation pipe
│   ├── config/                    # Configuration module
│   │   ├── commander.ts           # CLI argument parsing
│   │   ├── config.interface.ts    # Configuration interface
│   │   ├── configuration.service.ts  # Configuration service
│   │   └── util.ts                # Configuration utilities
