docs.title: Architecture and Design
docs.text: The microservice is built with the NestJS framework and runs commands with the execa library. A queue holds the execution requests, and a factory creates the runner instances.

docs.title: Core Components
docs.text:
classDiagram
    class AppController {
        -manager: ExecaManager
        +getHistory(): ExecuteCommandDto[]
        +newCommand(dto): void
        +cmdStatus(): CommandStatus
    }

    class ExecaManager {
        -commandQueue: Queue
        -config: Config
        +newCommand(name): [boolean, Map]
        +checkStatus(): CommandStatus
        +checkHistory(): ExecuteCommandDto[]
    }

    class Queue {
        -queue: Command[]
        +enqueue(command): void
        +checkHistory(): ExecuteCommandDto[]
        +activeCommand(): Command
    }

    class RunnerFactory {
        +create(command): Runner
    }

    class ExecaRunner {
        -command: string
        -stdout: string
        -stderr: string
        +run(): Promise~boolean~
        +checkLogs(): Map
    }

    class Config {
        -configValues: ConfigValues
        +loadConfig(options): void
        +permitCommands(): string[]
        +getPort(): number
        +getLocation(): string
    }

    AppController --> ExecaManager : uses
    ExecaManager --> Queue : uses
    ExecaManager --> Config : uses
    ExecaManager --> RunnerFactory : uses
    RunnerFactory --> ExecaRunner : creates

docs.title: REST API Controller
docs.text:
The AppController exposes three endpoints:

Endpoint Method Purpose / POST Submit a new command for execution / GET Get status of the current command /history GET Retrieve execution history

docs.title: Execution Manager
docs.text:
The ExecaManager service runs each command in these steps:

  1. Adds the command to the queue, marked invalid.
  2. Checks the command against the list of permitted commands.
  3. For a permitted command, creates a runner through the factory and runs the script from the configured location.
  4. Marks the command valid if the script succeeds, and returns the status and logs.

docs.title: Command Queue
docs.text: The Queue service keeps the execution history and tracks the active command. Each command is stored with its execution status (valid or invalid).

docs.title: Runner Interface
docs.text:
The Runner interface defines the contract for command executors:

interface Runner {
  run(): Promise<boolean>;
  checkLogs(): Map<string, string>;
}

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
The service reads its configuration from a YAML file (see config/runner.yaml.sample) with these settings:

Setting Purpose port HTTP server port location Base directory for executable scripts commands Allowlist of permitted command names

docs.title: Security Considerations
docs.text: The runner only executes commands that are listed in the configuration file. A request for any other command is recorded as invalid and not run, which prevents arbitrary command execution.

docs.title: Coding Agents
docs.text: Coding agents read their instructions from files in the repository. Every agent reads the same files, so the rules are written once.

docs.title: Instruction files
docs.text:
File Holds Read by AGENTS.md General coding guidelines Codex, OpenCode, GitHub Copilot and most other agents PROJECT.md Build and test commands, verification, shipping, pull request checks, code standards and per-project conventions Every agent, through AGENTS.md CLAUDE.md Imports AGENTS.md and PROJECT.md Claude Code .github/copilot-instructions.md A pointer to AGENTS.md and PROJECT.md GitHub Copilot

Change the rules in AGENTS.md or PROJECT.md; the other files only point to them.

docs.title: Skills
docs.text:
Task-specific instructions are Agent Skills. Each skill is a directory .agents/skills/<name>/ holding a SKILL.md file and, where needed, scripts. Codex and OpenCode find skills in .agents/skills/.

Claude Code reads skills from .claude/skills/ only. Each skill therefore has a stub .claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md with the same frontmatter, whose body sends the agent to the canonical file. A symbolic link would check out as a plain file on Windows clones without symlink support. The Lint Miscellaneous Scripts workflow fails when a stub's frontmatter differs from its canonical skill.

The repository provides these skills:

Skill Use it to upgrade-npm-packages Upgrade npm dependencies behind a ten-day release cooldown; see Upgrade NPM Packages capture-docs-screenshots Retake the user documentation screenshots from a running installation update-docs-diagrams Edit, restyle and export the documentation diagrams review-pull-request Check that a pull request passes every quality gate before merge check-code-quality Review the code quality of one component plan-before-coding Analyse the codebase and requirements before implementing architecture-design Design an architecture and its diagrams and documentation react-frontend-engineer Work on the React client playwright-tester Explore the website and write Playwright tests technical-debt-remediation-plan Plan the remediation of technical debt critical-thinking Challenge assumptions behind a proposed solution mentor Guide an engineer rather than writing the code for them

Seven of these skills are adapted from awesome-copilot under the MIT licence; see .github/REFERENCES.md.

docs.title: Adding a skill
docs.text:
1. Create .agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md. Its frontmatter needs name, equal to the directory name, and a description that says what the skill does and when to use it. The agent decides whether to load the skill from the description alone.
  2. Create .claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md with the same frontmatter and a body that points to the canonical file.
  3. Add the skill to the table above.
  4. Validate both directories with skills-ref: skills-ref validate .agents/skills/<name>.

docs.title: Using coding agents
docs.text: Contributors use coding agents for co-development, code review and draft pull requests. Disclose code that a coding agent generated, particularly when it carries significant program logic. Understand every line you contribute: review generated code before submitting it, and keep the critical thinking for yourself.

docs.title: Our Pledge
docs.text:
We as members, contributors, and leaders pledge to make participation in our community a harassment-free experience for everyone, regardless of age, body size, visible or invisible disability, ethnicity, sex characteristics, gender identity and expression, level of experience, education, socio-economic status, nationality, personal appearance, race, religion, or sexual identity and orientation.

We pledge to act and interact in ways that contribute to an open, welcoming, diverse, inclusive, and healthy community.

docs.title: Our Standards
docs.text:
Examples of behaviour that contributes to a positive environment for our community include:

  • Demonstrating empathy and kindness toward other people
  • Being respectful of differing opinions, viewpoints, and experiences
  • Giving and gracefully accepting constructive feedback
  • Accepting responsibility and apologizing to those affected by our mistakes, and learning from the experience
  • Focusing on what is best not just for us as individuals, but for the overall community

Examples of unacceptable behaviour include:

  • The use of sexualized language or imagery, and sexual attention or advances of any kind
  • Trolling, insulting or derogatory comments, and personal or political attacks
  • Public or private harassment
  • Publishing others' private information, such as a physical or email address, without their explicit permission
  • Other conduct which could reasonably be considered inappropriate in a professional setting

docs.title: Enforcement Responsibilities
docs.text:
Community leaders are responsible for clarifying and enforcing our standards of acceptable behaviour and will take appropriate and fair corrective action in response to any behaviour that they deem inappropriate, threatening, offensive, or harmful.

Community leaders have the right and responsibility to remove, edit, or reject comments, commits, code, wiki edits, issues, and other contributions that are not aligned to this Code of Conduct, and will communicate reasons for moderation decisions when appropriate.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text: This Code of Conduct applies within all community spaces, and also applies when an individual is officially representing the community in public spaces. Examples of representing our community include using an official e-mail address, posting via an official social media account, or acting as an appointed representative at an online or offline event.

docs.title: Enforcement
docs.text:
Instances of abusive, harassing, or otherwise unacceptable behaviour may be reported to the community leaders responsible for enforcement by opening a new issue in this repository. All complaints will be reviewed and investigated promptly and fairly.

All community leaders are obligated to respect the privacy and security of the reporter of any incident.

docs.title: Enforcement Guidelines
docs.text: Community leaders will follow these Community Impact Guidelines in determining the consequences for any action they deem in violation of this Code of Conduct:

docs.title: 1. Correction
docs.text:
Community Impact: Use of inappropriate language or other behaviour deemed unprofessional or unwelcome in the community.

Consequence: A private, written warning from community leaders, providing clarity around the nature of the violation and an explanation of why the behaviour was inappropriate. A public apology may be requested.

docs.title: 2. Warning
docs.text:
Community Impact: A violation through a single incident or series of actions.

Consequence: A warning with consequences for continued behaviour. No interaction with the people involved, including unsolicited interaction with those enforcing the Code of Conduct, for a specified period of time. This includes avoiding interactions in community spaces as well as external channels like social media. Violating these terms may lead to a temporary or permanent ban.

docs.title: 3. Temporary Ban
docs.text:
Community Impact: A serious violation of community standards, including sustained inappropriate behaviour.

Consequence: A temporary ban from any sort of interaction or public communication with the community for a specified period of time. No public or private interaction with the people involved, including unsolicited interaction with those enforcing the Code of Conduct, is allowed during this period. Violating these terms may lead to a permanent ban.

docs.title: 4. Permanent Ban
docs.text:
Community Impact: Demonstrating a pattern of violation of community standards, including sustained inappropriate behaviour, harassment of an individual, or aggression toward or disparagement of classes of individuals.

Consequence: A permanent ban from any sort of public interaction within the community.

docs.title: Docker Workflow for DTaaS
docs.text:
This document describes how the Docker files are built and used for developing and installing the DTaaS platform.

NOTE: The Docker workflows need a local Docker CE installation.

docs.title: Run
docs.text:
The developer/ directory holds two separate things:

  • developer/check/ checks that DTaaS functions on a developer machine. Follow the instructions in developer/check/README.md to start a localhost instance. It is an end-to-end test of the codebase as it exists in the local git directory.
  • developer/devenv/ is the containerised developer environment: the Node, Python and documentation toolchains needed to work on the code. See developer/devenv/README.md.

The diagram shows the localhost instance that developer/check/ starts: two user workspaces, the library and logger microservices and the client behind Traefik, with forward-auth signing users in through GitLab.

docs.title: CI Dockerfile Validation
docs.text:
A pull request that modifies client/**, servers/lib/**, servers/logger/** or the relevant Dockerfiles triggers a Docker build check. The check uses the reusable workflow .github/workflows/docker-build.yml and runs in parallel with the test jobs. It builds each image for both linux/amd64 and linux/arm64, each on a native runner (ubuntu-latest and ubuntu-24.04-arm), so an image that fails to build on either platform fails the check.

Workflow Dockerfile validated Notes .github/workflows/client.yml developer/check/client.dockerfile Full multi-stage build inside Docker .github/workflows/client.yml developer/check/client.built.dockerfile Validates the publish image Dockerfile .github/workflows/lib-ms.yml developer/check/libms.dockerfile Full multi-stage build inside Docker .github/workflows/logger-ms.yml developer/check/logger.dockerfile Full multi-stage build inside Docker

The Docker build checks also run on pushes. The push triggers of .github/workflows/client.yml and .github/workflows/lib-ms.yml cover only the source code directories (client/** and servers/lib/**).

The publish jobs of these two workflows run on pushes to, and manual runs on, the feature/distributed-demo branch. Because the push trigger covers only the source code directories, a change to a Dockerfile alone does not re-publish an already published package version.

In all three workflows, the Docker publish jobs wait for the Docker build check to pass on both platforms. A publish that has started is never cancelled by a newer push; only superseded pull request runs are.

The logger microservice workflow (.github/workflows/logger-ms.yml) also runs the image from developer/check/logger.dockerfile on amd64 and checks its health endpoint. It publishes that image on pushes to feature/* and release-v* branches, and its push trigger includes that Dockerfile.

docs.title: Publish Docker Images
docs.text:
Build and publish the Docker images. This step is needed only to publish images to Docker Hub.

The CI workflows publish every image for both linux/amd64 and linux/arm64. The docker build commands below build only for the platform of the machine they run on. To publish both platforms by hand, create a builder that supports multi-platform output once with docker buildx create --use, then run docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 --push with the same -t and -f arguments instead of docker build and docker push. The platform that differs from the host is built under QEMU emulation, which is several times slower. Docker Desktop and Rancher Desktop provide the emulation; on a plain Linux Docker Engine, register it first with docker run --privileged --rm tonistiigi/binfmt --install arm64.

Warning

Only project maintainers publish images. Other developers can skip this step.

The DTaaS development team publishes reusable packages, which together form the complete DTaaS application.

The packages are published on github, npmjs and docker hub.

The packages on github are published more often but are not user tested. The packages on npmjs and docker hub are published at least once per release. Regular users should use the packages from npm and Docker Hub.

The packages are:

Package Name Description Availability dtaas-web React web application docker hub and github libms Library microservice npmjs and github docker hub and github logger-ms Logger microservice npmjs and github docker hub and github runner REST API wrapper for multiple scripts/programs npmjs and github dt-automation Data and business-logic layer of the client npmjs and github

docs.title: React Website
docs.text:
docker build -t intocps/dtaas-web:latest -f ./developer/check/client.built.dockerfile .
docker tag intocps/dtaas-web:latest intocps/dtaas-web:<version>
docker push intocps/dtaas-web:latest
docker push intocps/dtaas-web:<version>

For example, to tag version 0.3.1, use

docker tag intocps/dtaas-web:latest intocps/dtaas-web:0.3.1

To test the React website container on localhost, use

docker run -d \
  -v ${PWD}/client/config/local.js:/dtaas/client/build/env.js \
  -p 4000:4000 intocps/dtaas-web:latest

docs.title: Library Microservice
docs.text:
The Dockerfile of the library microservice has a VERSION argument, which selects the package version to install from http://npmjs.com.

docker login -u <username> -p <password>
docker build -t intocps/libms:latest -f ./developer/check/libms.npm.dockerfile .
docker push intocps/libms:latest
docker build --build-arg="VERSION=<version>" \
  -t intocps/libms:<version> -f ./developer/check/libms.npm.dockerfile .
docker push intocps/libms:<version>

For example, to tag version 0.3.1, use

docker build --build-arg="VERSION=0.3.1" \
  -t intocps/libms:0.3.1 -f ./developer/check/libms.npm.dockerfile .

To test the library microservice on localhost, use

docker run -d -v ${PWD}/files:/dtaas/libms/files \
  -p 4001:4001 intocps/libms:latest

docs.title: Logger Microservice
docs.text:
The logger microservice image is built from the source code with logger.dockerfile. Use the version in servers/logger/package.json as the image tag.

docker login -u <username> -p <password>
docker build -t intocps/logger-ms:latest -f ./developer/check/logger.dockerfile .
docker tag intocps/logger-ms:latest intocps/logger-ms:<version>
docker push intocps/logger-ms:latest
docker push intocps/logger-ms:<version>

For example, to tag version 0.1.2, use

docker tag intocps/logger-ms:latest intocps/logger-ms:0.1.2

To test the logger microservice on localhost, use

mkdir logs
sudo chown -R 1000:1000 logs
docker run -d -v ${PWD}/logs:/dtaas/logger/logs \
  -p 4003:4003 intocps/logger-ms:latest

The captured events are written to logs/workflow-logs.jsonl.

docs.title: Secrets for GitHub Actions
docs.text:
The publishing jobs of the GitHub Actions need the following secrets from Docker Hub:

Secret Name Explanation DOCKERHUB_SCOPE Username or organisation name on Docker Hub DOCKERHUB_USERNAME Username on Docker Hub DOCKERHUB_TOKEN API token to publish images to Docker Hub, with Read, Write and Delete permissions

They also need this secret from npmjs:

Secret Name Explanation NPM_TOKEN Token to publish npm packages to the default npm registry.

Publishing to GitHub Packages uses the built-in GITHUB_TOKEN. The test jobs upload coverage with an optional CODECOV_TOKEN secret, which public repositories do not need.

The following repository variables are optional. When set, the npm package is published under the given name instead of the name in its package.json:

Variable Name Package PACKAGE_NAME Library microservice (servers/lib) NPM_RUNNER_PACKAGE_NAME Runner (servers/execution/runner) NPM_LOGGER_PACKAGE_NAME Logger microservice (servers/logger)

Add the secrets in the GitHub Secrets Setting of the fork, and the variables under Settings > Secrets and variables > Actions > Variables.

docs.title: Local Testing
docs.text: This guide gives a local test loop for contributors working in the DTaaS monorepo. The authoritative build and test command for each project is in the "Build and test commands" section of PROJECT.md; the commands below follow it. The development container in developer/devenv/ has every toolchain they need.

docs.title: Recommended Order
docs.text:
1. Run syntax and lint checks for the changed component.
  2. Run fast local tests (unit or focused integration).
  3. Run broader test suites before opening a pull request.
  4. Build the docs if markdown or navigation changed.

docs.title: Client (React + TypeScript)
docs.text:
Run from client/:

yarn syntax
yarn build
yarn config:test
yarn test:unit
yarn test:int

yarn config:test copies the test configuration into public/env.js and build/env.js. Use the yarn test:* scripts rather than bare jest: they load the setup files that the tests depend on.

For end-to-end checks:

yarn test:e2e

The end-to-end suite logs in through GitLab, so it needs a reachable GitLab instance configured in client/test/.env. GitHub Actions does not run it; run it locally before opening a pull request that changes client behaviour. See client/test/README.md.

docs.title: Library Microservice (NestJS)
docs.text:
Run from servers/lib/:

yarn syntax
yarn build
yarn test:all

For API-level checks of the cloudcmd integration, use yarn test:http. It needs a configured .env file and starts the library microservice under pm2.

docs.title: Runner Microservice (NestJS)
docs.text:
Run from servers/execution/runner/:

yarn syntax
yarn build
yarn test

yarn test:unit and yarn test:int run the unit and integration tests separately.

docs.title: Logger Microservice (NestJS)
docs.text:
Run from servers/logger/:

yarn syntax
yarn test

docs.title: DT Automation Library (TypeScript)
docs.text:
Run from lib/dt-automation/:

yarn syntax
yarn test:unit

The package has no test script.

docs.title: DTaaS CLI (Python)
docs.text:
Run from cli/:

poetry install
poetry run python src/pkg/build.py
poetry run pytest

The build step copies the shared code from lib/ into the package; the tests cannot be collected without it.

docs.title: GitLab Common Library (Python)
docs.text:
Run from lib/gitlab_common/:

poetry install
poetry run pytest

docs.title: Platform Services CLI (Python)
docs.text:
Run from deploy/services/cli/:

poetry install
poetry run python -m dtaas_services.pkg.build
CI=true poetry run pytest --ignore=tests/system_tests

The CLI checks for root before it validates arguments, so non-root runs need CI=true. The tests in tests/system_tests call docker.

docs.title: Documentation Validation
docs.text:
Run from the repository root:

python -m pytest script/docs
python script/docs/docs.py build

On Linux, to validate the full docs build including the PDF export:

python script/docs/docs.py build --pdf

docs.title: Practical Tip
docs.text: When changing several components, validate each package on its own first. Failures then stay local and are quicker to debug, and unrelated test errors do not get in the way.

docs.title: Publish NPM packages
docs.text: The DTaaS monorepo contains several npm packages.

docs.title: Default npm registry
docs.text:
The default registry for npm packages is npmjs. Public packages are published to npmjs.

GitHub Actions publish the library microservice (lib-ms.yml), the runner (runner.yml), the logger microservice (logger-ms.yml) and the @into-cps-association/dt-automation library (dt-automation.yml). Each workflow calls the reusable .github/workflows/publish-npm.yml workflow.

A package can also be published by hand:

npm login --registry="https://registry.npmjs.org"
cat ~/.npmrc  #shows the auth token for the registry
//registry.npmjs.org/:_authToken=xxxxxxxxxx
yarn publish --registry="https://registry.npmjs.org" \
  --no-git-tag-version --access public

At least one version of the runner package is published to this registry for each release of the DTaaS platform.

docs.title: GitHub npm registry
docs.text: The GitHub Actions of the project also publish the packages to the GitHub npm registry. Installing from this registry requires a personal access token from GitHub.

docs.title: Setup private npm registry
docs.text:
Publishing to npmjs is public and cannot be undone, so set up a private npm registry for local development. A private registry lets you publish and unpublish packages freely.

Verdaccio is the recommended registry. The following commands create a working private npm registry for development.

docker run -d --name verdaccio -p 4873:4873 verdaccio/verdaccio
npm adduser --registry http://localhost:4873 #create a user on the verdaccio registry
npm set registry http://localhost:4873/
yarn config set registry "http://localhost:4873"
yarn login --registry "http://localhost:4873" #login with the credentials for yarn utility
npm login #login with the credentials for npm utility

Open http://localhost:4873 in a browser and log in with the user credentials to see the published packages.

docs.title: Publish to private npm registry
docs.text:
To publish a package to the local registry, run:

yarn install
yarn build #the dist/ directory is needed for publishing step
yarn publish --no-git-tag-version #increments version in package.json, publishes to registry
yarn publish #increments version in package.json, publishes to registry and adds a git tag

The package version in package.json is updated accordingly. See the verdaccio docs for more information.

To unpublish a package, for example @into-cps-association/runner@0.0.2, run:

npm unpublish --registry http://localhost:4873/ \
  @into-cps-association/runner@0.0.2

To install or uninstall this utility for all users, run:

sudo npm install --registry http://localhost:4873 \
  -g @into-cps-association/runner
sudo npm list -g # should list @into-cps-association/runner in the packages
sudo npm remove --global @into-cps-association/runner

docs.title: Use the packages
docs.text:
Packages in the private npm registry are used like regular packages installed from npmjs.

For example, to use the @into-cps-association/runner@0.0.2 package, run:

sudo npm install --registry http://localhost:4873 \
  -g @into-cps-association/runner
runner # launch the digital twin runner

docs.title: Upgrade NPM Packages
docs.text:
A malicious npm release is usually found and pulled from the registry within days. The project therefore waits before taking any newly published package version.

  • Dependabot waits three days, through cooldown: default-days: 3 in .github/dependabot.yml.
  • Upgrades made by hand bypass Dependabot. Run them through the upgrade-npm-packages agent skill or its script, which wait ten days.

docs.title: Agent skill
docs.text: The upgrade-npm-packages skill in .agents/skills/ runs the script, explains every change, runs the project's build and tests, and pins back any upgrade that breaks them. Ask a coding agent to upgrade the npm packages of a project to use it. Coding Agents explains how skills are organised.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
The script needs Node.js 24 or later, npm 7 or later and yarn 1. It has no npm dependencies of its own. To run it without an agent:

node .agents/skills/upgrade-npm-packages/scripts/npm_pkg_upgrade.js client/package.json

The script takes the path to one package.json and performs these steps:

  1. Computes the cutoff date, ten days before now.
  2. For every entry in dependencies, devDependencies and optionalDependencies, picks the newest stable, non-deprecated version published on or before the cutoff that stays within the range the spec already allows. The range prefix (^, ~ or none) is kept.
  3. Writes the new versions into the package.json.
  4. Deletes the yarn.lock beside it and generates a fresh one.

The range follows npm's meaning of the prefix, and an exact version is treated like ^:

Spec Stays below ^6.0.3 or 6.0.3 7.0.0 ^0.18.9 0.19.0 ~30.4.2 30.5.0

The output lists every changed package as upgrade or DOWNGRADE, and every package left alone as skip, with the reason. A line starting with newer names a version outside the range, such as a new major release, which the script does not apply. Take such a version by editing the package.json and running the script again.

docs.title: Packages published from this repository
docs.text: Packages in the @into-cps-association/ scope, such as @into-cps-association/dt-automation, are built and published from this repository, so the cooldown does not apply to them. The script keeps their versions as written in the package.json, even when the release is only days old. Their provenance is tracked separately; see the issue on npm provenance attestations.

docs.title: How the new lockfile honours the cooldown
docs.text:
Yarn 1 has no setting to hold back recently published versions, and a fresh yarn install resolves every transitive dependency to its newest version. The script therefore builds the lockfile in an empty temporary directory, away from any existing node_modules:

  1. npm install --package-lock-only --before=<cutoff> resolves the whole dependency tree, transitive dependencies included, as it stood at the cutoff. The exempt @into-cps-association/ packages are left out of this step.
  2. A second npm install --package-lock-only, without --before, adds the exempt packages. It keeps every version the first step locked. Any package this step adds is printed as no cooldown: <name>@<version> for review.
  3. yarn_lock_from_npm.js converts the package-lock.json into a yarn.lock holding exactly the versions npm chose.
  4. yarn install --frozen-lockfile checks that yarn accepts the lockfile without resolving anything itself. The lockfile is then copied beside the package.json.

yarn import is not used. It reads an existing node_modules in preference to the package-lock.json, and it re-resolves some entries from the live registry, which lets recent versions back in.

Run yarn install afterwards to install the new versions.

docs.title: Review the result
docs.text:
The script applies the cooldown mechanically. Review the diff before committing it.

  • Downgrades. A version newer than the cutoff is replaced by the newest older version.
  • Newer versions outside the range. Review each newer line. A major release can break the build; for example, TypeScript 7 does not work with ts-jest, so the client stays on TypeScript 6.
  • Deliberate pins. A ~ range keeps a package on its minor release. For example, jest in servers/lib stays on ~30.4.2; see servers/lib/DEVELOPER.md.
  • Skipped entries. Ranges such as >=1.0.0, file: and npm: aliases, prerelease versions and packages missing from the registry are left unchanged.

Then run the build and test commands for the project; see PROJECT.md.

docs.title: Linting and tests
docs.text:
The Lint and Test Node Scripts job in .github/workflows/lint-scripts.yml checks the skill's scripts/ directory with eslint and prettier, runs its unit tests, and checks every skill's Claude Code stub. The linters are installed only in CI, at exact versions and without a package.json. To run the same checks locally:

cd .agents/skills/upgrade-npm-packages/scripts
npm install --no-save --no-package-lock --ignore-scripts \
  eslint@10.11.0 @eslint/js@10.0.1 prettier@3.9.9
npx eslint .
npx prettier --check .
node --test ./*.test.js

docs.title: System Overview
docs.text: The Digital Twin as a Service (DTaaS) platform supports the whole digital twin (DT) lifecycle. Users create, configure, execute and share digital twins built from reusable assets[1]. The architecture follows established principles for realising digital twins in practice[2] and also supports use cases such as runtime verification of autonomous systems[3].

docs.title: User Requirements
docs.text:
The platform provides the following capabilities:

  1. Author: create the assets of a DT on the platform itself. This requires software frameworks and tools built for authoring DT assets.
  2. Consolidate: consolidate the available DT assets and authoring tools so that users can navigate the library of reusable assets. This requires support for discovering available assets.
  3. Configure: select and configure DTs. This also requires validation of a given configuration.
  4. Execute: provision computing infrastructure on demand to execute a DT.
  5. Explore: interact with a DT and explore the results stored inside and outside the platform. Exploration may lead to analytical insights.
  6. Save: save the state of a DT that is already executing. This is needed to save and re-spawn DTs on demand.
  7. Services: integrate DTs with on-platform or external services that users can interact with.
  8. Share: share a DT with other users of their organisation.

docs.title: System Architecture
docs.text: The figure shows the system architecture of the DTaaS software platform.

docs.title: System Components
docs.text:
Users interact with the software platform through a web application. The service router is the single point of entry for direct access to platform services and controls user access to the microservice components. The service mesh provides microservice discovery, load balancing and authorization.

Further microservices manage DT reusable assets, platform services, the DT lifecycle, DT execution, accounting and security. The microservices are complementary and composable, and together they meet the core requirements of the system.

The microservices responsible for the user requirements are:

  1. The security microservice implements role-based access control (RBAC) in the platform.
  2. The accounting microservice keeps track of the live status of the platform, DT assets and infrastructure usage. It must enforce any licensing and usage restrictions. Accounting is a prerequisite for commercialising the platform. Because the platform makes heavy use of external infrastructure and resources, the accounting microservice needs to interface with the accounting systems of those external services.
  3. User Workspaces are virtual environments in which users perform lifecycle operations on DTs. These environments are either Docker containers or virtual machines that give users a desktop interface.
  4. Reusable Assets are the parts from which DTs are created. The assets page explains them further.
  5. Services are available to all DTs and users of the DTaaS platform. Services build on DTs and provide user interfaces to users.
  6. DT Execution Manager provides virtual and isolated execution environments for DTs. It also provisions cloud resources dynamically.
  7. DT Lifecycle Manager manages the lifecycle operations on all DTs. It directs the DT Execution Manager to execute, save and terminate DTs.

The web application can also carry domain-specific pages that come from separate npm packages. Client Extensions describes the current state and the proposed extension architecture.

Several of these components are not implemented yet; the table below gives their status. The architecture review describes the system as implemented.

The C4 diagram below shows the DTaaS architecture in more detail.

The table maps the architectural components to related pages in the documentation.

System Component Doc Page(s) Service Router Traefik Gateway Web Application React Web Application Reusable Assets Library Microservice Workflow Logs Logger Microservice Digital Twins and DevOps Integrated GitLab Platform Services Third-party Services (MQTT, InfluxDB, RabbitMQ, Grafana, MongoDB, PostgreSQL, and ThingsBoard) DT Lifecycle Manager Not available yet Security GitLab client OAuth 2.0 and server OAuth 2.0 Digital Twins as Services DT Runner Accounting Not available yet Execution Manager Not available yet

docs.title: Current Status
docs.text:
DTaaS is a monorepo under active development. It has deployment scenarios meant for production use, and work continues on execution automation, reusable assets and contributor tooling.

The C4 diagram shows the same status in more detail.

docs.title: Platform Snapshot
docs.text:
• React 19 client, built with Vite, with a typed backend abstraction over GitLab APIs.
  • NestJS library, runner and logger microservices.
  • @into-cps-association/dt-automation, an npm library with the data, state and GitLab operations for creating, managing and executing DTs.
  • @into-cps-association/bim-kit, maintained in the ifc-utils repository, for the Building Models page.
  • gitlab-common, a Python library shared by the two CLIs.
  • Python CLIs for DTaaS administration (dtaas) and platform services management (dtaas-services).
  • Scenario-based admin documentation for DTaaS and workspace deployments.

docs.title: Security and Access Model
docs.text:
Two authorization patterns are in use:

  • GitLab-centred OAuth flows for DTaaS package scenarios.
  • Keycloak-centred OIDC flows for secure workspace scenarios.

Traefik and its forward-auth middleware protect routes and mediate access at the gateway.

docs.title: Workspaces and Assets
docs.text: Workspace deployments give each user an isolated environment and share assets between users. Asset management currently uses file-system workflows and the library microservice, which is still evolving.

docs.title: Current Engineering Focus
docs.text:
• Improve scenario automation and configuration guidance.
  • Strengthen test coverage and CI reliability across packages.
  • Continue improving DevOps execution visibility in the client UI.
  • Evaluate the proposed client extension architecture, which adds domain-specific pages through npm packages.
  • Keep package publishing and release flows consistent across npm, Docker, and Poetry-based tools.

Contributions that improve reproducibility, documentation quality and integration between components are welcome.

docs.title: Client Extensions
docs.text: The web client uses npm packages for parts of its behaviour, and some of these packages are maintained outside this repository. This page lists them, describes how the Building Models page is wired into the client, and summarises the modular architecture proposed for domain-specific pages.

docs.title: Packages Used by the Client
docs.text:
Package Source Role in the client @into-cps-association/dt-automation lib/dt-automation/ in this repository Data, state and GitLab operations for creating, managing and executing DTs. The client takes it from npm (^0.2.0 in client/package.json). @into-cps-association/bim-kit ifc-utils IFC to glTF conversion in the browser, the binding manifest and the viewer of the Building Models page. The client pins version 0.1.1.

The client page describes the classes of dt-automation, and Publish Packages describes how it is released.

docs.title: The Building Models Page
docs.text:
The domain logic of the Building Models page lives in bim-kit. The client holds three wiring files in client/src/route/bim/:

  • Bim.tsx places the page in the DTaaS layout and hands the viewer the library URL of the signed-in user.
  • library.ts names the folder that holds the models, common/models.
  • persistGeometry.ts writes a model converted in the browser back to the library, so that each model is converted once.

A change to how a model is drawn reaches DTaaS as a new version of bim-kit. The page is still wired into the client by hand, in the route table (src/routes.tsx), the menu (src/page/MenuItems.tsx), the icon registry (src/components/appIcons.tsx) and package.json. A page for another domain would have to edit the same files.

docs.title: Proposed Modular Architecture
docs.text:
The modular architecture described here is a proposal. It is not merged into the client, and client/package.json does not depend on the SDK.

The dtaas-sdk repository holds @into-cps-association/dtaas-sdk, which defines a contract between the web client (the host) and domain extensions. In the proposal:

  • A domain extension is an npm package. It declares what it contributes, such as pages, navigation entries, digital twin tabs, asset previews, anchor kinds, converters, encoding presets and substrates, as one DtaasExtension object.
  • The host passes platform services to each extension through a HostServices object: authentication, the library, the workspace contents API, GitLab, live signals, the visualisation service, user interface helpers, logging, settings and configuration. An extension does not import client internals.
  • The client lists the extensions compiled into a build in one file, src/extensions.ts. A deployment can disable a compiled-in extension in env.js with REACT_APP_EXTENSIONS_DISABLED.
  • A common visualisation core, dtaas-visualisation, holds the parts that do not depend on the domain: live data transport, the temporal store, anchor resolution, encoding rules and the standard substrates.
  • bim-kit is moved onto the contract, and the wiring files in client/src/route/bim/ move into it.

The SDK declares a contract revision (sdk: 1) that is separate from its npm version, and a host built on the SDK refuses an extension built for another revision. The examples/bim folder of the SDK repository ports bim-kit 0.1.1 onto the contract as a private package.

The figure shows the direction of this architecture. Domain-specific extensions add pages to the web interface, and the common services are grouped into a generic set and a set for each domain, such as IFC for construction and buildings. Of the two extensions drawn, the Buildings page exists in the client today, as a hand-wired route.

The SDK repository documents the proposal in detail:

  • Modular architecture proposal
  • Writing an extension
  • Integrating the SDK into a host
  • The visualisation.json schema
  • The bim-kit port

docs.title: DTaaS Research Overview
docs.text: This document summarises the research behind the DTaaS platform for code contributors who need to understand the design rationale, the architectural decisions and the intended evolution of the system.

docs.title: 1. Introduction
docs.text:
A digital twin is a software representation of a physical asset that stays connected to its real-world counterpart through data exchange. The connection supports monitoring, analysis and prediction throughout the asset lifecycle. Digital twin platforms provide shared infrastructure for creating, managing and executing digital twins at scale.

DTaaS (Digital Twin as a Service) is an open-source platform that treats digital twins as compositions of reusable assets. The platform organises assets into four categories: data, models, functions (methods and scripts) and services. Users compose these assets into digital twin configurations that can be executed, monitored and evolved independently.

The platform targets operability: creating, configuring, executing, monitoring and evolving twins in long-running environments. This sets DTaaS apart from simulation-only tools and pure modelling frameworks.

docs.title: 2. Requirements
docs.text:
Eight requirements drive the platform design:

  1. Author: create and edit digital twin assets in isolated workspaces
  2. Consolidate: combine assets from different sources into coherent twin configurations
  3. Configure: set parameters for execution without modifying asset source code
  4. Execute: run digital twin configurations on demand or continuously
  5. Explore: browse available assets, twins and execution results
  6. Save: persist configurations, results and intermediate state
  7. What-if Analysis: evaluate alternative scenarios by varying parameters
  8. Collaborate: share assets and twins across users and organisations

These requirements apply across domains. Validated case studies include food fermentation process control, indoor climate management for firefighter training and structural health monitoring of civil infrastructure.

docs.title: 3. System Architecture
docs.text:
The architecture divides the platform into four concern areas:

  • Gateway and authentication: a Traefik reverse proxy with OAuth 2.0 / OpenID Connect for route protection and user identity management
  • Execution management: backend services that trigger, monitor and stop digital twin runs via GitLab CI/CD pipelines
  • Reusable-asset handling: a library microservice that serves assets from a local file system or git repositories and exposes asset discovery and retrieval APIs
  • Workspace isolation: per-user JupyterLab containers with private file systems for authoring and running assets

The current codebase implements these areas as follows. The React client handles user interaction and itself triggers and monitors the GitLab CI/CD pipelines that execute digital twins. Traefik manages routing and TLS. The library microservice serves reusable assets, and the DT runner executes commands inside a workspace. The architecture review describes this implemented architecture in detail.

docs.title: 4. User View
docs.text: Users see DTaaS as a single web interface for workspace operations, asset browsing, digital twin execution and result exploration. Each user works in their own isolated workspace and shares assets through the common library. The platform supports both class-level twin definitions (reusable templates) and instance-level twins (bound to specific physical assets).

docs.title: 5. Lifecycle-Driven Engineering
docs.text:
Lifecycle coverage is a core requirement. The platform supports the create, manage, execute and stop phases, with iterative reconfiguration between them. For this reason the contracts between the client and the backend cover both file management and execution tracking.

The lifecycle model assumes that digital twins evolve: models are updated as physical assets change, new data sources are integrated, and execution configurations are refined based on operational experience.

docs.title: 6. DevOps and Federation
docs.text:
GitLab-backed DevOps automation is a core platform capability. Repository structure, pipeline triggers and OAuth configuration are part of the platform contract and not only deployment details. The platform supports two execution modes, continuous (long-running services) and one-off (batch analysis jobs), and GitLab CI/CD pipelines manage both.

Related recordings:

  • DTaaS DevOps workflows
  • DTaaS and DevOps

The federation extension lets multiple DTaaS instances discover and reuse each other's assets across organisational boundaries. Federated digital twins can be organised as composites (assembled from assets on different instances), fleets (coordinated groups) or hierarchies (parent-child relationships).

Related recording:

  • Federated DTaaS video

docs.title: 7. Application: Structural Health Monitoring
docs.text:
Structural health monitoring (SHM) of civil infrastructure shows DTaaS used to integrate specialised engineering workflows. In this domain, digital twin assets include sensor data acquisition modules (accelerometers, distributed optical sensors), operational modal analysis functions, finite element model updating procedures and fatigue-based methods for estimating remaining useful life.

The SHM workflow composes these assets into a pipeline. Sensor data flows through modal analysis to extract structural properties. These feed into model updating, which calibrates a finite element model, and the calibrated model drives damage prognosis and remaining useful life estimation. Domain specialists build such workflows from reusable building blocks and keep their existing tools.

docs.title: Guidance for Contributors
docs.text:
When implementing or reviewing DTaaS changes:

  1. Map the change to one of the concern areas above (architecture, lifecycle, DevOps/federation, domain application, monitoring).
  2. Verify the change preserves the intended lifecycle and composability behaviour.
  3. Check whether the change shifts architecture boundaries (gateway/auth, execution manager, reusable-asset layer, workspace isolation).
  4. Document any intentional departure from design assumptions.

Anti-patterns to avoid:

  • Hard-coding one modelling or tooling workflow where the design expects heterogeneity.
  • Collapsing layered responsibilities into UI code for short-term convenience.
  • Treating DevOps and federation behaviour as optional.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
The research behind DTaaS is documented in the following papers.

  1. Composable Digital Twins on Digital Twin as a Service Platform defines the platform architecture, asset model, lifecycle phases and system requirements. (Talasila, Prasad, et al. "Composable digital twins on Digital Twin as a Service platform." Simulation 101.3 (2025): 287-311.)
  2. Realising Digital Twins positions DTaaS in the wider digital twin field, with a comparative survey of existing frameworks, cloud deployment strategies and fleet management concepts. (Talasila, Prasad, et al. "Realising digital twins." The engineering of digital twins. Cham: Springer International Publishing, 2024. 225-256.)
  3. Towards Federated Digital Twin Platforms extends DTaaS with multi-instance federation, DevOps integration and asset reuse across organisations. (Frasheri, Mirgita, Prasad Talasila, and Vanessa Scherma. "Towards federated digital twin platforms." arXiv preprint arXiv:2505.04324 (2025).)
  4. Structural Health Monitoring of Engineering Structures Using Digital Twins applies DTaaS to vibration-based SHM with modal analysis and model updating workflows. (Talasila, P., et al. "Structural health monitoring of engineering structures using digital twins: A digital twin platform approach." International Conference on Experimental Vibration Analysis for Civil Engineering Structures. Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland, 2025.)

docs.title: Architectural and Design Review
docs.text: This section contains an independent architectural and design review of the DTaaS codebase, performed against the feature/distributed-demo branch (commit e7f9dd6, July 2026). The findings describe the codebase at that commit.

docs.title: Scope and Method
docs.text:
The review covers the five deliverable packages of the monorepo, and the deployment scenarios that bind them together (the last row):

Package Path Technology React client client/ React 19, Redux Toolkit, oidc-client-ts Library microservice servers/lib/ NestJS, GraphQL (Apollo), cloudcmd DT Runner servers/execution/runner/ NestJS, REST, execa DTaaS CLI cli/ Python, click, python-on-whales Services manager deploy/services/cli/ Python, click (dtaas-services) Deployment scenarios deploy/dtaas/docker/, deploy/vagrant/ Traefik, docker compose

The review followed a standard system design review framework: requirements traceability, recovery of the high-level architecture from code and deployment artifacts, deep dives into each component, and an analysis of scale, reliability and security across components. Each finding was checked against the source files, and each claim in these documents cites the file it was observed in.

docs.title: Documents
docs.text:
1. Architecture Review: the architecture as implemented, recovered from code and compose files, with data flows and trade-off analysis.
  2. Design Review: component-level review of the client, microservices, CLIs and deployment tooling.
  3. Systemic Issues: issues that recur across components and releases, with evidence.
  4. Improvement Proposals: prioritised, incremental recommendations with migration paths and explicit trade-offs.

docs.title: Changes Since the Review
docs.text:
The findings describe commit e7f9dd6; only factual slips about that commit were corrected in place. These statements in them no longer describe the current branch:

  • Packages. Three packages added since then are not reviewed: the logger microservice (servers/logger/), the DT automation library (lib/dt-automation/) and the shared GitLab Python library (lib/gitlab_common/).
  • Services. The platform now runs three backend services: the library microservice, the DT Runner and the logger microservice.
  • Image pins. The docker compose files now pin intocps/dtaas-web:1.7.1 and intocps/libms:0.5.13 (at the review: 1.0.2 and 0.5.9), and add intocps/logger-ms.
  • Observability. The logger microservice exposes GET /logger/health and writes workflow events as JSON Lines (logs/workflow-logs.jsonl by default). The library microservice and the runner still have no health endpoint.
  • CI. The workspace.yml workflow is gone, and logger-ms.yml, dt-automation.yml, gitlab-common.yml, docs-publish.yml and qlty.yml have been added.
  • Resource limits. Users added through the DTaaS CLI get CPU, memory and process limits from the [common.resources] section of dtaas.toml (cli/src/templates/users.resources.yml). The finding on missing limits applies to the users defined directly in the base compose files.

docs.title: Summary Verdict
docs.text:
DTaaS has a clear product vision, unusually good documentation for a research platform and substantial test investment in the client. The main architectural risks are concentrated in four areas:

  • the gap between the documented and the implemented architecture;
  • the delegation of core platform logic (DT lifecycle, execution, state) to the browser and to GitLab;
  • a perimeter-only security model in which internal services trust the network;
  • a static per-user deployment model that limits scale.

None of these is fatal. All four can be addressed incrementally, and the improvements document proposes concrete paths.

docs.title: Architecture Review (As Implemented)
docs.text: The architecture page describes the intended architecture. This page documents the architecture that the code and deployment artifacts realised at the time of the review, because the two differ in important ways; see systemic issue SI-1.

docs.title: Requirements Traceability
docs.text:
The architecture page lists eight user requirements. Their implementation status, recovered from code, is:

Requirement Status Implemented by Author Implemented User workspaces (containers), integrated GitLab Consolidate Implemented Library microservice, client library pages Configure Partial Client editors (client/src/route/digitaltwins/editor, Monaco) Execute Partial GitLab CI pipelines triggered from the browser; DT Runner Explore Partial Client DevOps pages, IndexedDB execution history Save Not implemented None Services Implemented dtaas-services CLI (MQTT, InfluxDB, Grafana, …) Share Partial GitLab group/project visibility; common library files

Components named in the architecture but absent from the codebase are the DT Lifecycle Manager, DT Execution Manager, Accounting microservice, Security microservice (RBAC) and a service mesh. The architecture page's own component table already marks three of these "Not available yet", and the review found no partial implementations of any of them.

docs.title: High-Level Architecture (Recovered)
docs.text:
┌────────────────────────────┐
  Browser              │  Traefik (service router)  │
 ┌──────────────┐      │  + traefik-forward-auth    │
 │ React client │──────│  (OAuth2 via GitLab)       │
 │              │      └──────┬──────┬──────┬───────┘
 │ DT lifecycle │             │      │      │
 │ orchestration│      ┌──────┘      │      └──────────┐
 │ (gitbeaker)  │      ▼             ▼                 ▼
 │ IndexedDB    │  ┌────────┐  ┌───────────┐  ┌───────────────┐
 │ exec history │  │ libms  │  │ user1..N  │  │ static files, │
 └──────┬───────┘  │(NestJS)│  │ workspace │  │ client assets │
        │          └────────┘  │ containers│  └───────────────┘
        │ REST (direct)        └─────┬─────┘
        ▼                            │ DT Runner (NestJS)
 ┌─────────────────────┐             │ inside workspace
 │ GitLab              │◄────────────┘
 │ - OAuth provider    │
 │ - DT/asset storage  │
 │ - CI pipeline       │
 │   executor          │
 │ - trigger tokens    │
 └─────────────────────┘

Three facts define this architecture, and the intended-architecture diagram shows none of them:

  1. GitLab is the de facto platform backend. It provides identity (OAuth), asset and DT storage (repositories), the execution engine (CI pipelines and runners) and authorisation boundaries (group and project membership). Evidence: lib/dt-automation/src/gitlab/ implements pipeline start, cancel and log fetching against the GitLab REST API, and deploy/dtaas/docker/*/docker-compose.yml wires traefik-forward-auth to GitLab OAuth endpoints.

  2. The browser is the DT lifecycle manager. Orchestration runs client-side: resolving projects, fetching trigger tokens, starting pipelines, polling status and collecting logs (lib/dt-automation/src/gitlab/execution/pipelinePolling.ts, instance.ts). Execution history is persisted in the browser's IndexedDB (client/src/database/executionHistoryDB.ts), so the platform itself holds no record of DT executions.

  3. Security is perimeter-only. Traefik routes by path prefix and traefik-forward-auth authenticates at the edge. Behind the perimeter, no service authenticates its callers. The library microservice exposes GraphQL and cloudcmd without authentication checks (servers/lib/src/ contains no auth middleware), and the DT Runner executes configured commands for any caller (servers/execution/runner/src/app.controller.ts).

docs.title: Data Flows
docs.text:
DT execution flow (primary flow): when the user clicks Execute, the client resolves the GitLab project ID and trigger token, starts a GitLab CI pipeline with variables, polls the pipeline and job status, fetches the job logs and writes the results to browser IndexedDB. The platform's servers take no part in this loop; a network observer sees only browser-to-GitLab traffic.

Asset flow: library assets live either on the file system mounted into libms (local backend) or in git repositories (git backend, servers/lib/src/files/git/git-files.service.ts using isomorphic-git). The client queries them over GraphQL and renders file trees; cloudcmd provides direct file management.

User provisioning flow: an admin runs the Python CLI (cli/), which rewrites docker compose files from templates to add or remove per-user workspace services, then reconciles the running deployment via python-on-whales. Users are compose services, not data.

docs.title: Trade-off Analysis of the Current Architecture
docs.text:
The current shape was chosen for real benefits. This section states what each choice costs.

Delegating the backend to GitLab gave the team a large amount of functionality (auth, storage, CI, permissions, web IDE) for almost no implementation cost, which is a rational choice for a small research team. The price is hard vendor coupling, an execution model constrained to CI pipeline semantics, and a security model bounded by what GitLab OAuth scopes can express. The "backend abstraction" in lib/dt-automation/src/ has exactly one implementation, and its interfaces leak GitLab concepts such as pipelines and trigger tokens.

Putting lifecycle logic in the client avoided building and operating a lifecycle service. The price is that there is no headless API (a CLI or a scheduled job cannot execute a DT without a browser), state dies with the browser profile, trigger tokens are handled in browser memory, and every open tab generates its own polling load.

Perimeter-only security kept the microservices simple. The price is that a single misconfigured Traefik rule, or any foothold inside the docker network, reaches unauthenticated services, including one whose purpose is to execute shell commands.

Users as compose services made multi-user hosting possible with plain docker compose. The price is O(users) compose definitions, a restart of the stack topology to add users, no per-user resource quotas in the base scenarios, and a hard ceiling well below "as a Service" scale.

docs.title: Scale and Reliability Posture
docs.text: The platform services hold no state that matters for load (libms is stateless over mounted files and the runner runs per workspace), so the practical limits are the single Traefik instance, the single GitLab instance and the per-user container model. The single points of failure are Traefik, forward-auth and GitLab. The platform has no health, metrics or alerting support: no /health endpoints, no metrics export and no structured audit log of user actions (see SI-8). This is tolerable at current deployment sizes (tens of users per host), and it is the first thing to revisit if institutional deployments grow.

docs.title: Design Review (Per Component)
docs.text: This page collects findings for individual packages. Problems that cut across packages are in Systemic Issues.

docs.title: React Client (client/)
docs.text:
Strengths. The client is the most mature package. It has about 16 kLOC of source and about 28 kLOC of tests (unit, integration and Playwright end-to-end tests under client/test/), a documented internal architecture (lib/dt-automation/src/ARCHITECTURE.md), typed Redux slices, and runtime configuration injection via env.js that lets one build serve many deployments.

Findings.

  1. The backend abstraction leaks. BackendInterface and the builder/strategy design described in ARCHITECTURE.md promise swappable backends, but GitLab is the only implementation, and the abstractions expose GitLab concepts directly: the Pipeline and TriggerToken types (lib/dt-automation/src/interfaces/execution.ts) and the getTriggerToken methods of GitlabAPI (lib/dt-automation/src/gitlab/backend.ts) and GitlabInstance (lib/dt-automation/src/gitlab/instance.ts), along with pipeline refs. A second backend (for example Gitea) could not be written against these interfaces without changing them. Either commit to GitLab and simplify, or lift the abstraction to lifecycle verbs (start/stop/status/logs) and push the pipeline vocabulary down into the GitLab adapter.

  2. Too much platform logic lives here. Pipeline orchestration, polling, log collection, retries and status interpretation (gitlab/execution/) are platform behaviour rather than presentation. The consequences are detailed in SI-3.

  3. Execution and measurement history are browser-local. src/database/executionHistoryDB.ts and measurementHistoryDB.ts persist to IndexedDB. History is lost on another machine, in another browser or after clearing the profile, and users cannot share it, even though the platform otherwise emphasises sharing.

  4. Parallel util/ and utils/ directories (src/util/, src/utils/) and separate store trees (client/src/store/ and lib/dt-automation/src/store/) blur module boundaries. This is minor, but this kind of drift spreads.

  5. Benchmark and measurement task code ships with the product client. lib/dt-automation/src/gitlab/measure/tasks/ (scenarios with multiple identical DTs and with different runners) is experiment tooling embedded in the production bundle. It belongs in a separate package, or at least behind a build flag.

docs.title: Library Microservice (servers/lib/)
docs.text:
Strengths. The service is small and focused (about 600 LOC of source, with more test code than source). It has a clean NestJS module layout with a config service and a files module whose two swappable providers (local and git) sit behind files-service.factory.ts. This strategy pattern does not leak, unlike the client's.

Findings.

  1. No authentication or authorisation of its own. The GraphQL API and the embedded cloudcmd file manager trust the perimeter entirely. cloudcmd allows file modification and upload, so behind a single mis-scoped Traefik rule it becomes an unauthenticated file manager over the shared asset store.

  2. mock-fs is declared as a production dependency (package.json dependencies). Every production install and Docker image pulls in this test-only file system mocking library. It should be in devDependencies.

  3. Several API surfaces without a stated contract. The service exposes GraphQL (files resolver), cloudcmd's own HTTP/WebSocket API and git operations via isomorphic-git. The documentation does not say which surface is the supported integration contract; API.md and HTTP.md describe the surfaces separately.

docs.title: DT Runner (servers/execution/runner/)
docs.text:
Strengths. The runner is minimal by design (about 400 LOC): a whitelist of permitted commands from runner.yaml, Zod-validated DTOs and execa-based process management. The whitelist model is the right instinct.

Findings.

  1. No caller authentication. Any process that can reach the port can run any whitelisted command and read the execution history. The runner relies entirely on network placement. A bearer-token check, even a static shared secret from its YAML config, would be a cheap and meaningful hardening step.

  2. Queue is not a queue. queue.service.ts appends every command it receives to an array; activeCommand() returns the last element, nothing is ever dequeued, and checkHistory() returns the whole array. It is an unbounded execution log with a misleading name. Memory grows with every command, and the type does not express how concurrent commands are handled (is a second command rejected or queued?). Rename it, bound it and make the concurrency policy explicit.

  3. Silent failure channel. newCommand reduces every failure to one boolean, and the controller maps it to a generic invalid command response. The caller cannot tell "not whitelisted" from "spawned but exited non-zero" or "spawn failed".

docs.title: DTaaS CLI (cli/) and Services Manager (deploy/services/cli/)
docs.text:
Strengths. The new CLI (commit e7f9dd6) consolidates user and configuration management with templates (dtaas.toml, generated compose files), validation, and reconcile and uninstall flows. This is the right direction for reducing the deployment matrix. dtaas-services has its own test tree for each service.

Findings.

  1. Two Python CLIs with overlapping missions. cli/ (platform installation, users) and deploy/services/cli/ (third-party services, including its own GitLab compose template) both template compose files and wrap docker, and they are packaged and released separately. The boundary between them is historical rather than conceptual, and admins must learn both.

  2. Compose-file rewriting as the user model. Users are managed by editing YAML service definitions. This works at current scale, but it couples user management to file-format details and requires file system access to the deployment host. There is no API that an admin UI could call. (Accepted for now; see improvement I-7 before investing here.)

docs.title: Deployment Scenarios (deploy/)
docs.text:
Findings.

  1. Four docker scenarios, Vagrant and two CLIs form the real installation matrix (localhost, server, secure-server, secure-server with GitLab, and a single Vagrant machine in deploy/vagrant/ with optional developer provisioning). Each scenario has its own compose file and CONFIG.md, and drift between them is already visible (see the next point). Each new scenario adds to the testing and documentation burden.

  2. Image version drift and unpinned images. The docker compose files pin versions of the intocps/dtaas-web and intocps/libms images that can lag behind the latest releases on Docker Hub. traefik-forward-auth uses the :latest tag of a third-party image whose upstream maintenance has stalled. The release process does not update the compose files (see SI-7).

  3. No resource limits on user workspaces. Workspace containers in the base scenarios have no CPU or memory limits, so one user can starve a shared host. The intended architecture assigns these accounting and quota functions to the accounting service, which has not been built.

docs.title: Documentation and CI
docs.text: The documentation tree is a real asset: per-package DEVELOPER.md files, admin scenario guides, a test pyramid description and MkDocs publishing. CI runs per package (client, lib-ms, runner, Python CLIs, docs, workspace) with Codecov upload and SonarCloud badges. The gaps: no integration pipeline exercises a composed deployment end to end, and quality gates differ between packages. The client has extensive end-to-end tests, the runner and libms have unit, integration and end-to-end Jest tests but no browser-level tests, and STATUS.md does not show coverage for the Python packages.

docs.title: Improvement Proposals
docs.text: These proposals are prioritised and incremental. Each names the systemic issues it addresses, sketches a migration path that avoids a big-bang rewrite, and states the trade-off it accepts. The priorities are P1 (do next; unblocks the rest), P2 (do after the P1 seams exist) and P3 (continuous or opportunistic).

docs.title: I-1 (P1): Introduce a minimal DT Lifecycle service
docs.text:
Addresses SI-1, SI-3; enables I-2, I-4, I-7.

Create the first real increment of the documented DT Lifecycle Manager: a small NestJS service (matching the team's existing skills and the libms and runner idioms) that owns the verbs start / stop / status / logs / history for DT executions. Its first version implements them by calling GitLab exactly as the client does today. The orchestration code in lib/dt-automation/src/gitlab/execution/ serves as a de facto specification and can be ported almost mechanically.

Migration path: (1) stand the service up behind Traefik next to libms; (2) port the pipeline start, poll and log logic from the client; (3) switch the client's BackendInterface implementation to call the lifecycle service instead of GitLab, removing gitbeaker from the browser bundle; (4) move trigger tokens server-side. The client's existing abstraction is the right cut point, and this is where building it pays off.

Trade-off: one more service to deploy and operate, and the direct path from browser to GitLab, which currently keeps that traffic off the platform, becomes platform traffic. This is accepted because every further platform capability (headless API, history, accounting, quotas) needs this seam.

docs.title: I-2 (P1): Server-side execution history
docs.text:
Addresses SI-3, SI-8; prerequisite for accounting.

Give the lifecycle service a persistent store (SQLite per deployment is enough at first; the schema in client/src/database/executionHistoryDB.ts is a starting point) and record every execution with user, DT, timestamps and outcome. IndexedDB can stay as an offline cache, but the server becomes the source of truth. This also produces the audit trail that SI-8 notes is missing.

Trade-off: this introduces the platform's first stateful service, so the admin docs need a note on backup and restore. This is accepted, because IndexedDB cannot serve as the system of record for a multi-user platform.

docs.title: I-3 (P1): Second security layer behind the perimeter
docs.text:
Addresses SI-4.

Three cheap, independent steps:

  1. Validate the identity issued by forward-auth at each service. Forward-auth already forwards X-Forwarded-User; services should reject requests without it, and the Traefik edge should strip the header so that it cannot be spoofed from outside.
  2. Add a shared-secret or JWT check to the DT Runner. It executes commands, so it must not be open.
  3. Replace thomseddon/traefik-forward-auth:latest with a maintained, version-pinned equivalent (for example oauth2-proxy), or at least pin a digest.

A small shared NestJS guard package keeps this uniform across libms, the runner and the new lifecycle service.

Trade-off: slightly more configuration per service and a migration note for existing deployments. There is no architectural cost; the current design simply omits this defence in depth.

docs.title: I-4 (P2): Reshape the backend abstraction around lifecycle verbs
docs.text:
Addresses SI-2.

After I-1, the GitLab vocabulary (pipelines, trigger tokens, refs) lives in exactly one adapter inside the lifecycle service. Define the provider interface there in DT terms (execute(dt, config), status(execution), logs(execution)) and keep GitLab as the reference implementation. Do not build a second provider speculatively. The goal is an honest seam, so that a Gitea, GitHub or local-executor provider becomes a bounded project when a concrete adopter needs one.

Trade-off: the abstraction has to be maintained without a second implementation to validate it. Deriving the interface from verbs already in use, rather than from anticipated generality, reduces this risk.

docs.title: I-5 (P2): Collapse the deployment matrix
docs.text:
Addresses SI-6, SI-7.

Declare the new DTaaS CLI (cli/) the single supported entry point for platform deployment, and turn the four docker scenario directories into generated artifacts (or examples explicitly marked as frozen) instead of parallel copies maintained by hand. Remove the overlap between cli/ and deploy/services/cli/, either by making the services CLI a dependency that the platform CLI invokes or by merging the packages. In CI, add one composed smoke test: bring up the localhost scenario via the CLI, log in, list library assets and run one trivial DT. This single job catches the cross-package breakage that per-package workflows cannot detect.

Trade-off: scenario flexibility narrows and some existing installation habits break, so a deprecation cycle of one release is needed. This is accepted because the matrix is the project's largest hidden maintenance cost.

docs.title: I-6 (P2): Release-time consistency checks
docs.text:
Addresses SI-7.

Automate what is currently coordinated by hand. Add a release workflow step that (1) rewrites image tags in the compose scenarios (generated, after I-5) to the versions being released; (2) fails on any :latest tag; (3) runs npm pkg-level checks such as "no test libraries in dependencies". Moving mock-fs to devDependencies in libms can happen immediately, independent of the rest. These steps take hours of CI work.

docs.title: I-7 (P3): Quotas and the path to the Execution Manager
docs.text:
Addresses SI-5; depends on I-1, I-2.

In the near term, add CPU and memory limits to the workspace container templates. This takes one line per service and protects shared hosts immediately. In the medium term, once the lifecycle service records executions (I-2), quota enforcement has both a data source and an enforcement point. "Users as data" (an API-driven provisioner wrapping the docker API, replacing compose-file rewriting) then becomes the first real slice of the Execution Manager. Defer any discussion of Kubernetes until a deployment outgrows one host; compose with limits is the right tool at current scale.

docs.title: I-8 (P3): Truth-first documentation and ADRs
docs.text:
Addresses SI-1.

Restructure the architecture page into "Implemented architecture" (the recovered diagram in the architecture review can seed it) and "Target architecture", and make the status column of the component table prominent. Record the load-bearing decisions that are currently implicit (GitLab as backend, perimeter auth, users as services, browser-side orchestration) as short ADRs. The repository has no adr/ directory today. ADRs let future contributors tell decisions made for stated reasons from ones that accumulated. This proposal costs only writing time and can begin immediately.

docs.title: Observability note (cross-cutting)
docs.text: Fold this into I-1 and I-3 instead of running a separate project: every service gains a /health endpoint (NestJS Terminus is one dependency), and the lifecycle service logs structured events. Grafana is already in the list of supported services, so pointing it at the platform's own signals closes SI-8 with tooling that admins already deploy.

docs.title: What to Revisit as the System Grows
docs.text:
These signals should trigger a re-evaluation of decisions that this review otherwise endorses:

  • more than about 50 workspaces on a host, or any multi-host deployment (revisit compose-based provisioning, I-7);
  • a concrete non-GitLab adopter (fund the second provider, I-4);
  • commercial accounting requirements (the SQLite store of I-2 becomes Postgres and event-shaped);
  • a need for interactive or long-running DT execution. Then the CI pipeline execution model itself becomes the constraint, not just where it runs. That is a larger redesign and should get its own ADR when it arrives.

docs.title: Systemic Issues
docs.text: These issues cut across packages. They recur in several packages, survive individual refactorings and shape what the platform can become. Each is stated with evidence and consequences; the remedies are in Improvement Proposals.

docs.title: SI-1: Documented vs implemented architecture
docs.text:
The architecture page presents a microservice architecture with a service mesh, security (RBAC), accounting, a DT lifecycle manager and an execution manager. None of these five components exists in any form in the codebase, and the implemented system (edge auth, three services and GitLab) has a very different security and data topology. The page's own component table admits three gaps ("Not available yet"), but the prose and diagrams above it describe the planned system as if it were current.

Consequence: new contributors and adopters evaluating the platform form a wrong model of the system, and design discussions argue from components that do not exist. The architecture that is actually implemented, which is defensible on its own terms, is not written down anywhere. The current-status page partly compensates but does not describe the topology.

docs.title: SI-2: GitLab is a hard dependency, not a backend choice
docs.text:
Identity, asset storage, DT execution and authorisation all resolve to GitLab. The client's backend abstraction has one implementation whose interface leaks GitLab vocabulary (trigger tokens, pipelines). Forward-auth is configured against GitLab OAuth URLs, the DevOps integration assumes GitLab CI semantics, and even the services CLI ships a GitLab compose template. There is no seam where a different provider could be inserted without touching every layer.

Consequence: every GitLab breaking change is a platform breaking change. Institutions that run GitHub, Gitea or plain git cannot adopt DTaaS without also adopting GitLab. The execution model is permanently constrained to CI pipeline semantics (batch jobs, per-commit refs, runner scheduling), even where DTs need long-running or interactive execution.

docs.title: SI-3: The browser is the platform
docs.text:
DT lifecycle orchestration, pipeline polling, log aggregation and the only persistent record of executions (IndexedDB) live in the React client. The platform's own servers neither mediate nor observe DT executions.

Consequence: no headless automation (CLI, cron job, external system) can run a DT. Execution history is stored per browser profile and cannot support auditing, accounting or the "Save" requirement. Closing a tab orphans in-flight orchestration, and secrets (trigger tokens) pass through browser memory. The unbuilt Lifecycle Manager (SI-1) also becomes harder to introduce, because its logic keeps accumulating client-side in TypeScript coupled to React state.

docs.title: SI-4: Perimeter-only trust
docs.text:
A single enforcement point (Traefik with forward-auth) protects every service. libms (including cloudcmd file management), the runner (command execution) and the workspace containers accept any request that reaches them. Authorisation works at the granularity of path prefixes. The forward-auth component is a third-party image pulled at :latest.

Consequence: one routing misconfiguration, one compromised container on the docker network or one forward-auth regression exposes the entire platform, including arbitrary (whitelisted) command execution in workspaces. The design has no defence in depth, and nothing in the codebase currently provides a second layer that could be turned on.

docs.title: SI-5: Static, file-edited user model
docs.text:
Users are docker compose services that the CLI generates from templates. Provisioning requires access to the host file system and a reconciliation of the stack, and per-user resources are unbounded in the base scenarios.

Consequence: scale is capped by compose-file size and the capacity of a single host. Onboarding cannot be self-service or API-driven. Quotas and accounting (a stated prerequisite for commercialisation) have no enforcement point. This is the concrete form of the missing Execution Manager.

docs.title: SI-6: Sprawling deployment and configuration matrix
docs.text:
The matrix spans four docker scenarios, each with integrated or external GitLab, plus Vagrant variants. Two Python CLIs both generate compose files, and there are at least four configuration mechanisms (env.js runtime injection, .env files, YAML service configs, dtaas.toml). The documentation covers each cell, CI does not, and drift between cells is already visible.

Consequence: maintenance effort grows with the matrix rather than with features. Every release must be reasoned through N scenarios by hand, and users on the less common paths find the breakage first.

docs.title: SI-7: Release engineering gaps
docs.text:
