Compose scenarios pin superseded image versions (dtaas-web:1.0.2 against the released 1.3.0; libms:0.5.9 against 0.5.11). One security-critical image floats on :latest. A test library (mock-fs) ships in the libms production dependencies. Versions across npm, Docker Hub, PyPI and the compose files are coordinated by hand.

Consequence: installing from the repository and installing the release give different systems. The floating tag creates supply-chain exposure, and misplaced dependencies bloat images and widen the attack surface.

docs.title: SI-8: No observability plane
docs.text:
No platform service exposes health or metrics endpoints, there is no structured audit log of user or DT activity, and the admin docs give no monitoring guidance. The only operational signals are container logs and GitLab's own UI.

Consequence: operators learn about failures from user reports, accounting (SI-5) has no data source, and SLO-style operation of an institutional deployment is not possible.

docs.title: Interdependency Map
docs.text:
The issues depend on each other. SI-2 and SI-3 together block the Lifecycle and Execution managers whose absence makes up SI-1. SI-5 and SI-8 together block accounting. SI-4 is cheap to fix only while the number of services is small, that is, before fixing SI-1 adds services. The improvement proposals are prioritised in this dependency order:

SI-3 (browser logic) ──► fix first: creates the server-side seam
    │
    ├──► enables server-side history/audit ──► SI-8, then SI-5 quotas
    │
    └──► shrinks GitLab surface area ──► makes SI-2 tractable
SI-4 (perimeter trust) ── fix in parallel: cheapest now
SI-6/SI-7 (matrix, releases) ── continuous reduction, CI-enforced
SI-1 (docs) ── fix immediately: writing, not engineering

docs.title: OAuth Username Resolution in the React Client
The Problem
docs.text:
The client used to extract the logged-in username in Authentication.ts with a single, GitLab-specific method:

const profileUrl = auth.user.profile.profile ?? '';
const username = profileUrl.split('/').filter(Boolean).pop() ?? '';

This assumed that the OIDC provider always exposes a profile claim holding a URL whose last path segment is the username, which is what GitLab does (https://gitlab.example.com/username). It failed silently for other providers:

  • Keycloak exposes preferred_username, not a profile URL.
  • Native Dex also exposes preferred_username and no profile URL. A companion Python proxy was built to inject a synthetic profile URL as a workaround.
  • For any OIDC provider without a profile URL, the username became "" with no error.

AccountTabData.tsx made the same assumption when displaying and linking the profile.

docs.title: The Solution: a provider-agnostic resolver module
docs.text: client/src/util/auth/oauthUserProfile.ts holds all claim resolution logic in one module. It exports three functions.

docs.title: resolveOAuthUsername(profile)
docs.text:
Walks a fixed priority chain and returns the first usable value:

1. preferred_username   ← Keycloak, Dex, most OIDC
2. username             ← some custom providers
3. nickname             ← OpenID standard optional claim
4. login                ← GitHub-style providers
5. local part of email  ← Dex connector fallback (e.g. "alice" from "alice@example.com")
6. local part of upn    ← Azure AD / Entra ID
7. last path segment of profile URL  ← GitLab (preserves old behaviour)
8. sub                  ← worst-case fallback, always present

The chain is ordered by reliability and specificity. GitLab's URL-based extraction sits at step 7 for backward compatibility, and sub is the last resort.

isSafeUsername() checks each candidate before it is accepted. A candidate is used only if it matches ^[A-Za-z0-9._@+-]+$ and does not contain ..; otherwise the chain falls through to the next claim. Because the check applies to every candidate, sub included, the function returns an empty string when no claim yields a path-safe value, even if other claims are present. This protects the URL paths described in Downstream coupling.

docs.title: resolveOAuthProfileUrl(profile)
docs.text: Looks for profile, then html_url (GitHub). Before returning, it passes the candidate through isSafeExternalUrl(), which rejects any protocol other than http: or https:. This prevents XSS through javascript: or data: URLs placed in the href of the profile link. The function returns undefined instead of an unsafe URL.

docs.title: resolveOAuthPictureUrl(profile)
docs.text: Looks for picture (GitLab), then avatar_url, and applies the same isSafeExternalUrl() check. It returns undefined when the provider supplies no usable picture, and the caller falls back to an initial or an icon.

docs.title: Authentication.ts: useGetAndSetUsername
docs.text:
A single call replaces the GitLab-specific URL parsing:

// before
const profileUrl = auth.user.profile.profile ?? '';
const username = profileUrl.split('/').filter(Boolean).pop() ?? '';
sessionStorage.setItem('username', username ?? '');

// after
const username = resolveOAuthUsername(auth.user.profile);
sessionStorage.setItem('username', username);

This is where the username is written to Redux state and sessionStorage, from where the rest of the application reads it.

docs.title: AccountTabData.tsx: ProfileTab and SettingsTab
docs.text:
Both components call the resolver functions. When the provider does not expose a profile URL (Keycloak by default, Dex), the UI shows "Your OAuth provider did not expose a profile URL." instead of a broken link:

{profileUrl ? profileSettingsText : profileNotAvailableText}

MenuToolbar.tsx, route/auth/PrivateRoute.tsx and util/envUtil.ts also call resolveOAuthUsername, and MenuToolbar.tsx calls resolveOAuthPictureUrl for the avatar.

docs.title: Internal module structure
docs.text:
oauthUserProfile.ts is built from small private functions:

  • getClaim reads a string claim from the profile, trims it and returns undefined for missing, non-string or empty values.
  • getEmailLocalPart splits on @ and returns the local part.
  • pathFromProfileUrl parses the value with new URL() and returns its pathname. For a value that is not an absolute URL, it falls back to the raw path when the value contains /.
  • getUsernameFromProfileUrl returns the last segment of that path.
  • isSafeExternalUrl parses with new URL() (no regex) and allows only http: and https:.
  • isSafeUsername restricts a resolved username to a URL-path-safe character set and rejects .., so an unsafe claim is skipped.
  • firstDefinedValue returns the first entry of an array that is not undefined. resolveOAuthProfileUrl and resolveOAuthPictureUrl use it.

None of the seven is exported. The module's public surface is the three resolve* functions (resolveOAuthUsername, resolveOAuthProfileUrl and resolveOAuthPictureUrl).

docs.title: Downstream coupling: username as GitLab namespace
docs.text:
The resolver is provider-agnostic, but the resolved username is more than a display string. It is stored in sessionStorage and Redux, and the GitLab backend layer then uses it as a namespace, inserted unencoded into URL paths such as:

${authority}/${group}/${username}/-/raw/${branch}/...

(lib/dt-automation/src/digitalTwin.ts, lib/dt-automation/src/libraryAsset.ts, and the workbench and service links in util/envUtil.ts and route/workbench).

This has two consequences:

  1. Security: because the value ends up unencoded in a URL path, isSafeUsername validates it at the single point of resolution, so a crafted claim cannot inject path separators or .. traversal. The input is a signed OIDC token and GitLab enforces authorization on the server, so this is defence in depth, not a fix for an exploitable hole.
  2. Operations: for a provider other than GitLab (Keycloak, Dex, GitHub), the resolved username must match an existing GitLab account. Otherwise sign-in succeeds while every GitLab-backed request fails. The client is provider-agnostic, but the backend identity model is still GitLab, so keep provider usernames aligned with GitLab usernames.

docs.title: Effect on provider-specific infrastructure
docs.text:
A companion Python service for Dex used to exist only to work around the old GitLab assumption. It intercepted /dex/userinfo responses and injected a synthetic profile URL of the form {issuer}/{preferred_username} so that the GitLab-specific parser could extract the username.

Because preferred_username is now checked first, Keycloak and Dex both resolve usernames from standard claims. The companion service is no longer needed and is not part of deploy/workspace/dex/localhost/.

docs.title: GitLab CI/CD Infrastructure
docs.text: The files in the Library are stored in a Git repository, so DTaaS uses GitLab's parent-child pipelines to run them. A parent pipeline starts another pipeline, the child pipeline, in the same project. GitLab's documentation on CI/CD Pipelines describes pipelines in more detail.

docs.title: CI/CD Pipelines
docs.text:
Continuous Integration (CI) and Continuous Deployment (CD) are two parts of the DevOps methodology.

CI means integrating code changes into a shared repository often. Each integration triggers automated builds and tests, so problems are detected early. Changes are checked quickly, which reduces integration problems.

CD automates the release process: code changes are tested and prepared for deployment automatically. Teams using CD can deploy updates quickly and reliably. Together, CI/CD automates the software delivery pipeline and removes most or all of the manual work needed to move a code change from a commit to a production environment. The process covers compilation, testing (unit, integration and regression), deployment and infrastructure provisioning.

GitLab explains CI/CD practices in more detail in this article.

A CI/CD pipeline is a series of automated processes that carry out CI and CD. Once started, a pipeline runs without manual intervention.

GitLab covers the whole DevOps lifecycle in one application, including everything CI/CD needs. Its pipeline documentation was the main reference for this design.

A pipeline is made of jobs and stages. Jobs define the tasks to carry out, and stages define the order in which jobs run. When all jobs in a stage succeed, the pipeline moves on to the next stage. If any job fails, the pipeline stops.

When a pipeline starts, its jobs are distributed among the available runners.

GitLab runners are agents of the GitLab Runner application. They execute jobs according to their configuration and the available resources. Runners can run on virtual machines, in containers or on physical servers, and can be managed locally or in the cloud.

DTaaS uses this parent-child pipeline setup to execute the digital twins stored in a user's GitLab repository.

Note

The recommended way to modify these pipelines is through the Digital Twins Preview Page.

docs.title: Parent Pipeline
docs.text:
The parent pipeline is the top-level element. It has a single stage, triggers, which triggers the child pipelines.

The .gitlab-ci.yml file in the user repository holds the triggers for the DTs. Each trigger belongs to one DT and becomes active when the API call provides the matching value of the DTName variable. The RunnerTag variable sets a custom runner tag that executes each job in the DT's pipeline.

For one parent pipeline execution, the generated DTName rules must activate exactly one trigger job. The client treats zero downstream pipelines as a transitional state and rejects multiple downstream pipelines as a configuration error; it never picks the first result in API order.

The keywords used in the pipeline configuration are:

  • image: the Docker image, such as fedora:41, that provides the environment for the pipeline.
  • stages: the phases of the pipeline, such as triggers, which run in order.
  • trigger: starts another pipeline, using the configuration from an external file.
  • include: imports configuration from another file.
  • rules: conditions for running a job, based on variables or states.
  • if: a condition within rules that decides, from the value of a variable, whether a job runs.
  • when: when the job runs, such as always.
  • variables: variables, like RunnerTag, passed to the pipeline.

Here is an example YAML file that registers a trigger for a DT named mass-spring-damper:

image: fedora:41

stages:
  - triggers

trigger_mass-spring-damper:
  stage: triggers
  trigger:
    include: digital_twins/mass-spring-damper/.gitlab-ci.yml
  rules:
    - if: '$DTName == "mass-spring-damper"'
      when: always
  variables:
    RunnerTag: $RunnerTag

docs.title: Digital Twin Structure
docs.text:
The digital_twins folder contains DTs built by one or more users. They are meant to be flexible enough to reconfigure for specific use cases.

For example, the dtaas/user1 repository on gitlab.com has a digital_twins directory with a hello_world example. Its file structure is:

hello_world/
├── lifecycle/
│   ├── clean
│   ├── create
│   ├── execute
│   └── terminate
├── .gitlab-ci.yml
└── description.md

The lifecycle directory contains four files, clean, create, execute and terminate, which are simple BASH scripts. They correspond to stages in a digital twin's lifecycle.

docs.title: Child Pipelines
docs.text:
Each DT folder contains a child pipeline that automates the DT's lifecycle. Each child pipeline ignores the image given in the parent pipeline and uses the image set in its own YAML configuration, or Ruby's default image if none is set.

The keywords used in a child pipeline, based on GitLab's CI/CD YAML syntax reference, are:

  1. stage: the steps of the pipeline, such as create, execute and clean, which run in a fixed order.
  2. script: the commands to run at each step, for example changing directories, modifying permissions or running lifecycle scripts.
  3. tags: which runner runs the jobs, giving control over where and how they run.

For the mass-spring-damper DT, the stages create, execute and terminate the DT simulation, then clean up the environment so it is ready for the next execution. Here is an example configuration that defines create, execute and clean in the child pipeline:

image: ubuntu:20.04

stages:
    - create
    - execute
    - clean

create_mass-spring-damper:
    stage: create
    script:
        - cd digital_twins/mass-spring-damper
        - chmod +x lifecycle/create
        - lifecycle/create
    tags:
        - $RunnerTag

execute_mass-spring-damper:
    stage: execute
    script:
        - cd digital_twins/mass-spring-damper
        - chmod +x lifecycle/execute
        - lifecycle/execute
    tags:
        - $RunnerTag

clean_mass-spring-damper:
    stage: clean
    script:
        - cd digital_twins/mass-spring-damper
        - chmod +x lifecycle/terminate
        - chmod +x lifecycle/clean
        - lifecycle/terminate
    tags:
        - $RunnerTag

docs.title: Direct API Calls
docs.text:
A GitLab DevOps pipeline can be triggered through an API call with a pipeline trigger token created on the GitLab instance. The call needs these values:

  1. <trigger_token>: the user's GitLab trigger token.
  2. <digital_twin_name>: the name of the DT (e.g. mass-spring-damper).
  3. <runner_tag>: the tag of the GitLab runner the user wants to use.
  4. <project_id>: the ID of the GitLab project, shown on the project overview page.

The example below sets the DTName variable to the DT name and the RunnerTag variable to the GitLab Runner tag, and runs the pipeline on the main branch:

    curl --request POST \
      --form "token=<trigger_token>" \
      --form ref=main \
      --form "variables[DTName]=<digital_twin_name>" \
      --form "variables[RunnerTag]=<runner_tag>" \
      "https://intocps.org/gitlab/api/v4/projects/<project_id>/trigger/pipeline"

docs.title: Reference
docs.text: Vanessa Scherma, Design and implementation of an integrated DevOps framework for Digital Twins as a Service software platform, Master's Degree Thesis, Politecnico Di Torino, 2024.

docs.title: OAuth 2.0 and Keycloak Summary
docs.text:
DTaaS uses OAuth 2.0/OIDC at two levels:

  • Browser-side login for the web client.
  • Gateway-side protection for backend routes and workspaces.

docs.title: 1. GitLab-Centred OAuth
docs.text:
The DTaaS packages that use GitLab as the identity provider follow this pattern.

  • The web client authenticates users through the OAuth/OIDC settings in its runtime config.
  • traefik-forward-auth handles gateway authorization.
  • GitLab applications provide the client ID and client secret values that DTaaS components use.

docs.title: 2. Keycloak-Centred OIDC
docs.text:
Workspace secure-server deployments use this pattern.

  • Keycloak provides the realm, users and OIDC clients.
  • traefik-forward-auth validates sessions and tokens and enforces route access.
  • Workspace routes stay protected when users access different sub-paths.

docs.title: Control Plane vs Data Plane
docs.text:
• Control plane: provider setup, secret management and callback URI configuration.
  • Data plane: the request flow through Traefik and forward-auth before it reaches DTaaS.

docs.title: Core Runtime Values
docs.text:
The secure-server OIDC variables include:

  • KEYCLOAK_ISSUER_URL
  • KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_ID
  • KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_SECRET
  • OAUTH_SECRET

GitLab-based scenarios set the equivalent OAuth authority and client values in their own configuration files.

docs.title: Debugging Login Failures
docs.text:
When debugging a login failure, first identify which identity provider pattern is active. Most failures come from a mismatch in one of these:

  • Redirect/callback URL.
  • Client ID and secret.
  • Hostname and TLS assumptions.
  • User whitelist or route policy in the forward-auth config.

Check the configuration first, then the gateway and provider logs.

docs.title: Definition of Software Testing
docs.text: Software testing investigates the quality of a software product across different scenarios. It can also be defined as the process of verifying and validating that a program works as expected and meets the business and technical requirements that guided its design and development.

docs.title: Importance of Software Testing
docs.text: Testing finds defects introduced during the different development phases and checks that the product works as expected in the expected scenarios. A stronger test suite gives more confidence in the product. Tests also let developers make incremental changes to the source code and check that those changes do not break existing functionality.

docs.title: Test Driven Development (TDD)
docs.text: Test Driven Development (TDD) is a development process built on repeating a very short cycle. The developer first writes an automated test case, which initially fails, that defines a desired improvement or new function. They then write the minimum code needed to pass that test, and finally refactor the new code to acceptable standards. TDD is closer to specification than to validation: it gives a method for thinking through requirements or design before writing functional code.

docs.title: Behaviour Driven Development (BDD)
docs.text: Behaviour Driven Development (BDD) grew out of TDD. It keeps the practice of writing tests first, but its tests describe behaviour instead of verifying a unit of implementation. Development and management teams get a shared set of tools and a shared process for working together. BDD usually relies on a simple domain-specific language (DSL) with natural language constructs (e.g., English-like sentences) that express behaviour and expected outcomes. The Mocha and Cucumber testing libraries are built around BDD.

docs.title: Testing Workflow
docs.text:
(Ref: Ham Vocke, The Practical Test Pyramid)

The DTaaS project follows the test pyramid shown above. Testing of a new feature starts with isolated tests and moves towards full integration. The types of tests are explained below, in the order in which they should be performed.

docs.title: Unit Tests
docs.text:
Unit testing tests the individual units or components of a piece of software. Its aim is to isolate a section of code and verify that it is correct.

Ideally, each test case is independent of the others. Substitutes such as method stubs, mock objects and spies help test a module in isolation.

docs.title: Benefits of Unit Testing
docs.text:
• Unit tests increase confidence when changing and maintaining code. When good unit tests run every time the code changes, defects introduced by the change are found quickly.
  • Code designed with fewer interdependencies, to make unit testing easier, suffers fewer unintended effects from changes.
  • Fixing a defect found during unit testing costs less time, effort and money than fixing one found at a higher level.

docs.title: Unit Tests in DTaaS
docs.text: Each DTaaS component uses its own technology stack, so the unit test packages differ between components. The client uses Jest and React Testing Library, and the NestJS servers use Jest. The Python CLIs and libraries use pytest. The build and test command for each project is listed in PROJECT.md in the repository root.

docs.title: Integration Tests
docs.text:
Integration testing combines individual software modules and tests them as a group. The DTaaS project uses an integration server for both software development and integration testing.

The existing integration tests work at the component level. Integration tests between components have not been implemented yet and are deferred to future work.

docs.title: End-to-End Tests
docs.text:
Testing code changes through the end-user interface shows whether the code has the intended effect for users. End-to-End tests in DTaaS require a working setup.

The client has end-to-end tests written with Playwright. The library microservice, the runner and the logger microservice have end-to-end tests run with Jest (yarn test:e2e).

docs.title: Feature Tests
docs.text:
A software feature is a change to the system that adds new functionality or modifies existing functionality. New features should be tested when they are implemented, along with checks that they do not break existing features.

The DTaaS project does not have feature tests yet. Cucumber is planned for implementing them.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Arthur Hicken, Shift left approach to software testing
  2. Justin Searls and Kevin Buchanan, Contributing Tests wiki.
  3. This wiki has a good explanation of TDD and test doubles.

docs.title: Auth Microservice
docs.text: This page describes the workflow and implementation of the DTaaS Auth Microservice. Read the System Design and the OAuth 2.0 summary first.

docs.title: User Identity using OAuth 2.0
docs.text:
This discussion uses the following constants:

  • CLIENT ID: the OAuth 2.0 Client ID of the Auth MS.
  • CLIENT SECRET: the OAuth 2.0 Client Secret of the Auth MS.
  • REDIRECT URI: the URI to which the user is redirected after approving sharing of information with the client.
  • STATE: a random string that identifies a specific "GET authcode" request.
  • AUTHCODE: the single-use authorization code that the OAuth 2.0 provider (the GitLab instance) returns in response to "GET authcode" after the user approves.

Assume also that DTaaS uses a dedicated GitLab instance at https://gitlab.intocps.org (instead of https://intocps.org).

A successful OAuth 2.0 workflow has the following steps:

  • The user requests a resource, say GET/BackendMS.
  • The Auth MS intercepts this request and starts the OAuth 2.0 process.
  • The Auth MS sends an authorization request to the GitLab instance.

The diagram abbreviates this request as GET/authcode. The actual request (a user redirect) looks like:

https://gitlab.intocps.org/oauth/
authorize?
response_type=code&
client_id=OAUTH_CLIENT_ID&
redirect_uri=REDIRECT_URI&
scope=read_user&state=STATE

Here gitlab.intocps.org/oauth/authorize is the GitLab endpoint that handles authorization code requests.

The query parameters include the expected response type, which is fixed as code, meaning that an authorization code is expected. The other parameters are the client ID, the redirect URI, the scope (read_user here) and the state, the random string that identifies the request.

  • The OAuth 2.0 provider redirects the user to the login page, where the user logs into their protected account with their username or email ID and password.

  • The OAuth 2.0 provider then asks the user to approve or deny sharing the requested information with the Auth MS. The user must approve for authentication to succeed.

  • After approval, the GitLab instance redirects the user to the REDIRECT URI, in this form:

REDIRECT_URI?code=AUTHCODE&state=STATE

The REDIRECT URI is the one set when the OAuth 2.0 client was initialised, which is also the one the Auth MS sent in the "GET authcode" request. The GitLab instance adds the query parameters: the AUTHCODE that the Auth MS requested, and the STATE, which is the same random string as in the "GET authcode" request.

  • The Auth MS reads these query parameters and checks that STATE matches the random string it sent in the "GET authcode" request. This confirms that the AUTHCODE answers its own request.

  • The Auth MS exchanges the single-use AUTHCODE for an access token. The access token can be used more than once but expires after a set time. For the exchange, the Auth MS makes another request to the GitLab instance. The sequence diagram abbreviates it as GET/access_token. The actual request is:

POST https://gitlab.intocps.org/oauth/token,
parameters = 'client_id=OAUTH_CLIENT_ID&
client_secret=OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET&
code=AUTHCODE&
grant_type=authorization_code&
redirect_uri=REDIRECT_URI'

For most OAuth 2.0 providers, exchanging an authorization code for a token is a POST request. The https://gitlab.intocps.org/oauth/token endpoint handles token exchange requests. The POST request carries the client ID, the client secret, the AUTHCODE and the redirect URI. The grant type is always authorization_code, which says that an authorization code is being exchanged for an access token.

  • The GitLab instance exchanges a valid AUTHCODE for an access token and sends it to the Auth MS. An example response:
{
  "access_token": "d8aed28aa506f9dd350e54",
  "token_type": "bearer",
  "expires_in": 7200,
  "refresh_token":"825f3bffb2544b976633a1",
  "created_at": 1607635748
}

The access_token field holds the string to use as an access token in the headers of requests for user information. The token_type field is usually bearer. The expires_in field gives the number of seconds the token stays valid, and created_at is the Unix timestamp at which it was created. The refresh_token field holds a string that can extend the access token's lifetime, but the Auth MS does not use it: when an access token expires, the Auth MS requests a new one. Below, TOKEN stands for the access token string from this response.

  • The Auth MS now has an access token that it can use to retrieve the user's information. If the Auth MS already held a valid access token for this user, it would skip the steps above, which exist only to obtain that token.

  • The Auth MS makes a final request to the GitLab instance, abbreviated as GET user_details in the sequence diagram. The actual request is:

GET https://gitlab.intocps.org/api/v4/user
"Authorization": Bearer <TOKEN>

Here, https://gitlab.intocps.org/api/v4/user is the API endpoint that returns user information. The request needs an authorization header with a valid access token; TOKEN is the access token that the Auth MS holds.

  • The GitLab instance verifies the access token and, if it is valid, responds with the user's information, including the username and email ID. An example response:
{
  "id": 8,
  "username": "UserX",
  "name": "XX",
  "state": "active",
  "web_url": "http://gitlab.intocps.org/UserX",
  "created_at": "2023-12-03T10:47:21.970Z",
  "bio": "",
  "location": "",
  "public_email": null,
  "skype": "",
  "linkedin": "",
  "twitter": "",
  "organization": "",
  "job_title": "",
  "work_information": null,
  "followers": 0,
  "following": 0,
  "is_followed": false,
  "local_time": null,
  "last_sign_in_at": "2023-12-13T12:46:21.223Z",
  "confirmed_at": "2023-12-03T10:47:21.542Z",
  "last_activity_on": "2023-12-13",
  "email": "UserX@localhost",
  "projects_limit": 100000
}

The important fields in this response are email and username. Each is unique to a user, so either one identifies the user.

  • The Auth MS reads candidate key fields such as email and username from the response. The Auth MS now knows who the user is.

docs.title: Checking User permissions - Authorization
docs.text:
The Auth MS also enforces access policies for DTaaS resources. Some resources or microservices may need to be restricted to certain users. For example, /BackendMS/user1 might be open only to the user with username user1, and /BackendMS/group3 only to users with an email ID in the @gmail.com domain. The Auth MS has to impose such restrictions. This takes two steps:

  • First, the Auth MS must know and trust the user's identity, that is, believe that the user is who they claim to be. The previous section achieves this.

  • Second, the Auth MS checks this identity against a set of rules or a database of allowed users to decide whether the user may access the requested resource.

The second step needs, for every service, either a set of rules that defines which users may access it, or a database of the user identities allowed to access it. The rules or database use the user identity, here the email ID or username, to make the decision. Rules are written against the form of the username or email ID, for example as a regular expression. A database uses the user identity as its key, and a simple lookup decides whether the user is allowed or denied.

In the sequence diagram, the Auth MS has a self-request marked "Checks user permissions" after it receives the user identity from the GitLab instance. At this point the Auth MS compares the user's identity with the rules or database for the requested service. If the identity has access to the resource, the Auth MS responds with 200 OK. Authentication has then succeeded and the user can access the resource.

Note: the Auth MS and the user never communicate directly. The Auth MS sends and receives all requests and responses through the Traefik gateway. It is the external server of the route's ForwardAuth middleware and talks only to that middleware. If authentication succeeds, the gateway forwards the request to the resource when it receives the 200 OK; otherwise it drops the request and returns the error code to the user.

docs.title: Traefik-forward-auth
docs.text:
The Auth MS is the open-source thomseddon/traefik-forward-auth, configured for DTaaS.

traefik-forward-auth is published as a docker.io image and runs as a Docker container, so it brings no dependency management issues. It is added to Traefik routers as a middleware server, so it needs Traefik to work, as well as the services whose access it controls. Traefik, the traefik-forward-auth service and the other services run together as a stack of Docker containers, and most of the setup is in the docker-compose.yml file.

Configuring the Auth MS takes three steps.

  • Configure the traefik-forward-auth service. First set the environment variables. Because GitLab is the provider, the generic-oauth provider configuration is used. The required variables include the OAuth 2.0 Client ID, Client Secret and scope, as well as the API endpoints for getting an AUTHCODE, exchanging the code for an access token and getting user information.

Also create a router for the REDIRECT URI path, with traefik-forward-auth itself as its middleware. After approval, the user is sent to the REDIRECT URI; this router lets the gateway pass that request to the Auth service for the token exchange. The configuration also defines the ForwardAuth middleware, which the design above requires, and a load balancer for the service. A conf file holding the selective authorization rules (described later) is mounted as a volume. This follows the suggested configuration. The following is added to the Docker services:

traefik-forward-auth:
  image: thomseddon/traefik-forward-auth:latest
  volumes:
    - <filepath>/conf:/conf
  environment:
    - DEFAULT_PROVIDER=generic-oauth
    - PROVIDERS_GENERIC_OAUTH_AUTH_URL=https://gitlab.intocps.org/oauth/authorize
    - PROVIDERS_GENERIC_OAUTH_TOKEN_URL=https://gitlab.intocps.org/oauth/token
    - PROVIDERS_GENERIC_OAUTH_USER_URL=https://gitlab.intocps.org/api/v4/user
    - PROVIDERS_GENERIC_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID=OAUTH_CLIENT_ID
    - PROVIDERS_GENERIC_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET=OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET
    - PROVIDERS_GENERIC_OAUTH_SCOPE=read_user
    - SECRET=a-random-string
    # INSECURE_COOKIE is required if
    # not using a https entrypoint
    - INSECURE_COOKIE=true
  labels:
    - "traefik.enable=true"
    - "traefik.http.routers.redirect.entryPoints=web"
    - "traefik.http.routers.redirect.rule=PathPrefix(`/_oauth`)"
    - "traefik.http.routers.redirect.middlewares=traefik-forward-auth"
    - "traefik.http.middlewares.traefik-forward-auth.forwardauth.address=http://traefik-forward-auth:4181"
    - "traefik.http.middlewares.traefik-forward-auth.forwardauth.authResponseHeaders=X-Forwarded-User"
    - "traefik.http.services.traefik-forward-auth.loadbalancer.server.port=4181"
  • Add the traefik-forward-auth service to the backend services as a middleware.

To do this, add the following lines to the docker-compose configuration of each service:

    - "traefik.http.routers.<service-router>.rule=Path(`/<path>`)"
    - "traefik.http.routers.<service-router>.middlewares=traefik-forward-auth"

This creates a router for the route and attaches the auth middleware to it.

  • Finally, set user permissions by writing rules in the conf file. Each rule has a name (its identifier) and the route on which it applies. A rule also has an action, either auth or allow. With allow, requests on the route skip even the OAuth 2.0 identification. With auth, requests on the route require OAuth 2.0 user identification and follow the sequence diagram. For auth rules, the Auth MS retrieves the user information and uses the user's email ID as the identity. Two kinds of restriction can be configured on this identity:

  • Whitelist: a list of user identities (email IDs in DTaaS) that may access the route.

  • Domain: a domain (for example, gmail.com). Only email IDs in that domain (for example, johndoe@gmail.com) may access the route.

Setting either property on an auth rule gives selective access control over the route. If an auth rule sets neither, the OAuth 2.0 process still runs and retrieves the user identity, but every known user (every user who completes OAuth 2.0) may access the resource.

DTaaS currently uses only whitelist rules.

The rules can be used in three ways, shown below with the lines to add to the conf file.

  • No Auth: serves the Path(`/public`) route with an allow rule.
rule.noauth.action=allow
rule.noauth.rule=Path(`/public`)
  • User specific: serves the Path(`/user1`) route with a rule that allows only the user1@localhost identity.
rule.onlyu1.action=auth
rule.onlyu1.rule=Path(`/user1`)
rule.onlyu1.whitelist=user1@localhost
  • Common Auth: serves the Path(`/common`) route with a rule that requires OAuth 2.0 (action=auth) but allows every valid, known user identity.
rule.all.action = auth
rule.all.rule = Path(`/common`)

docs.title: System Design of DTaaS Authorization Microservice
docs.text: DTaaS needs backend authorization to protect its backend services and user workspaces. This page describes the system design of the DTaaS Auth Microservice, which provides it.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
The Auth MS only has to answer requests of the general form "Is User X allowed to access /BackendMS/example?".

If the GitLab OAuth 2.0 provider verifies the user's identity AND the user is allowed to access the requested microservice or action, the Auth MS responds with a 200 (OK) code and lets the request pass through the gateway to the microservice or server.

If identity verification through GitLab OAuth 2.0 fails OR the user is not permitted to access the requested resource, the Auth MS responds with a 40X (NOT OK) code and stops the request.

docs.title: Forward Auth Middleware in Traefik
docs.text:
Traefik lets you attach middlewares to the routes configured in it. A middleware intercepts requests on a route and can analyse or modify them before passing them on to the services. Traefik's ForwardAuth middleware delegates authentication to an external service. If the external authentication server responds with a 2XX code, the middleware acts as a proxy and lets the request through to the service. If the external server responds with any other code, the middleware drops the request and returns that response code to the user.

(source: Traefik documentation)

An Auth Microservice can therefore be added to the existing gateway and DTaaS system by making it the external authentication server for ForwardAuth middlewares. These middlewares can be attached to any route that needs authentication. DTaaS attaches it to all routes, because the platform requires at least identity verification for every request through the gateway.

docs.title: Auth MS Design
docs.text:
The sequence diagram shows how the integrated Auth MS works.

  • The user makes every request through the React website, the frontend of the DTaaS platform.

  • The request goes through the Traefik gateway, where the route's ForwardAuth middleware intercepts it.

  • The middleware asks the Auth MS whether this request from this user should be allowed.

  • The Auth MS (the auth server) verifies the user's identity using OAuth 2.0 with GitLab, and checks whether the user may make this request.

  • If the user is verified and allowed to make the request, the auth server responds with 200 OK to the Traefik gateway (more precisely, to the middleware in Traefik).

  • Traefik then forwards the request to the service. Any response from the service passes back along the chain to the user.

  • If the user is not verified or not allowed to make the request, the auth server responds with a 40X code to the Traefik gateway.

  • Traefik then drops the request and tells the client that the request was forbidden, passing on the auth server's response code.

docs.title: OAuth 2.0 Summary
docs.text: The Authentication Microservice (Auth MS) follows the OAuth 2.0 RFC specification. This page summarises OAuth 2.0 and how the DTaaS platform uses it.

docs.title: Entities
docs.text:
OAuth 2.0, when used to verify user identity, has three main entities:

  • The User: the entity whose identity the platform is trying to verify. In DTaaS, this is the user of the DTaaS software.
  • The Client: the entity that wants to know or verify the identity of a user. In DTaaS, this is the Auth MS, initialised with a GitLab application. Do not confuse it with the DTaaS frontend website, which the rest of the documentation also calls the client.
  • The OAuth 2.0 Identity Provider: the entity that lets the client know the identity of the user. In DTaaS, this is GitLab. Users usually already have a protected account with this provider. The account is registered under a unique key, such as an email ID or username, and is usually password protected so that only its owner can log in. After logging in, the user is asked to approve sharing their profile information with the client. If they approve, the client gets access to the user's email ID, username and other profile information, which it uses to verify the user's identity.

Note: In general, the authorization server (which requests user approval) and the resource (user identity) provider can be two different servers. In DTaaS, the GitLab instance handles both through different API endpoints. The concepts stay the same, so this page talks about three entities: the User, the OAuth 2.0 Client and the GitLab instance.

docs.title: The OAuth 2.0 Client
docs.text:
Many platforms can initialise an OAuth 2.0 client. DTaaS does it by creating an "application" in GitLab. The client does not have to be initialised on the same platform as the identity provider; the two are separate concerns. The DTaaS OAuth 2.0 client is a GitLab instance-wide application, and its configuration has two main elements:

  • Redirect URI: the URI to which users are redirected after they approve sharing information with the client.
  • Scopes: the types and levels of access the client has to the user's profile. DTaaS needs only the read_user scope, which allows access to the user's profile information for identity verification.

Creating the GitLab application generates a Client ID and a Client Secret. Any application that holds these credentials becomes an OAuth 2.0 Client, so the Client Secret must never be shared. The DTaaS Auth MS uses the Client ID and Client Secret to act as an OAuth 2.0 Client and follow the OAuth 2.0 workflow to verify user identity.

docs.title: OAuth 2.0 Workflows
docs.text: The DTaaS platform uses two OAuth 2.0 flows.

docs.title: OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code Flow
docs.text:
In this flow, the client exchanges an authorization code for access tokens. The DTaaS Auth MS, which secures all backend DTaaS services, uses this flow.

The Client (Auth MS) starts the workflow whenever it needs to verify a user's identity. It sends an authorization request to GitLab and tries to obtain an access token, which lets it fetch user information. With that information, the Auth MS verifies the user's identity and decides whether the user may access the requested resource.

The diagram shows the requests from the Auth MS to the OAuth 2.0 provider in abbreviated form. The Auth MS implementation documentation explains the DTaaS workflow in detail.

docs.title: OAuth 2.0 PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange) Flow
docs.text:
PKCE is an extension to the OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code Flow that adds security for public clients, which cannot store client secrets securely. It protects against attacks such as authorization code interception.

The DTaaS client website uses the PKCE flow for login. The Auth0 documentation describes this flow in more detail.

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
The DTaaS software platform offers:

  • Support for heterogeneous Digital Twin implementations
  • CFD, Simulink, co-simulation, FEM, ROM, ML, and other paradigms
  • Integration with existing Digital Twin frameworks
  • Digital Twins offered as a service
  • Collaboration and reuse of assets
  • Private workspaces for verifying reusable assets and trying out DT executions
  • Lower cost through shared infrastructure

docs.title: Software Features
docs.text:
Each installation of the DTaaS platform includes the features shown in the following diagram.

Every user gets a dedicated workspace. These workspaces are containerized Linux desktops. The user desktops are isolated, so software installed and customisations made in one workspace do not affect other user workspaces. Graphical digital twins can be executed in these private workspaces.

Each user workspace comes with pre-installed development tools, which are accessed through a web browser. The following tools are currently available:

Tool Advantage Jupyter Lab Create and use digital twins and their components in a web browser. All native JupyterLab use cases are supported. Jupyter Notebook Manage files and library assets in a web browser. VS Code in the browser A widely used IDE for software development. Digital twin assets can be developed in this environment. ungit An interactive git client for managing repositories in a web browser.

In addition, an xfce-based remote desktop is accessible through a VNC client that runs in the web browser. Desktop software supported by xfce can also be executed in the workspace.

The workspaces have Internet access, so Digital Twins running in a workspace can interact with both internal and external services.

A DT automation layer manages DT automation tasks. It creates, modifies and executes DTs on both on-premise infrastructure and commercial cloud (DevOps) service providers.

The web client also has a Building Models page that draws IFC building models from the user's library and colours them by the readings of their sensors.

The DTaaS software platform includes several pre-installed services. The currently available services are:

Service Advantage InfluxDB Internet of Things (IoT) device management and data visualisation platform. This service stores data for digital twins and provides alerting capabilities. RabbitMQ Communication broker for message exchange between physical and digital twins. Grafana Visualisation dashboard service for presenting digital twin data. MQTT Lightweight data transfer broker for IoT devices and physical twins providing data to digital twins. MongoDB NoSQL document database for storing metadata from physical twins. PostgreSQL SQL database server for storing historical and time-series data. ThingsBoard Internet of Things (IoT) device management and data visualisation platform.

Users can publish and reuse the digital twin assets available on the platform. Digital twins can also be executed and offered as services to external clients. These clients do not need to be registered users of the DTaaS installation.

docs.title: References
docs.text: Talasila, Prasad, et al. "Composable digital twins on Digital Twin as a Service platform." Simulation 101.3 (2025): 287-311.

docs.title: User Guide
docs.text:
This guide is for users of the DTaaS platform. You need access to a live installation of the DTaaS platform. The simplest option is the workspace localhost installation scenario.

These Slides and Video explain the concepts behind the DTaaS platform.

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
A central question for Digital Twin (DT) software platforms is how to support collaborative activities:

  • Building digital twins (DTs)
  • Using DTs independently
  • Sharing DTs with other users
  • Providing existing DTs as a service to other users

DT software platforms must also offer:

  • Support for DT lifecycle management
  • Scalability through flexible convention over configuration

docs.title: Existing Approaches
docs.text:
Recent literature proposes several solutions to these challenges, including:

  • Focus on data from Physical Twins (PTs) for analysis, diagnosis, and planning
  • Sharing DT assets across upstream and downstream stakeholders
  • Evaluating different models of PT
  • DevOps methodologies for Cyber Physical Systems (CPS)
  • Scaling DT execution and ensemble management of related DTs
  • Support for PT product lifecycle

docs.title: The DTaaS Approach
docs.text:
The DTaaS platform follows these principles[1]:

  • Support for transition from existing workflows to DT frameworks
  • Creation of DTs from reusable assets
  • Enabling users to share DT assets
  • Offering DTs as a Service
  • Integration of DTs with external software systems
  • Separation of configurations for independent DT components

docs.title: References
docs.text: [1]: Talasila, Prasad, et al. "Composable digital twins on Digital Twin as a Service platform." Simulation 101.3 (2025): 287-311.

docs.title: Create a Digital Twin
docs.text:
A digital twin is built from the assets available in the workspace. To bring assets or files from a local computer into the DTaaS workspace, follow the instructions in library assets.

The library assets depend on one another as shown below.

A digital twin is created by linking assets in a meaningful way. The relationship can be written as:

\[ D_t: \{ D{^*},M^{*},(FT)^{+} \}C_{dt} \]

where D denotes data, M denotes models, F denotes functions, T denotes tools, \(C_{dt}\) denotes DT configuration, and \(D_t\) is a symbolic notation for a digital twin itself. The \(\{ D{^*},M^{*},(FT)^{+} \}C_{dt}\) expression denotes composition of a DT from D, M, T, and F assets. The \(*\) indicates zero or more instances of an asset, and \(+\) indicates one or more instances of an asset.

The DT configuration specifies which assets to use and any parameters to set for them. When a DT requires RabbitMQ, InfluxDB, or similar services supported by the platform, the DT configuration must include access credentials for these services.

This generic DT definition is based on DT examples observed in practice, and a DT may deviate from it. The only requirement is that the DT can be executed from either the command line or a graphical desktop environment.

Tip

If you are new to digital twins and do not have separate digital twin assets, only a single directory containing all components, upload this monolithic digital twin into the digital_twins/your_digital_twin_name directory.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
The Examples repository contains a co-simulation setup for a mass-spring-damper system. The example shows how co-simulation can be used in a digital twin.

The file system contents for this example are:

workspace/
  data/
    mass-spring-damper
        input/
        output/

  digital_twins/
    mass-spring-damper/
      cosim.json
      time.json
      lifecycle/
        analyze
        clean
        evolve
        execute
        save
        terminate
      README.md

  functions/
  models/
    MassSpringDamper1.fmu
    MassSpringDamper2.fmu

  tools/
  common/
    data/
    functions/
    models/
    tools/
        maestro-2.3.0-jar-with-dependencies.jar

The workspace/data/mass-spring-damper/ directory contains input and output data for the mass-spring-damper digital twin.

The two FMU models required for this digital twin are in the models/ directory.

The co-simulation digital twin requires the Maestro co-simulation orchestrator. Maestro is reusable across all co-simulation-based DTs, so it is placed in the common/tools/ directory.

The digital twin configuration is in the digital_twins/mass-spring-damper directory. The co-simulation configuration is defined in two JSON files: cosim.json and time.json. Documentation for the digital twin goes in digital_twins/mass-spring-damper/README.md.

The launch program for this digital twin is digital_twins/mass-spring-damper/lifecycle/execute. It runs the co-simulation until completion and then exits. The programs in digital_twins/mass-spring-damper/lifecycle manage the lifecycle of this digital twin. The lifecycle page explains these programs.

Execution of a Digital Twin

A frequent question concerns the run time of a digital twin. The natural intuition is that a digital twin must operate as long as its physical twin is in operation. If a digital twin runs for a finite time and then ends, can it be called a digital twin? Yes. The Industry 4.0 use cases seen among SMEs have digital twins that run for a finite time. Users often run these digital twins when they choose to.

To execute this digital twin:

  1. Open the Workbench page of the DTaaS website and click the Desktop tool. The desktop opens in a new browser tab.
  2. The tab shows the VNC Desktop with a connect button. Click Connect to connect to the Linux desktop of the workspace.
  3. Open a terminal (the black rectangular icon in the top left region of the tab) and enter the commands below.

  4. Download the example files by following the instructions in the examples overview.

  5. Go to the digital twin directory and run:

cd /workspace/examples/digital_twins/mass-spring-damper
lifecycle/execute

The last command executes the mass-spring-damper digital twin and stores the co-simulation output in data/mass-spring-damper/output.

docs.title: Digital Twin Lifecycle
docs.text:
Physical products in the real world go through a product lifecycle. A simplified four-stage product lifecycle is shown here.

A digital twin that tracks physical products (twins) must evolve together with the corresponding physical twin.

The figure shows the activities that can take place in each lifecycle phase.

(Ref: Minerva, R, Lee, GM and Crespi, N (2020) Digital Twin in the IoT context: a survey on technical features, scenarios and architectural models. Proceedings of the IEEE, 108 (10). pp. 1785-1824. ISSN 0018-9219.)

docs.title: Lifecycle Phases
docs.text:
The four-phase lifecycle has been extended to a lifecycle with seven phases. This section lists the phase names and the typical activities in each phase[1].

A DT lifecycle consists of explore, create, execute, save, analyse, evolve and terminate phases.

Phase Main Activities explore Selection of suitable assets based on user requirements and verification of their compatibility for DT creation. create Specification of DT configuration. For existing DTs, no creation phase is required at the time of reuse. execute Automated or manual execution of a DT based on its configuration. The DT configuration must be verified before starting execution. analyse Examination of DT outputs and decision-making. Outputs may include text files or visual dashboards. evolve Reconfiguration of DT primarily based on analysis results. save Preservation of DT state to enable future recovery. terminate Cessation of DT execution.

A digital twin that faithfully tracks the physical twin lifecycle must support all the phases. Digital twin engineers may also add their own phases, so the DTaaS platform is designed to accommodate different DTs.

The phases do not have to run in a fixed order. A digital twin can repeat or skip phases as needed.

A code structure with one program per phase is not mandatory, but it makes DT creation and management within the DTaaS platform easier. The recommended structure is:

workspace/
  digital_twins/
    digital-twin-1/
      lifecycle/
        analyze
        clean
        evolve
        execute
        save
        terminate

Each phase of the DT lifecycle has its own program. A program can be as simple as a script that launches other programs or sends messages to a live digital twin.

Note

The recommended way to implement lifecycle phases within DTaaS is with scripts, for example shell scripts.

docs.title: Example Lifecycle Scripts
docs.text:
The following example scripts manage three phases in the lifecycle of the mass-spring-damper DT.

lifecycle/execute
#!/bin/bash
mkdir -p /workspace/data/mass-spring-damper/output
#cd ..
java -jar /workspace/common/tools/maestro-2.3.0-jar-with-dependencies.jar \
    import -output /workspace/data/mass-spring-damper/output \
    --dump-intermediate sg1 cosim.json time.json -i -vi FMI2 \
    output-dir>debug.log 2>&1

The execute phase uses the DT configuration, the FMU models and the Maestro tool to execute the digital twin. The script stores the co-simulation output in /workspace/data/mass-spring-damper/output.

A DT may not support every lifecycle phase. An unsupported phase can be an empty script, with a message if needed.

lifecycle/analyze
#!/bin/bash
printf "operation is not supported on this digital twin"

The lifecycle programs can invoke other programs in the codebase. For example, the lifecycle/terminate program calls another script to do its work.

lifecycle/terminate
#!/bin/bash
lifecycle/clean

docs.title: References
docs.text: [1]: Talasila, Prasad, et al. "Composable digital twins on Digital Twin as a Service platform." Simulation 101.3 (2025): 287-311.

docs.title: Capabilities
docs.text:
Besides creating and editing digital twins, you can run them and adjust their execution parameters. The DTaaS can run several digital twins at the same time, and you can change settings while they run without fetching the data manually: the data loads again when you return to the branch and group used for the execution. The settings cover both repository and execution options. All twins can be run and checked from the Execute tab of the Digital Twins Page.

Read more about Settings, Setting Values and Concurrent Execution on their own pages.

The following sections describe what each of these features can do.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
The table below lists the test setups (valid, invalid, and so on), the behaviour that was expected and the behaviour that was observed. Each table is followed by a summary and a list of problems found.

Setting Expected behaviour Observed behaviour Test method Runner tag valid Job is picked up by runner with relevant tag and completes without error. Pass: Same as expected. Go to the Settings tab of the Account page. Change Runner Tag. Go back one page. Execute Hello world twin. Verify runner name based on tag (repeat with 2nd runner) Runner tag invalid Job is never picked up. Runner times out after 10 minutes. Pass: Same as expected. Change Runner Tag to "foo" (nonexistent). Run Hello World twin. Runner Tag no value Configuration saves. Running a twin succeeds if appropriate runner exists. Fail: Not picked up, times out. Set run_untagged = false in local gitlab runner config. Mark "Run untagged jobs" as true in gitlab instance (https://dtaas-digitaltwin.com/gitlab). Change Runner Tag to the empty string on application. Run Hello world twin. Branch valid Job runs with the correct branch and completes without error. Pass: Same as expected. Make new branch in GitLab instance project. Change Branch Name to "master-2". Execute Hello world twin. Verify ref matches branch in execution log. Branch invalid Execute tab gracefully displays no twins as branch does not exist. Fail: IF twins are not cached: Throws an error displayed to user: An error occurred while fetching assets: GitbeakerRequestError. IF twins are cached: Job fails. Snackbar says "Execution error for [twin name]". No log available in execution history. Change Branch Name to "master-1" (nonexistent). IF twins are cached: Execute Hello world twin. Group name valid The twin is runnable. Pass: Same as expected. Click "Reset to Defaults". Run twin. Group name invalid Execute tab gracefully displays no twins as group does not exist. Fail: Same as Branch invalid case. Change Group Name to "Foo" (nonexistent). IF twins are cached: Execute Hello world twin. Common name valid Library twins are visible. Pass: Same as expected. *Private twins also show up in Common twins. Click "Reset to Defaults". Go to the Library Page. Go to common twins. Inspect twin visibility. Common name invalid Library twins gracefully not visible. Fail: Displays error: An error occurred while fetching assets: Error: Common project foo not found Change Common Library Project Name to "Foo" (nonexistent). Go to common twins. Inspect visibility. DT directory valid Twins are visible. Pass: Same as expected. Click "Reset to Defaults". Go to the Library Page. Go to the Execute tab. Inspect twin visibility. DT directory name invalid Twins gracefully not visible. Fail: Depends on the cache. Displays error if there is none: An error occurred while fetching assets: GitbeakerRequestError Change DT Directory to "Foo" (nonexistent). Go to the Execute tab. Inspect twin visibility. Group Name, DT Directory, Common Library Project Name, Branch name no value Invalid value caught early. Cannot save, appropriate feedback of invalid form fill out. Fail: Same as Branch invalid case. Change Group Name, DT Directory, Common Library Project Name, Branch Name to the empty string.

Summary: Changing to valid settings works. At best, invalid settings display an error in the page (no cache); otherwise the page shows stale twins.

Problems:

  • Stale state is kept after settings are updated unless the page is refreshed.
  • Technical errors are shown to the user when the settings are invalid.
  • Invalid values such as empty strings are accepted when a value is required.
  • Runners without tags may not work, though this may be a local problem.
  • Private twins show up as common twins.

Note

These tests were run against an earlier version of the website. The Settings form now rejects an empty value in any of these fields and shows a "... is required" message, so the no value cases can no longer be saved.

docs.title: Concurrent Execution
docs.text: Expected behaviour Observed behaviour Test method Both twins run successfully simultaneously. Pass: Same as expected. Run the same twin twice at the same time. All twins run successfully simultaneously. Pass: Same as expected. Run different twins at the same time.

docs.title: Concurrent Execution Across Different Runners
docs.text:
Expected behaviour Observed behaviour Test method Both twins run successfully simultaneously. They report the correct runner name in the Execution logs. Pass: Same as expected. Set up 2 ubuntu GitLab runners with different tags. Change Runner Tag to first runner's tag. Execute twin. Change Runner Tag to second runner tag. Execute another twin. History stays after editing, it is still executing. Pass: Same as expected. Execute → Edit settings → Execute. Check: is history still there? Does it look correct?

Summary:

All functionality works according to the tests. The logs remain after settings change, and any combination of twins and runners works (only Ubuntu runners were tested).

docs.title: Implementing Backends
docs.text: By default the DTaaS uses GitLab as its execution and storage backend, but other combinations may suit some installations better. The code base is designed so that a new backend does not require a rewrite from scratch. Future versions of the DTaaS may include more backends by default, such as GitHub and Azure.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Digital twins can be queued as needed, and changing settings while they run does not lose data, so several setups can be tested at the same time. Developers can also add new backends.

docs.title: Running Multiple Digital Twins at the Same Time
docs.text: The DTaaS platform can execute several digital twins at once. This saves time with long-running digital twins or when they run on different resources.

docs.title: Running Digital Twins
docs.text:
To run a digital twin, open the Execute tab of the Digital Twins Page. Click Automation in the menu on the left, then click the Digital Twins Page card. The page opens in the same browser tab.

The Execute tab shows a card for each digital twin, with its name, a short description and the Start and History buttons. Start sends a job to the backend, which runs the simulation defined by the digital twin's lifecycle files. You can inspect and change these files with the Reconfigure button on the Manage tab.

docs.title: Running Multiple Twins
docs.text:
Pressing Start several times queues several simulations. You can also queue different digital twins.

The deployment service (for example, GitLab) balances the load across the available runners, so it can be configured once and then left to run.

docs.title: The Execution Log
docs.text:
History opens a list of all current and past runs, showing the time of execution and the status (Running, Completed, Failed, Canceled or Timed out). To review the results of a run, click an entry (or the arrow on the right of the entry) to expand it. The log of each job in the pipeline is then shown.

To delete an entry, click the trash icon and confirm the deletion in the dialog. The Clear All button deletes all entries of a digital twin.

Click the stop icon of a running entry to stop that execution:

docs.title: Changing Runners
docs.text: The runners that pick up jobs can be changed in the settings. See these and other settings.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This page described the Execute tab: running several digital twins at once, and inspecting and deleting their logs.

docs.title: Setting Allowed Values
docs.text:
Some setting values cause problems. This page lists the values that are allowed and those that are not, with the errors to expect and troubleshooting steps.

The settings are on the Settings tab of the Account page. The settings page explains what each parameter does.

Note: the user must have access rights to all the resources connected to the application.

The Settings form rejects an empty value in any of these fields and shows a "... is required" message under the field.

docs.title: Runner Tag
docs.text:
• Allowed values

This parameter is a text string such as "linux", "ubuntu" or "2", and it must match a tag of a runner on the execution service:

Multiple values, such as "linux, windows", are not supported and are treated as one tag.

  • Not allowed values

If the Runner Tag field does not match a runner, no runner picks up the job and it times out. If the twins time out unexpectedly, check the spelling of the tag.

Some services, such as GitLab, allow jobs without a tag, which any runner configured to pick up untagged jobs can run. The DTaaS requires a tag, so the field cannot be left blank.

  • Visual examples

docs.title: Branch Name
docs.text:
• Allowed values

The Branch Name field must be a text string matching a branch in the user and common library repositories. For example: "main" or "master":

  • Not allowed values

The field cannot be left empty. Do not set it to a value that does not match a branch in both repositories: the form accepts such a value, but it causes errors or unexpected behaviour.

Expected error:

An error occurred while fetching assets: GitbeakerRequestError: 404 Tree Not Found

  • Visual examples

docs.title: Group name
docs.text:
• Allowed values

The Group Name field is a text string that must match a group in the storage service (for example, GitLab).

Example:

DTaaS

Group names are case insensitive on GitLab, but matching the case exactly is recommended for consistency and to rule it out as a source of error.

  • Not allowed values

If the group does not exist, errors occur when digital twins and other assets are loaded.

Expected error:

An error occurred while fetching assets: GitbeakerRequestError: 404 Group Not Found

  • Visual examples

docs.title: Common Library Project name
docs.text:
• Allowed values

The Common Library Project Name parameter is a text string. It must match the repository that holds the shared resources. Examples: "common" and "library":

If it does not match a repository, the Digital Twins Page and the Library Page cannot load their assets.

Expected error:

An error occurred while fetching assets: Error: Common project <name> not found

  • Not allowed values

Do not set this field to a value that does not match a repository. It should not match a user repository either.

  • Visual examples

docs.title: DT directory
docs.text:
• Allowed values

This is also a text string. It must match the name of the folder in the common library and, above all, in the user repository where the digital twins are stored.

  • Not allowed values

Do not set this to a folder that does not exist. It fails silently: the digital twins do not load, or digital twins from a previous setup show up.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
The digital twins are not showing up:

Check that Group Name, Branch Name, Common Library Project Name and DT Directory match the backend exactly.

The digital twins are timing out:

Check that the Runner Tag is a single tag, not a list, and that a runner with that tag is active.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Every field must be a text string that matches the corresponding repository, group, branch or runner tag on the backend. The troubleshooting steps above cover the most common problems.

docs.title: Digital Twin File Structure in GitLab
docs.text:
GitLab is the file store for DevOps on digital twins. The user interface page is a front end for this GitLab-backed file storage.

Each DTaaS installation comes with an integrated GitLab. It must have a GitLab group named dtaas and a GitLab repository for each user, named after the username. For example, if a DTaaS installation has two users, user1 and user2, the following repositories must exist on the linked GitLab installation.

https://intocps.org/gitlab/dtaas/common.git
https://intocps.org/gitlab/dtaas/user1.git
https://intocps.org/gitlab/dtaas/user2.git

Warning

By default, the assets shown on the Library Page and the Digital Twins Page come from the master branch of the backing GitLab project. Create a branch named master and make it the default branch in all the user repositories, including the common repository. A different branch can be set in the Branch Name field of the settings.

Each user repository must have the following structure.

<username>/
├── common/
├── data/
├── digital_twins/
├── functions/
├── models/
├── tools/
├── .gitlab-ci.yml
└── README.md

This is the same structure the user sees on the Library page.

docs.title: Digital Twin Structure
docs.text:
The digital_twins folder contains DTs that one or more users have built. They are meant to be flexible enough to be reconfigured for specific use cases.

For an example of such a configuration, see the dtaas/user1 repository on gitlab.com. Its digital_twins directory contains a hello_world example with this file structure:

hello_world/
├── lifecycle/ (at least one lifecycle script)
│   ├── clean
│   ├── create
│   ├── execute
│   └── terminate
├── .gitlab-ci.yml (GitLab DevOps config for executing lifecycle scripts)
└── description.md (optional but is recommended)
└── README.md (optional but is recommended)

The lifecycle directory here contains four files, clean, create, execute and terminate, which are simple BASH scripts. They correspond to stages in a digital twin's lifecycle. The lifecycle stages page explains them further.

The .gitlab-ci.yml at the top of the user repository contains one trigger job per digital twin. When the website executes a digital twin, the matching trigger job runs the pipeline defined in that digital twin's own .gitlab-ci.yml. Saving a new digital twin on the Create tab adds its trigger job, and deleting a digital twin removes it.

docs.title: Performance Measurement
docs.text: The DTaaS has a built-in tool that measures the execution time of Digital Twin features. Developers can use it to understand performance and to record baselines for later optimization.

docs.title: Accessing the Measurement Page
docs.text: Open the measurement page from the Measurement card on the Automation page, or at http://localhost:4000/insights/measure or https://intocps.org/insights/measure. Only signed-in users can open this page.

docs.title: Measurement Tasks
docs.text:
The measurement suite includes the following tasks, each measuring a different aspect of Digital Twin execution:

Task Description Valid Setup Digital Twin Execution Runs the primary Digital Twin with current setup Multiple Identical Digital Twins Simultaneously Runs the primary Digital Twin twice at once Multiple different Digital Twins Simultaneously Runs the primary and secondary Digital Twins at once Different Runners same Digital Twin Runs the primary Digital Twin twice with 2 different runners Different Runners different Digital Twins Runs the primary and secondary Digital Twins with 2 different runners

By default, the primary Digital Twin is hello-world and the secondary is mass-spring-damper. Both can be changed in the measurement settings.

docs.title: Configuration Options
docs.text:
The configuration is in the Measurement Settings section of the Settings tab on the Account page.

  • Trial Number: number of times each task is repeated to calculate the average execution time (default: 3).
  • Measurement Secondary Runner Tag: the runner tag used for multi-runner measurement tests. The primary runner tag is the Runner Tag field of the same settings tab.
  • Primary Digital Twin: the Digital Twin used in single-DT and same-DT measurement tasks (default: hello-world).
  • Secondary Digital Twin: the Digital Twin used as the second DT in multi-DT measurement tasks (default: mass-spring-damper).

Note: the first time the settings page is visited in a session, the Primary Digital Twin and Secondary Digital Twin dropdowns load the list of available Digital Twins. They stay disabled until loading completes.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
• Start: begin the measurement suite from the first task
  • Stop: cancel all running executions (asks for confirmation)
  • Restart: discard all current results and start again (asks for confirmation)
  • Export: download all measurement results as a JSON file (available when results exist)
  • Purge: delete all stored measurement data from the database

docs.title: Status Values
docs.text: Status Meaning PENDING Task has not started yet RUNNING Task is currently executing SUCCESS All trials completed successfully FAILURE One or more trials failed STOPPED Task was interrupted by user

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
• Average Duration: mean execution time across all trials of a task
  • Total Time: time for the complete measurement suite (shown after completion)

docs.title: Measurement Table Columns
docs.text:
The measurement results table has the following columns:

Column Description Task Task number, name, and description Status Current execution status (PENDING, RUNNING, SUCCESS, FAILURE, or STOPPED); a dash before the task is queued Average Duration Mean execution time across all completed trials, displayed in seconds Trials Visual cards showing each trial's execution details and status. Each trial represents one iteration of the task Data Download button to export individual task results as JSON

Click a row to expand it and show a toggle next to the task description. A disabled task is skipped during execution.

docs.title: Data Storage
docs.text:
Measurement data is stored in the browser's IndexedDB, separately from the regular execution history. As a result:

  • measurements do not mix with normal DT execution logs
  • measurement data can be purged without affecting execution history
  • results can be downloaded as JSON for further analysis

docs.title: Per-Task Download
docs.text: After a task completes successfully, click Download Task Results in the Data column to export that task's measurements as JSON.

docs.title: Full Results Download
docs.text:
The Export button in the controls toolbar downloads all measurement results as JSON. It is available whenever results exist.

The figure below shows both options after a completed measurement run.

docs.title: JSON Format
docs.text:
The exported JSON describes each task and its trials. Each trial is one iteration of a task and contains an executions array with the pipeline execution details. The configuration is shared at the task level, and each execution includes its runner tag. The task records its own start and end times. A trial carries an Error field only when it records an error.

The exported JSON has the following structure:

{
  "totalTimeSeconds": number,
  "tasks": [
    {
      "Task Name": string,
      "Description": string,
      "config": {
        "Branch name": string,
        "Group name": string,
        "Common Library project name": string,
        "DT directory": string
      },
      "trials": [
        {
          "Time Start": "ISO8601 timestamp",
          "Time End": "ISO8601 timestamp",
          "Status": "PENDING | RUNNING | SUCCESS | FAILURE | STOPPED",
          "Error": { "message": string, "error": object },
          "executions": [
            {
              "dtName": string,
              "pipelineId": number,
              "status": string,
              "Runner tag": string
            }
          ]
        }
      ],
      "Time Start": "ISO8601 timestamp",
      "Time End": "ISO8601 timestamp",
      "Average Time (s)": number,
      "Status": string
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Timing Behaviour
docs.text:
The measurement system waits 750ms between some requests so that the GitLab instance does not receive them all at once:

  • Between trials: a 750ms delay is applied before each trial except the first. Trial 0 starts immediately; trials 1, 2, and so on each wait 750ms after the previous trial completes.
  • Between executions within a trial: when a task runs several Digital Twins (for example, "Multiple different Digital Twins Simultaneously"), each execution is staggered by 750ms. The first execution starts immediately, the second after 750ms, the third after 1500ms, and so on.

After starting each pipeline, the measurement also waits 10 seconds and checks that GitLab accepted it. A pipeline that failed or was canceled in that time is started again.

The Average Duration of a task includes the stagger delay between executions and the 10-second acceptance check. It does not include the delay between trials, because each trial's timer starts after that delay.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Run measurements when the system is lightly used, to get consistent results.
  2. Use several trials (3-5) for more reliable averages.
  3. Make sure runners are available before starting the measurement.
  4. You can navigate to other pages while a measurement runs; execution continues in the background. However, changing the URL, refreshing or closing the tab stops the measurement. Notifications tell you when the measurement completes or stops.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Issue Solution Task appears stuck, old pipelines appear Reauthenticate the app by refreshing the tab Tasks time out Verify runners are online, use the tag and are accessible
