docs.title: Digital Twins and DevOps
docs.text:
DevOps is a well-established software development practice. The DTaaS has an experimental feature that brings DevOps to digital twins.

Recordings of the latest workflows:

  • DTaaS DevOps workflows
  • Automation layer demo

This feature requires a specific installation setup:

  1. Integrated GitLab installation
  2. A valid GitLab repository for the logged-in user. See an example repository. You can clone this repository and customise it as needed.
  3. A GitLab Runner linked to the user's GitLab repository.

To open the feature, click Automation in the menu and then the Digital Twins Page card.

docs.title: DT Lifecycle
docs.text:
The Digital Twins Page implements the Create, Manage and Execute stages of a DT lifecycle. The suggested order of the lifecycle stages is:

Each of the Create, Manage and Execute stages has its own tab. The DT assets for the Create stage are selected on the Library Page. The Manage tab reconfigures digital twins. Execution and termination happen on the Execute tab.

docs.title: Create Tab
docs.text:
Users select reusable DT assets on the Library Page and then arrive on the Create tab. The following figure shows the Create tab after mass-spring-damper was selected as a reusable asset for the new DT.

The menu on the left lets you create the necessary structure and elements of a new DT. Each reusable asset selected for the new DT appears in this menu, and its configuration can be updated.

The files in the left menu fall into three categories.

  • Description: contains README.md, a full description of the DT, and description.md, a brief description. The brief description is shown on the DT cards. The Details button on the Manage tab shows the complete README.md.
  • Configuration: contains a .gitlab-ci.yml for running the lifecycle scripts and other operations of the DT. You can add more JSON and YAML files to configure the new DT.
  • Lifecycle: the DT lifecycle scripts.

The Add New File button adds new files in any of the three categories. Click the Save button to save the new DT. Newly created DTs appear on the Manage and Execute tabs straight away.

docs.title: Manage Tab
docs.text:
The Manage tab offers these operations on a digital twin:

  • Check the details (Details button)
  • Delete (Delete button)
  • Modify or reconfigure (Reconfigure button)

A digital twin placed in the DTaaS has a recommended structure. See the assets page for an explanation and this example.

The Details button shows the README.md stored in the digital twin directory.

The Reconfigure button opens an editor with all the files of a digital twin, and all of them can be updated. The files fall into the same three categories.

  • Description
  • Configuration
  • Lifecycle

docs.title: Execute Tab
docs.text: The Execute tab can run several digital twins at once. When an execution of a digital twin finishes, its execution log is available.

docs.title: DTaaS Examples
docs.text:
The DTaaS platform comes with several example digital twins. Work through the steps in this Examples section to try the features of the platform and to learn good practice for managing digital twins on it. The following slides and video give an overview of these examples.

The following demos show the DTaaS in use in two projects:

Project Slides and Videos CP-SENS project Project Introduction: slides and video Wind turbine testing with the demo inside user workspace Python package and demo video Videos of a digital twin for structural health monitoring applications: Data Acquisition System: Part-1, Data Acquisition System: Part-2, Operational Modal Analysis, and Model Updating Incubator video

docs.title: Workspace Examples
docs.text: These examples run interactively inside the DTaaS user workspace. The workspace examples overview lists them and explains how to download and run them.

docs.title: Automation Examples
docs.text:
These examples use GitLab DevOps pipelines to run the lifecycle scripts of digital twins on the DTaaS platform. See the automation examples overview for details.

DTaaS examples

docs.title: Automation Examples
docs.text: These examples use the DevOps features of the DTaaS platform. GitLab CI/CD pipelines run the lifecycle scripts of each digital twin, such as create, execute, and clean, without manual steps.

docs.title: Available Examples
docs.text: Example Description Mass Spring Damper Co-simulation DT with automated lifecycle via GitLab CI/CD Structural Health Monitoring SHM DT with automated system identification and model update Heart Digital Twin Real-time cardiovascular monitoring with web interface Heart Digital Twin (PaaS) Cloud deployment of Heart DT using PaaS strategies

docs.title: Codebase
docs.text: The source code for these examples is available in the DTaaS-examples repository.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The Heart Digital Twin is a real-time cardiovascular monitoring system that uses ECG data from the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database. It shows live ECG plots with anomaly detection, alongside an interactive 3D heart model that beats in time with the cardiac rhythm.

docs.title: Example Structure
docs.text:
The Heart Digital Twin has these components:

  • ECG Data Processing: Real-time processing and visualisation of electrocardiogram signals from the MIT-BIH database
  • 3D Heart visualisation: Interactive 3D heart model with synchronised pumping animation
  • Anomaly Detection: Real-time identification and highlighting of cardiac anomalies
  • Web Interface: Flask-based web application for real-time monitoring and control

docs.title: MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database
docs.text:
This digital twin uses the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database, which contains 48 half-hour excerpts of two-channel ambulatory ECG recordings. The database includes:

  • Records from 47 subjects studied by the BIH Arrhythmia Laboratory
  • 360 Hz sampling frequency with 11-bit resolution
  • Expert annotations for arrhythmia detection and classification
  • Multiple ECG channels (MLII, V1, V2, V4, V5) depending on the record

Records 100-109 are available for simulation. Each contains different types of cardiac rhythms and anomalies.

docs.title: Digital Twin Configuration
docs.text:
This example uses the following assets:

Asset Type Names of Assets Visibility Reuse in Other Examples Data MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database Records (100-109) Public Yes Models 3D Heart Model (Beating heart.glb) Public Yes Functions ECG Processing & Anomaly Detection Public Yes Tools Flask Web Server & UI Components Public Yes

You can customise the heart digital twin with these parameters:

  • Record Selection: Choose from records 100-109
  • Channel Selection: Switch between available ECG channels
  • Window Size: Adjust the time window for real-time display
  • Update Frequency: Control the refresh rate of the simulation

docs.title: 3D Heart Animation
docs.text:
The digital twin includes a synchronised 3D heart pumping animation:

  • Real-time Synchronisation: Heart model animation matches the ECG rhythm
  • Interactive Controls:
  • Camera controls for 360° viewing
  • Auto-rotate functionality
  • Reset view option
  • Animation Features:
  • Realistic beating heart model
  • Smooth cardiac cycle animation
  • Pause/resume functionality synchronised with ECG simulation
  • Model Format: GLB (GL Transmission Format Binary) 3D model
  • Rendering: WebGL-based rendering using model-viewer component

The 3D heart moves in step with the electrical activity shown in the ECG, which helps to relate the electrical signals to the mechanical function of the heart.

docs.title: Lifecycle Phases
docs.text: Lifecycle Phase Completed Tasks Create Sets up Python virtual environment and installs required dependencies (NumPy, Pandas, Matplotlib, WFDB, Flask) Execute Starts the Flask web server and launches the heart monitoring interface accessible via web browser Clean Terminates the running application and removes the virtual environment

docs.title: DevOps Automation
docs.text: This example uses the DevOps features of the DTaaS platform. GitLab DevOps pipelines run its lifecycle scripts.

docs.title: Pipeline Configuration
docs.text:
The .gitlab-ci.yml file sets the order in which the lifecycle scripts of the heart digital twin run. It defines two stages:

  • create: Sets up the Python virtual environment and installs dependencies
  • execute: Runs the heart digital twin application

docs.title: Runner Requirements
docs.text:
This digital twin requires a shell-based GitLab runner. The application needs:

  • Access to the host system's Python environment
  • Ability to create and manage Python virtual environments
  • File system access for model loading and data processing
  • Network access for the web application

Docker-based runners may restrict the network or file system access that this digital twin needs.

docs.title: Alternative Execution Mode: Docker
docs.text:
The heart digital twin can also run in a Docker container, still on a shell-based GitLab runner.

The GitLab CI file for this approach is .gitlab-ci-docker.yml.

To use it, change the root .gitlab-ci.yml to reference this Docker-based pipeline (.gitlab-ci-docker.yml) instead of the default one.

docs.title: Artifacts and Outputs
docs.text: The create stage saves the Python virtual environment as a GitLab pipeline artefact, which the execute stage reuses. The artefact expires after one hour.

docs.title: Run the example
docs.text:
To run the example, go to the following directory:

cd /workspace/examples/digital_twins/heart_dt

If required, make the lifecycle scripts executable:

chmod +x lifecycle/create
chmod +x lifecycle/execute
chmod +x lifecycle/clean

Now, run the following scripts:

docs.title: Create
docs.text:
Sets up the Python environment and installs the required dependencies, including WFDB for MIT-BIH data access, Flask for the web interface, and scientific computing libraries.

lifecycle/create

docs.title: Execute
docs.text:
Starts the Heart Digital Twin web application in the background. Open it in a web browser for real-time ECG monitoring and 3D heart visualisation.

lifecycle/execute

The application is available at http://localhost:5001. On start-up it:

  • Loads the required MIT-BIH records
  • Initialises the ECG data processing
  • Starts real-time visualisation
  • Enables 3D heart model synchronisation

docs.title: Examine the results
docs.text:
Use the web interface to:

  • Monitor Real-time ECG: View live electrocardiogram signals
  • Control Simulation: Select different records, channels, and update frequencies
  • Interact with 3D Heart: Rotate, zoom, and control the heart animation
  • Detect Anomalies: Observe highlighted cardiac irregularities
  • Pause/Resume: Control the simulation flow

The application writes its logs to the logs/heart_dt.log file.

docs.title: Clean
docs.text:
Stops the running application and cleans up the environment.

lifecycle/clean

This script:

  • Stops the Flask web server
  • Removes the Python virtual environment

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The mass spring damper digital twin (DT) has two mass spring dampers and shows how a co-simulation based DT can be used within DTaaS.

docs.title: Example Structure
docs.text: The study includes two simulators, each representing a mass spring damper system. The first simulator calculates the mass displacement and speed of \(m_1\) for a given force \(F_k\) acting on mass \(m_1\). The second simulator calculates force \(F_k\) given a displacement and speed of mass \(m_1\). By coupling these simulators, the evolution of the position of the two masses is computed.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This example applies digital twin methodology to structural health monitoring (SHM). The digital twin workflow shown below was developed for the SHM use cases.

The complete source code for this example is available online.

docs.title: Example Structure
docs.text:
This digital twin consists of:

  • SHM package: implements the digital twin workflow. The package also contains data recorded from the physical twin and replay functions that stream this data into the digital twin workflow.
  • replay.json: MQTT configuration file for replaying the recorded data

The package provides these experimental scenarios:

  • replay replays the recorded readings from the cantilever beam setup.
  • acceleration_readings shows how the Accelerometer class extracts accelerometer measurements from an MQTT data stream.

  • aligning_readings shows how the Aligner class collects and aligns accelerometer measurements from multiple MQTT data streams.

  • sysid demonstrates sysid with four cases:

    1. sysid-and-plot: plots natural frequencies.
    2. sysid-and-print: prints sysid output to the console.
    3. sysid-and-publish: publishes one set of sysid output via MQTT to the broker given in the sysid section of the config.
    4. live-sysid-publish: publishes sysid output continuously via MQTT to the broker given in the sysid section of the config.

  • Clustering demonstrates clustering with four cases:

    1. clustering-with-local-sysid: gets the sysid output by running sysid locally, then runs mode clustering.
    2. clustering-with-remote-sysid: gets the sysid output by subscribing, then runs mode clustering once.
    3. live-clustering-with-remote-sysid: gets the sysid output by subscribing, then runs mode clustering in a loop.
    4. live-clustering-with-remote-sysid-and-publish: gets the sysid output by subscribing, then runs mode clustering in a loop and publishes the cluster results.

  • mode-tracking demonstrates mode_tracking with three cases:

    1. mode-tracking-with-local-sysid: gets the sysid output by running sysid locally, then runs mode clustering and mode tracking.
    2. mode-tracking-with-remote-sysid: gets the sysid output by subscribing, then runs mode clustering and mode tracking once.
    3. live-mode-tracking-with-remote-sysid: gets the sysid output by subscribing, then runs mode clustering and mode tracking in a loop.

  • model-update demonstrates model_update with three cases:

    1. model-update-with-local-sysid: gets the sysid output, then uses it to update the model and get updated system parameters.
    2. live-model-update-with-remote-sysid: gets the sysid output by subscribing to an MQTT topic, then runs mode clustering and uses the result to update the model and get updated system parameters.
    3. live-model-update-with-remote-clustering: gets the mode clustering output by subscribing to an MQTT topic, then uses it to update the model and get updated system parameters.

The following scenarios can run in the automated execution mode:

  • acceleration_readings shows how the Accelerometer class extracts accelerometer measurements from an MQTT data stream.

  • aligning_readings shows how the Aligner class collects and aligns accelerometer measurements from multiple MQTT data streams.

  • sysid prints the sysid output to the console.

  • Clustering demonstrates sysid and clustering.

  • mode-tracking demonstrates sysid and mode_tracking.

  • model-update runs the digital twin workflow up to model_update.

docs.title: Workspace Examples
docs.text: These digital twins run interactively inside the DTaaS user workspace. You can download each example and run it with its lifecycle scripts.

docs.title: Copy Examples
docs.text:
Copy all the example code into the user workspace with this script:

wget https://raw.githubusercontent.com/INTO-CPS-Association/DTaaS-examples/main/getExamples.sh
bash getExamples.sh

This copies all examples into the /workspace/examples directory.

The script also works when run as root. The examples are then given to the user who ran sudo, or to the owner of the directory containing the examples, so that the workspace user can run them. Set REPOSITORY and BRANCH to download the examples from another repository or branch, for example REPOSITORY=<user>/DTaaS-examples BRANCH=<branch> bash getExamples.sh.

The lifecycle scripts locate the models, tools, data and common assets relative to their own location. The examples work from /workspace/examples and from any other directory that contains a copy of the DTaaS-examples repository.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: This example shows bidirectional communication between a mock physical twin and a digital twin of a mobile robot (Desktop Robotti). A RabbitMQ broker carries the messages between them.

docs.title: Example Structure
docs.text:
Two Python scripts make up the mock physical twin of the mobile robot:

  1. data/drobotti_rmqfmu/rmq-publisher.py
  2. data/drobotti_rmqfmu/consume.py

The mock physical twin sends its location as (x,y) coordinates and expects the digital twin to return the Cartesian distance \(\sqrt(x^2 + y^2)\).

The rmq-publisher.py script reads the recorded (x,y) coordinates of the mobile robot from a data file and publishes them to the RabbitMQ broker, where the digital twin consumes them.

The consume.py script subscribes to the RabbitMQ broker and waits for the distance calculated by the digital twin.

The digital twin is an FMI-based co-simulation, with Maestro as the co-orchestration engine. The co-simulation uses two FMUs: the RMQ FMU (rmqfmu-vhost.fmu) and the distance FMU (distance_from_zero.fmu). The RMQ FMU receives the (x,y) coordinates from rmq-publisher.py and sends the calculated distance to consume.py. It uses the RabbitMQ broker to communicate with the mock mobile robot, that is, rmq-publisher.py and consume.py. The distance FMU calculates the distance between (0,0) and (x,y). The two FMUs exchange values during the co-simulation.

docs.title: Digital Twin Configuration
docs.text:
This example uses two models, one tool, one data file and two scripts that form the mock physical twin. The specific assets used are:

Asset Type Names of Assets Visibility Reuse in Other Examples Models distance_from_zero.fmu Private No rmqfmu-vhost.fmu Private Yes Tool maestro-4.1.0-jar-with-dependencies.jar Common Yes Data drobotti_playback_data.csv Private No Mock PT rmq-publisher.py Private No consume.py Private No

The DT has several configuration files. coe.json and multimodel.json are used to execute the digital twin and can be modified to customise the DT.

The RabbitMQ access credentials go in multimodel.json for the RMQ FMU and in rabbitMQ-credentials.json for the mock PT Python scripts. Add the appropriate credentials to both files.

docs.title: Lifecycle Phases
docs.text: Lifecycle Phase Completed Tasks Create Installs Java Development Kit for Maestro tool and Python packages for python scripts Execute Runs both DT and mock PT Clean Clears run logs and outputs

docs.title: Run the example
docs.text:
To run the example, change to the example directory.

cd /workspace/examples/digital_twins/drobotti_rmqfmu

If required, give the lifecycle scripts execute permission, for example:

chmod +x lifecycle/create

Now run the following scripts.

docs.title: Create
docs.text:
Installs Open Java Development Kit 21 in the workspace, along with the Python packages needed by the rmq-publisher.py and consume.py scripts and by the distance_from_zero.fmu model (python3-pika, python3-protobuf and python3-zmq).

lifecycle/create

docs.title: Execute
docs.text:
Starts the Python scripts of the mock physical twin and then the digital twin. Since this is a co-simulation based digital twin, the Maestro co-simulation tool runs the co-simulation with the two FMU models.

lifecycle/execute

docs.title: Examine the results
docs.text:
The results are in the /workspace/examples/digital_twins/drobotti_rmqfmu directory.

Executing the DT generates and launches a co-simulation (RMQFMU and distance FMU) and two Python scripts: one publishes data read from a file, and the other consumes what the distance FMU sends.

In this example the DT runs for 10 seconds with a step size of 100 ms. Afterwards, the logs are in /workspace/examples/digital_twins/drobotti_rmqfmu/target. The outputs.csv file records the outputs of each FMU: xpos and ypos for the RMQFMU, and the distance for the distance FMU. Each FMU and the publisher scripts also write their own logs. Note that the RMQFMU sends data only when the current input differs from the previous one.

docs.text:
Terminate to clean up the debug files and co-simulation output files.

lifecycle/terminate

docs.text:
The RabbitMQ FMU GitHub repository contains the documentation and source code of the RabbitMQ FMU.

More information about the case study is available in:

Frasheri, Mirgita, et al. "Addressing time discrepancy between digital
and physical twins." Robotics and Autonomous Systems 161 (2023): 104347.

docs.title: Flex Cell Digital Twin with Two Industrial Robots
Overview
docs.text:
The flex-cell digital twin is a case study with two industrial robotic arms, a UR5e and a Kuka LBR iiwa 7, working together in a manufacturing cell.

The case study focuses on positioning the robots in the discrete Cartesian space of the flex-cell. Both robots accept (X,Y,Z) commands that give the target hole and height to move to.

The TwinManager (formerly DT Manager) manages the flex-cell case study. It is packaged as a jar library in the tools and run from a Java main file.

The TwinManager uses Maestro as a slave for co-simulation, so it generates the co-simulation output and, with the proper configuration and setup, can interact with the real robots at the same time. The main file can be changed to suit the application, that is, /workspace/examples/tools/flex-cell/FlexCellDTaaS.java can be modified to get a different result.

The /workspace/examples/models/flex-cell/ folder contains the .fmu files for the kinematic models of the robotic arms, the .urdf files for visualisation (including the grippers), and the .aasx files for the schema representation as an Asset Administration Shell.

The case study also uses the RabbitMQ FMU to inject values into the co-simulation, so the models folder contains that FMU as well. For now, the RabbitMQ FMU only injects values into the co-simulation and does not send values out of it. The TwinManager reads the values from the co-simulation output and the current state of the physical twins.

docs.title: Example Structure
docs.text:
The example structure shows the components of the flex-cell DT implementation using the TwinManager architecture.

The TwinManager orchestrates the flex-cell DT through the Flex-cell DT System, which is composed of two smaller digital twins, the DT UR5e and the DT Kuka lbr iiwa 7. The TwinManager also provides the interface to the physical twins, PT UR5e and PT Kuka lbr iiwa 7. Each physical twin and digital twin system has its own endpoint (with a different specialization), which is initialized from configuration files and a data model (twin schema).

The current endpoints used in this implementation are:

Digital or Physical Twin Endpoint Flex-cell DT System MaestroEndpoint DT UR5e FMIEndpoint DT Kuka lbr iiwa 7 FMIEndpoint PT UR5e MQTTEndpoint and RabbitMQEndpoint PT Kuka lbr iiwa 7 MQTTEndpoint and RabbitMQEndpoint

The Flex-cell DT System has a separate configuration for its integration with the Maestro co-simulation engine.

In the lower part of the diagram, the Flex-cell System is the composed physical twin, including the two robotic arms and the controller. The Flex-cell Simulation is the mock-up of the real system, implemented by FMU blocks and their connections.

docs.title: Lifecycle Phases
docs.text:
The example covers these lifecycle phases:

  1. Installing dependencies in the create phase.
  2. Preparing the connection credentials in the prepare phase.
  3. Running the experiment in the execute phase.
  4. Saving experiments in the save phase.
  5. Plotting the co-simulation results and the real data from the robots in the analyze phase.
  6. Stopping the background processes in the terminate phase and cleaning up the outputs in the clean phase.
Lifecycle Phase Completed Tasks Create Installs Java Development Kit 21 and Maven, compiles the source code of TwinManager to create a usable jar package (used as tool) Prepare Takes the RabbitMQ and MQTT credentials in connections.conf file and configures different assets of DT. Execute The TwinManager executes the flex-cell DT and produces output in data/flex-cell/output directory Save Save the experimental results Analyze Uses plotting functions to generate plots of co-simulation results Terminate Terminating the background processes Clean Cleans up the output data

docs.title: Run the example
docs.text:
To run the example, change to the example directory.

cd /workspace/examples/digital_twins/flex-cell

If required, give the lifecycle scripts execute permission, for example:

chmod +x lifecycle/create

This example requires Java 21 because Maestro 4.1.0 needs it. The create script installs Java 21. If other Java versions are already installed, the default java may point to another version. Check and change the default version with these commands.

java -version
update-alternatives --config java

Now run the following scripts.

docs.title: Create
docs.text:
Installs Open Java Development Kit 21, Maven, and a Python virtual environment with pip dependencies. It also builds the TwinManager tool (TwinManagerFramework-0.0.2.jar) from source code.

lifecycle/create

docs.title: Prepare
docs.text:
This step configures the DT assets with connection credentials, using the functions/flex-cell/prepare.py script. To set up the connection, update /workspace/examples/data/flex-cell/input/connections.conf with the connection parameters for MQTT and RabbitMQ, then run the prepare script.

lifecycle/prepare

The script writes the configuration into these files, which need credentials to connect to the RabbitMQ and MQTT brokers:

  1. /workspace/examples/digital_twins/flex-cell/kuka_actual.conf
  2. /workspace/examples/digital_twins/flex-cell/ur5e_actual.conf
  3. /workspace/examples/data/flex-cell/input/publisher-flexcell-physical.py
  4. modelDescription.xml of the RabbitMQ FMU

docs.title: Execute
docs.text:
Executes the flex-cell digital twin using the TwinManager, which in turn runs the co-simulation using Maestro. The co-simulation output file outputs.csv is written to /workspace/examples/data/flex-cell/output. Stop the execution with control + c, because the TwinManager runs the application in an endless loop.

lifecycle/execute

docs.title: Save
docs.text:
Each execution of the DT is treated as a single run. The save script stores the results of one execution as a time-stamped co-simulation output file in the data/flex-cell/output/saved_experiments directory.

lifecycle/save

The execute and save scripts can be run in that order any number of times. Each iteration adds a new file to the data/flex-cell/output/saved_experiments directory.

docs.title: Analyze
docs.text:
The plotting functions are in functions/flex-cell/plots.py. The script plots the co-simulation results against the recorded values from the two robots.

lifecycle/analyze

docs.title: Terminate
docs.text:
Stops Maestro running in the background, along with any other Java process started during the execute phase.

lifecycle/terminate

docs.title: Clean
docs.text:
Removes the output generated during the execute phase.

lifecycle/clean

docs.title: Examining the Results
docs.text:
Executing this digital twin generates a co-simulation output. The results can also be monitored by adding a set of getAttributeValue calls to /workspace/examples/tools/flex-cell/FlexCellDTaaS.java, as shown in the code. The main file runs the digital twin and the physical twin online and compares them at the same time and at the same abstraction level.

The output is written to the /workspace/examples/data/flex-cell/output folder. To keep a specific experiment, the save lifecycle script stores the co-simulation results in the /workspace/examples/data/flex-cell/output/saved_experiments folder.

In the default example, the co-simulation runs for 10.5 seconds in steps of 0.2 seconds. Both the duration and the step size can be changed. The output stored in outputs.csv contains the joint positions of both robotic arms and the current discrete (X,Y,Z) position of the robot TCP. More variables can be added, such as the discrete (X,Y,Z) position of the other joints.

When connected to the real robots, the tools urinterface and kukalbrinterface log their data at a higher sampling rate.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
The RabbitMQ FMU GitHub repository contains the documentation and source code of the RabbitMQ FMU.

More information about the TwinManager (formerly DT Manager) and the case study is available in:

  1. D. Lehner, S. Gil, P. H. Mikkelsen, P. G. Larsen and M. Wimmer, "An Architectural Extension for Digital Twin Platforms to Leverage Behavioral Models," 2023 IEEE 19th International Conference on Automation Science and Engineering (CASE), Auckland, New Zealand, 2023, pp. 1-8, doi: 10.1109/CASE56687.2023.10260417.
  2. S. Gil, P. H. Mikkelsen, D. Tola, C. Schou and P. G. Larsen, "A Modeling Approach for Composed Digital Twins in Cooperative Systems," 2023 IEEE 28th International Conference on Emerging Technologies and Factory Automation (ETFA), Sinaia, Romania, 2023, pp. 1-8, doi: 10.1109/ETFA54631.2023.10275601.
  3. S. Gil, C. Schou, P. H. Mikkelsen, and P. G. Larsen, “Integrating Skills into Digital Twins in Cooperative Systems,” in 2024 IEEE/SICE International Symposium on System Integration (SII), 2024, pp. 1124–1131, doi: 10.1109/SII58957.2024.10417610.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This example puts a building model in the DTaaS library and gives each of its rooms a simulated temperature sensor. The building is the FZK-Haus, a two-storey house modelled by the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT) as an IFC example. Its model has 7 rooms (IfcSpace) and no sensors, so the example proposes one temperature sensor per room. Rooms are not drawn in the 3D view, so each sensor is bound by its IFC GlobalId to a wall or column inside the room, the one nearest to the room's centre that no other room has taken. When a room has none left, the sensor goes on another drawn object in it, such as a door.

The Buildings page of the DTaaS client draws the model from the library. The binding manifest written by this example tells the page which reading belongs to which room. A publisher sends a simulated temperature for every room over MQTT, on the topics the manifest lists.

The model is AC20-FZK-Haus.ifc from the KIT IFC examples, which KIT provides for unrestricted use. Its content is unchanged, and only its line endings are stored as LF. As KIT asks, publications that use it credit the Institute for Automation and Applied Informatics (IAI) / Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT).

docs.title: Example Structure
docs.text:
File What it does models/fzk_haus.ifc The building model, IFC4 lifecycle/make_manifest.py Proposes one sensor per room, places it on a wall of the room and writes the binding manifest lifecycle/publish_readings.py Publishes a simulated temperature per room over MQTT lifecycle/show_readings.py Prints the first readings that reach the broker lifecycle/requirements.txt The IFC converters from ifc-utils and the MQTT client lifecycle/constraints.txt The versions of the packages those tools pull in, each at least ten days old when pinned

The create phase writes four files into /workspace/common/models, the folder the Buildings page reads:

File Contents fzk_haus.ifc A copy of the building model fzk_haus.glb The geometry, so the page does not convert the model in the browser fzk_haus.json The property tree shown when you click an object fzk_haus.manifest.json One binding per room, from room to MQTT topic

docs.title: Digital Twin Configuration
docs.text:
Asset Type Names of Assets Visibility Reuse in Other Examples Model fzk_haus.ifc Common Yes Tools ifc-explorer, ifc-converter Installed by create Yes

The publisher reads the broker from these environment variables:

Variable Default Meaning MQTT_HOST localhost Host name of the MQTT broker MQTT_PORT 1883 MQTT port of the broker MQTT_USERNAME not set User name, when the broker asks for one MQTT_PASSWORD not set Password, when the broker asks for one MQTT_TLS not set Set to 1 to connect over TLS, for example on port 8883

Without MQTT_TLS, the user name and password travel unencrypted, so set it whenever the broker is not on the same machine.

The lifecycle scripts work from any directory, as the other examples do. Two more variables change where they read and write:

Variable Default Meaning EXAMPLES_PATH the repository root Where models/fzk_haus.ifc is read from WORKSPACE the folder above EXAMPLES_PATH, /workspace inside the workspace The library whose common/models receives the model

docs.title: Lifecycle Phases
docs.text: Lifecycle Phase Completed Tasks Create Installs the tools, places the model and writes the derived files Execute Starts the publisher in the background Terminate Stops the publisher and clears its log Clean Clears the publisher log and PID file

docs.title: Run the Example
docs.text:
Change to the example directory:

cd /workspace/examples/digital_twins/fzk_haus

If required, give the lifecycle scripts execute permission:

chmod +x lifecycle/*

docs.title: Create
docs.text:
Installs ifc-explorer, ifc-converter and paho-mqtt into a virtual environment in .venv. Then copies the model into /workspace/common/models and writes the geometry, the property tree and the binding manifest beside it. This takes about a minute, most of it for the installation.

lifecycle/create

Open Buildings in the DTaaS menu and choose Projekt-FZK-Haus, the name the model gives its project, to see it.

docs.title: Execute
docs.text:
Starts publishing a temperature for each room every two seconds. Point it at the MQTT broker of your installation first, for example the one installed with the DTaaS platform services:

export MQTT_HOST=<broker host>
lifecycle/execute

Each reading goes to dtaas/examples/fzk-haus/room-NN/temperature as one line of comma-separated fields:

timestamp,measurement,type,unit,value
20261013T10:00:00,temperature,simulation,°C,21.40

The type field says simulation, so a subscriber can tell these values apart from measured ones. The log is in publisher.log.

To see the readings arrive through the broker, print the first round of them:

.venv/bin/python lifecycle/show_readings.py /workspace/common/models/fzk_haus.manifest.json

It prints one line per room, such as 1, Flur temperature: 22.10 °C at 12:02:14, and stops with an error when no reading arrives within 10 seconds.

docs.title: Terminate
docs.text:
Stops the publisher and removes its log:

lifecycle/terminate

docs.title: Current Limits
docs.text: The Buildings page draws the model and resolves the manifest, but the DTaaS client does not subscribe to MQTT yet. Until it does, the readings reach any other MQTT subscriber, such as a dashboard, and not the page. The demo video shows this: the readings reach the terminal through the broker, and the page draws the model and its sensors, whose cards wait for a first reading.

docs.title: References
docs.text: The converters come from the ifc-utils repository. The manifest format and the Buildings page are described in DTaaS issue 1762.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The Heart Digital Twin is a real-time cardiovascular monitoring system that uses ECG data from the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database. It shows live ECG plots with anomaly detection, alongside an interactive 3D heart model that beats in time with the cardiac rhythm.

docs.title: Example Structure
docs.text:
The Heart Digital Twin has these components:

  • ECG Data Processing: Real-time processing and visualisation of electrocardiogram signals from the MIT-BIH database
  • 3D Heart visualisation: Interactive 3D heart model with synchronised pumping animation
  • Anomaly Detection: Real-time identification and highlighting of cardiac anomalies
  • Web Interface: Flask-based web application for real-time monitoring and control

docs.title: MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database
docs.text:
This digital twin uses the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database, which contains 48 half-hour excerpts of two-channel ambulatory ECG recordings. The database includes:

  • Records from 47 subjects studied by the BIH Arrhythmia Laboratory
  • 360 Hz sampling frequency with 11-bit resolution
  • Expert annotations for arrhythmia detection and classification
  • Multiple ECG channels (MLII, V1, V2, V4, V5) depending on the record

Records 100-109 are available for simulation. Each contains different types of cardiac rhythms and anomalies.

docs.title: Digital Twin Configuration
docs.text:
This example uses the following assets:

Asset Type Names of Assets Visibility Reuse in Other Examples Data MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database Records (100-109) Public Yes Models 3D Heart Model (Beating heart.glb) Public Yes Functions ECG Processing & Anomaly Detection Public Yes Tools Flask Web Server & UI Components Public Yes

You can customise the heart digital twin with these parameters:

  • Record Selection: Choose from records 100-109
  • Channel Selection: Switch between available ECG channels
  • Window Size: Adjust the time window for real-time display
  • Update Frequency: Control the refresh rate of the simulation

docs.title: 3D Heart Animation
docs.text:
The digital twin includes a synchronised 3D heart pumping animation:

  • Real-time Synchronisation: Heart model animation matches the ECG rhythm
  • Interactive Controls:
  • Camera controls for 360° viewing
  • Auto-rotate functionality
  • Reset view option
  • Animation Features:
  • Realistic beating heart model
  • Smooth cardiac cycle animation
  • Pause/resume functionality synchronised with ECG simulation
  • Model Format: GLB (GL Transmission Format Binary) 3D model
  • Rendering: WebGL-based rendering using model-viewer component

The 3D heart moves in step with the electrical activity shown in the ECG, which helps to relate the electrical signals to the mechanical function of the heart.

docs.title: Lifecycle Phases
docs.text: Lifecycle Phase Completed Tasks Create Sets up Python virtual environment and installs required dependencies (NumPy, Pandas, Matplotlib, WFDB, Flask) Execute Starts the Flask web server and launches the heart monitoring interface accessible via web browser Clean Terminates the running application and removes the virtual environment

docs.title: Run the example
docs.text:
To run the example, go to the following directory:

cd /workspace/examples/digital_twins/heart_dt

If required, make the lifecycle scripts executable:

chmod +x lifecycle/create
chmod +x lifecycle/execute
chmod +x lifecycle/clean

Now, run the following scripts:

docs.title: Create
docs.text:
Sets up the Python environment and installs the required dependencies, including WFDB for MIT-BIH data access, Flask for the web interface, and scientific computing libraries.

lifecycle/create

docs.title: Execute
docs.text:
Starts the Heart Digital Twin web application in the background. Open it in a web browser for real-time ECG monitoring and 3D heart visualisation.

lifecycle/execute

The application is available at http://localhost:5001. On start-up it:

  • Loads the required MIT-BIH records
  • Initialises the ECG data processing
  • Starts real-time visualisation
  • Enables 3D heart model synchronisation

docs.title: Examine the results
docs.text:
Use the web interface to:

  • Monitor Real-time ECG: View live electrocardiogram signals
  • Control Simulation: Select different records, channels, and update frequencies
  • Interact with 3D Heart: Rotate, zoom, and control the heart animation
  • Detect Anomalies: Observe highlighted cardiac irregularities
  • Pause/Resume: Control the simulation flow

The application writes its logs to the logs/heart_dt.log file.

docs.title: Clean
docs.text:
Stops the running application and cleans up the environment.

lifecycle/clean

This script:

  • Stops the Flask web server
  • Removes the Python virtual environment

docs.title: References
docs.text:
More information about the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database and cardiac monitoring:

Moody GB, Mark RG. The impact of the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database.
IEEE Eng in Med and Biol 20(3):45-50 (May-June 2001).

Goldberger, A., et al. PhysioBank, PhysioToolkit, and PhysioNet:
Components of a new research resource for complex physiologic signals.
Circulation 101(23):e215-e220, 2000.

The MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database is available at: https://physionet.org/content/mitdb/

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This case study of an incubator shows the steps involved in developing a digital twin system. The incubator is an insulated container that can maintain a temperature by heating, but it cannot cool. A picture of the incubator is shown below.

The system reaches a set temperature inside a box and holds that temperature regardless of the content. An overview of the system is shown below:

The system consists of:

  • 1x Styrofoam box as the insulated container
  • 1x heat source to heat the content of the Styrofoam box
  • 1x fan to distribute the heat within the box
  • 2x temperature sensors to monitor the temperature inside the box
  • 1x temperature sensor to monitor the temperature outside the box
  • 1x controller that actuates the heat source and the fan, reads the temperature sensors, and communicates with the digital twin

The example comes from the original repository. This trimmed version of the codebase leaves out:

  • docker support
  • tests
  • datasets

The original repository has the complete documentation of the example, including the full system architecture and instructions for running with a physical twin or a 3D visualisation of the incubator.

docs.title: Digital Twin Structure
docs.text:
This diagram shows the main components and the interfaces they use to communicate. All components communicate through the RabbitMQ message exchange, and the data is stored in a time series database. RabbitMQ and InfluxDB are platform services hosted by the DTaaS.

The Incubator digital twin is pre-packaged. It can be used as is or integrated with other digital twins.

The mock physical twin runs from the incubator/mock_plant/real_time_model_solver.py script.

docs.title: Digital Twin Configuration
docs.text:
This example uses many Python scripts to run the digital twin. By default, it runs with a mock physical twin. It also needs RabbitMQ and InfluxDB instances.

There is one configuration file: simulation.conf. The RabbitMQ and InfluxDB configuration parameters must be updated.

docs.title: Lifecycle Phases
docs.text:
The example covers these lifecycle phases:

Lifecycle Phase Completed Tasks Create Installs missing system packages and the Python dependencies in a virtual environment Execute Executes the Incubator digital twin and produces output in the terminal and in incubator/log.log. Clean Removes the log file.

docs.title: Run the example
docs.text:
To run the example, change to its directory.

cd /workspace/examples/digital_twins/incubator

If required, make the lifecycle scripts executable, for example:

chmod +x lifecycle/create

Now, run the following scripts:

docs.title: Create
docs.text:
Installs any missing system packages (Python 3 and venv) and the Python dependencies in a virtual environment in common/digital_twins/incubator/.venv.

lifecycle/create

docs.title: Execute
docs.text:
Executes the Incubator digital twin with a mock physical twin. Writes the results to the terminal, incubator/log.log and InfluxDB.

lifecycle/execute

docs.title: Clean
docs.text:
Removes the output log file.

lifecycle/clean

docs.title: Incubator Digital Twin with NuRV FMU Monitoring Service
Overview
docs.text: This example shows how an FMU can serve as a runtime monitoring service (here generated with NuRV[1]) and be connected to the Incubator digital twin to verify the runtime behaviour of the Incubator.

docs.title: Simulated scenario
docs.text:
This example simulates a scenario where the lid of the Incubator is removed and later put back on. The Incubator has anomaly detection, which can detect anomalous behaviour such as the removal of the lid. When it detects an anomaly, the Incubator switches to an energy saving mode in which the heater is turned off.

The monitor checks that the energy saving mode is turned on within 3 messages of an anomaly detection. The property for this is:

\(G(anomaly \rightarrow (F_{[0,3]}\space energy\_saving))\).

The monitor outputs the unknown state as long as the property is satisfied and moves to the false state once it detects a violation.

The simulated scenario progresses as follows:

  • Initialization: The services are initialized and the Kalman filter in the Incubator is given 2 minutes to stabilize. The anomaly detection algorithm sometimes detects an anomaly at startup even though the lid is still on. This disappears after about 15 seconds.
  • After 2 minutes: The lid is lifted and an anomaly is detected. The energy saver is turned on shortly after.
  • After another 30 seconds: The energy saver is manually disabled, producing a false verdict.
  • After another 30 seconds: The lid is put back on and the anomaly detection is given time to detect that the lid is back on. The monitor is then reset, producing an unknown verdict again. The simulation then ends.

docs.title: Example structure
docs.text:
The diagram below shows the logical software structure of the example.

The execute script starts the NuRV service and then runs the Python script that controls the scenario (execute.py).

The execute.py script starts the Incubator services and runs the example scenario. Once the Incubator DT is started, a RabbitMQ client is created that subscribes to changes in the anomaly and energy_saving states of the DT, as well as the verdicts produced by the NuRV service. Each time an update arrives, the full state or the verdict is printed to the console.

docs.title: Digital Twin Configuration
docs.text:
Before running the example, configure the simulation.conf file with the appropriate RabbitMQ credentials.

The example uses the following assets:

Asset Type Names of Assets Visibility Reuse in other Examples Tools common/tools/NuRV/NuRV Common Yes Other common/fmi2_headers Common Yes DT common/digital_twins/incubator Common Yes Specification safe-operation.smv Private No Script execute.py Private No

The safe-operation.smv file contains the default monitored specification described in the Simulated scenario section. It can be changed as needed.

docs.title: Lifecycle phases
docs.text:
The lifecycle phases for this example are:

Lifecycle phase Completed tasks create Creates a virtual python environment with the necessary dependencies and generates the monitor FMU from the NuRV specification execute Runs a python script that starts up the necessary services as well as the Incubator simulation. Various status messages are printed to the console, including the monitored system states and monitor verdict.

If required, make the lifecycle scripts executable with the following command.

chmod +x lifecycle/{script}

where {script} is the name of the script, for example create or execute.

docs.title: Running the example
docs.text:
To run the example, first run the following command in a terminal:

cd /workspace/examples/digital_twins/incubator-NuRV-fmu-monitor-service/

Then run the create script followed by the execute script using the following command:

lifecycle/{script}

The execute script then prints the system states and the monitor verdict about every 3 seconds. System states are printed in this format:

"State: {anomaly state} & {energy_saving state}"

where "anomaly" means that an anomaly is detected and "!anomaly" means that no anomaly is currently detected. The energy_saving state uses the same format. NuRV verdicts are printed in this format:

"Verdict from NuRV: {verdict}".

The monitor verdict can be false or unknown. Unknown means that the monitor does not yet have enough information to decide whether the property is satisfied. Because of the G operator, the monitor never produces a true verdict: satisfaction can only be confirmed over the entire trace. The unknown state can therefore be read as a tentative true verdict.

An example output trace is provided below:

....

Using INCUBATOR_PATH: /workspace/examples/digital_twins/incubator-NuRV-fmu-monitor-service/lifecycle/../../../common/digital_twins/incubator
Starting NuRV FMU Monitor Service, see output at /tmp/nurv-fmu-service.log

Starting incubator
Connected to rabbitmq server.
Running scenario with initial state: lid closed and energy saver on
Setting energy saver mode: enable
Setting G_box to: 0.5763498

State: !anomaly & !energy_saving

Verdict from NuRV: unknown

Verdict from NuRV: unknown

docs.title: Incubator Digital Twin with NuRV monitoring service
Overview
docs.text: This example shows how a runtime monitoring service (here NuRV[1]) can be connected to the Incubator digital twin to verify the runtime behaviour of the Incubator.

docs.title: Simulated scenario
docs.text:
This example simulates a scenario where the lid of the Incubator is removed and later put back on. The Incubator has anomaly detection, which can detect anomalous behaviour such as the removal of the lid. When it detects an anomaly, the Incubator switches to an energy saving mode in which the heater is turned off.

The monitor checks that the energy saving mode is turned on within 3 simulation steps of an anomaly detection. The property for this is: \(G(anomaly \rightarrow (F_{[0,3]}\space energy\_saving))\). The monitor outputs the Unknown state as long as the property is satisfied and moves to the False state once it detects a violation.

The simulated scenario progresses as follows:

  • Initialization: The services are initialized and the Kalman filter in the Incubator is given 2 minutes to stabilize. The anomaly detection algorithm sometimes detects an anomaly at startup even though the lid is still on. This disappears after about 15 seconds.
  • After 2 minutes: The lid is lifted and an anomaly is detected. The energy saver is turned on shortly after.
  • After another 30 seconds: The energy saver is manually disabled, producing a False verdict.
  • After another 30 seconds: The lid is put back on and the anomaly detection is given time to detect that the lid is back on. The monitor is then reset, producing an Unknown verdict again. The simulation then ends.

docs.title: Example structure
docs.text:
The diagram below shows the logical software structure of the example.

The execute.py script orchestrates and starts all the services in this example: the Incubator DT, the CORBA naming service (omniNames) and the NuRV monitor server. It also implements the Monitor connector component, which connects the DT output to the NuRV monitor server.

The NuRV monitor server registers under a specific name with a CORBA naming service. A client can query the naming service for that name to obtain a reference to the monitor server. For more information on how the NuRV monitor server works, refer to [1].

After the connection with the NuRV monitor server is established, the Incubator DT starts and a RabbitMQ client subscribes to changes in the anomaly and energy_saving states of the DT. Each time either state changes, the full state (the updated state and the last value of the other state) is pushed to the NuRV monitor server, and the verdict is printed to the console.

docs.title: Digital Twin Configuration
docs.text:
Before running the example, configure the simulation.conf file with the appropriate RabbitMQ credentials.

The example uses the following assets:

Asset Type Names of Assets Visibility Reuse in other Examples Service common/services/NuRV/NuRV_orbit Common Yes DT common/digital_twins/incubator Common Yes Specification safe-operation.smv Private No Script execute.py Private No

The safe-operation.smv file contains the default monitored specification described in the Simulated scenario section. It can be changed as needed.

docs.title: Lifecycle phases
docs.text:
The lifecycle phases for this example are:

Lifecycle phase Completed tasks create Downloads the necessary tools and creates a virtual python environment with the necessary dependencies. The omniORBpy CORBA library is compiled from source because there are no packages of it for Python 3.12 execute Runs a python script that starts up the necessary services as well as the Incubator simulation. Various status messages are printed to the console, including the monitored system states and monitor verdict. clean Removes created data directory and incubator log files.

If required, make the lifecycle scripts executable with the following command

chmod +x lifecycle/{script}

where {script} is the name of the script, for example create or execute.

docs.title: Running the example
docs.text:
To run the example, first run the following command in a terminal:

cd /workspace/examples/digital_twins/incubator-NuRV-monitor-service/

Then run the create script, which can take a few minutes depending on the network connection, followed by the execute script, using the following command:

lifecycle/{script}

The execute script then prints the system states and the monitor verdict about every 3 seconds, in the format "State: {anomaly state} & {energy_saving state}, verdict: {Verdict}", where "anomaly" means that an anomaly is detected and "!anomaly" means that no anomaly is currently detected. The energy_saving state uses the same format.

The monitor verdict can be False or Unknown. Unknown means that the monitor does not yet have enough information to decide whether the property is satisfied. Because of the G operator, the monitor never produces a True verdict: satisfaction can only be confirmed over the entire trace. The Unknown state can therefore be read as a tentative True verdict.

An example output trace is provided below:

....
Running scenario with initial state: lid closed and energy saver on
Setting energy saver mode: enable
Setting G_box to: 0.5763498
State: !anomaly & !energy_saving, verdict: Unknown
State: !anomaly & !energy_saving, verdict: Unknown
....
State: anomaly & !energy_saving, verdict: Unknown
State: anomaly & energy_saving, verdict: Unknown
State: anomaly & energy_saving, verdict: Unknown
....
State: anomaly & energy_saving, verdict: Unknown
State: anomaly & !energy_saving, verdict: Unknown
State: anomaly & !energy_saving, verdict: Unknown
State: anomaly & !energy_saving, verdict: Unknown
State: anomaly & !energy_saving, verdict: Unknown
State: anomaly & !energy_saving, verdict: False

The connection to the NuRV server often fails at startup and takes a few attempts to establish. The script retries automatically.

docs.title: Incubator Co-Simulation Digital Twin validation with NuRV Monitor
Overview
docs.text: This example shows how to validate digital twin components using FMU monitors. Here the monitors are generated with NuRV[1].

docs.title: Simulated scenario
docs.text:
This example validates some components of the Incubator digital twin through a simulation in which the components are wrapped inside FMUs and inspected at runtime by an FMU monitor generated by NuRV. The link to the Incubator digital twin is given only for the details of the incubator physical twin. The digital twin (DT) presented here is a co-simulation DT of the Incubator.

The input data for the simulation comes from a purpose-built FMU component named source, which supplies test data to the anomaly detector and simulates an anomaly at time t=60s. A second component, the watcher, checks whether the energy saver activates in response to an anomaly reported by the anomaly detector.

The output of the watcher is then passed to the monitor, which checks that the energy saver activates within three simulation cycles of a detected anomaly.

docs.title: Incubator Digital Twin with TeSSLa monitoring service
Overview
docs.text: This example demonstrates how a runtime enforcement service (in this example implemented with the specification language TeSSLa[1]) can be connected with the Incubator Digital Twin to steer the behavior of the Incubator.

docs.title: Simulated scenario
docs.text:
The incubator is a device used to maintain the temperature inside a box within a pre-defined range. In this specific scenario, the lid of the incubator is removed and later replaced. The incubator is equipped with anomaly detection capabilities that can detect anomalous behaviour (i.e. the removal of the lid). If an anomaly is detected, the incubator will, after a period of time, enter a power saving mode where the heating is turned off. The runtime enforcer provides the control signal for the power saving mode.

The simulated scenario is as follows:

  • Initialisation: The services are initialised and the Kalman filter in the incubator is given 2 minutes to stabilise.
  • After 2 minutes*: The lid is lifted and an anomaly is detected. The power saver is activated shortly after.
  • After a further 30 seconds: The lid is replaced and the anomaly detector is given time to detect that the lid is back on. The simulation ends.

docs.title: Example structure
docs.text:
A diagram showing the logical software structure of the example is shown below.

The execute.py script is responsible for orchestrating and starting all relevant services in this example. This includes the incubator DT, the TeSSLa runtime enforce as well as telegraf and the TeSSLa telegraf connector for communication between the DT and TeSSLa.

The telegraf client subscribes to the RabbitMQ server used by the DT for communication and forwards the messages on the topics incubator.diagnosis.plant.lidopen and incubator.energysaver.status to the TeSSLa telegraf connector, which feeds them as inputs to TeSSLa. TeSSLa then generates a control signal to activate or deactivate the energy saver mode. The signal is then sent back to Telegraf via the connector and published to RabbitMQ and printed on the console.

The example uses the following assets:

The safe-operation.tessla file contains the default monitored specification as described in the Simulated scenario section. These can be configured as desired.

Various status messages are printed to the console, including the monitored system states and the monitor verdict. clean Removes the created data directory and the incubator log files.

docs.title: Incubator Digital Twin with TeSSLa Monitoring Service
Overview
docs.text: This example demonstrates how a runtime monitoring service (in this example TeSSLa[1]) can be connected to the Incubator Digital Twin to verify the runtime behaviour of the incubator.

docs.title: Simulated scenario
docs.text:
This example simulates a scenario where the lid of the incubator is removed and later replaced. The incubator is equipped with anomaly detection capabilities that can detect anomalous behaviour (i.e. removal of the lid). If an anomaly is detected, the incubator will enter an energy saving mode where the heating is switched off.

From a monitoring perspective, we want to verify that within approximately 3 simulation steps of an anomaly being detected, the energy saving mode is turned on. To verify this behaviour we construct the property: \(G(anomaly \rightarrow (F_{[0,3]}\space energy\_saving))\). The monitor will output the normal state as long as the property is satisfied, and will switch to the alert state as soon as a violation is detected.

The simulated scenario is as follows

  • Initialisation: The services are initialised and the Kalman filter in the incubator is given 2 minutes to stabilise.
  • After 2 minutes*: The lid is lifted and an anomaly is detected. The power saver is activated shortly after.
  • After a further 30 seconds: The power saver is manually deactivated, resulting in a False verdict.
  • After another 30 seconds: The lid is replaced and anomaly detection is given time to detect that the lid is back on. The monitor is then reset, producing a normal verdict again. The simulation ends.

docs.title: Example structure
docs.text:
A diagram showing the logical software structure of the example is shown below.

The execute.py script is responsible for orchestrating and starting all relevant services in this example. This includes the incubator DT, the TeSSLa monitor and the telegraf and TeSSLa telegraf connector for communication between the DT and the TeSSLa monitor.

The telegraf client subscribes to the RabbitMQ server used by the DT for communication and forwards the messages on the topics incubator.diagnosis.plant.lidopen and incubator.energysaver.status to the TeSSLa telegraf connector, which feeds them as inputs to the TeSSLa monitor. TeSSLa then makes a judgement based on this new state together with the previously received states. The judgement is then sent back to Telegraf via the connector and published to the incubator.energysaver.alert topic and printed on the console.

The execute script will then start outputting system states and the monitor verdict approx every 3 seconds. The output is printed as follows "State: {anomaly state} & {energy_saving state}, verdict: {Verdict}" where "anomaly" indicates that an anomaly is detected and "!anomaly" indicates that an anomaly is not currently detected. The same format is used for the energy_saving state.

The monitor verdict can be normal or alert, where the latte indicates that the monitor does not yet have sufficient informationto determine the satisfaction of the property. The monitor will never produce a True verdict as the entire trace must be verified to ensure satisfaction due to the G operator. Thus the normal state can be viewed as a tentative True verdict.

This digital twin is derived from the Mass Spring Damper digital twin.

The mass spring damper digital twin (DT) has two mass spring dampers. It shows how to use a co-simulation based DT within the DTaaS. This version of the example adds a monitor generated by NuRV. More information about NuRV is available on the NuRV tool page.

docs.title: Example Structure
docs.text:
The study includes two simulators, each representing a mass spring damper system. The first simulator calculates the displacement and speed of mass \(m_1\) for a given force \(F_k\) acting on \(m_1\). The second simulator calculates the force \(F_k\) from a given displacement and speed of mass \(m_1\). Coupling the two simulators computes how the positions of the two masses evolve.

docs.title: Firefighter Mission in a Burning Building
docs.text: During a firefighter mission, the oxygen level of each firefighter's Self Contained Breathing Apparatus (SCBA) must be monitored in the context of the mission.

docs.title: Physical Twin Overview
docs.text:
Image: Schematic overview of a firefighter mission. Note the mission commander on the lower left documenting the air supply pressure levels provided by radio communication from the firefighters inside and around the burning building. This image was created with the assistance of DALL·E.

The following scenario is assumed:

  • a set of firefighters work to extinguish a burning building
  • they each use an SCBA with pressurised oxygen to breathe
  • a mission commander outside coordinates the efforts and monitors the oxygen levels

docs.title: Digital Twin Overview
docs.text:
This example implements a monitor that calculates how much time the firefighters have left before they need to leave the building. It uses these inputs:

  • a 3D model of the building in which the mission takes place,
  • pressure data from a firefighter's SCBA, and
  • the firefighter's location inside the building

to estimate:

  • the shortest way out,
  • how long it takes, and
  • how much time is left until the SCBA runs out of oxygen.

The remaining mission time is monitored, and the firefighters receive a warning if it drops below a threshold.

This example implements the paper Digital Twin for Rescue Missions--a Case Study by Leucker et al.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Waste water treatment (WWT) plants must keep substance and species concentrations within regulatory limits to ensure water quality. This is usually checked by taking periodic samples and analysing them in the laboratory, so plant operators lack continuous information for their decisions and set operating setpoints higher than needed to guarantee water quality. Some WWT processes consume a lot of power, so adjusting the setpoints could reduce energy consumption significantly.

docs.title: Physical Twin Overview
docs.text:
This example shows the communication between a physical ultraviolet (UV) disinfection process (the tertiary treatment of a WWT plant) and its digital twin, which is based on Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) and compartment models. The digital twin provides "virtual sensors" that give the plant operator continuous information for decision making.

The physical twin is an ultraviolet channel. A PLC controls the power of the UV lamps needed to kill all the pathogens in the flow. The channel has 3 groups of UV lamps, so the real channel (and its mathematical model) is divided into 7 zones: 4 without UV lamps (the entrance and exit of the channel, plus 2 zones between lamp groups) and 3 for the UV lamps.

The dose to apply (related to the power) changes with the residence time, computed from the measured volume flow, and with the UV intensity measured by the intensity sensor.

The volumetric flow and the power in the three parts of the channel are transmitted to the PLC of the plant. The PLC also works as an OPC UA server that sends data to and receives data from an OPC UA client. Some sizing parameters and initial values, such as the initial concentrations of disinfectant and pathogens, are read from a spreadsheet that the plant operator fills in. The spreadsheet is an Open Office file (.ods) because of the software installed on the SCADA PC. Some of the values the operator defines are input signals that are not measured yet but are expected to be measured in the future.

docs.title: Digital Twin Overview
docs.text: The digital twin is a reduced model, written in C, that solves the physical conservation laws (mass, energy and momentum) but simplifies details, mainly the geometry, to calculate in real time while keeping the results accurate. Its results are compared with those of the CFD model. An OpenModelica model uses the C solver, and OpenModelica exports it as an FMU so that the OPC UA client (client-opcua.py) can integrate it.

docs.title: Digital Twin Configuration
docs.text:
Asset Type Name of Asset Visibility Reuse in Other Examples Model Test_DTCONEDAR.mo private No Data configuration_freeopcua.ods private No model_description.csv (generated by client-opcua.py) private No Mock OPC UA Server: opcua-mock-server.py private No Tool OPC UA Client: client-opcua.py private No FMU builder: create-fmu.mos private No

This example uses a dummy model of the plant instead of the real model. The simplified model, which does not contain the real equations, is written in OpenModelica (Test_DTCONEDAR.mo). The FMU is generated with OpenModelica to obtain the binaries needed to run it. A previously generated FMU can be used, but to make sure the right binaries are used, install the OpenModelica compiler and run create-fmu.mos to build the FMU from the Modelica file Test_DTCONEDAR.mo.

The FMU model description file (modelDescription.xml inside Test_DTCONEDAR.fmu) holds the value references, and configuration_freeopcua.ods holds the OPC-UA node IDs. The variable name links the two.

The client Python script (client-opcua.py) performs these actions:

  • Reads the variable names and value references from the model description file of Test_DTCONEDAR.fmu.
  • Reads configuration_freeopcua.ods to obtain the OPC UA node IDs and assigns them to the variables read from the FMU.
  • Reads configuration_freeopcua.ods to set initial values, parameters and some inputs (a reasonable value is assumed for inputs that are not measured).
  • Reads values from the PLC using an OPC UA client.

  • Runs the algorithm with the FMPy library, using the FMU created from the compartment model (based on CFD):

  • Obtains the results.

  • Sends the results to the PLC over OPC UA, so that they appear in the SCADA and help the plant operator make decisions.

docs.title: Input Data Variables
docs.text: The configuration_freeopcua.ods data file sets the initial input data values used by the server.

docs.title: DT Config
docs.text:
The config.json file specifies the configuration parameters of the OPC UA client.

These optional parameters can be modified:

  • stop_time
  • step_size
  • record = True, to save the simulation results
  • record_interval. When the simulation step_size is small, the results file can become too big. For instance, if the step_size is 0.01 seconds, increase the record_interval to reduce the file size.
  • record_variables: the list of variables to record.
  • enable_send = True, to send the results to the OPC UA server.

docs.title: Waste Water Plant with OPC UA
docs.text: NOTE: This directory contains complete version of the digital_twins/opc-ua-waterplant digital twin. This directory contains code for multiple versions of mock physical twin and the example given here works on both Windows and Linux.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Waste water treatment (WWT) plants must comply with substance and species concentration limits established by regulation in order to ensure the good quality of the water. This is usually done taking periodic samples that are analyzed in the laboratory. This means that plant operators do not have continuous information for making decisions and, therefore, operation setpoints are set to higher values than needed to guarantee water quality. Some of the processes involved in WWT plants consume a lot of power, thus adjusting setpoints could significantly reduce energy consumption.

docs.title: Physical Twin Overview
docs.text:
This example demonstrates the communication between a physical ultraviolet (UV) disinfection process (the tertiary treatment of a WWT plant) and its digital twin, which is based on Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) and compartment models. The aim of this digital twin is to develop "virtual sensors" that provide continuous information that facilitates the decision making process for the plant operator.

The physical twin of the waste water plant is composed of an ultraviolet channel controlled by a PLC that controls the power of the UV lamps needed to kill all the pathogens of the flow. The channel has 3 groups of UV lamps, therefore the real channel (and is mathematical model) is subdivided in 7 zones: 4 correspond to zones without UV lamps (2 for the entrance and exit of the channel + 2 zones between UV lamps) and the 3 reamaining for the UV lamps.

The dose to be applied (related with the power) changes according to the residence time (computed from the measure of the volume flow) and the UV intensity (measured by the intensity sensor). The information of the volumetric flow and power (in the three parts of the channel) is transmitted to the PLC of the plant. Furthermore, the PLC is working as OPC UA Server to send and receive data to and from an OPC UA client. Additionally, some sizing parameters and initial values are read from a spreadsheet filled in by the plant operator. In this case, the spreadsheet is an Open Office file (.ods) due to the software installed in the SCADA PC. Some of the variables like initial concentration of disinfectant and pathogens are included, among others. Some values defined by the plant operator correspond to input signals that are not currently being measured, but are expected to be measured in the future.

docs.title: Digital Twin Overview
docs.text:
The digital twin is a reduced model (developed in C) that solves physical conservation laws (mass, energy and momentum), but simplifies details (geometry, mainly) to ensure real-time calculations and accurate results. The results are compared to the ones obtained by the CFD. C solver developed is used by the OpenModelica model. OpenModelica converts it into FMI standard, to be integrated in the main script execution (client-opcua.py).

The main python script (client-opcua.py) does the following actions:

  • Read values from PLC using a client OPC.
  • Read the spreadsheet to fix initial values, parameters and some inputs (those inputs that are not being measured, a reasonable value is assumed). And read the node IDs assigned to each input and output variable of the OPC UA server.
  • Execute the algorithm with the FMPy library using the .fmu created from the compartment model (based on CFD)
  • Obtain results.
  • Send by OPC UA protocol the result values to the PLC, to visualize them in the SCADA and with the aim to improve the decision-making process of the plant operator.

The configurationXXX.ods file is used for customizing the initial values to your needs. In this example, a dummy model representation of the plant is used, instead of the real model. The simplified model (with not the real equations) is developed in Modelica (Test_DTCONEDAR.mo). The FMU is generated from the Open Modelica interface in Linux and Windows to obtain the needed binaries to run the FMU in both operating systems. It is possible to run an FMU previously generated, however, to ensure that we are using the right binaries it is recommended to install Open Modelica Compiler and run create-fmu.mos to build the FMU from de Modelica file Test_DTCONEDAR.mo

docs.title: Install and Demonstrate
docs.text:
1. Install GLIBC 2.33 or newer versions. The Windows has Visual Studio Redistributable which comes with GLIBC equivalent libraries.
  2. Linux: You can install with sudo apt-get install -y glibc-source on Ubuntu 22.04. Please see install GLIBC-2.35 for Ubuntu 20.04.
  3. Windows: Install Visual Studio Redistributable to install the newest version of GLIBC.
  4. Install Open Modelica Compiler for Linux or Windows. The minimal installation is enough since the graphical clients (OMEdit, OMShell and OMNotebook) are not necessary. This allows to compile an FMU from the terminal, therefore if the FMU is already built with the correct binaries, this step is optional
  5. Run the create-fmu.mos file to compile the FMU from the Modelica file.

Linux

sudo apt-get install cmake
omc create-fmu.mos

Windows: omc usually is located in a path like this

"C:\Program Files\OpenModelica1.21.0-64bit\bin\omc.exe" create-fmu.mos

Two FMUs, namely Test_DTCONEDAR_linux.fmu and Test_DTCONEDAR_windows.fmu have been provided as samples. The Test_DTCONEDAR_linux.fmu has been generated on Ubuntu Linux 22.04 and the Test_DTCONEDAR_windows.fmu has been generated on Windows 10.

  1. Install Python 3.8 or above. It has been tested in 3.8, 3.10 and 3.11 versions. However version 3.10 is recommended:
  2. Linux: Install Python 3.10.

  3. Windows: Install Python 3.10

  4. Install pip for Python

  5. Linux: Install pip3 for python3.10. curl -sS https://bootstrap.pypa.io/get-pip.py | python3.10

  6. Windows: pip is installed by default when installing Python.

  7. Upgrade pip and install pip dependencies.

Linux

  ``` bash
  sudo apt-get install python-is-python3 python3-pip
  python3 -m pip install --upgrade pip
  python3 -m pip install -r requirements_linux.txt
  ```

  Windows

  ```cmd
  py -m pip install --upgrade pip
  py -m pip install -r requirements_windows.txt
  ```
  1. Configure an OPC UA simulation server. Two options are available.

  2. Use Free OPC-UA Library. This is the recommended approach, because its configuration is more straightforward. Two libraries are provided within Free OPC-UA Library.

    • opcua is deprecated, but still works fine to create OPC-UA servers and clients.
    • asyncua is very similar, but allows asynchronous programming through the asyncio Python native library.

  3. Download and install Prosys OPC UA Simulation Server. This server is not running properly in DTaaS user workspace but works well on Ubuntu 22.04. It seems there is a bug in the OPC UA server. This needs debugging. To configure Prosys OPC UA Simulation Server see How to configure Prosys.

  4. Start the OPC-UA Server (two options available):

  5. Free OPC-UA Library: run any of these scripts (server-opcua.py, server-opcua-xml.py, server-asyncua.py, server-asyncua-xml.py). All of them create the same server, the difference between them is that ones use opcua library and others asyncua and ones define each node by hand and others import a list of nodes from a .xml file.

  6. Prosys OPC UA Simulation Server: just run the application.

  7. Configure parameters and inputs of the simulation model in the file configuration.ods.

  8. Open the configuration file config.json and fill in the values:

  9. Replace "url" : "opc.tcp://0.0.0.0:4840" with new Connection Address. The default localhost is:

    • opc.tcp://0.0.0.0:4840 for Linux
    • opc.tcp://localhost:4840 for Windows

  10. Select the .ods configuration file.

    • If using Free OPC-UA select configuration_freeopcua.ods
    • If using Prosys select configuration_prosys.ods

  11. Make sure that your are running the FMU that suits your Operating System. The easiest way is to provide the same fmu_filename that has been created after running step 3.

  12. Besides the mentioned parameters, optional parameters can be modified:

    • stop_time
    • step_size
    • record = True, if we want to save the results of the simulation
    • record_interval. Sometimes the simulation step_size is small and a the size of the results file can be too big. For instance, if the simulation step_size is 0.01 seconds, we can increase the record_interval so as to reduce the result file size.
    • record_variables: we can specify the list of variables that we want to record.
    • enable_send = True, if we want to send results to the OPC UA Server.

  13. Run any of the following client scripts: client-opcua.py or client-asyncua.py

docs.title: How to configure Prosys
docs.text:
1. Start OPC UA server once and then close. This action will create ~/.prosysopc/prosys-opc-ua-simulation-server directory (within your operating system).
  2. Go to prosys folder (within this repository) and copy default.simconf file into ~/.prosysopc/prosys-opc-ua-simulation-server directory. After that, when running again Prosys OPC UA the following nodes should appear.
  3. Start the OPC UA server again. Make sure that the server is running at a port. Copy Connection Address (UA TCP) from the Status tab.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The three-tank system is a simple case study of three components coupled in a cascade: the first tank is connected to the input of the second tank, and the output of the second tank is connected to the input of the third tank.

This example contains only simulated components, so there is no configuration for a connection to the physical system.

The TwinManager manages the three-tank system. It is packaged as a jar library in the tools and run from a Java main file. The TwinManager uses Maestro as a slave for co-simulation, so it generates the output of the co-simulation.

The main file can be changed to suit the application, that is, /workspace/examples/tools/three-tank/TankMainDTaaS.java can be modified to get a different result.

The /workspace/examples/models/three-tank/ folder contains Linear.fmu, a non-realistic model of a tank with an input and an output, and TankSystem.aasx, the schema representation as an Asset Administration Shell. The three tank instances use the same .fmu file and the same schema because they belong to the same object class. The TwinManager reads the values from the co-simulation output.

docs.text:
