The DT has several configuration files. The Maestro tool uses coe.json and multimodel.json. The files tank1.conf, tank2.conf and tank3.conf configure three instances of one model (Linear.fmu).

docs.title: Examining the results
docs.text:
Executing this digital twin generates a co-simulation output. The results can also be monitored by adding a set of getAttributeValue calls to /workspace/examples/tools/three-tank/TankMainDTaaS.java, as shown in the code.

The main file runs the digital twin and its internal components online.

The co-simulation output is written to the /workspace/examples/data/three-tank/output folder.

In the default example, the co-simulation runs for 10 seconds in steps of 0.5 seconds. Both the duration and the step size can be changed. The output stored in outputs.csv contains the level, in/out flow and leak values.

The example neither generates nor uses data from the physical twin.

docs.title: Water Tank Fault Injection with NuRV Runtime Monitor
Overview
docs.text:
This example shows a digital twin (DT) with fault injection (FI). A live DT receives simulated faults from the environment. The faults are part of the DT configuration and can be changed for new instances of the DT. This version of the example adds a monitor generated by NuRV. More information about NuRV is available on the NuRV tool page.

This co-simulation based DT uses a water tank case study. The co-simulation consists of a tank and a controller, and its goal is to keep the water level in the tank between Level-1 and Level-2. Faults are injected into the output of the water tank controller (watertankcontroller-c.fmu) from 12 to 20 time units. The faults close the tank outlet for a period of time, and the water level rises above the desired level (Level-2). A monitor added to the simulation checks at runtime whether the water level stays below a maximum threshold.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This example shows multi-stage execution and dynamic reconfiguration of a digital twin (DT). It demonstrates two features of DTs:

  • Fault injection into a live DT
  • Dynamic auto-reconfiguration of a live DT

The DT is built with the co-simulation methodology.

docs.title: Configuration of assets
docs.text:

Asset Type Names of Assets Visibility Reuse in Other Examples Models watertankcontroller-c.fmu Private Yes singlewatertank-20sim.fmu Private Yes leak_detector.fmu Private No leak_controller.fmu Private No Tool maestro-4.1.0-jar-with-dependencies.jar Common Yes

The DT is executed in two stages, and each stage has its own configuration files. The following table lists the configuration files and their purpose.

Configuration file name Execution Stage Purpose mm1.json stage-1 DT configuration wt_fault.xml, FaultInject.mabl stage-1 faults injected into DT during stage-1 mm2.json stage-2 DT configuration simulation-config.json Both stages Configuration for specifying DT execution time and output logs

docs.text:
To run the example, change to the example directory.

cd /workspace/examples/digital_twins/water_tank_swap

If required, make the lifecycle scripts executable, for example:

chmod +x lifecycle/create

docs.title: Create
docs.text:
Installs Open Java Development Kit 21 and, from the Ubuntu repositories, the Python packages used by the plotting script and the Python FMUs (python3-pandas, python3-matplotlib, python3-protobuf and python3-zmq).

lifecycle/create

docs.title: Execute
docs.text:
This DT runs in two stages. The first stage runs a co-simulation of the watertankcontroller-c.fmu and singlewatertank-20sim.fmu models. During this stage, faults are injected into one of the models (watertankcontroller-c.fmu) and the system performance is checked.

The second stage runs another co-simulation with three FMUs: watertankcontroller-c, singlewatertank-20sim and leak_detector. The Maestro tool has a built-in monitor, which is enabled during this stage, and a swap condition is set at the start of the stage. When the swap condition is satisfied, Maestro swaps out the watertankcontroller-c.fmu model and swaps in the leak_controller.fmu model. This model swap demonstrates the dynamic reconfiguration of a DT.

At the end of the execution phase, the outputs.csv file of each stage is copied to the stage1 and stage2 subdirectories of /workspace/examples/data/water_tank_swap/output.

The run-time model (FMU) swap mechanism used in this example is described in the paper:

Ejersbo, Henrik, et al. "fmiSwap: Run-time Swapping of Models for
Co-simulation and Digital Twins." arXiv preprint arXiv:2304.07328 (2023).

Runtime reconfiguration of a co-simulation by changing the Functional Mockup Units (FMUs) it uses is described further in the paper:

Ejersbo, Henrik, et al. "Dynamic Runtime Integration of
New Models in Digital Twins." 2023 IEEE/ACM 18th Symposium on
Software Engineering for Adaptive and Self-Managing Systems
(SEAMS). IEEE, 2023.

docs.title: Working with GitLab
docs.text:
The DTaaS platform uses GitLab for two purposes:

  1. OAuth 2.0 authorization service
  2. DevOps service

The admin documentation covers the OAuth 2.0 authorization configuration. This guide covers the git commands and project structure for the GitLab DevOps service within the DTaaS.

docs.title: Preparation
docs.text:
First, create a GitLab project named after your username in the GitLab group named dtaas.

The user must have ownership permissions over the project.

Warning

By default, the DTaaS website expects a branch named master to exist and performs all git operations on it. A different branch can be set in the Branch Name field of the settings page.

docs.title: Git commands
docs.text:
Use the standard git commands and workflows. A GitLab project can be used as a remote git server in two ways:

  1. Over SSH using a personal SSH key
  2. Over HTTPS using personal access tokens (PAT)

This tutorial uses a PAT to work with the GitLab server.

First, create a PAT.

Copy the token and use it to clone the git repository.

docs.title: Library Assets
docs.text:
GitLab stores the reusable Library assets of all users. Library assets, including digital twins, must follow a mandatory structure. A properly initialized GitLab project has the following structure.

Pay special attention to .gitlab-ci.yml. It must be a valid GitLab DevOps configuration. The example repo has a sample structure.

For example, with PAT1 as the PAT for the dtaas/user1 repository, the command to clone the repository is:

$git clone \
  https://user1:PAT1@dtaas-digitaltwin.com/gitlab/dtaas/user1.git
$cd user1

After adding the required Library assets:

$git push origin

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
A GitLab runner must be linked to the project repository. Some runners may already be installed with the DTaaS platform; check the runners page of the GitLab project. You can also install custom runners and link them to the repository.

You can then use the Digital Twins Page to access the DevOps features of the DTaaS platform.

docs.title: Reusable Assets and DevOps
docs.text:
DevOps is a well-established software development practice. The DTaaS platform has an experimental feature that brings DevOps to digital twins.

This feature requires a specific installation setup:

  1. Integrated GitLab installation
  2. A valid GitLab repository for the logged-in user. See an example repository. You can clone this repository and customise it as needed.
  3. A GitLab Runner linked to the user's GitLab repository.

Once these requirements are met, open the Library Page by clicking Automation in the menu and then the Library Page card. The page shows all the reusable assets stored in the linked GitLab repository. A category with no assets shows an empty list.

Otherwise the page lists the existing assets. The following figure shows all the available DTs.

Click Add on an asset to add it to the Selection pane on the right. After selecting all the required assets, click the Create a Digital Twin button to go to the DT create stage.

docs.title: Runner
docs.text:
A utility service for the safe execution of remote scripts and commands. The user launches it from the command line, and the utility manages the commands to be executed.

The runner runs as a service and provides a REST API for executing remote commands safely. Several runners can be active at the same time on one computer. Commands are sent through the REST API and executed on the computer running the runner.

Info

The runner works on Linux and Windows. On Windows, it runs the PowerShell version of each script.

docs.title: NPM Registry
docs.text:
The package is available on npmjs.

Install the package with the following command:

sudo npm install -g @into-cps-association/runner

docs.title: GitHub Registry
docs.text:
The package is available in GitHub packages registry.

Set the registry and install the package with the following commands:

sudo npm config set @into-cps-association:registry \
  https://npm.pkg.github.com
sudo npm install -g @into-cps-association/runner

The npm install command asks for a username and password. The username is your GitHub username and the password is a GitHub personal access token. For npm to download the package, the personal access token needs the read:packages scope.

docs.title: Configure
docs.text:
The utility needs a configuration file in YAML format. The template configuration file is:

port: 5000
location: 'scripts'  # directory of scripts, relative to this config file
commands:  # list of permitted scripts
  - create
  - execute
  - terminate

Name the configuration file runner.yaml and place it in the directory from which the runner microservice is run.

location is the path of the scripts directory relative to the runner.yaml file.

You can choose any configuration filename and any location. The path to the configuration file can be relative or absolute, but the location path is always relative to the configuration file.

Note

The commands must be executable. On Linux, make sure the commands have execute permission.

docs.title: Create Commands
docs.text:
The runner needs commands or scripts to run. Place them in the location directory specified in the runner.yaml file. The location is relative to the directory of the runner.yaml file.

On Windows, each command needs a PowerShell script with the .ps1 extension, for example create.ps1 for the create command. The runner executes it with powershell.exe -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File. A directory can hold both versions of a script, so that the same commands work on Linux and Windows.

The runner can also run in a docker container. See the docker instructions.

docs.title: Use
docs.text:
Display help.

$runner -h
Usage: runner [options]

Remote code execution for humans

Options:
  -v --version          package version
  -c --config <string>  runner config file specified in yaml format (default: "runner.yaml")
  -h --help             display help

The config option is optional. Without it, runner looks for runner.yaml in the directory from which it is run. Once launched, the utility listens on the port specified in the runner.yaml file.

runner  #use runner.yaml of the present working directory
runner -c FILE-PATH       #absolute or relative path to config file
runner --config FILE-PATH #absolute or relative path to config file

On the computer where it runs, the service is available at http://localhost:<port>.

Other computers on the network can reach it at http://<ip or hostname>:<port>/.

docs.title: Application Programming Interface (API)
docs.text:
Three REST API methods are available. Their routes and responses are:

REST API Route HTTP Method Return Value Comment localhost:port POST Returns the execution status of command Executes the command provided. Each invocation appends to array of commands executed so far. localhost:port GET Returns the execution status of the last command sent via POST request. localhost:port/history GET Returns the array of POST requests received so far.

docs.title: Library Microservice
docs.text:
The lib microservice serves the library assets of the DTaaS platform. Clients use its API endpoints to list and fetch these assets.

This page explains how to use the library microservice.

The assets page describes the suggested storage conventions for library assets.

Assets stored in the library are available in the user workspace.

docs.title: Application Programming Interface (API)
docs.text:
The lib microservice provides services at two endpoints:

GraphQL API Endpoint: http://intocps.org/lib

HTTP Endpoint: http://intocps.org/lib/files

docs.title: HTTP protocol
docs.text:
Endpoint: localhost:PORT/lib/files

Enable this endpoint with the -H http.json flag. It provides the usual file upload and download options.

Sample screenshots:

docs.title: GraphQL protocol
docs.text:
Endpoint: localhost:PORT/lib

The http://intocps.org/lib URL opens GraphiQL, a GraphQL web page.

GraphiQL shows the query schema and lets you test sample queries. It sends the queries with your DTaaS sign-in, so they work on an installation that requires one. Outside GraphiQL, send GraphQL queries as HTTP POST requests.

The library microservice provides two API calls:

  • List the contents of a directory
  • Fetch a file

Both calls can be sent from GraphiQL or as plain HTTP POST requests. The accepted queries are shown below.

docs.title: Provide list of contents for a directory
docs.text:
To list the files in a directory, use the following GraphQL query.

Replace the path value with the directory path.

Send requests to: https://intocps.org/lib

docs.title: GraphQL query for list of contents
docs.text:
query {
  listDirectory(path: "user1") {
    repository {
      tree {
        blobs {
          edges {
            node {
              name
              type
            }
          }
        }
        trees {
          edges {
            node {
              name
              type
            }
          }
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

              {

                }

docs.text:
This query takes a file path and returns the contents of the file.

To try this query, create a file files/user2/data/welcome.txt containing hello world.

The path is the file path to look at. For example, user1 looks at the files of user1, and user1/functions looks at the contents of the functions/ directory.

docs.title: Reusable Assets
docs.text: Reusable assets make it easier to work with digital twins, and reusability of assets is a fundamental feature of the platform[1].

docs.title: Kinds of Reusable Assets
docs.text: The DTaaS platform sorts all reusable library assets into five categories:

docs.title: Data
docs.text: The data sources and sinks available to a digital twin. Typical data sources are sensor measurements from Physical Twins and test data provided by manufacturers for calibrating models. Typical data sinks are visualisation software, external users and data storage services. Some outputs, such as events and commands, are akin to control outputs from a Digital Twin. These control outputs usually go to Physical Twins, but they can also go to another Digital Twin.

docs.title: Models
docs.text: Model assets describe different aspects of Physical Twins and their environment, at different levels of abstraction, so the same Physical Twin can have several models. For example, a flexible robot used in a car production plant may have structural models that help track the wear and tear of parts. The same robot can have behavioural models describing the safety guarantees provided by the robot manufacturer, and functional models describing what parts the robot can manufacture.

docs.title: Tools
docs.text: Tool assets are software used to create, evaluate and analyse models. These tools run on a computing platform, such as an operating system, a virtual machine like the Java virtual machine, or a docker container. Tools tend to be platform specific, which makes them less reusable than models. A tool can be packaged to run on a local or distributed virtual machine, so the most suitable execution environment can be chosen for a Digital Twin. Most models need tools to evaluate them against data inputs. In some cases, executable packages run as binaries in a computing environment. Each of these packages combines models and tools into a ready-to-use Digital Twin.

docs.title: Functions
docs.text: Functions pre-process and post-process data inputs, data outputs and control outputs. Data science libraries and functions can be used to create function assets for the platform. Some Digital Twin models need calibration before use; functions written by domain experts, together with the right data inputs, can calibrate them. Functions can also process the sensor and actuator data of both Physical Twins and Digital Twins.

docs.title: Digital Twins
docs.text: Ready-to-use digital twins created by one or more users. They can be reconfigured later for specific use cases.

docs.title: File System Structure
docs.text:
Each user's assets are stored in five directories, one for each category above. In addition, common library assets are available to all users. A simplified example of the structure is:

workspace/
  data/
    data1/ (ex: sensor)
      filename (ex: sensor.csv)
      README.md
    data2/ (ex: turbine)
      README.md (remote source; no local file)
    ...
  digital_twins/
    digital_twin-1/ (ex: incubator)
      config (yaml and json)
      README.md (usage instructions)
      description.md (short summary of digital twin)
      lifecycle/ (directory containing lifecycle scripts)
    digital_twin-2/ (ex: mass spring damper)
      config (yaml and json)
      README.md (usage instructions)
      description.md (short summary of digital twin)
      lifecycle/ (directory containing lifecycle scripts)
    digital_twin-3/ (ex: model swap)
      config (yaml and json)
      README.md (usage instructions)
      description.md (short summary of digital twin)
      lifecycle/ (directory containing lifecycle scripts)
    ...
  functions/
    function1/ (ex: graphs)
      filename (ex: graphs.py)
      README.md
    function2/ (ex: statistics)
      filename (ex: statistics.py)
      README.md
    ...
  models/
    model1/ (ex: spring)
      filename (ex: spring.fmu)
      README.md
    model2/ (ex: building)
      filename (ex: building.skp)
      README.md
    model3/ (ex: rabbitmq)
      filename (ex: rabbitmq.fmu)
      README.md
    ...
  tools/
    tool1/ (ex: maestro)
      filename (ex: maestro.jar)
      README.md
    ...
  common/
    data/
    functions/
    models/
    tools/

Tip

The DTaaS is agnostic to the format of assets. The only requirement is that they are files that can be uploaded on the Library page. Directories can be compressed into single files and uploaded, then decompressed from a terminal or the xfce Desktop available on the Workbench page.

A recommended file system structure for storing assets is also available in DTaaS examples.

docs.title: Upload Assets
docs.text:
Users can upload assets into their workspace from the Library page of the website.

Open a directory and click the upload button to upload files or directories into the workspace. The uploaded assets are then available in all workbench tools. The new dropdown menu creates new text-based files on the page. Other files must be uploaded with the upload button.

The user workbench provides the following services:

  • Jupyter Notebook and Lab
  • VS Code
  • XFCE Desktop Environment available via VNC
  • Terminal

Users can also bring DT assets into their workspaces from external sources with any of these services. Developers using git repositories can clone from and push to remote git servers. Users can also use common file transfer protocols such as FTP and SCP to bring DT assets into their workspaces.

docs.title: References
docs.text: [1]: Talasila, Prasad, et al. "Composable digital twins on Digital Twin as a Service platform." Simulation 101.3 (2025): 287-311.

docs.title: Logger Microservice
docs.text: The logger microservice receives workflow interaction events from the DTaaS client and stores them as JSON Lines: one JSON object per line, one line per event. The format suits command-line tools such as jq and data analysis libraries alike.

docs.title: How Events Reach the Logger
docs.text:
The website records page navigation, button and tab clicks, form changes and notifications. When remote logging is on, the browser sends each event to the logger with the Beacon API, which does not wait for a reply, so logging never slows the website down. The logger checks each event and appends it to its log file.

flowchart LR
    A[DTaaS website<br>in the browser] -- "POST /logger<br>one event" --> B[Logger<br>microservice]
    B -- "appends a line" --> C[(workflow-logs.jsonl)]
    A -. "local activity log" .-> D[(Browser storage)]

The local activity log is separate. It stays in the browser and is shown on the Logs page.

docs.title: Enabling Remote Logging
docs.text:
Remote logging is off by default. When the installation has a logger, the Logging Settings section on the Settings tab of the Account page shows a Send logs to ... checkbox, followed by the logger's host name. Select it and click Save Settings.

The two checkboxes are independent. Keep a local activity log stores the events in the browser, and Send logs to ... sends them to the logger. Keep remote logging on only with the consent of the person whose activity is being recorded.

docs.title: What a Log File Contains
docs.text:
The following lines were recorded while a user opened the Digital Twins Page from Automation, switched to the Execute tab, opened and closed the execution history of Hello World, and then went to the Logs page. Download them as workflow-logs-sample.jsonl.

{"sessionId":"70327d05-9dbc-454a-a358-6b8914fb37b9","userHash":"0a041b9462caa4a31bac3567e0b6e6fd9100787db2ab433d96f6d178cabfce90","timestamp":"2026-10-10T20:29:34.686Z","event":"navigation","page":"/account","element":"page","label":"/account","context":{}}
{"sessionId":"70327d05-9dbc-454a-a358-6b8914fb37b9","userHash":"0a041b9462caa4a31bac3567e0b6e6fd9100787db2ab433d96f6d178cabfce90","timestamp":"2026-10-10T20:29:36.233Z","event":"navigation","page":"/automation","page_transition":{"src":"/account","target":"/automation"},"element":"page","label":"/automation","context":{}}
{"sessionId":"70327d05-9dbc-454a-a358-6b8914fb37b9","userHash":"0a041b9462caa4a31bac3567e0b6e6fd9100787db2ab433d96f6d178cabfce90","timestamp":"2026-10-10T20:29:40.379Z","event":"navigation","page":"/preview/digitaltwins","page_transition":{"src":"/automation","target":"/preview/digitaltwins"},"element":"page","label":"/preview/digitaltwins","context":{}}
{"sessionId":"70327d05-9dbc-454a-a358-6b8914fb37b9","userHash":"0a041b9462caa4a31bac3567e0b6e6fd9100787db2ab433d96f6d178cabfce90","timestamp":"2026-10-10T20:29:44.317Z","event":"click","page":"/preview/digitaltwins","element":"tab","label":"Execute","context":{"dt":{"tab":"execute"}}}
{"sessionId":"70327d05-9dbc-454a-a358-6b8914fb37b9","userHash":"0a041b9462caa4a31bac3567e0b6e6fd9100787db2ab433d96f6d178cabfce90","timestamp":"2026-10-10T20:29:48.369Z","event":"click","page":"/preview/digitaltwins","element":"button","label":"History","context":{"dt":{"name":"hello-world","button":"history","executionCount":0}}}
{"sessionId":"70327d05-9dbc-454a-a358-6b8914fb37b9","userHash":"0a041b9462caa4a31bac3567e0b6e6fd9100787db2ab433d96f6d178cabfce90","timestamp":"2026-10-10T20:29:50.435Z","event":"click","page":"/preview/digitaltwins","element":"button","label":"Close","context":{"dt":{"name":"hello-world","button":"close-history"}}}
{"sessionId":"70327d05-9dbc-454a-a358-6b8914fb37b9","userHash":"0a041b9462caa4a31bac3567e0b6e6fd9100787db2ab433d96f6d178cabfce90","timestamp":"2026-10-10T20:29:52.481Z","event":"navigation","page":"/insights/log","page_transition":{"src":"/preview/digitaltwins","target":"/insights/log"},"element":"page","label":"/insights/log","context":{}}

Each line has the same fields:

Field Meaning in the sample sessionId A random identifier for one browser session. All seven events share it userHash The SHA-256 hash of the username, computed in the browser. The logger never receives the username itself timestamp When the event happened, in UTC event navigation for a page change and click for a tab or button. The other types are change, notification and dismiss page The page on which the event happened page_transition On navigation events only: the page the user came from (src) and went to (target) element and label What was used, such as the button labelled History context Details that depend on the page. On the Digital Twins Page, dt names the digital twin and the action

The hash is the same every time a user signs in, so events can still be grouped by user across sessions. It is a pseudonym, not anonymity.

docs.title: Analysing a Log File
docs.text:
The logger writes to logs/workflow-logs.jsonl unless it is configured otherwise. These jq commands work on that file and on the sample.

Count the events of each type:

jq -s -c 'group_by(.event) | map({event: .[0].event, count: length})' \
  workflow-logs.jsonl

[{"event":"click","count":3},{"event":"navigation","count":4}]

Follow the path a user took through the website:

jq -r 'select(.page_transition)
| "\(.timestamp) \(.page_transition.src) -> \(.page_transition.target)"' \ |
  workflow-logs.jsonl

2026-10-10T20:29:36.233Z /account -> /automation
2026-10-10T20:29:40.379Z /automation -> /preview/digitaltwins
2026-10-10T20:29:52.481Z /preview/digitaltwins -> /insights/log

List what was done to digital twins:

jq -c 'select(.context.dt) | {timestamp, label, dt: .context.dt}' \
  workflow-logs.jsonl

{"timestamp":"2026-10-10T20:29:44.317Z","label":"Execute","dt":{"tab":"execute"}}
{"timestamp":"2026-10-10T20:29:48.369Z","label":"History","dt":{"name":"hello-world","button":"history","executionCount":0}}
{"timestamp":"2026-10-10T20:29:50.435Z","label":"Close","dt":{"name":"hello-world","button":"close-history"}}

When the active file reaches its size limit, the logger renames it and starts a new one, keeping a fixed number of old files. To analyse everything, pass all of them to jq.

docs.title: Configuring the Website
docs.text:
The client sends events to the URL configured in LOGGER_URL. Include the /logger route prefix, for example:

LOGGER_URL: "https://example.com/logger";

For non-Docker local development, use the logger's direct port:

LOGGER_URL: "http://localhost:4003/logger";

The API is specified in servers/logger/API.md. Installing and configuring the logger is covered in the administrator guide.

docs.title: Building Models
docs.text:
The Building Models page draws a building from the user's own library and colours it with the readings its sensors report, so you can see, for example, which of forty rooms is the warm one. A time-series dashboard cannot show that. Open it from Buildings in the menu.

This page describes the asset layout, the binding manifest and the conversion workflow. It is the user documentation for DTaaS issue 1762. The developer documentation, covering what the route contains and what it leaves out, is in client/src/route/bim/README.md.

docs.title: What the Page Needs
docs.text:
The page reads up to four files per model, all in the user's library under common/models. The page links to that folder above the viewer.

File Required What it holds model.ifc yes The building, as the authoring tool exported it model.glb no The geometry converted from the IFC file. The page writes it the first time the model is converted model.json no The property tree: every object, its IFC class, its storey, its property sets model.manifest.json no The binding manifest, mapping each sensor to the object it measures

An IFC file on its own is enough to see the building. With the geometry file, the next visit loads the model instead of converting it again. The property tree adds the panel that opens when you click an object, and the manifest adds the readings. Nothing fails when the last three files are missing.

docs.title: How a Model Is Named
docs.text:
The IFC Model menu names each model by what its own file says the building is called: the project's long name, then its name, then the building's. Only the first 64 KB of each file is read for this. The menu skips template text that an authoring tool leaves behind, such as Project Name, and names that two files share. Those models are shown by their file name, with underscores read as spaces.

To give a name to a file that has none, use ifc-set-name from the ifc-utils repository. It writes the name into the file and changes nothing else. DTaaS stores nothing about the names.

docs.title: The Geometry Format
docs.text:
The model is converted to glTF binary, .glb. The issue offered OBJ as an alternative. OBJ was rejected because it cannot carry a stable identifier per object, which is the property the issue itself relies on.

The binding key is the IFC GlobalId, a 22-character identifier that the schema expects to stay the same across exports of the same model. glTF carries arbitrary data per node in its extras field, so the converter writes the GlobalId there and the viewer resolves a binding by reading it back. OBJ has no such field. A marker on an OBJ model can only be placed by node name, and names are not unique. Two walls are often both called Wall, and the resolver refuses that case instead of guessing which one the reading belongs to. A model without a stable identity per object cannot carry a binding that someone can review.

docs.title: The Binding Manifest
docs.text:
The manifest is plain JSON beside the model, and it is validated with zod before anything is drawn. People write it by hand and it will often contain mistakes, so every error names the binding and the field that caused it, for example bindings[3].display.ramp, instead of only reporting that the file is invalid.

{
  "model": {
    "source": "substation.ifc",
    "source_sha256": "60b1b94ee88a2b087080200c3c347edaf2347e768c1accb4b3608c6a129fbb09",
    "converter": "ifc_explorer.to_manifest 0.1.0"
  },
  "bindings": [
    {
      "selector": { "globalId": "0_sgz7bzz4Jh2ckU1ehFe$" },
      "label": "HX-1 temperature TS-01",
      "source": {
        "live": { "transport": "mqtt", "topic": "swim/B1/temperature/TS-01" },
        "history": { "bucket": "swim", "measurement": "temperature" }
      },
      "display": { "unit": "°C", "ramp": [10, 50] }
    }
  ]
}

Four design decisions shape the format:

  • selector is a small union of globalId, nodeName and expressId, so a non-IFC asset can use the same manifest instead of a second schema. A selector names exactly one of the three. If it named two, the resolver would have to choose between them, and the result would depend on that choice.
  • live and history are separate. MQTT supplies the current value shown on the model, and the time-series database supplies the panel that opens on a click. The 3D view does not reimplement charting.
  • source_sha256 is required. Without it there is no way to tell whether a derived artifact still describes the file beside it. The literal unknown is accepted, for a generator that never read the source, and anything else has to be a SHA-256.
  • display.ramp is the range the colour scale spans, and the viewer also reads it as the range the sensor is expected to stay inside. A value outside it raises an alert on the sensor card.

A binding whose object is missing from the geometry is reported and counted. This happens when an object is deleted and drawn again, or when the exporting tool does not keep the GlobalId and writes a new one. If the manifest asks for six markers and only four objects are found, the viewer says which two are missing instead of silently drawing four.

docs.title: Conversion
docs.text: Conversion runs in the browser of whoever opens the model. Putting an IFC file in the library is the whole workflow. You do not need a terminal or a separate service, and there is no step to repeat when the file changes.

docs.title: Why the Parser Ships Inside the Package
docs.text:
The issue asked that the WebAssembly parser and its workers be served from the DTaaS origin, so the feature works in a localhost install with no external network, and it proposed a postinstall copy step to achieve that.

The converter package meets the same requirement differently. The web-ifc WebAssembly binary is embedded in the JavaScript as base64 at build time, so the published package contains it and there is no separate .wasm file to serve. A production build of the client contains no .wasm files and fetches none.

This was chosen over the copy step for three reasons.

First, there is no extra step to forget. A postinstall copy sits outside the dependency graph. It has to be present in the host's build and survive every change to that build. When it is missing, the failure shows up at runtime in somebody else's deployment as a parser that cannot load. An embedded binary either installs or does not.

Second, it saves a request and a content type. Serving .wasm requires the right MIME type from the reverse proxy in front of the deployment, and a Content Security Policy that permits wasm-unsafe-eval. Both are configured in files this project does not own. A base64 payload inside a JavaScript chunk is served as JavaScript, which every deployment already handles correctly.

Third, the cost is paid only when needed. Base64 is one third larger than the binary it encodes. That extra size stays out of the main bundle: the parser is in a chunk that is fetched the first time a model has to be converted, and a user who never opens the page never downloads it. The entry chunk of a production build has no reference to the renderer or the parser.

The result is a larger download for the one page that needs it, in exchange for a deployment step that cannot be done wrong. DTaaS is installed on localhost and in air-gapped environments, where the second matters more.

docs.title: Converting Once Instead of on Every Visit
docs.text:
When a model has no .glb beside it, the page converts it in the browser and writes the result back into the library, next to the .ifc. The next visit finds the file and loads it, so only the first person to open the model waits for the conversion.

The write goes through the workspace's own Jupyter Contents API, the same interface the Library page reads through. It writes in pieces of 512 KB, because the server in front of Jupyter refuses a request body of a megabyte. The write has limits: the destination has to be a single file directly inside common/models, and an address that already holds a file is left alone, so a geometry produced outside the browser is never replaced. When the page cannot tell whether a file is there, it does not write.

The bytes are written to model.glb.part, and the file takes its real name only when the last piece has landed. A write that fails, or that stops because the person left the page, deletes its model.glb.part. If the .part file could not be deleted because the tab was closed, it stays visible in JupyterLab beside the model. It is safe to delete, and the next conversion of that model replaces it anyway.

If the server in front of the workspace refuses a piece as too large, the write starts over once in pieces of half the size.

A failed write shows nothing on the page, by design: a model that is not stored is simply converted again on the next visit. One case is worth knowing about. On a workspace with Jupyter XSRF protection enabled, the token is in an HttpOnly cookie that scripts cannot read, so every write is refused. The failure is written to the browser console.

For a large model it is still better to produce the .glb outside the browser with ifc-to-glb from the ifc-utils repository, as the administrator documentation recommends. The browser conversion covers the case where nobody has done that.

docs.title: Recording Where an Artifact Came From
docs.text: The manifest records the hash of the source it was made from and the name and version of the converter that made it, and the schema refuses a manifest without them. This makes it possible to detect a stale manifest. A .glb does not carry that record yet, whether ifc-to-glb wrote it or the browser did. It names the tool that generated it and says nothing about the source.

docs.title: Live Readings
docs.text:
The viewer draws whatever readings it is given and does not subscribe to anything. It knows neither the broker nor the topic scheme, so the same component can serve a demonstration fed by a local publisher and a deployment fed by the platform.

How readings reach the client is not decided yet. There are two options, and they are not equivalent:

  • The client subscribes to MQTT over WebSocket against the platform's RabbitMQ, through the rabbitmq_web_mqtt plugin, and passes the latest value to the viewer.
  • A platform service, the MQTT Agent described in the DTaaS material, subscribes, validates, stores, and serves the latest value to the client.

The second option separates concerns better, but it depends on that service existing and running, which has not been confirmed. Until this is settled the route shows models without readings. That is already the correct behaviour for a model that declares no sensors, and most architectural models declare none.

docs.title: What Is Not Built Yet
docs.text:
• History on click: the manifest already carries the history block, with bucket, measurement and tags, so the Grafana address can be built from it. Opening that panel from a marker is not implemented.
  • Federation: viewing several discipline models together as one building is not supported. Each model is drawn on its own.

docs.title: DTaaS Website Screenshots
docs.text:
This page walks through the DTaaS website with screenshots. A short screen recording is also available.

This tutorial uses https://intocps.org as an example base URL. Replace it with the URL of your installation.

docs.title: Visit the DTaaS Installation
docs.text:
URL: https://intocps.org (specified in config/client.js file)

Start by visiting the website of the DTaaS installation you are registered with.

docs.title: Redirected to Authorization Provider
docs.text:
URL: https://gitlab.com/xxxx (specified in config/.env file)

The browser redirects to the GitLab authorization page for the DTaaS.

Enter the email or username and password of the GitLab account whose email ID is registered with the DTaaS.

The browser then redirects to the OAuth 2.0 application page.

docs.title: Permit DTaaS Server to Use GitLab
docs.text:
URL: https://gitlab.com/xxxx

Clicking Authorize lets the OAuth 2.0 application access the information associated with the GitLab account. This step is required.

After successful authentication, the browser returns to the sign-in page of the DTaaS website.

URL: https://intocps.org

The DTaaS website adds a second layer of security with the OAuth 2.0 third-party authorization protocol. Only users with an active account at the selected OAuth 2.0 provider can access the installation. This installation also uses GitLab as the OAuth 2.0 provider.

The sign-in page shows a Sign In button. Clicking it redirects to the GitLab instance that authorizes users for the DTaaS. You do not need to sign in to GitLab again unless you have explicitly logged out of your GitLab account.

docs.title: Permit DTaaS Website to Use GitLab
docs.text:
URL: https://gitlab.com/xxxx

The DTaaS website needs permission to use the GitLab account for authorization. Click the Authorize button.

After successful authorization, the browser opens the Library page of the DTaaS website.

URL: https://intocps.org/library/xxxx

The application bar at the top of every page shows the DTaaS logo and title in the middle. On the right are three buttons. The GitHub icon opens the DTaaS code repository and the question-mark icon opens this documentation. The round avatar, which shows your profile picture or the first letter of your username, opens a menu with Account and Logout. The Account page has a Profile tab and a Settings tab where you can change settings.

The footer at the bottom of every page links to the documentation, the source code, the issue tracker, the INTO-CPS Association and the license.

docs.title: Check Website Access
docs.text: To troubleshoot sign-in problems, open https://intocps.org/config/user to check the website configuration. The page below means the application is configured correctly. A signed-in user can run the same check from Insights > Config, which shows it inside the application. Its link to the full list of configuration values also stays inside the application.

docs.title: Menu Items
docs.text:
The menu is a sidebar on the left of the page. By default it is collapsed to a narrow rail that shows only the icons, and hovering over an icon shows its name. Click the three horizontal bars icon in the top-left corner to expand the sidebar with the names of the pages. The arrow at the top of the expanded sidebar collapses it again.

The menu has six items:

Library: Manage reusable library assets. You can upload, download, create and modify files on this page.

Digital Twins: Manage digital twins. The page embeds Jupyter Lab, from which digital twins can be executed.

Automation: Links to the Library Page, the Digital Twins Page and the Measurement page. These pages show the integration of the DTaaS with GitLab CI/CD and are experimental.

Buildings: Opens the Building Models page, which draws the IFC building models in your library and colours them by the readings their sensors report.

Workbench: Not every digital twin can be managed in Jupyter Lab. This page links to the other tools in your workspace.

Insights: Information the platform can give you about itself: the Logs of this website and the configuration check described above.

docs.title: Library Page
docs.text:
The page has five tabs, one for each type of digital twin asset. Each tab has a description of its asset type.

Functions

The functions responsible for pre- and post-processing of data inputs, data outputs and control outputs. The data science libraries and functions can be used to create useful function assets for the platform. In some cases, Digital Twin models require calibration prior to their use; functions written by domain experts along with the right data inputs can make model calibration achievable. Functions can also process the sensor and actuator data of both Physical Twins and Digital Twins.

Models

The model assets describe different aspects of Physical Twins and their environment, at different levels of abstraction. Therefore, it is possible to have multiple models for the same Physical Twin. For example, a flexible robot used in a car production plant may have structural models that are useful for tracking the wear and tear of parts. The same robot can have behavioural models describing the safety guarantees provided by the robot manufacturer. The same robot can also have functional models describing the part manufacturing capabilities of the robot.

Tools

The software tool assets are software used to create, evaluate and analyse models. These tools run on top of a computing platform, i.e., an operating system, a virtual machine such as the Java virtual machine, or inside docker containers. Tools tend to be platform specific, which makes them less reusable than models. A tool can be packaged to run on a local or distributed virtual machine environment, so the most suitable execution environment can be selected for a Digital Twin. Most models require tools to evaluate them in the context of data inputs. In some cases executable packages are run as binaries in a computing environment. Each of these packages is a pre-packaged combination of models and tools that makes a ready-to-use Digital Twin.

Data

The data sources and sinks available to digital twins. Typical examples of data sources are sensor measurements from Physical Twins and test data provided by manufacturers for calibration of models. Typical examples of data sinks are visualisation software, external users and data storage services. There are also special outputs, such as events and commands, which are akin to control outputs from a Digital Twin. These control outputs usually go to Physical Twins, but they can also go to another Digital Twin.

Digital Twins

These are ready-to-use digital twins created by one or more users. These digital twins can be reconfigured later for specific use cases.

Each asset tab has two sub-tabs: Private and Common. Private library assets are visible only to the signed-in user. Common library assets are available to all users.

The assets page explains where to place reusable assets of each type and the directory structure on the server.

Note

Assets (files) can be uploaded using the upload button.

Note

The file manager is based on Jupyter Notebook, and all tasks available in Jupyter Notebook can be performed here.

docs.title: Digital Twins Page
docs.text:
URL: https://intocps.org/digitaltwins

The Digital Twins page has three tabs, Create, Execute and Analyze, and each tab shows Jupyter Lab below its description. The descriptions suggest tasks for these lifecycle phases of a digital twin. The lifecycle phases of digital twin page explains them further.

Create

Create digital twins from tools provided within user workspaces. Each digital twin has one directory. Users are advised to provide one bash shell script to run their digital twin. Users can create the required scripts and other files with the tools on the Workbench page.

Execute

Digital twins are executed from within user workspaces. The given bash script is executed from the digital twin directory. Terminal-based digital twins can be executed from VSCode and graphical digital twins can be executed from VNC GUI. The results of execution can be placed in the data directory.

Analyze

Analysing a digital twin requires running the digital twin script from the user workspace. Analysis scripts process the execution results placed in the data directory and put their results back in the data directory. These scripts can be executed from VSCode, or from VNC GUI when they produce graphical results.

Note

The reusable assets (files) shown in the file manager are also available in Jupyter Lab. Jupyter Lab also has a git plugin for linking files with external git repositories.

docs.title: Workbench
docs.text:
URL: https://intocps.org/workbench

The Workbench Tools page shows a card for each tool running in your workspace. A card has the tool's name, a one-line description and the address it opens. A standard workspace has four tools:

  • Desktop
  • VSCode
  • JupyterLab
  • Jupyter Notebook

The page lists only the tools your workspace reports. If it reports none, the page says so instead of showing cards.

Each card opens its tool in a new browser tab. The Workspace page shows what each tool looks like.

docs.title: Automation
docs.text:
URL: https://intocps.org/automation

The Automation page has three cards for the DevOps-based implementation of composable digital twins. Each card opens its page in the same browser tab.

  • Library Page
  • Digital Twins Page
  • Measurement

The trials, runner tags and digital twins that the Measurement page uses are set on the Settings tab of the Account page.

docs.title: Library Preview Page
docs.text:
URL: https://intocps.org/preview/library

This page, titled Library Page, follows the same idea as the Library page and has a similar interface.

Unlike the Library page, it uses digital twin assets stored in a GitLab repository. You compose a new digital twin by selecting the library assets it needs. The selected assets are listed on the page.

Clicking the Create a Digital Twin button opens the Create tab of the Digital Twins Page. The Clear button empties the selection. Both buttons are disabled until at least one asset is selected.

docs.title: Digital Twins Preview Page
docs.text:
URL: https://intocps.org/preview/digitaltwins

This page, titled Digital Twins Page, manages digital twins with the DevOps methodology. It has three tabs: Create, Manage and Execute.

docs.title: Create Tab
docs.text: The Create tab uses the selected library assets to create new digital twins. New digital twins are saved in the linked GitLab repository. Remember to add a valid .gitlab-ci.yml configuration, because it is used to execute the digital twin.

docs.title: Manage Tab
docs.text:
The Details button shows the full description of a digital twin.

The Delete button removes a digital twin from the workspace along with all its data. The Reconfigure button changes the configuration of a digital twin.

docs.title: Execute Tab
docs.text: Digital twins are executed with GitLab CI/CD workflows. Several digital twins can run at the same time.

docs.title: Insights
docs.text:
URL: https://intocps.org/insights

The Insights page has two cards. Logs opens the activity log this browser keeps once logging is enabled, and Config runs the configuration check.

docs.title: Finally logout
docs.text:
Click the avatar in the top-right corner and choose Logout.

Close the browser to exit the DTaaS software platform completely.

docs.title: Logs
docs.text: The DTaaS website can record how you use it: page navigation, button and link clicks, form changes and notifications. The events are captured in the browser and can be reviewed on the Workflow Logs page.

docs.title: Enabling Logging
docs.text:
Logging is off by default. To turn it on, select the Keep a local activity log checkbox in the Logging Settings section of the Settings page (Account > Settings). Nothing is stored in the browser until this checkbox is selected, so the pages described below stay empty until then.

If the DTaaS installation is configured to stream events to a remote logging server, the Settings page shows a second checkbox, Send logs to followed by the server name. It is also off by default and works independently of the local log. Keep remote logging on only with the consent of the person whose activity is being recorded.

docs.title: Viewing the Logs
docs.text:
URL: https://intocps.org/insights/log or http://localhost:4000/insights/log

Open the logs from Insights in the menu and then the Logs card, or go to /insights/log on the DTaaS installation. The page is titled Workflow Logs. The icon next to the title shows a short description of the page.

The toolbar above the log list has these controls:

Control Description Filter logs Shows only the entries that match the search text (see Filtering). Refresh Reloads the log entries from local storage. Raw view Switches between the card view and the raw JSON Lines view. Clear logs Permanently deletes all stored log entries, after confirmation. Download All JSONL Exports the displayed entries as a .jsonl file. Live update Streams new events into the view as they are recorded.

docs.title: Log Entries (Card View)
docs.text:
Each entry is shown as a card with:

  • A coloured chip for the event type: click, change, navigation, notification or dismiss.
  • The label of the element that triggered the event.
  • The timestamp of the event.
  • The element type and the path of the page where the event occurred.
  • Any extra context recorded for the event, shown as small chips (for example a link's target URL or the new value of a form field).

docs.title: Filtering Logs
docs.text:
Type into the Filter logs box to show only the entries whose event type, label, element, page or context contains the search text. The count above the log list shows how many of the entries match, for example 3 of 10 log entries.

While a filter is active, the Download All JSONL button becomes Download Filtered JSONL and exports only the entries shown.

docs.title: Raw View
docs.text:
Raw view shows the same entries as pretty-printed JSON Lines instead of cards and adds a Copy to clipboard button. To keep the page responsive, both views render at most the newest 500 entries and show a note when more exist. The download button and Copy to clipboard ignore this limit and always cover every displayed entry (that is, every entry that matches the filter, if there is one).

Each line is a single JSON object. Entries are shown newest first, so a click on Digital Twins in the menu followed by the page navigation it causes appears as:

{
  "timestamp": "2026-07-22T20:19:02.736Z",
  "event": "navigation",
  "label": "/digitaltwins",
  "element": "page",
  "page": "/digitaltwins",
  "page_transition": {
    "src": "/library",
    "target": "/digitaltwins"
  },
  "context": {},
  "sessionId": "eaba3642-324e-4f3b-bd21-4204ddd10ebe",
  "userHash": "dee55bf8057abd8211bf80d6513577ff260e739d627c20762d9d617a393a89db"
}

{
  "timestamp": "2026-07-22T20:19:01.245Z",
  "event": "click",
  "label": "Digital Twins",
  "element": "nav-link",
  "page": "/library",
  "context": {
    "nav": {
      "link": "/digitaltwins",
      "active": false
    }
  },
  "sessionId": "eaba3642-324e-4f3b-bd21-4204ddd10ebe",
  "userHash": "dee55bf8057abd8211bf80d6513577ff260e739d627c20762d9d617a393a89db"
}

docs.title: Log Event Fields
docs.text: Field Description timestamp UTC time the event was recorded, in ISO 8601 format. event The event type: click, change, navigation, notification or dismiss. label A human-readable label for the element involved. element The type of UI element involved, e.g. nav-link, button, link, page. page The URL path of the page on which the event occurred. page_transition Present on navigation events after the first; records the source and target page. context Extra metadata specific to the event, e.g. a link's target URL. sessionId A random identifier generated for the current browser session. userHash A SHA-256 hash of the username, which links events without storing the name in plain text.

docs.title: Live Updates
docs.text: Live update subscribes the page to new log events as they are recorded elsewhere in the browser (including other open tabs) and reloads the list automatically. It is off by default, because reloading a large log store continuously is unnecessary when you are only reviewing past entries.

docs.title: Clearing Logs
docs.text: The icon opens a confirmation dialog, and Clear Logs in that dialog permanently deletes all stored log entries. This cannot be undone. It only clears the entries stored in the browser and has no effect on copies already sent to a remote logging server.

docs.title: Privacy and Storage
docs.text:
• Log entries are stored locally in the browser (IndexedDB) and never leave the device, unless the DTaaS installation is configured with a remote logging server and remote logging is turned on. Then the entries are also sent to that server.
  • The local log store is limited to about 25 MB. The oldest entries are removed automatically once the limit is reached.
  • The userHash field is a hash of the username, not the username itself. It pseudonymizes the user while still allowing their events to be linked together.
  • The sessionId field is a random value generated per browser session and is not linked to the user's identity.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This page described the logging feature of the DTaaS website: turning it on in Settings, viewing and filtering events on the Workflow Logs page, switching between the card and raw JSON Lines views, downloading and clearing logs, and how the stored data protects privacy.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text: You need the settings when you first set up the DTaaS and again whenever you work with a different configuration. The main settings are collected on one page for both cases.

docs.title: Changing Settings
docs.text:
The parameters for sending information to and receiving it from the storage and execution services (e.g., GitLab) may need to be adjusted to match your infrastructure. Click the avatar in the top-right corner, choose Account, and open the Settings tab to see the adjustable parameters:

The settings are in three sections: Application Settings, Measurement Settings and Logging Settings. Application settings are used by the DevOps features. Measurement settings are used to benchmark the DevOps features. Logging settings control the activity log described on the Logs page.

Each parameter is described below.

docs.title: Group Name
docs.text:
The Group Name is the group on the storage service, the highest level of organisation there. The DTaaS requires a GitLab group. The group holds projects whose names must match the usernames of system users. See the file organisation for details. Set this parameter to the name of the group; it is case-insensitive.

Default: DTaaS

docs.title: Common Library Project Name
docs.text:
One project in the group is the Digital Twins Library. All users can access the files in the Library through the DTaaS and copy them to their own projects as needed. This parameter must match the project name of the Library.

Default: common

docs.title: DT Directory
docs.text:
In the common library and in user projects, files related to Digital Twins are stored in a designated folder. This parameter is the name of that folder.

Default: digital_twins

docs.title: Branch Name
docs.text:
This parameter sets the branch that is searched for data (Twins, Functions, etc.) in user and library projects. Digital Twins are also executed from this branch.

Default: master

docs.title: Runner Tag
docs.text:
The (GitLab) runners that execute Digital Twin code must have a tag. Only one tag can be given, and it cannot be left blank; otherwise the job that runs the twin is not processed. This is a limitation of the DTaaS.

Default: linux

docs.title: Trial Number
docs.text:
The number of times each task is repeated during a benchmark run. The execution times are averaged over the trials. The value must be at least 1.

Default: 3

docs.title: Measurement Secondary Runner Tag
docs.text:
Some benchmark runs require two GitLab runners. The Runner Tag in Application Settings points to the first runner, and the Measurement Secondary Runner Tag points to the second runner.

Default: windows

docs.title: Primary Digital Twin
docs.text:
Select the first digital twin from the drop-down list of available digital twins. It is used in the single digital twin and same digital twin measurement tasks.

Default: hello-world, or the first digital twin in the list if hello-world is not available

docs.title: Secondary Digital Twin
docs.text:
Select the second digital twin from the drop-down list of available digital twins. It is used as the second digital twin in the multiple digital twin measurement tasks. The refresh button next to the list reloads the available digital twins using the Branch Name and DT Directory entered above.

Default: mass-spring-damper, or the first digital twin in the list if mass-spring-damper is not available

docs.title: Keep a Local Activity Log
docs.text:
The Keep a local activity log checkbox controls whether the DTaaS records workflow events in your browser (stored locally in IndexedDB). It is off by default.

If the installation is configured with a remote logger, a second checkbox, Send logs to followed by the name of the logging server, also sends the events to that server. It is off by default as well. See Logs for viewing and downloading logs at /insights/log.

docs.title: Saving and Resetting Changes
docs.text:
When you are satisfied with the changes, press Save Settings so that they persist after you leave the Settings page. To undo a mistake, press Reset to Defaults to restore the default values. The reset values are saved automatically, so you do not need to save them again. The two buttons are shown below:

The default values are defined in the code and can be changed there if needed.

You can now return to the DevOps pages (i.e., the Digital Twins Preview page). When you change the Group Name, Common Library Project Name, DT Directory or Branch Name, saving fetches the digital twins again from the remote repository. The Digital Twins should then be visible and ready to be executed, edited and shared.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This page described how to edit the settings, both to initialise the DTaaS for a project and during continuous use (for example, to change the Runner Tag or Branch Name). It also covered saving changes and restoring the default values after a mistake.

docs.title: Workspace
docs.text:
This page walks through the website of the workspace software platform with screenshots. A short screen recording is also available.

The user workspace in DTaaS is a personal Linux environment given to each registered user. This page uses https://intocps.org as an example base URL. Replace it with the URL of your installation.

docs.title: Visit the Workspace Installation
docs.text:
URL: https://intocps.org (specified in config/client.js file)

Start by visiting the website of the DTaaS installation you are registered with.

docs.title: Redirected to Authorization Provider
docs.text:
URL: https://intocps.org/auth/realms/dtaas/xxxx (specified in config/.env file)

The browser redirects to the Keycloak authorization page for the DTaaS Workspace.

Enter your email or username and password.

The browser then redirects to the application page.

After successful authentication, the browser returns to the sign-in page of the DTaaS website.

URL: https://intocps.org

The DTaaS website adds a second layer of security with the OIDC third-party authorization protocol. Only users with an active account at the selected OIDC provider can access the installation. This installation uses Keycloak as the OIDC provider. The Sign In button on the sign-in page starts the authorization.

After successful authorization, the browser opens the Library page of the DTaaS website.

URL: https://intocps.org/library/xxxx

The application bar at the top of every page shows the DTaaS logo and title in the middle. On the right are three buttons. The GitHub icon opens the DTaaS code repository and the question-mark icon opens this documentation. The round avatar, which shows your profile picture or the first letter of your username, opens a menu with Account and Logout. The Account page has a Settings tab where you can change settings.

docs.title: Menu Items
docs.text:
The menu is a sidebar on the left of the page. By default it is collapsed to a narrow rail that shows only the icons. Click the three horizontal bars icon in the top-left corner to expand it.

The menu items are described on the website page.

docs.title: Library Page
docs.text:
The page has five tabs, one for each type of digital twin asset. Each tab has a description of its asset type.

Functions

The functions responsible for pre- and post-processing of data inputs, data outputs and control outputs. The data science libraries and functions can be used to create useful function assets for the platform. In some cases, Digital Twin models require calibration prior to their use; functions written by domain experts along with the right data inputs can make model calibration achievable. Functions can also process the sensor and actuator data of both Physical Twins and Digital Twins.

Models

The model assets describe different aspects of Physical Twins and their environment, at different levels of abstraction. Therefore, it is possible to have multiple models for the same Physical Twin. For example, a flexible robot used in a car production plant may have structural models that are useful for tracking the wear and tear of parts. The same robot can have behavioural models describing the safety guarantees provided by the robot manufacturer. The same robot can also have functional models describing the part manufacturing capabilities of the robot.

Tools

The software tool assets are software used to create, evaluate and analyse models. These tools run on top of a computing platform, i.e., an operating system, a virtual machine such as the Java virtual machine, or inside docker containers. Tools tend to be platform specific, which makes them less reusable than models. A tool can be packaged to run on a local or distributed virtual machine environment, so the most suitable execution environment can be selected for a Digital Twin. Most models require tools to evaluate them in the context of data inputs. In some cases executable packages are run as binaries in a computing environment. Each of these packages is a pre-packaged combination of models and tools that makes a ready-to-use Digital Twin.

Data

The data sources and sinks available to digital twins. Typical examples of data sources are sensor measurements from Physical Twins and test data provided by manufacturers for calibration of models. Typical examples of data sinks are visualisation software, external users and data storage services. There are also special outputs, such as events and commands, which are akin to control outputs from a Digital Twin. These control outputs usually go to Physical Twins, but they can also go to another Digital Twin.

Digital Twins

These are ready-to-use digital twins created by one or more users. These digital twins can be reconfigured later for specific use cases.

Each asset tab has two sub-tabs: Private and Common. Private library assets are visible only to the signed-in user. Common library assets are available to all users.

The assets page explains where to place reusable assets of each type and the directory structure on the server.

Note

Assets (files) can be uploaded using the upload button.

Note

The file manager is based on Jupyter Notebook, and all tasks available in Jupyter Notebook can be performed here.

docs.title: Digital Twins Page
docs.text:
URL: https://intocps.org/digitaltwins

The Digital Twins page has three tabs, Create, Execute and Analyze, and each tab shows Jupyter Lab below its description. The descriptions suggest tasks for these lifecycle phases of a digital twin. The lifecycle phases of digital twin page explains them further.

Create

Create digital twins from tools provided within user workspaces. Each digital twin has one directory. Users are advised to provide one bash shell script to run their digital twin. Users can create the required scripts and other files with the tools on the Workbench page.

Execute

Digital twins are executed from within user workspaces. The given bash script is executed from the digital twin directory. Terminal-based digital twins can be executed from VSCode and graphical digital twins can be executed from VNC GUI. The results of execution can be placed in the data directory.

Analyze

Analysing a digital twin requires running the digital twin script from the user workspace. Analysis scripts process the execution results placed in the data directory and put their results back in the data directory. These scripts can be executed from VSCode, or from VNC GUI when they produce graphical results.

Note

The reusable assets (files) shown in the file manager are also available in Jupyter Lab. Jupyter Lab also has a git plugin for linking files with external git repositories.

docs.title: Workbench
docs.text:
URL: https://intocps.org/workbench

The Workbench Tools page shows a card for each tool running in your workspace. A standard workspace has four tools:

Tool Description Desktop XFCE-based Linux desktop environment in the browser VSCode Browser-based VS Code editor (code-server) JupyterLab Interactive notebook environment Jupyter Notebook Classic Jupyter interface

Each card opens its tool in a new browser tab. The sections below show the page each tool opens.

docs.title: VS Code Workspace
docs.text:
The VS Code interface has:

  • File explorer for navigating the workspace
  • Integrated terminal for running commands
  • Extensions for Python, Markdown, and other languages

docs.title: XFCE Desktop
docs.text: The XFCE desktop is a full graphical Linux environment in the browser. Use it to run GUI-based tools that cannot be used from a terminal alone.

docs.title: JupyterLab
docs.text: JupyterLab combines notebooks, terminals and a file browser in one window. The Digital Twins page embeds the same interface.

docs.title: Jupyter Notebook
docs.text: The classic notebook interface opens on the file list of the workspace. The Library page embeds the same interface.

docs.title: Workspace File System
docs.text:
Each user's workspace container mounts two directories:

/workspace/           # Private user files (read-write)
├── data/
├── digital_twins/
├── functions/
├── models/
└── tools/

/workspace/common/    # Shared library assets
├── data/
├── digital_twins/
├── functions/
├── models/
└── tools/

Files in /workspace/ are private to each user. Files in /workspace/common/ are shared across all users. Administrators can mount /workspace/common as read-only in the compose configuration.

docs.title: Installing Software
docs.text:
Users can install more software in their workspace from the XFCE Desktop, Jupyter Lab or VSCode:

sudo apt-get install <package>
pip install <package>

Installed software is private to each user's workspace and persists across sessions.

docs.title: Running Digital Twins
docs.text:
To execute a digital twin stored in /workspace/digital_twins/, run its lifecycle scripts in the terminal:

cd /workspace/digital_twins/<dt-name>
lifecycle/create
lifecycle/execute

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The DTaaS workspace gives each user a private, persistent Linux environment with a desktop, a terminal and development tools in the browser. Users can install software, run digital twins and develop new DT assets in their workspace.
